paragraphs: This paper introduces a learning algorithm for storing both steady patterns and repeating activity cycles in recurrent analog networks. For a network with n nodes, it gives storage of n static attractors or n/2 periodic attractors. A memory can therefore take the form of an ongoing rhythm.

The method separates programming the network’s dynamics from choosing the patterns to store. It allows control over pattern stability, the shapes of attraction basins, and convergence speed. When the patterns are orthonormal, learning simplifies to a periodic version of an outer-product rule, with updates that are local, additive, order-independent, and incremental.

Stored cycles can form standing or traveling waves resembling oscillating spatial activity in olfactory structures. During simulated inspiration, these attractors emerge through a multiple Hopf bifurcation, a transition that creates oscillatory behavior. Near this transition, a very small input can select the resulting attractor. The approach thus links a programmable memory mechanism to the selection of rhythmic patterns in a biologically inspired recognition model.
summary.tldr: A learning algorithm programs stable memories and rhythmic attractors while controlling their dynamics and sensitivity to small selecting inputs.

title: A Bifurcation Theory Approach to the Programming of Periodic Attractors in Network Models of Olfactory Cortex

abstract: Learning how to adjust to an opponent's position is critical to the success of having intelligent agents collaborating towards the achievement of specific tasks in unfriendly environments. This pa(cid:173) per describes our work on a Memory-based technique for to choose an action based on a continuous-valued state attribute indicating the position of an opponent. We investigate the question of how an agent performs in nondeterministic variations of the training situ(cid:173) ations. Our experiments indicate that when the random variations fall within some bound of the initial training, the agent performs better with some initial training rather than from a tabula-rasa.

This pa(cid:173) per describes our work on a Memory-based technique for to choose an action based on a continuous-valued state attribute indicating the position of an opponent. We investigate the question of how an agent performs in nondeterministic variations of the training situ(cid:173) ations. Our experiments indicate that when the random variations fall within some bound of the initial training, the agent performs better with some initial training rather than from a tabula-rasa.

paragraphs: An agent facing an opponent must adapt its actions to where that opponent is located. This paper studies that problem in robotic soccer using a memory-based learning technique. The relevant state information is a continuous-valued attribute describing the opponent's position, and the learner uses that information to choose an action.

The central question concerns how useful earlier training remains when situations vary unpredictably. Exact repetition of a training situation would provide a narrow test of adaptation. The experiments instead consider nondeterministic variations around the situations the agent initially encountered, examining whether prior experience still provides an advantage.

The reported result is conditional: when random variations remain within some bound of the initial training conditions, a trained agent performs better than one starting without prior training. This supports the usefulness of remembered experience for nearby variations in an opponent's position. The stated bound is central to the finding, because the demonstrated benefit concerns variation within a range around prior experience.
summary.tldr: Memory-based training helps a robotic soccer agent handle bounded random variations in an opponent's position.

title: Beating a Defender in Robotic Soccer: Memory-Based Learning of a Continuous Function

abstract: We present an algorithm that infers the model structure of a mix(cid:173) ture of factor analysers using an efficient and deterministic varia(cid:173) tional approximation to full Bayesian integration over model pa(cid:173) rameters. This procedure can automatically determine the opti(cid:173) mal number of components and the local dimensionality of each component (Le. the number of factors in each factor analyser) . Alternatively it can be used to infer posterior distributions over number of components and dimensionalities. Since all parameters are integrated out the method is not prone to overfitting. Using a stochastic procedure for adding components it is possible to per(cid:173) form the variational optimisation incrementally and to avoid local maxima. Results show that the method works very well in practice and correctly infers the number and dimensionality of nontrivial synthetic examples. By importance sampling from the variational approximation we show how to obtain unbiased estimates of the true evidence, the exact predictive density, and the KL divergence between the varia(cid:173) tional posterior and the true posterior, not only in this model but for variational approximations in general.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bayesian algorithm for learning the structure of a mixture of factor analysers. It can determine both the number of mixture components and the number of factors within each component. Alternatively, it can infer posterior distributions over these choices, retaining uncertainty about the appropriate model structure.

The method uses an efficient, deterministic variational approximation to Bayesian integration over parameters. The authors attribute resistance to overfitting to integrating out those parameters. A stochastic procedure for adding components also permits incremental variational optimization and can help avoid local maxima. In nontrivial synthetic examples, the method correctly identifies the component counts and their dimensionalities.

A further contribution uses importance sampling from the variational approximation to obtain unbiased estimates of the true evidence, exact predictive density, and divergence between approximate and true posteriors. These quantities respectively concern model support, prediction, and approximation quality. The authors present this sampling technique as applicable beyond factor-analyser mixtures to variational approximations more generally.
summary.tldr: Variational Bayesian inference learns mixture size and local dimensionality, while importance sampling provides unbiased estimates of key Bayesian quantities.

title: Variational Inference for Bayesian Mixtures of Factor Analysers

abstract: I present a simple variation of importance sampling that explicitly search(cid:173) es for important regions in the target distribution. I prove that the tech(cid:173) nique yields unbiased estimates, and show empirically it can reduce the variance of standard Monte Carlo estimators. This is achieved by con(cid:173) centrating samples in more significant regions of the sample space.
originalAbstract: I present a simple variation of importance sampling that explicitly search(cid:173) es for important regions in the target distribution. I prove that the tech(cid:173) nique yields unbiased estimates, and show empirically it can reduce the variance of standard Monte Carlo estimators. This is achieved by con(cid:173) centrating samples in more significant regions of the sample space.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo estimation uses samples to approximate quantities associated with a probability distribution. This paper proposes a simple variation of importance sampling that explicitly searches for important regions of the target distribution. Its central idea is to concentrate sampling effort where samples contribute more significantly to the estimation task.

Searching for important regions changes how samples are allocated, making the correctness of the resulting estimate a central question. The author proves that the technique yields unbiased estimates. Unbiasedness means that the estimator's average over repeated sampling agrees with the quantity being estimated; it does not mean that each individual estimate is exact.

The paper also gives empirical evidence that this concentration of samples can reduce the variance of standard Monte Carlo estimators. Lower variance means less fluctuation between repeated estimates. The evidence therefore combines a proven property with an observed benefit: unbiasedness is established theoretically, while variance reduction is demonstrated empirically as something the method can achieve. The contribution connects active search for significant regions with valid Monte Carlo estimation.
summary.tldr: Greedy importance sampling searches significant regions while preserving unbiasedness and can empirically reduce estimator variance.

title: Greedy Importance Sampling

abstract: The problem that we address in this paper is how a mobile robot can plan in order to arrive at its goal with minimum uncertainty. Traditional motion planning algo(cid:173) rithms often assume that a mobile robot can track its position reliably, however, in real world situations, reliable localization may not always be feasible. Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) provide one way to maximize the certainty of reaching the goal state, but at the cost of computational intractability for large state spaces. The method we propose explicitly models the uncertainty of the robot's position as a state variable, and generates trajectories through the augmented pose-uncertainty space. By minimizing the positional uncertainty at the goal, the robot reduces the likelihood it becomes lost. We demonstrate experimentally that coastal navigation reduces the uncertainty at the goal, especially with degraded localization.

The method we propose explicitly models the uncertainty of the robot's position as a state variable, and generates trajectories through the augmented pose-uncertainty space. paragraphs: The paper studies how a mobile robot can plan a route that leaves it with little uncertainty about its position when it reaches its goal. This matters because reliable localization cannot always be assumed. A route must therefore be evaluated partly by how uncertain the robot's position may become along the way.

The proposed method makes positional uncertainty an explicit part of the planning state. It generates trajectories through a space containing both the robot's pose and its uncertainty. This allows the planner to seek routes that minimize uncertainty at the destination. The motivation includes the computational difficulty of using partially observable Markov decision processes for large state spaces.

Experiments show that coastal navigation reduces uncertainty at the goal, especially when localization is degraded. The result supports accounting for localization quality during route planning. By seeking a destination state with lower positional uncertainty, the method reduces the likelihood of the robot becoming lost, making confidence about arrival part of the planning objective.
summary.tldr: Planning jointly over robot pose and positional uncertainty reduces uncertainty at the goal, especially with degraded localization.

title: Coastal Navigation with Mobile Robots

abstract: We propose a method for the fast estimation of hyperparameters in large networks, based on the linear response relation in the cav(cid:173) ity method, and an empirical measurement of the Green's func(cid:173) tion. Simulation results show that it is efficient and precise, when compared with cross-validation and other techniques which require matrix inversion.
originalAbstract: We propose a method for the fast estimation of hyperparameters in large networks, based on the linear response relation in the cav(cid:173) ity method, and an empirical measurement of the Green's func(cid:173) tion. Simulation results show that it is efficient and precise, when compared with cross-validation and other techniques which require matrix inversion.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational cost of estimating hyperparameters in large networks. Its goal is to obtain useful estimates quickly while maintaining precision. The proposed approach uses information about a network's response, bringing together a theoretical response relation and an empirical measurement as the basis for parameter estimation.

Specifically, the method draws on the linear-response relation from the cavity method and measures a Green's function empirically. The Green's function supplies response information used by the estimation procedure. The important connection is between that measured behavior and the theoretical relation: together they provide a way to estimate hyperparameters in the large-network setting considered by the authors.

Simulation results compare the method with cross-validation and other techniques requiring matrix inversion. The authors report that their approach is efficient and precise in those comparisons. This supports response-based estimation as a promising computational alternative for the evaluated problems, with the reported evidence coming from simulations rather than a universal claim about every network or estimation task.
summary.tldr: Empirically measured Green's functions support a hyperparameter-estimation method reported to be efficient and precise in large-network simulations.

title: Fast Parameter Estimation Using Green's Functions

abstract: In the problem of probability forecasting the learner’s goal is to output, given a training set and a new object, a suitable probability measure on the possible values of the new object’s label. An on-line algorithm for probability forecasting is said to be well-calibrated if the probabilities it outputs agree with the observed frequencies. We give a natural non- asymptotic formalization of the notion of well-calibratedness, which we then study under the assumption of randomness (the object/label pairs are independent and identically distributed). It turns out that, although no probability forecasting algorithm is automatically well-calibrated in our sense, there exists a wide class of algorithms for “multiprobability forecasting” (such algorithms are allowed to output a set, ideally very narrow, of probability measures) which satisfy this property; we call the algorithms in this class “Venn probability machines”. Our experimental results demonstrate that a 1-Nearest Neighbor Venn probability machine performs reasonably well on a standard benchmark data set, and one of our theoretical results asserts that a simple Venn probability machine asymptotically approaches the true conditional probabilities regardless, and without knowledge, of the true probability measure generating the examples.

paragraphs: The paper studies probability forecasts whose stated probabilities agree with observed frequencies. It introduces a finite-sample formalization of this calibration requirement and analyzes it under the assumption that object-label pairs are independent and identically distributed. The task is to forecast possible labels for a new object using training examples.

Under the proposed definition, no ordinary probability-forecasting algorithm is automatically calibrated. The authors instead allow a forecast to be a set of probability measures, ideally a narrow set. They identify a broad class of such multiprobability algorithms that satisfies the calibration property and call them Venn probability machines. Allowing a set changes what the forecasting procedure can guarantee.

Experiments show that a Venn machine based on one-nearest-neighbor performs reasonably well on a standard benchmark. A separate theoretical result establishes that a simple Venn machine approaches the true conditional probabilities asymptotically, without knowing the generating distribution. Within the stated randomness setting, the paper thus combines a finite-sample calibration framework with a long-run probability-estimation result.
summary.tldr: Under independent, identically distributed sampling, Venn probability machines achieve a finite-sample calibration property by outputting sets of probability measures.

title: Self-calibrating Probability Forecasting

abstract: We consider the question of how well a given distribution can be approx- imated with probabilistic graphical models. We introduce a new param- eter, effective treewidth, that captures the degree of approximability as a tradeoff between the accuracy and the complexity of approximation. We present a simple approach to analyzing achievable tradeoffs that ex- ploits the threshold behavior of monotone graph properties, and provide experimental results that support the approach.
originalAbstract: We consider the question of how well a given distribution can be approx- imated with probabilistic graphical models. We introduce a new param- eter, effective treewidth, that captures the degree of approximability as a tradeoff between the accuracy and the complexity of approximation. We present a simple approach to analyzing achievable tradeoffs that ex- ploits the threshold behavior of monotone graph properties, and provide experimental results that support the approach.

paragraphs: This paper asks how closely a probability distribution can be represented by a probabilistic graphical model of manageable complexity. The central issue is a tradeoff: an approximation should retain enough of the original distribution to be accurate, while its graphical representation should remain sufficiently simple. The authors study that balance rather than treating approximation quality and model complexity as separate questions.

They introduce effective treewidth, a parameter designed to describe this accuracy-versus-complexity relationship. Its role is to characterize how well a distribution can be approximated at different levels of complexity. This gives the analysis a way to express degrees of approximability instead of reducing the question to whether a particular representation is possible.

The proposed analysis uses threshold behavior in monotone graph properties to investigate achievable tradeoffs. This connects changes in graph structure with the approximation problem. Experiments support the approach, providing empirical backing for the analysis. The stated contribution is both a new descriptive parameter and a way to reason about the compromises available when choosing a graphical approximation.
summary.tldr: Effective treewidth characterizes the tradeoff between accuracy and complexity when approximating distributions with graphical models.

title: Approximability of Probability Distributions

abstract: Probabilistic temporal planning attempts to ﬁnd good policies for acting in domains with concurrent durative tasks, multiple uncertain outcomes, and limited resources. These domains are typically modelled as Markov decision problems and solved using dynamic programming methods. This paper demonstrates the application of reinforcement learning — in the form of a policy-gradient method — to these domains. Our emphasis is large domains that are infeasible for dynamic programming. Our ap- proach is to construct simple policies, or agents, for each planning task. The result is a general probabilistic temporal planner, named the Factored Policy-Gradient Planner (FPG-Planner), which can handle hundreds of tasks, optimising for probability of success, duration, and resource use.

paragraphs: The paper addresses planning when tasks can overlap, take time to finish, have uncertain outcomes, and compete for limited resources. A useful policy must decide how to act under these interacting conditions. Such problems are commonly modeled as Markov decision problems, but the authors focus on domains too large for dynamic programming to be feasible.

Their approach applies reinforcement learning through a policy-gradient method. They construct a simple policy, or agent, for each planning task. This produces a factored representation of the planner, organizing its behavior around individual tasks while using policy-gradient learning to improve the resulting choices.

The resulting system, called the Factored Policy-Gradient Planner, can handle hundreds of tasks. It optimizes criteria involving success probability, duration, and resource use. The contribution demonstrates that policy-gradient methods can support probabilistic temporal planning at this scale. Its significance is the combination of task-level policies with learning in domains where concurrency, uncertainty, and resource limits make planning computationally demanding.
summary.tldr: The Factored Policy-Gradient Planner learns task-level policies for large temporal planning problems involving uncertainty, concurrency, and limited resources.

title: Policy-Gradient Methods for Planning

abstract: Correlation between instances is often modelled via a kernel function using in- put attributes of the instances. Relational knowledge can further reveal additional pairwise correlations between variables of interest. In this paper, we develop a class of models which incorporates both reciprocal relational information and in- put attributes using Gaussian process techniques. This approach provides a novel non-parametric Bayesian framework with a data-dependent covariance function for supervised learning tasks. We also apply this framework to semi-supervised learning. Experimental results on several real world data sets verify the usefulness of this algorithm.
originalAbstract: Correlation between instances is often modelled via a kernel function using in- put attributes of the instances. Relational knowledge can further reveal additional pairwise correlations between variables of interest. In this paper, we develop a class of models which incorporates both reciprocal relational information and in- put attributes using Gaussian process techniques. This approach provides a novel non-parametric Bayesian framework with a data-dependent covariance function for supervised learning tasks. We also apply this framework to semi-supervised learning. Experimental results on several real world data sets verify the usefulness of this algorithm.

paragraphs: Learning systems often describe relationships between examples through a kernel computed from their input attributes. However, known relationships among examples can reveal additional correlations between the quantities being predicted. This paper develops Gaussian process models that use both sources of information within a single learning framework.

The approach combines reciprocal relational information with the attributes of individual instances. It does so through a covariance function that depends on the data, giving relational evidence a role in how the model represents correlations. The resulting formulation is a nonparametric Bayesian framework for supervised learning, with covariance as the point where the two information sources meet.

The authors also apply the framework to semi-supervised learning and report experiments on several real-world datasets that support its usefulness. The contribution broadens the information available to Gaussian process learning: predictions can reflect relationships supplied alongside the examples, as well as similarity inferred from their attributes. The empirical finding supports that combined approach in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process framework combines instance attributes and relational information through a data-dependent covariance function.

title: Relational Learning with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) provides an unprecedented window into the complex functioning of the human brain, typically detailing the activity of thousands of voxels during hundreds of sequential time points. Unfortunately, the interpretation of fMRI is complicated due both to the relatively unknown connection between the hemodynamic response and neural activity and the unknown spatiotemporal characteristics of the cognitive patterns themselves. Here, we use data from the Experience Based Cognition competition to compare global and local methods of prediction applying both linear and nonlinear techniques of dimensionality reduction. We build global low dimensional representations of an fMRI dataset, using linear and nonlinear methods. We learn a set of time series that are implicit functions of the fMRI data, and predict the values of these times series in the future from the knowledge of the fMRI data only. We find effective, low-dimensional models based on the principal components of cognitive activity in classically-defined anatomical regions, the Brodmann Areas. Furthermore for some of the stimuli, the top predictive regions were stable across subjects and episodes, including WernickeÕs area for verbal instructions, visual cortex for facial and body features, and visual-temporal regions (Brodmann Area 7) for velocity. These interpretations and the relative simplicity of our approach provide a transparent and conceptual basis upon which to build more sophisticated techniques for fMRI decoding. To our knowledge, this is the first time that classical areas have been used in fMRI for an effective prediction of complex natural experience.

paragraphs: An fMRI recording contains activity measurements from thousands of voxels across time, making prediction and interpretation difficult. This paper compares global and local prediction methods using linear and nonlinear dimensionality reduction. It uses data from the Experience Based Cognition competition to study how compact representations can support prediction of natural experience.

The authors build low-dimensional representations and learn time series whose future values are predicted from fMRI data alone. They find effective models using principal components within anatomically defined Brodmann Areas. This connects dimensionality reduction with recognizable brain regions, making the predictive representation easier to interpret than a description based only on a large collection of individual voxels.

Reported examples include Wernicke's area for verbal instructions, visual cortex for face and body features, and Brodmann Area 7 for velocity. These qualified findings support anatomically organized, low-dimensional decoding as a transparent foundation for more sophisticated methods.
summary.tldr: Low-dimensional models within anatomical brain regions effectively predict aspects of natural experience, with stable predictive regions for some stimuli.

title: Locality and low-dimensions in the prediction of natural experience from fMRI

abstract: We provide statistical performance guarantees for a recently introduced kernel classifier that optimizes the $L_2$ or integrated squared error (ISE) of a difference of densities. The classifier is similar to a support vector machine (SVM) in that it is the solution of a quadratic program and yields a sparse classifier. Unlike SVMs, however, the $L_2$ kernel classifier does not involve a regularization parameter. We prove a distribution free concentration inequality for a cross-validation based estimate of the ISE, and apply this result to deduce an oracle inequality and consistency of the classifier on the sense of both ISE and probability of error. Our results can also be specialized to give performance guarantees for an existing method of $L_2$ kernel density estimation.

The classifier is similar to a support vector machine (SVM) in that it is the solution of a quadratic program and yields a sparse classifier. Unlike SVMs, however, the $L_2$ kernel classifier does not involve a regularization parameter. paragraphs: This paper analyzes a kernel classifier whose objective is the integrated squared error of a difference between densities. Like a support vector machine, it is obtained by solving a quadratic program and produces a sparse classifier. A distinguishing feature is that the formulation does not involve a regularization parameter.

The authors establish a distribution-free concentration inequality for a cross-validation estimate of integrated squared error. Such a result controls how the estimated error relates to its statistical target. They use this foundation to derive an oracle inequality and prove consistency for both the density-difference error criterion and the probability of misclassification.

These guarantees connect the quantity optimized by the method to the prediction behavior ultimately of interest. The analysis therefore goes beyond the classifier's computational resemblance to an SVM and supplies a statistical basis for evaluating it. The results can also be specialized to an existing L2 kernel density estimator, extending their relevance from classification to the related task of estimating a density.
summary.tldr: Statistical guarantees establish consistency of an L2 kernel classifier in both integrated squared error and misclassification probability.

title: Performance analysis for L\_2 kernel classification

abstract: In this study, we present a method for estimating the mutual information for a localized pattern of fMRI data. We show that taking a multivariate information approach to voxel selection leads to a decoding accuracy that surpasses an univariate inforamtion approach and other standard voxel selection methods. Furthermore,we extend the multivariate mutual information theory to measure the functional connectivity between distributed brain regions. By jointly estimating the information shared by two sets of voxels we can reliably map out the connectivities in the human brain during experiment conditions. We validated our approach on a 6-way scene categorization fMRI experiment. The multivariate information analysis is able to ﬁnd strong information ﬂow between PPA and RSC, which conﬁrms existing neuroscience studies on scenes. Furthermore, by exploring over the whole brain, our method identifies other interesting ROIs that share information with the PPA, RSC scene network,suggesting interesting future work for neuroscientists.

Furthermore,we extend the multivariate mutual information theory to measure the functional connectivity between distributed brain regions. Furthermore, by exploring over the whole brain, our method identifies other interesting ROIs that share information with the PPA, RSC scene network,suggesting interesting future work for neuroscientists.

paragraphs: The paper studies information carried by patterns of fMRI measurements across multiple voxels. Its method estimates mutual information for a local pattern rather than assessing each voxel separately. This matters because the usefulness of a group of measurements can depend on their joint behavior. The authors report that selecting voxels this way improves decoding accuracy over univariate information selection and other standard selection methods.

They extend the same multivariate perspective to functional connectivity between distributed brain regions. Instead of examining a single measurement from each location, they jointly estimate information shared by two sets of voxels. This provides a way to map relationships between regions under the experimental conditions.

Validation uses an fMRI experiment with six scene categories. The analysis finds strong shared information between PPA and RSC, consistent with existing scene-related neuroscience findings. A whole-brain exploration also identifies other regions sharing information with that network. These additional relationships suggest directions for future neuroscience research.
summary.tldr: Joint information analysis of fMRI voxel groups improves decoding and identifies shared information within and beyond a scene-processing network.

title: Exploring Functional Connectivities of the Human Brain using Multivariate Information Analysis

abstract: In this paper, we point out that there exist scaling and initialization problems in most existing multiple kernel learning (MKL) approaches, which employ the large margin principle to jointly learn both a kernel and an SVM classifier. The reason is that the margin itself can not well describe how good a kernel is due to the negligence of the scaling. We use the ratio between the margin and the radius of the minimum enclosing ball to measure the goodness of a kernel, and present a new minimization formulation for kernel learning. This formulation is invariant to scalings of learned kernels, and when learning linear combination of basis kernels it is also invariant to scalings of basis kernels and to the types (e.g., L1 or L2) of norm constraints on combination coefficients. We establish the differentiability of our formulation, and propose a gradient projection algorithm for kernel learning. Experiments show that our method significantly outperforms both SVM with the uniform combination of basis kernels and other state-of-art MKL approaches.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we point out that there exist scaling and initialization problems in most existing multiple kernel learning (MKL) approaches, which employ the large margin principle to jointly learn both a kernel and an SVM classifier. The reason is that the margin itself can not well describe how good a kernel is due to the negligence of the scaling. We use the ratio between the margin and the radius of the minimum enclosing ball to measure the goodness of a kernel, and present a new minimization formulation for kernel learning. This formulation is invariant to scalings of learned kernels, and when learning linear combination of basis kernels it is also invariant to scalings of basis kernels and to the types (e.g., L1 or L2) of norm constraints on combination coefficients. We establish the differentiability of our formulation, and propose a gradient projection algorithm for kernel learning. Experiments show that our method significantly outperforms both SVM with the uniform combination of basis kernels and other state-of-art MKL approaches.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning selects a kernel while training a support vector machine. This paper argues that relying on the classification margin alone creates scaling and initialization problems in many existing approaches. A margin can change with the scale of the representation, so its size by itself does not adequately characterize kernel quality.

The authors instead evaluate the margin relative to the radius of the minimum ball enclosing the data and develop a corresponding minimization formulation. The objective is invariant to scaling the learned kernel. For linear combinations of basis kernels, it is also invariant to scaling those basis kernels and to the choice of norm constraint on the combination coefficients.

The paper establishes differentiability of the formulation and proposes a gradient projection algorithm to optimize it. Experiments report significant improvements over an SVM using a uniform kernel combination and other state-of-the-art multiple kernel learning approaches. The contribution connects a scale-aware geometric criterion to an optimization method and demonstrates its empirical usefulness in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: A margin-to-radius kernel criterion removes specified scaling sensitivities and improves on competing kernel-learning methods in experiments.

title: Learning Kernels with Radiuses of Minimum Enclosing Balls

abstract: We consider structured multi-armed bandit tasks in which the agent is guided by prior structural knowledge that can be exploited to efficiently select the optimal arm(s) in situations where the number of arms is large, or even infinite. We pro- pose a new optimistic, UCB-like, algorithm for non-linearly parameterized bandit problems using the Generalized Linear Model (GLM) framework. We analyze the regret of the proposed algorithm, termed GLM-UCB, obtaining results similar to those recently proved in the literature for the linear regression case. The analysis also highlights a key difficulty of the non-linear case which is solved in GLM-UCB by focusing on the reward space rather than on the parameter space. Moreover, as the actual efficiency of current parameterized bandit algorithms is often deceiving in practice, we provide an asymptotic argument leading to significantly faster convergence. Simulation studies on real data sets illustrate the performance and the robustness of the proposed GLM-UCB approach.

Structural knowledge can connect their rewards and guide selection even when the action set is infinite. This paper studies that setting using generalized linear models, which allow rewards to depend nonlinearly on shared parameters.

The proposed GLM-UCB algorithm uses an optimistic, upper-confidence-bound approach to action selection. Its regret analysis obtains results similar to those established for linear regression bandits. A central difficulty arises from the nonlinear parameterization. The authors address it by focusing the analysis and algorithm on reward space rather than parameter space.

The paper also tackles the gap between theoretical guarantees and practical efficiency in parameterized bandit algorithms. An asymptotic argument leads to significantly faster convergence, and simulation studies using real datasets illustrate performance and robustness. Together, these contributions extend structured optimistic exploration to the generalized linear setting while attending to how quickly the method learns in practice.
summary.tldr: GLM-UCB extends optimistic bandit learning to generalized linear reward models, with regret guarantees and an approach to faster convergence.

title: Parametric Bandits: The Generalized Linear Case

abstract: This paper outlines a hierarchical Bayesian model for human category learning that learns both the organization of objects into categories, and the context in which this knowledge should be applied. The model is fit to multiple data sets, and provides a parsimonious method for describing how humans learn context specific conceptual representations.
originalAbstract: This paper outlines a hierarchical Bayesian model for human category learning that learns both the organization of objects into categories, and the context in which this knowledge should be applied. The model is fit to multiple data sets, and provides a parsimonious method for describing how humans learn context specific conceptual representations.

paragraphs: Category learning involves deciding how objects should be grouped, but the usefulness of a grouping also depends on context. This paper treats those as connected learning problems. Its model learns both the organization of objects into categories and the circumstances in which that category knowledge should be applied.

The proposed account is hierarchical and Bayesian. Its explanatory focus is therefore broader than assigning an object to a category: it also includes learning when a conceptual representation is relevant. This matters because the same account must describe category structure and its context-specific use. Learning the context is part of the representation-building process described by the model, rather than an unrelated decision considered afterward.

The authors fit the model to multiple datasets and present it as a parsimonious description of human learning. The stated contribution is a compact account of how people acquire conceptual representations tied to context. Its significance lies in joining the content of category knowledge with the conditions for applying it within a single modeling approach.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model jointly learns object categories and the contexts in which that knowledge should apply.

title: Learning the context of a category

abstract: We consider large matrices of low rank. We address the problem of recovering such matrices when most of the entries are unknown. Matrix completion finds applications in recommender systems. In this setting, the rows of the matrix may correspond to items and the columns may correspond to users. The known entries are the ratings given by users to some items. The aim is to predict the unobserved ratings. This problem is commonly stated in a constrained optimization framework. We follow an approach that exploits the geometry of the low-rank constraint to recast the problem as an unconstrained optimization problem on the Grassmann manifold. We then apply first- and second-order Riemannian trust-region methods to solve it. The cost of each iteration is linear in the number of known entries. Our methods, RTRMC 1 and 2, outperform state-of-the-art algorithms on a wide range of problem instances.

paragraphs: Matrix completion seeks to recover missing entries of a matrix using its known entries and an assumption of low rank. In a recommendation setting, the observed entries can be user ratings for items, and the missing entries are ratings to predict. This paper develops methods for large matrices with most entries unobserved.

The authors use the geometry of the low-rank constraint to reformulate the problem on the Grassmann manifold. This turns the constrained problem into an unconstrained optimization problem on that geometric space. They then apply first- and second-order Riemannian trust-region methods, producing the algorithms RTRMC 1 and RTRMC 2.

Each iteration has a cost linear in the number of observed entries, tying the stated computational workload to the available data. The methods outperform state-of-the-art algorithms across a wide range of tested problem instances. The contribution combines a geometric formulation of low rank with optimization methods suited to that formulation, providing an effective approach to recovering sparsely observed matrices.
summary.tldr: RTRMC exploits low-rank geometry to complete matrices with trust-region methods whose iteration cost is linear in the number of observed entries.

title: RTRMC: A Riemannian trust-region method for low-rank matrix completion

abstract: The brain uses population codes to form distributed, noise-tolerant representations of sensory and motor variables. Recent work has examined the theoretical optimality of such codes in order to gain insight into the principles governing population codes found in the brain. However, the majority of the population coding literature considers either conditionally independent neurons or neurons with noise governed by a stimulus-independent covariance matrix. Here we analyze population coding under a simple alternative model in which latent input noise" corrupts the stimulus before it is encoded by the population. This provides a convenient and tractable description for irreducible uncertainty that cannot be overcome by adding neurons, and induces stimulus-dependent correlations that mimic certain aspects of the correlations observed in real populations. We examine prior-dependent, Bayesian optimal coding in such populations using exact analyses of cases in which the posterior is approximately Gaussian. These analyses extend previous results on independent Poisson population codes and yield an analytic expression for squared loss and a tight upper bound for mutual information. We show that, for homogeneous populations that tile the input domain, optimal tuning curve width depends on the prior, the loss function, the resource constraint, and the amount of input noise. This framework provides a practical testbed for examining issues of optimality, noise, correlation, and coding fidelity in realistic neural populations."

paragraphs: Neural population codes distribute information across many neurons, but adding neurons cannot remove uncertainty already present in their shared input. This paper studies a model in which noise corrupts the stimulus before population encoding. The construction produces stimulus-dependent correlations and represents an irreducible source of uncertainty.

The authors analyze Bayesian optimal coding with dependence on the prior distribution of stimuli, focusing on cases where the posterior is approximately Gaussian. Their analyses extend earlier results for independent Poisson population codes. They derive an analytic expression for squared loss and a tight upper bound on mutual information, giving two ways to assess the fidelity of the population representation.

Thus, even within this structured setting, optimal width depends on several modeling choices and environmental properties. The framework offers a tractable testbed for studying how shared uncertainty, correlations, and coding objectives jointly affect neural representations.
summary.tldr: A shared-input-noise model shows how optimal neural tuning depends jointly on stimulus priors, coding objectives, resources, and irreducible noise.

title: Optimal prior-dependent neural population codes under shared input noise

abstract: Spectral methods of moments provide a powerful tool for learning the parameters of latent variable models. Despite their theoretical appeal, the applicability of these methods to real data is still limited due to a lack of robustness to model misspecification. In this paper we present a hierarchical approach to methods of moments to circumvent such limitations. Our method is based on replacing the tensor decomposition step used in previous algorithms with approximate joint diagonalization. Experiments on topic modeling show that our method outperforms previous tensor decomposition methods in terms of speed and model quality.

Despite their theoretical appeal, the applicability of these methods to real data is still limited due to a lack of robustness to model misspecification. In this paper we present a hierarchical approach to methods of moments to circumvent such limitations. Our method is based on replacing the tensor decomposition step used in previous algorithms with approximate joint diagonalization. Experiments on topic modeling show that our method outperforms previous tensor decomposition methods in terms of speed and model quality.

paragraphs: Spectral methods of moments learn the parameters of latent-variable models from statistical summaries of observed data. Although these methods have appealing theoretical properties, the paper identifies a practical obstacle: they can lack robustness when the assumed model does not match the data. That mismatch limits how readily their theoretical appeal translates into useful results on real datasets.

The authors propose a hierarchical approach to methods of moments. Its central computational change replaces the tensor-decomposition step used by earlier algorithms with approximate joint diagonalization. This changes a key operation in parameter learning while retaining the broader methods-of-moments approach. The replacement is presented as a way to address difficulties associated with model misspecification.

Experiments in topic modeling show improvements over previous tensor-decomposition methods in both speed and model quality. These two findings matter together: the alternative computation is faster in the reported tests and also produces better models. The evidence supports the hierarchical approach for the evaluated topic-modeling setting, without making robustness to every possible model mismatch a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: Replacing tensor decomposition with approximate joint diagonalization improves reported topic-modeling speed and quality.

title: Hierarchical Methods of Moments

abstract: Random projections have been increasingly adopted for a diverse set of tasks in machine learning involving dimensionality reduction. One specific line of research on this topic has investigated the use of quantization subsequent to projection with the aim of additional data compression. Motivated by applications in nearest neighbor search and linear learning, we revisit the problem of recovering inner products (respectively cosine similarities) in such setting. We show that even under coarse scalar quantization with 3 to 5 bits per projection, the loss in accuracy tends to range from negligible'' to moderate''. One implication is that in most scenarios of practical interest, there is no need for a sophisticated recovery approach like maximum likelihood estimation as considered in previous work on the subject. What we propose herein also yields considerable improvements in terms of accuracy over the Hamming distance-based approach in Li et al. (ICML 2014) which is comparable in terms of simplicity

paragraphs: Random projections compress data by reducing its dimension, and quantizing the projected values can compress it further. This paper asks how accurately inner products and cosine similarities can be recovered from those coarsely stored projections. The question matters for nearest neighbor search and linear learning, where such comparisons are central to using the compressed representation.

The authors find that using only three to five bits per projection tends to produce an accuracy loss ranging from negligible to moderate. They propose simple recovery strategies and argue that, in most practically relevant scenarios, sophisticated recovery procedures such as maximum likelihood estimation are unnecessary. This is a qualified practical conclusion, rather than a guarantee for every possible dataset.

The proposed strategies also improve accuracy considerably over a previously studied Hamming-distance approach with comparable simplicity. The contribution therefore concerns both compression and reconstruction: coarse storage can preserve useful similarity information, and recovering it need not require a complex estimator. The reported comparison supports better accuracy without sacrificing the simplicity of the recovery procedure.
summary.tldr: Simple estimators recover useful inner products from projections stored with three to five bits, often making more elaborate recovery unnecessary.

title: Simple strategies for recovering inner products from coarsely quantized random projections

abstract: In many machine learning applications, submodular functions have been used as a model for evaluating the utility or payoff of a set such as news items to recommend, sensors to deploy in a terrain, nodes to influence in a social network, to name a few. At the heart of all these applications is the assumption that the underlying utility/payoff function is known a priori, hence maximizing it is in principle possible. In real life situations, however, the utility function is not fully known in advance and can only be estimated via interactions. For instance, whether a user likes a movie or not can be reliably evaluated only after it was shown to her. Or, the range of influence of a user in a social network can be estimated only after she is selected to advertise the product. We model such problems as an interactive submodular bandit optimization, where in each round we receive a context (e.g., previously selected movies) and have to choose an action (e.g., propose a new movie). We then receive a noisy feedback about the utility of the action (e.g., ratings) which we model as a submodular function over the context-action space. We develop SM-UCB that efficiently trades off exploration (collecting more data) and exploration (proposing a good action given gathered data) and achieves a $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound after $T$ rounds of interaction. Given a bounded-RKHS norm kernel over the context-action-payoff space that governs the smoothness of the utility function, SM-UCB keeps an upper-confidence bound on the payoff function that allows it to asymptotically achieve no-regret. Finally, we evaluate our results on four concrete applications, including movie recommendation (on the MovieLense data set), news recommendation (on Yahoo! Webscope dataset), interactive influence maximization (on a subset of the Facebook network), and personalized data summarization (on Reuters Corpus). In all these applications, we observe that SM-UCB consistently outperforms the prior art.

Across these applications, the authors report consistent improvements over prior methods.
summary.tldr: SM-UCB learns unknown submodular payoffs through interaction, with conditional no-regret guarantees and reported gains across four applications.

title: Interactive Submodular Bandit

abstract: We introduce the factored bandits model, which is a framework for learning with limited (bandit) feedback, where actions can be decomposed into a Cartesian product of atomic actions. Factored bandits incorporate rank-1 bandits as a special case, but significantly relax the assumptions on the form of the reward function. We provide an anytime algorithm for stochastic factored bandits and up to constants matching upper and lower regret bounds for the problem. Furthermore, we show that with a slight modification the proposed algorithm can be applied to utility based dueling bandits. We obtain an improvement in the additive terms of the regret bound compared to state of the art algorithms (the additive terms are dominating up to time horizons which are exponential in the number of arms).

paragraphs: Bandit learning involves choosing actions while receiving only limited feedback about their rewards. This paper considers actions built by combining smaller, atomic choices. Its factored-bandit model represents the action space as a Cartesian product, giving the learning problem an explicit structure even when the set of complete actions contains many combinations.

The model includes rank-one bandits as a special case while substantially relaxing their assumptions about the reward function. For stochastic factored bandits, the authors provide an anytime algorithm, which can operate without a predetermined stopping horizon. They establish upper and lower regret bounds that match up to constant factors, characterizing the achievable learning performance within this problem formulation.

A small modification also makes the algorithm applicable to utility-based dueling bandits. In that setting, the authors improve additive terms in the regret bound relative to existing algorithms. These terms can dominate until horizons exponential in the number of arms, so improving them can matter across a substantial range of learning durations, rather than only changing a negligible part of the guarantee.
summary.tldr: Factored bandits model actions assembled from atomic choices and admit an anytime algorithm with regret bounds matching up to constants.

title: Factored Bandits

abstract: In the $k$-nearest neighborhood model ($k$-NN), we are given a set of points $P$, and we shall answer queries $q$ by returning the $k$ nearest neighbors of $q$ in $P$ according to some metric. This concept is crucial in many areas of data analysis and data processing, e.g., computer vision, document retrieval and machine learning. Many $k$-NN algorithms have been published and implemented, but often the relation between parameters and accuracy of the computed $k$-NN is not explicit. We study property testing of $k$-NN graphs in theory and evaluate it empirically: given a point set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^\delta$ and a directed graph $G=(P,E)$, is $G$ a $k$-NN graph, i.e., every point $p \in P$ has outgoing edges to its $k$ nearest neighbors, or is it $\epsilon$-far from being a $k$-NN graph? Here, $\epsilon$-far means that one has to change more than an $\epsilon$-fraction of the edges in order to make $G$ a $k$-NN graph. We develop a randomized algorithm with one-sided error that decides this question, i.e., a property tester for the $k$-NN property, with complexity $O(\sqrt{n} k^2 / \epsilon^2)$ measured in terms of the number of vertices and edges it inspects, and we prove a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{n / \epsilon k})$. We evaluate our tester empirically on the $k$-NN models computed by various algorithms and show that it can be used to detect $k$-NN models with bad accuracy in significantly less time than the building time of the $k$-NN model.

Many algorithms construct such graphs, but their settings do not always clearly indicate how accurate the result will be. This paper asks whether a graph can be checked efficiently after construction, without inspecting its entire collection of connections.

The authors formulate this as property testing: distinguish a correct k-nearest-neighbor graph from one requiring changes to more than an epsilon fraction of its edges. The contribution is therefore an efficient quality check with a precisely defined error criterion, rather than a replacement method for constructing nearest-neighbor graphs.
summary.tldr: A randomized property tester detects substantially incorrect nearest-neighbor graphs while inspecting only part of their structure.

title: A Theory-Based Evaluation of Nearest Neighbor Models Put Into Practice

abstract: Neural attention has become central to many state-of-the-art models in natural language processing and related domains. Attention networks are an easy-to-train and effective method for softly simulating alignment; however, the approach does not marginalize over latent alignments in a probabilistic sense. This property makes it difficult to compare attention to other alignment approaches, to compose it with probabilistic models, and to perform posterior inference conditioned on observed data. A related latent approach, hard attention, fixes these issues, but is generally harder to train and less accurate. This work considers variational attention networks, alternatives to soft and hard attention for learning latent variable alignment models, with tighter approximation bounds based on amortized variational inference. We further propose methods for reducing the variance of gradients to make these approaches computationally feasible. Experiments show that for machine translation and visual question answering, inefficient exact latent variable models outperform standard neural attention, but these gains go away when using hard attention based training. On the other hand, variational attention retains most of the performance gain but with training speed comparable to neural attention.

paragraphs: Neural attention provides an effective, trainable approximation to alignment, but ordinary soft attention does not probabilistically sum over latent alignments. This complicates combining it with probabilistic models and inferring alignments after observing data. Hard attention offers a latent-variable alternative, yet the abstract identifies harder training and lower accuracy as practical obstacles.

The result supports a practical middle ground between efficient soft attention and expensive exact latent-alignment inference.
summary.tldr: Variational attention preserves most observed gains from exact latent alignment while training at speeds comparable to standard attention.

title: Latent Alignment and Variational Attention

abstract: The state-of-the-art methods for solving optimization problems in big dimensions are variants of randomized coordinate descent (RCD). In this paper we introduce a fundamentally new type of acceleration strategy for RCD based on the augmentation of the set of coordinate directions by a few spectral or conjugate directions. As we increase the number of extra directions to be sampled from, the rate of the method improves, and interpolates between the linear rate of RCD and a linear rate independent of the condition number. We develop and analyze also inexact variants of these methods where the spectral and conjugate directions are allowed to be approximate only. We motivate the above development by proving several negative results which highlight the limitations of RCD with importance sampling.

paragraphs: Randomized coordinate descent tackles high-dimensional optimization by choosing coordinate directions for its updates. This paper proposes accelerating it by expanding the collection of directions available for sampling. Alongside the original coordinates, the method can select a few spectral or conjugate directions that provide additional ways to move through the optimization space.

The analysis shows that adding more of these directions improves the convergence rate. The resulting progression connects the linear rate of randomized coordinate descent to a linear rate independent of the condition number. This describes how the rate changes as the direction set is enriched, making the choice of available directions central to the acceleration strategy.

The authors also develop and analyze inexact versions in which the additional directions need only be approximate. This extends the framework beyond requiring exact spectral or conjugate information. Finally, they prove negative results exposing limitations of coordinate descent with importance sampling. Those results motivate changing the set of directions itself as another route to faster optimization.
summary.tldr: Adding spectral or conjugate directions to randomized coordinate descent improves its analyzed convergence rate, with extensions allowing approximate directions.

title: Stochastic Spectral and Conjugate Descent Methods

abstract: This paper presents a general mean-field game (GMFG) framework for simultaneous learning and decision-making in stochastic games with a large population. It first establishes the existence of a unique Nash Equilibrium to this GMFG, and explains that naively combining Q-learning with the fixed-point approach in classical MFGs yields unstable algorithms. It then proposes a Q-learning algorithm with Boltzmann policy (GMF-Q), with analysis of convergence property and computational complexity. The experiments on repeated Ad auction problems demonstrate that this GMF-Q algorithm is efficient and robust in terms of convergence and learning accuracy. Moreover, its performance is superior in convergence, stability, and learning ability, when compared with existing algorithms for multi-agent reinforcement learning.

The mean-field viewpoint describes interactions through population-level behavior, providing a way to reason about strategic learning when many agents are involved.

The authors establish the existence of a unique Nash equilibrium for their framework. They also explain why simply combining Q-learning with the fixed-point approach used in classical mean-field games produces unstable algorithms. This separates the existence of a well-defined equilibrium from the practical challenge of learning how to reach it.

Their proposed GMF-Q algorithm combines Q-learning with a Boltzmann policy, and the paper analyzes its convergence and computational complexity. Experiments use repeated advertising auctions to examine the learning procedure. In those experiments, GMF-Q is efficient and robust in convergence and learning accuracy, and outperforms existing multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms in convergence, stability, and learning ability. The results support the proposed integration of learning and equilibrium computation in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: GMF-Q combines Q-learning with a Boltzmann policy for mean-field games, with theoretical analysis and strong repeated-auction results.

title: Learning Mean-Field Games

abstract: Reducing the precision of weights and activation functions in neural network training, with minimal impact on performance, is essential for the deployment of these models in resource-constrained environments. We apply mean field techniques to networks with quantized activations in order to evaluate the degree to which quantization degrades signal propagation at initialization. We derive initialization schemes which maximize signal propagation in such networks, and suggest why this is helpful for generalization. Building on these results, we obtain a closed form implicit equation for $L_{\max}$, the maximal trainable depth (and hence model capacity), given $N$, the number of quantization levels in the activation function. Solving this equation numerically, we obtain asymptotically: $L_{\max}\propto N^{1.82}$.

This paper studies how that reduction in precision affects the passage of signals through a network at initialization. Its focus is the relationship between activation quantization and the depth that a network can support.

The authors apply mean field techniques to analyze signal propagation and derive initialization schemes that maximize it for quantized activations. This connects the choice of numerical precision with the choice of initial network parameters. They also suggest why preserving signals in this way could help generalization, rather than establishing that benefit as an unconditional result.

The analysis produces an implicit equation connecting the number of activation levels, N, to the maximal trainable depth, L_max. Numerically solving that equation gives the asymptotic relationship L_max proportional to N raised to 1.82. Within this theoretical account, adding quantization levels permits greater depth, making precision and model capacity linked design choices.
summary.tldr: A mean field analysis links activation precision to trainable network depth and derives initialization schemes that improve signal propagation.

title: A Mean Field Theory of Quantized Deep Networks: The Quantization-Depth Trade-Off

abstract: Due to the foveated nature of the human vision system, people can focus their visual attention on a small region of their visual field at a time, which usually contains only a single object. Estimating this object of attention in first-person (egocentric) videos is useful for many human-centered real-world applications such as augmented reality applications and driver assistance systems. A straightforward solution for this problem is to pick the object whose bounding box is hit by the gaze, where eye gaze point estimation is obtained from a traditional eye gaze estimator and object candidates are generated from an off-the-shelf object detector. However, such an approach can fail because it addresses the where and the what problems separately, despite that they are highly related, chicken-and-egg problems. In this paper, we propose a novel unified model that incorporates both spatial and temporal evidence in identifying as well as locating the attended object in firstperson videos. It introduces a novel Self Validation Module that enforces and leverages consistency of the where and the what concepts. We evaluate on two public datasets, demonstrating that Self Validation Module significantly benefits both training and testing and that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: This paper estimates which object a person is attending to in first-person video. A straightforward approach estimates a gaze point, detects objects separately, and selects the object whose bounding box contains that point. The authors argue that this separation can fail because identifying the object and locating attention are closely connected problems.

Their proposed network addresses both questions together, using evidence from image locations and changes over time. Its Self Validation Module encourages consistency between the predicted attention location and the identity of the attended object. The useful idea is that these predictions can check and inform each other, rather than relying entirely on a final overlap test between independently produced outputs.

Evaluation on two public datasets shows that the module benefits both training and testing, and the authors report performance exceeding the state of the art. These findings support jointly modeling where attention falls and what it selects for the evaluated first-person videos. The task has potential relevance to applications such as augmented reality and driver assistance, where an attended object can be more informative than a gaze coordinate alone.
summary.tldr: A unified network improves attended-object estimation in first-person video by making object identity and attention location mutually consistent.

title: A Self Validation Network for Object-Level Human Attention Estimation

abstract: The simplest and most widely applied method for guaranteeing differential privacy is to add instance-independent noise to a statistic of interest that is scaled to its global sensitivity. However, global sensitivity is a worst-case notion that is often too conservative for realized dataset instances. We provide methods for scaling noise in an instance-dependent way and demonstrate that they provide greater accuracy under average-case distributional assumptions. Specifically, we consider the basic problem of privately estimating the mean of a real distribution from i.i.d. samples. The standard empirical mean estimator can have arbitrarily-high global sensitivity. We propose the trimmed mean estimator, which interpolates between the mean and the median, as a way of attaining much lower sensitivity on average while losing very little in terms of statistical accuracy. To privately estimate the trimmed mean, we revisit the smooth sensitivity framework of Nissim, Raskhodnikova, and Smith (STOC 2007), which provides a framework for using instance-dependent sensitivity. We propose three new additive noise distributions which provide concentrated differential privacy when scaled to smooth sensitivity. We provide theoretical and experimental evidence showing that our noise distributions compare favorably to others in the literature, in particular, when applied to the mean estimation problem.

This paper studies private mean estimation from independent, identically distributed samples, where the ordinary empirical mean can have arbitrarily large global sensitivity. It asks how noise can instead reflect the dataset at hand.

The authors propose using a trimmed mean, an estimator between the mean and median. Under their average-case distributional assumptions, it achieves much lower sensitivity while giving up little statistical accuracy. They combine this estimator with smooth sensitivity, a framework for safely adapting privacy noise to an instance-dependent measure of how much the statistic can change.

Theoretical analysis and experiments show favorable comparisons with existing noise distributions, particularly for estimating means. The accuracy improvements are supported under the stated average-case assumptions, making the result a way to exploit typical dataset behavior while retaining a formal privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: Trimmed means and new smooth-sensitivity noise distributions improve private mean estimation under average-case distributional assumptions.

title: Average-Case Averages: Private Algorithms for Smooth Sensitivity and Mean Estimation

abstract: Designing effective model-based reinforcement learning algorithms is difficult because the ease of data generation must be weighed against the bias of model-generated data. In this paper, we study the role of model usage in policy optimization both theoretically and empirically. We first formulate and analyze a model-based reinforcement learning algorithm with a guarantee of monotonic improvement at each step. In practice, this analysis is overly pessimistic and suggests that real off-policy data is always preferable to model-generated on-policy data, but we show that an empirical estimate of model generalization can be incorporated into such analysis to justify model usage. Motivated by this analysis, we then demonstrate that a simple procedure of using short model-generated rollouts branched from real data has the benefits of more complicated model-based algorithms without the usual pitfalls. In particular, this approach surpasses the sample efficiency of prior model-based methods, matches the asymptotic performance of the best model-free algorithms, and scales to horizons that cause other model-based methods to fail entirely.

paragraphs: A learned environment model can generate additional experience for reinforcement learning, but its errors can bias policy training. This paper studies how much to trust model-generated data. It first analyzes an algorithm with a step-by-step improvement guarantee, then examines why that analysis can be too pessimistic to guide effective model use in practice.

The initial analysis favors real data collected under other policies over synthetic data generated under the current policy. Incorporating an empirical estimate of model generalization provides a way to justify using the model. Motivated by this reasoning, the authors propose short simulated rollouts that begin from real data, making limited model use the core of the practical procedure.

The reported experiments show better sample efficiency than prior model-based methods and eventual performance matching the best model-free algorithms. The approach also handles horizons where other model-based methods fail. These findings support short rollouts from real experience as a useful balance between obtaining extra training data and controlling the consequences of model error in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Short model-generated rollouts starting from real data improve sample efficiency while preserving strong eventual policy performance in the reported experiments.

title: When to Trust Your Model: Model-Based Policy Optimization

abstract: With the introduction of the variational autoencoder (VAE), probabilistic latent variable models have received renewed attention as powerful generative models. However, their performance in terms of test likelihood and quality of generated samples has been surpassed by autoregressive models without stochastic units. Furthermore, flow-based models have recently been shown to be an attractive alternative that scales well to high-dimensional data. In this paper we close the performance gap by constructing VAE models that can effectively utilize a deep hierarchy of stochastic variables and model complex covariance structures. We introduce the Bidirectional-Inference Variational Autoencoder (BIVA), characterized by a skip-connected generative model and an inference network formed by a bidirectional stochastic inference path. We show that BIVA reaches state-of-the-art test likelihoods, generates sharp and coherent natural images, and uses the hierarchy of latent variables to capture different aspects of the data distribution. We observe that BIVA, in contrast to recent results, can be used for anomaly detection. We attribute this to the hierarchy of latent variables which is able to extract high-level semantic features. Finally, we extend BIVA to semi-supervised classification tasks and show that it performs comparably to state-of-the-art results by generative adversarial networks.

paragraphs: BIVA addresses a performance gap between variational autoencoders and other generative models. Its central idea is to make effective use of a deep hierarchy of stochastic latent variables, allowing the model to represent complex relationships within data. Different parts of the hierarchy can capture different aspects of the distribution being learned.

The architecture combines a generative model with skip connections and an inference network whose stochastic path runs in both directions. This arrangement is designed to make the deep hierarchy useful for modeling complex covariance structure. The authors report state-of-the-art test likelihoods together with generated natural images that are sharp and coherent.

The paper also explores uses beyond image generation. It observes that BIVA can detect anomalies and attributes this ability to high-level semantic features extracted through the latent hierarchy. That explanation is the authors' interpretation of the observation. An extension to semi-supervised classification performs comparably to state-of-the-art generative adversarial network results, suggesting that the learned hierarchy can also support prediction when labels are only partly available.
summary.tldr: BIVA combines a deep latent hierarchy with bidirectional inference to achieve strong generative performance and support anomaly detection and semi-supervised classification.

title: BIVA: A Very Deep Hierarchy of Latent Variables for Generative Modeling

abstract: We study the performance of optimistic regret-minimization algorithms for both minimizing regret in, and computing Nash equilibria of, zero-sum extensive-form games. In order to apply these algorithms to extensive-form games, a distance-generating function is needed. We study the use of the dilated entropy and dilated Euclidean distance functions. For the dilated Euclidean distance function we prove the first explicit bounds on the strong-convexity parameter for general treeplexes. Furthermore, we show that the use of dilated distance-generating functions enable us to decompose the mirror descent algorithm, and its optimistic variant, into local mirror descent algorithms at each information set. This decomposition mirrors the structure of the counterfactual regret minimization framework, and enables important techniques in practice, such as distributed updates and pruning of cold parts of the game tree. Our algorithms provably converge at a rate of $T^{-1}$, which is superior to prior counterfactual regret minimization algorithms. We experimentally compare to the popular algorithm CFR+, which has a theoretical convergence rate of $T^{-0.5}$ in theory, but is known to often converge at a rate of $T^{-1}$, or better, in practice. We give an example matrix game where CFR+ experimentally converges at a relatively slow rate of $T^{-0.74}$, whereas our optimistic methods converge faster than $T^{-1}$. We go on to show that our fast rate also holds in the Kuhn poker game, which is an extensive-form game. For games with deeper game trees however, we find that CFR+ is still faster. Finally we show that when the goal is minimizing regret, rather than computing a Nash equilibrium, our optimistic methods can outperform CFR+, even in deep game trees.

title: Optimistic Regret Minimization for Extensive-Form Games via Dilated Distance-Generating Functions

abstract: A spatial point process can be characterized by an intensity function which predicts the number of events that occur across space. In this paper, we develop a method to infer predictive intensity intervals by learning a spatial model using a regularized criterion. We prove that the proposed method exhibits out-of-sample prediction performance guarantees which, unlike standard estimators, are valid even when the spatial model is misspecified. The method is demonstrated using synthetic as well as real spatial data.
