The method is demonstrated using synthetic as well as real spatial data.

paragraphs: A spatial point process describes events distributed across space. Its intensity function predicts how many events occur in different locations, making intensity estimation central to spatial prediction. This paper develops a method that produces predictive intensity intervals, expressing predictions through ranges rather than relying only on a single estimated intensity.

The method learns a spatial model using a regularized criterion. Its central theoretical contribution is a guarantee about prediction performance outside the data used for fitting. Crucially, the guarantee remains valid when the spatial model is misspecified, meaning that the chosen model does not correctly describe the actual process generating the observations.

That robustness to misspecification matters because the prediction guarantee does not depend on having selected the correct spatial model. The authors contrast this property with standard estimators and demonstrate the method on both synthetic and real spatial data. The contribution brings interval prediction and theoretical out-of-sample assurance into the same modeling procedure, with model mismatch explicitly covered by the stated result.
summary.tldr: A regularized spatial model produces predictive intensity intervals with out-of-sample guarantees that remain valid under model misspecification.

title: Prediction of Spatial Point Processes: Regularized Method with Out-of-Sample Guarantees

abstract: The standard approach to fitting an autoregressive spike train model is to maximize the likelihood for one-step prediction. This maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) often leads to models that perform poorly when generating samples recursively for more than one time step. Moreover, the generated spike trains can fail to capture important features of the data and even show diverging firing rates. To alleviate this, we propose to directly minimize the divergence between neural recorded and model generated spike trains using spike train kernels. We develop a method that stochastically optimizes the maximum mean discrepancy induced by the kernel. Experiments performed on both real and synthetic neural data validate the proposed approach, showing that it leads to well-behaving models. Using different combinations of spike train kernels, we show that we can control the trade-off between different features which is critical for dealing with model-mismatch.

paragraphs: Autoregressive spike-train models are commonly fitted to predict the next time step by maximum likelihood. Yet good one-step prediction can coexist with poor behavior when the model repeatedly generates its own future inputs. Generated neural activity may miss important data features or even develop diverging firing rates.

This paper instead directly compares recorded spike trains with spike trains generated by the model. It uses spike-train kernels to define a maximum mean discrepancy, a measure of difference between the recorded and generated distributions. The authors develop a stochastic method for minimizing this discrepancy, making generated behavior itself the object of optimization.

Experiments on real and synthetic neural data show that the approach produces well-behaving models. Different combinations of kernels also let the authors control trade-offs among the spike-train features being matched. This matters when the model cannot reproduce every aspect of the data: the kernel combination provides a way to choose the balance among those features during fitting.
summary.tldr: Directly matching generated and recorded spike trains improves recursive model behavior and allows control over which activity features are emphasized.

title: Rescuing neural spike train models from bad MLE

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a discrete variant of the Meta-learning framework. Meta-learning aims at exploiting prior experience and data to improve performance on future tasks. By now, there exist numerous formulations for Meta-learning in the continuous domain. Notably, the Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) formulation views each task as a continuous optimization problem and based on prior data learns a suitable initialization that can be adapted to new, unseen tasks after a few simple gradient updates. Motivated by this terminology, we propose a novel Meta-learning framework in the discrete domain where each task is equivalent to maximizing a set function under a cardinality constraint. Our approach aims at using prior data, i.e., previously visited tasks, to train a proper initial solution set that can be quickly adapted to a new task at a relatively low computational cost. This approach leads to (i) a personalized solution for each task, and (ii) significantly reduced computational cost at test time compared to the case where the solution is fully optimized once the new task is revealed. The training procedure is performed by solving a challenging discrete optimization problem for which we present deterministic and randomized algorithms. In the case where the tasks are monotone and submodular, we show strong theoretical guarantees for our proposed methods even though the training objective may not be submodular. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on two real-world problem instances where we observe that our methods lead to a significant reduction in computational complexity in solving the new tasks while incurring a small performance loss compared to when the tasks are fully optimized.

This paper transfers that idea to discrete optimization, where each task selects a set of items subject to a size constraint. summary.tldr: Submodular meta-learning learns reusable initial sets that reduce new-task optimization costs with a small empirical performance loss.

title: Submodular Meta-Learning

abstract: We study symmetric spiked matrix models with respect to a general class of noise distributions. Given a rank-1 deformation of a random noise matrix, whose entries are independently distributed with zero mean and unit variance, the goal is to estimate the rank-1 part. For the case of Gaussian noise, the top eigenvector of the given matrix is a widely-studied estimator known to achieve optimal statistical guarantees, e.g., in the sense of the celebrated BBP phase transition. However, this estimator can fail completely for heavy-tailed noise. In this work, we exhibit an estimator that works for heavy-tailed noise up to the BBP threshold that is optimal even for Gaussian noise. We give a non-asymptotic analysis of our estimator which relies only on the variance of each entry remaining constant as the size of the matrix grows: higher moments may grow arbitrarily fast or even fail to exist. Previously, it was only known how to achieve these guarantees if higher-order moments of the noises are bounded by a constant independent of the size of the matrix. Our estimator can be evaluated in polynomial time by counting self-avoiding walks via a color coding technique. Moreover, we extend our estimator to spiked tensor models and establish analogous results.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a rank-one signal hidden in a symmetric random matrix. Its noise model has independent entries with zero mean and unit variance. With Gaussian noise, the leading eigenvector achieves a well-known optimal statistical threshold, but heavy-tailed noise can make this estimator fail completely.

The authors construct an alternative estimator that reaches the BBP threshold even with heavy-tailed noise. Their finite-size analysis only requires the entry variances to remain constant as the matrix grows. Higher moments may increase arbitrarily quickly or may not exist. This substantially relaxes earlier guarantees that required higher-order moments to stay bounded independently of matrix size.

The estimator is computable in polynomial time by counting self-avoiding walks using a color-coding technique. The authors also extend the construction to spiked tensors and obtain analogous results. The contribution combines statistical robustness under weak moment assumptions with computational feasibility: matching the stated Gaussian-noise threshold does not require the stronger tail restrictions imposed by previous analyses.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-time estimator recovers rank-one signals at the BBP threshold under heavy-tailed noise without bounded higher-moment assumptions.

title: Estimating Rank-One Spikes from Heavy-Tailed Noise via Self-Avoiding Walks

abstract: We present BlockGAN, an image generative model that learns object-aware 3D scene representations directly from unlabelled 2D images. Current work on scene representation learning either ignores scene background or treats the whole scene as one object. Meanwhile, work that considers scene compositionality treats scene objects only as image patches or 2D layers with alpha maps. Inspired by the computer graphics pipeline, we design BlockGAN to learn to first generate 3D features of background and foreground objects, then combine them into 3D features for the whole scene, and finally render them into realistic images. This allows BlockGAN to reason over occlusion and interaction between objects’ appearance, such as shadow and lighting, and provides control over each object’s 3D pose and identity, while maintaining image realism. BlockGAN is trained end-to-end, using only unlabelled single images, without the need for 3D geometry, pose labels, object masks, or multiple views of the same scene. Our experiments show that using explicit 3D features to represent objects allows BlockGAN to learn disentangled representations both in terms of objects (foreground and background) and their properties (pose and identity).

paragraphs: BlockGAN learns to generate images using a scene representation that separates foreground objects from the background in three dimensions. This addresses a weakness of approaches that represent an entire scene as one object or describe its components only as image patches and flat layers. The goal is to make individual objects controllable while preserving a realistic overall image.

Its generation process follows a computer graphics pipeline. The model first creates 3D features for the background and individual foreground objects, combines them into scene features, and then renders an image. Composing objects before rendering allows it to account for occlusion and interactions in appearance, including lighting and shadows.

Training uses unlabelled single images without requiring 3D geometry, pose annotations, object masks, or multiple views of a scene. Experiments show that the explicit 3D features support separation both between objects and between properties such as pose and identity. These results support the model's ability to control an object's 3D pose and identity while maintaining image realism.
summary.tldr: BlockGAN learns separate, controllable 3D object representations from unlabelled single images and combines them to generate realistic scenes.

title: BlockGAN: Learning 3D Object-aware Scene Representations from Unlabelled Images

abstract: We study sequential decision-making problems in which each agent aims to maximize the expected total reward while satisfying a constraint on the expected total utility. We employ the natural policy gradient method to solve the discounted infinite-horizon Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) problem. Specifically, we propose a new Natural Policy Gradient Primal-Dual (NPG-PD) method for CMDPs which updates the primal variable via natural policy gradient ascent and the dual variable via projected sub-gradient descent. Even though the underlying maximization involves a nonconcave objective function and a nonconvex constraint set under the softmax policy parametrization, we prove that our method achieves global convergence with sublinear rates regarding both the optimality gap and the constraint violation. Such a convergence is independent of the size of the state-action space, i.e., it is~dimension-free. Furthermore, for the general smooth policy class, we establish sublinear rates of convergence regarding both the optimality gap and the constraint violation, up to a function approximation error caused by restricted policy parametrization. Finally, we show that two sample-based NPG-PD algorithms inherit such non-asymptotic convergence properties and provide finite-sample complexity guarantees. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees of policy-based primal-dual methods for solving infinite-horizon discounted CMDPs. We also provide computational results to demonstrate merits of our approach.

title: Natural Policy Gradient Primal-Dual Method for Constrained Markov Decision Processes

abstract: There has been growing progress on theoretical analyses for provably efficient learning in MDPs with linear function approximation, but much of the existing work has made strong assumptions to enable exploration by conventional exploration frameworks. Typically these assumptions are stronger than what is needed to find good solutions in the batch setting. In this work, we show how under a more standard notion of low inherent Bellman error, typically employed in least-square value iteration-style algorithms, we can provide strong PAC guarantees on learning a near optimal value function provided that the linear space is sufficiently ``explorable''. We present a computationally tractable algorithm for the reward-free setting and show how it can be used to learn a near optimal policy for any (linear) reward function, which is revealed only once learning has completed. If this reward function is also estimated from the samples gathered during pure exploration, our results also provide same-order PAC guarantees on the performance of the resulting policy for this setting.

paragraphs: An agent may need to explore an environment before knowing which reward will define its eventual task. This paper studies that reward-free setting with linear function approximation. It aims to obtain efficient learning guarantees under assumptions closer to those used for learning from an already collected batch of data.

The analysis assumes low inherent Bellman error and that the linear representation space is sufficiently explorable. The first condition concerns how well the representation supports the value-iteration updates; the second ensures that exploration can gather the information needed within that space. Under these conditions, the authors establish strong probably approximately correct guarantees for learning a near-optimal value function.

The paper provides a computationally tractable algorithm whose exploration supports a near-optimal policy for any linear reward revealed after learning. If rewards must themselves be estimated from the exploration samples, the resulting policy retains guarantees of the same order. This connects reusable, reward-independent exploration with later task solving while keeping the representation and explorability assumptions explicit.
summary.tldr: Reward-free exploration can support near-optimal policies for later linear rewards under low Bellman error and sufficient explorability.

title: Provably Efficient Reward-Agnostic Navigation with Linear Value Iteration

abstract: Prototype-driven text generation uses non-parametric models that first choose from a library of sentence "prototypes" and then modify the prototype to generate the output text. While effective, these methods are inefficient at test time as a result of needing to store and index the entire training corpus. Further, existing methods often require heuristics to identify which prototypes to reference at training time. In this paper, we propose a novel generative model that automatically learns a sparse prototype support set that, nonetheless, achieves strong language modeling performance. This is achieved by (1) imposing a sparsity-inducing prior on the prototype selection distribution, and (2) utilizing amortized variational inference to learn a prototype retrieval function. In experiments, our model outperforms previous prototype-driven language models while achieving up to a 1000x memory reduction, as well as a 1000x speed-up at test time. More interestingly, we show that the learned prototypes are able to capture semantics and syntax at different granularity as we vary the sparsity of prototype selection, and that certain sentence attributes can be controlled by specifying the prototype for generation.

paragraphs: Prototype-driven text generation first retrieves an example sentence and then modifies it to produce new text. Keeping and indexing the entire training corpus makes this approach expensive at generation time. Existing methods can also rely on hand-designed rules to decide which examples should act as prototypes during training.

The proposed generative model learns a small support set of prototypes automatically. A sparsity-inducing prior encourages the selection distribution to concentrate on fewer examples, while amortized variational inference learns the retrieval function. Together, these components address both the size of the stored prototype library and the way prototypes are selected.

Experiments show better language modeling performance than earlier prototype-driven models, alongside memory reductions and test-time speedups reaching 1,000-fold. Changing the degree of sparsity also changes the granularity of semantic and syntactic information captured by the prototypes. Specifying a prototype can control certain sentence attributes. Thus, the learned library offers both computational savings and a handle on some properties of generated text.
summary.tldr: A learned sparse prototype library improves prototype-based language modeling while sharply reducing storage and generation costs.

title: Learning Sparse Prototypes for Text Generation

abstract: Several machine learning applications involve the optimization of higher-order derivatives (e.g., gradients of gradients) during training, which can be expensive with respect to memory and computation even with automatic differentiation. As a typical example in generative modeling, score matching~(SM) involves the optimization of the trace of a Hessian. To improve computing efficiency, we rewrite the SM objective and its variants in terms of directional derivatives, and present a generic strategy to efficiently approximate any-order directional derivative with finite difference~(FD). Our approximation only involves function evaluations, which can be executed in parallel, and no gradient computations. Thus, it reduces the total computational cost while also improving numerical stability. We provide two instantiations by reformulating variants of SM objectives into the FD forms. Empirically, we demonstrate that our methods produce results comparable to the gradient-based counterparts while being much more computationally efficient.

paragraphs: Some training objectives require derivatives of derivatives, which can consume substantial computation and memory even with automatic differentiation. Score matching provides an example in generative modeling because its objective involves the trace of a Hessian. This paper seeks a less expensive way to handle those derivative-dependent quantities during learning.

The authors rewrite score matching and related objectives using directional derivatives. They then introduce a general finite-difference strategy for approximating directional derivatives of any order. The approximation uses function evaluations that can run in parallel, without computing gradients for the derivative approximation itself. This reformulation reduces the computational burden and is also reported to improve numerical stability.

The paper gives two concrete versions by converting score-matching variants into finite-difference objectives. Empirical results show outcomes comparable to the corresponding gradient-based approaches with substantially greater computational efficiency. The significance is that an expensive mathematical ingredient can be approximated through simpler evaluations while preserving comparable generative-modeling results in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Finite-difference reformulations make score-matching training substantially more efficient while producing comparable empirical results.

title: Efficient Learning of Generative Models via Finite-Difference Score Matching

abstract: In offline reinforcement learning (RL), the goal is to learn a highly rewarding policy based solely on a dataset of historical interactions with the environment. This serves as an extreme test for an agent's ability to effectively use historical data which is known to be critical for efficient RL. Prior work in offline RL has been confined almost exclusively to model-free RL approaches. In this work, we present MOReL, an algorithmic framework for model-based offline RL. This framework consists of two steps: (a) learning a pessimistic MDP using the offline dataset; (b) learning a near-optimal policy in this pessimistic MDP. The design of the pessimistic MDP is such that for any policy, the performance in the real environment is approximately lower-bounded by the performance in the pessimistic MDP. This enables the pessimistic MDP to serve as a good surrogate for purposes of policy evaluation and learning. Theoretically, we show that MOReL is minimax optimal (up to log factors) for offline RL. Empirically, MOReL matches or exceeds state-of-the-art results on widely used offline RL benchmarks. Overall, the modular design of MOReL enables translating advances in its components (for e.g., in model learning, planning etc.) to improvements in offline RL.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning seeks a rewarding policy using only previously collected interactions. MOReL approaches this through a learned model of the environment. It first constructs a pessimistic Markov decision process from the historical dataset and then learns a near-optimal policy inside that constructed decision process.

The pessimism has a specific theoretical role: for any policy, its performance in the constructed model approximately lower-bounds its performance in the real environment. The model therefore provides a conservative surrogate for evaluating and learning policies. Optimizing within it is motivated by the relationship between modeled performance and real performance, rather than simply trusting a learned environment model without such a relationship.

The authors prove minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors and report results matching or exceeding state-of-the-art performance on widely used offline benchmarks. The framework is modular, separating model construction from policy learning. That organization allows improvements in components such as model learning or planning to contribute to improvements in offline reinforcement learning within the same overall approach.
summary.tldr: MOReL learns policies in a pessimistic environment model and achieves minimax-optimal offline learning up to logarithmic factors.

title: MOReL: Model-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in episodic Markov decision processes with unknown transition kernels, where the goal is to optimize the total reward under the risk measure of exponential utility. We propose two provably efficient model-free algorithms, Risk-Sensitive Value Iteration (RSVI) and Risk-Sensitive Q-learning (RSQ). These algorithms implement a form of risk-sensitive optimism in the face of uncertainty, which adapts to both risk-seeking and risk-averse modes of exploration. We prove that RSVI attains an \ensuremath{\tilde{O}\big(\lambda(|\beta| H^2) \cdot \sqrt{H^{3} S^{2}AT} \big)}$ regret, while RSQ attains an $\ensuremath{\tilde{O}\big(\lambda(|\beta| H^2) \cdot \sqrt{H^{4} SAT} \big)}$ regret, where $\lambda(u) = (e^{3u}-1)/u$ for $u>0$. In the above, $\beta$ is the risk parameter of the exponential utility function, $S$ the number of states, $A$ the number of actions, $T$ the total number of timesteps, and $H$ the episode length. On the flip side, we establish a regret lower bound showing that the exponential dependence on $|\beta|$ and $H$ is unavoidable for any algorithm with an $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret (even when the risk objective is on the same scale as the original reward), thus certifying the near-optimality of the proposed algorithms. Our results demonstrate that incorporating risk awareness into reinforcement learning necessitates an exponential cost in $|\beta|$ and $H$, which quantifies the fundamental tradeoff between risk sensitivity (related to aleatoric uncertainty) and sample efficiency (related to epistemic uncertainty). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first regret analysis of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning with the exponential utility.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic reinforcement learning when transition probabilities are unknown and the objective evaluates rewards through exponential utility. A risk parameter controls whether the learner is risk-seeking or risk-averse. The authors introduce two model-free algorithms, Risk-Sensitive Value Iteration and Risk-Sensitive Q-learning, that adapt optimistic exploration to these different attitudes toward risk.

Their regret guarantees grow roughly with the square root of total interaction time, alongside factors involving states, actions, episode length, and risk sensitivity. A central feature is an exponential cost involving the magnitude of the risk parameter and the episode length. The authors also prove a lower bound: exponential dependence on these quantities is unavoidable for algorithms with square-root-time regret in the studied setting.

That lower bound supports the claimed near-optimality of the algorithms' risk-sample tradeoff, rather than treating the exponential factor as merely an implementation weakness. It persists even when the risk objective is scaled comparably to the original reward. The results distinguish sensitivity to randomness in outcomes from uncertainty caused by limited experience, and quantify how demanding stronger risk awareness can be for sample-efficient learning.
summary.tldr: Two risk-sensitive learning algorithms achieve regret guarantees whose exponential risk-related cost is shown to be unavoidable for square-root-time regret.

title: Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning: Near-Optimal Risk-Sample Tradeoff in Regret

abstract: Works on lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH) and single-shot network pruning (SNIP) have raised a lot of attention currently on post-training pruning (iterative magnitude pruning), and before-training pruning (pruning at initialization). The former method suffers from an extremely large computation cost and the latter usually struggles with insufficient performance. In comparison, during-training pruning, a class of pruning methods that simultaneously enjoys the training/inference efficiency and the comparable performance, temporarily, has been less explored. To better understand during-training pruning, we quantitatively study the effect of pruning throughout training from the perspective of pruning plasticity (the ability of the pruned networks to recover the original performance). Pruning plasticity can help explain several other empirical observations about neural network pruning in literature. We further find that pruning plasticity can be substantially improved by injecting a brain-inspired mechanism called neuroregeneration, i.e., to regenerate the same number of connections as pruned. We design a novel gradual magnitude pruning (GMP) method, named gradual pruning with zero-cost neuroregeneration (GraNet), that advances state of the art. Perhaps most impressively, its sparse-to-sparse version for the first time boosts the sparse-to-sparse training performance over various dense-to-sparse methods with ResNet-50 on ImageNet without extending the training time. We release all codes in https://github.com/Shiweiliuiiiiiii/GraNet.

paragraphs: Pruning removes neural network connections to reduce computation, but its timing affects both cost and performance. This paper focuses on pruning during training and studies pruning plasticity: how well a network can recover its original performance after connections are removed. The authors use this perspective to explain several empirical observations about pruning.

They find that recovery can be substantially improved through neuroregeneration, which restores the same number of connections as were pruned. This mechanism is incorporated into GraNet, a gradual magnitude pruning method. The key idea is to improve the network's ability to adapt after pruning by allowing connections to be regenerated during training.

The authors report that GraNet advances the state of the art. In particular, its sparse-to-sparse version outperforms various dense-to-sparse methods for ResNet-50 on ImageNet without increasing training time. That result supports the value of regeneration when training begins with a sparse network, while the broader analysis identifies recovery capacity as a useful way to understand the effects of pruning throughout training.
summary.tldr: GraNet improves recovery from pruning by regenerating connections, achieving strong sparse-training results without extending the reported training time.

title: Sparse Training via Boosting Pruning Plasticity with Neuroregeneration

abstract: The standard tools of causal inference have been developed to answer simple causal queries which can be easily formalized as a small number of statistical estimands in the context of a particular structural causal model (SCM); however, scientific theories often make diffuse predictions about a large number of causal variables. This article proposes a framework for parameterizing such complex causal queries as the maximum difference in causal effects associated with two sets of causal variables that have a researcher specified probability of occurring. We term this estimand the Maximum Causal Set Effect (MCSE) and develop an estimator for it that is asymptotically consistent and conservative in finite samples under assumptions that are standard in the causal inference literature. This estimator is also asymptotically normal and amenable to the non-parametric bootstrap, facilitating classical statistical inference about this novel estimand. We compare this estimator to more common latent variable approaches and find that it can uncover larger causal effects in both real world and simulated data.

paragraphs: Scientific theories can predict patterns across many causal variables, making them difficult to express through a few conventional causal quantities. This paper introduces the Maximum Causal Set Effect, or MCSE, to turn these broader questions into an explicit statistical target that can be estimated and tested.

MCSE asks for the largest difference in causal effects associated with two sets of causal variables, with the probability of those sets occurring specified by the researcher. That probability requirement is part of how the query is defined. It gives the framework a way to express a broad causal comparison while retaining a concrete quantity for statistical analysis.

Under assumptions described as standard in causal inference, the proposed estimator is consistent as sample size grows and conservative in finite samples. It also has asymptotic normality and supports the nonparametric bootstrap, enabling classical inference. Comparisons with latent-variable approaches uncover larger causal effects in real and simulated data, demonstrating how the chosen formulation can reveal effects that those alternatives capture less strongly.
summary.tldr: MCSE formalizes broad causal questions as maximum effect differences between probability-constrained sets and provides an estimator with conditional statistical guarantees.

title: Answering Complex Causal Queries With the Maximum Causal Set Effect

abstract: We study linear and kernel classification in the streaming model. For linear classification, we improve upon the algorithm of (Tai, et al. 2018), which solves the $\ell_1$ point query problem on the optimal weight vector $w_* \in \mathbb{R}^d$ in sublinear space. We first give an algorithm solving the more difficult $\ell_2$ point query problem on $w_*$, also in sublinear space. We also give an algorithm which solves the $\ell_2$ heavy hitter problem on $w_*$, in sublinear space and running time. Finally, we give an algorithm which can $\textit{deterministically}$ solve the $\ell_1$ point query problem on $w_*$, with sublinear space improving upon that of (Tai, et al. 2018). For kernel classification, if $w_* \in \mathbb{R}^{d^p}$ is the optimal weight vector classifying points in the stream according to their $p^{th}$-degree polynomial kernel, then we give an algorithm solving the $\ell_2$ point query problem on $w_*$ in $\text{poly}(\frac{p \log d}{\varepsilon})$ space, and an algorithm solving the $\ell_2$ heavy hitter problem in $\text{poly}(\frac{p \log d}{\varepsilon})$ space and running time. Note that our space and running time are polynomial in $p$, making our algorithms well-suited to high-degree polynomial kernels and the Gaussian kernel (approximated by the polynomial kernel of degree $p = \Theta(\log T)$).

We first give an algorithm solving the more difficult $\ell_2$ point query problem on $w_*$, also in sublinear space. We also give an algorithm which solves the $\ell_2$ heavy hitter problem on $w_*$, in sublinear space and running time. Finally, we give an algorithm which can $\textit{deterministically}$ solve the $\ell_1$ point query problem on $w_*$, with sublinear space improving upon that of (Tai, et al. 2018). For kernel classification, if $w_* \in \mathbb{R}^{d^p}$ is the optimal weight vector classifying points in the stream according to their $p^{th}$-degree polynomial kernel, then we give an algorithm solving the $\ell_2$ point query problem on $w_*$ in $\text{poly}(\frac{p \log d}{\varepsilon})$ space, and an algorithm solving the $\ell_2$ heavy hitter problem in $\text{poly}(\frac{p \log d}{\varepsilon})$ space and running time. Note that our space and running time are polynomial in $p$, making our algorithms well-suited to high-degree polynomial kernels and the Gaussian kernel (approximated by the polynomial kernel of degree $p = \Theta(\log T)$).

paragraphs: Streaming classification must process incoming data with limited memory. This paper focuses on obtaining information about the optimal classifier's weight vector without storing that full vector. Its targets are point queries, which estimate individual coordinates, and heavy-hitter queries, which identify coordinates with large contributions under the specified norm.

For linear classification, the authors provide sublinear-space algorithms for the more demanding l2 point-query problem and sublinear-space, sublinear-time algorithms for l2 heavy hitters. They also give a deterministic l1 point-query algorithm with improved space requirements. These are distinct guarantees for accessing important information about the optimal weights under restricted resources.

For polynomial kernels, the implicit weight vector can have dimension d to the power p. The proposed query algorithms instead use space polynomial in p log d divided by the accuracy parameter, with a corresponding time bound for heavy hitters. Polynomial dependence on degree makes the approach suitable for high-degree kernels and for the stated polynomial approximation to a Gaussian kernel.
summary.tldr: New streaming algorithms estimate classifier weights and identify large coordinates using sublinear resources, including for high-dimensional polynomial-kernel representations.

title: Linear and Kernel Classification in the Streaming Model: Improved Bounds for Heavy Hitters

abstract: We provide the first coreset for clustering points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that have multiple missing values (coordinates). Previous coreset constructions only allow one missing coordinate. The challenge in this setting is that objective functions, like \kMeans, are evaluated only on the set of available (non-missing) coordinates, which varies across points. Recall that an $\epsilon$-coreset of a large dataset is a small proxy, usually a reweighted subset of points, that $(1+\epsilon)$-approximates the clustering objective for every possible center set.Our coresets for $k$-Means and $k$-Median clustering have size $(jk)^{O(\min(j,k))} (\epsilon^{-1} d \log n)^2$, where $n$ is the number of data points, $d$ is the dimension and $j$ is the maximum number of missing coordinates for each data point. We further design an algorithm to construct these coresets in near-linear time, and consequently improve a recent quadratic-time PTAS for $k$-Means with missing values [Eiben et al., SODA 2021] to near-linear time.We validate our coreset construction, which is based on importance sampling and is easy to implement, on various real data sets. Our coreset exhibits a flexible tradeoff between coreset size and accuracy, and generally outperforms the uniform-sampling baseline. Furthermore, it significantly speeds up a Lloyd's-style heuristic for $k$-Means with missing values.

paragraphs: Clustering incomplete data is difficult because each point may have a different set of observed coordinates. Distances and clustering costs are evaluated only where values are available, so the information used varies from point to point. This paper constructs coresets for data with multiple missing coordinates, extending earlier constructions that allowed only one.

A coreset is a small proxy dataset, typically a weighted subset, that approximately preserves the clustering objective for every possible choice of centers. The authors provide such constructions for both k-means and k-median. Their size depends on accuracy, dimension, dataset size, the number of clusters, and the maximum number of missing coordinates per point.

The importance-sampling construction runs in near-linear time. It also turns an existing quadratic-time approximation scheme for k-means with missing values into a near-linear-time method. On real datasets, the coresets offer a size-versus-accuracy trade-off, generally beat uniform sampling, and substantially accelerate a Lloyd-style clustering heuristic. These results connect the formal approximation guarantee with practical computational savings.
summary.tldr: Small weighted summaries preserve clustering costs for data with multiple missing coordinates and enable faster clustering.

title: Coresets for Clustering with Missing Values

abstract: The Dynamic Pickup and Delivery Problem (DPDP) is an essential problem in the logistics domain, which is NP-hard. The objective is to dynamically schedule vehicles among multiple sites to serve the online generated orders such that the overall transportation cost could be minimized. The critical challenge of DPDP is the orders are not known a priori, i.e., the orders are dynamically generated in real-time. To address this problem, existing methods partition the overall DPDP into fixed-size sub-problems by caching online generated orders and solve each sub-problem, or on this basis to utilize the predicted future orders to optimize each sub-problem further. However, the solution quality and efficiency of these methods are unsatisfactory, especially when the problem scale is very large. In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical optimization framework to better solve large-scale DPDPs. Specifically, we design an upper-level agent to dynamically partition the DPDP into a series of sub-problems with different scales to optimize vehicles routes towards globally better solutions. Besides, a lower-level agent is designed to efficiently solve each sub-problem by incorporating the strengths of classical operational research-based methods with reinforcement learning-based policies. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed framework, real historical data is collected from the order dispatching system of Huawei Supply Chain Business Unit and used to build a functional simulator. Extensive offline simulation and online testing conducted on the industrial order dispatching system justify the superior performance of our framework over existing baselines.

paragraphs: Dynamic pickup and delivery requires scheduling vehicles while new orders continue to arrive. The objective is to keep transportation costs low, but planners cannot know all future requests in advance. Existing approaches collect incoming orders into fixed-size groups and solve each group, sometimes using predictions of future demand. The paper addresses the quality and efficiency difficulties these approaches face at large scales.

The proposed framework divides the work between two agents. An upper-level agent decides how to partition the ongoing scheduling problem into subproblems of different sizes. This makes the grouping itself part of the optimization, with the aim of improving routes across the larger problem. A lower-level agent solves each resulting subproblem by combining classical operations research methods with reinforcement learning policies.

The authors build a simulator from historical orders collected from Huawei's supply chain dispatching system. They evaluate the framework through offline simulations and online tests in the industrial system, reporting better performance than existing baselines. The findings support learning both how to divide the scheduling workload and how to solve the resulting pieces.
summary.tldr: A two-level learning framework dynamically groups delivery orders and solves the resulting routing problems, outperforming baselines in industrial simulations and online tests.

title: A Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning Based Optimization Framework for Large-scale Dynamic Pickup and Delivery Problems

abstract: Despite the predominant use of first-order methods for training deep learning models, second-order methods, and in particular, natural gradient methods, remain of interest because of their potential for accelerating training through the use of curvature information. Several methods with non-diagonal preconditioning matrices, including KFAC, Shampoo, and K-BFGS, have been proposed and shown to be effective. Based on the so-called tensor normal (TN) distribution, we propose and analyze a brand new approximate natural gradient method, Tensor Normal Training (TNT), which like Shampoo, only requires knowledge of the shape of the training parameters. By approximating the probabilistically based Fisher matrix, as opposed to the empirical Fisher matrix, our method uses the block-wise covariance of the sampling based gradient as the pre-conditioning matrix. Moreover, the assumption that the sampling-based (tensor) gradient follows a TN distribution, ensures that its covariance has a Kronecker separable structure, which leads to a tractable approximation to the Fisher matrix. Consequently, TNT's memory requirements and per-iteration computational costs are only slightly higher than those for first-order methods. In our experiments, TNT exhibited superior optimization performance to state-of-the-art first-order methods, and comparable optimization performance to the state-of-the-art second-order methods KFAC and Shampoo. Moreover, TNT demonstrated its ability to generalize as well as first-order methods, while using fewer epochs.

paragraphs: Natural gradient methods use curvature information to guide training, offering a possible route to faster optimization than first-order methods. Their computational demands make approximations important. This paper introduces Tensor Normal Training, or TNT, an approximate natural gradient method that requires knowledge of the shape of the model's training parameters.

TNT approximates the probabilistic Fisher matrix using blockwise covariance of sampling-based gradients. Its key assumption is that these tensor-shaped gradients follow a tensor normal distribution. It also generalizes as well as first-order methods while using fewer epochs. These findings support the practical promise of its structured curvature approximation, with the tensor normal assumption providing the mechanism that keeps the calculation manageable.
summary.tldr: TNT uses a tensor normal gradient assumption to make natural-gradient training tractable, achieving strong optimization with modest per-iteration overhead.

title: Tensor Normal Training for Deep Learning Models

abstract: We propose a toolkit for developing and comparing reinforcement learning (RL)-based traffic signal controllers. The toolkit includes implementation of state-of-the-art deep-RL algorithms for signal control along with benchmark control problems that are based on realistic traffic scenarios. Importantly, the toolkit allows a first-of-its-kind comparison between state-of-the-art RL-based signal controllers while providing benchmarks for future comparisons. Consequently, we compare and report the relative performance of current RL algorithms. The experimental results suggest that previous algorithms are not robust to varying sensing assumptions and non-stylized intersection layouts. When more realistic signal layouts and advanced sensing capabilities are assumed, a distributed deep-Q learning approach is shown to outperform previously reported state-of-the-art algorithms in many cases.

paragraphs: Comparing reinforcement learning traffic-signal controllers requires shared control problems and implementations. This paper introduces a toolkit that supplies both, combining implementations of leading deep reinforcement learning methods with benchmark problems based on realistic traffic scenarios. It establishes a common setting for comparing existing controllers and evaluating future proposals.

Using the toolkit, the authors examine how algorithms perform when sensing assumptions and intersection layouts vary. Their experiments suggest that earlier methods are not robust to those changes, particularly when intersections depart from simplified layouts. This matters because the information available to a controller and the structure of its signals are part of the control problem itself.

Under more realistic signal layouts and advanced sensing assumptions, a distributed deep-Q learning approach outperforms previously reported leading algorithms in many cases. The result is conditional on those settings and does not establish a universally best controller. Together, the toolkit and comparisons show why traffic-control evaluations should make sensing and layout assumptions explicit when interpreting relative performance.
summary.tldr: A shared traffic-control toolkit shows that reinforcement learning rankings depend on sensing assumptions and intersection layouts.

title: Reinforcement Learning Benchmarks for Traffic Signal Control

abstract: We present Second Thoughts, a new learning paradigm that enables language models (LMs) to re-align with human values. By modeling the chain-of-edits between value-unaligned and value-aligned text, with LM fine-tuning and additional refinement through reinforcement learning, Second Thoughts not only achieves superior performance in three value alignment benchmark datasets but also shows strong human-value transfer learning ability in few-shot scenarios. The generated editing steps also offer better interpretability and ease for interactive error correction. Extensive human evaluations further confirm its effectiveness.

The generated editing steps also offer better interpretability and ease for interactive error correction. Extensive human evaluations further confirm its effectiveness.

paragraphs: Second Thoughts treats alignment with human values as a process of revising text. The method models a chain of edits connecting text that is unaligned with those values to text that is aligned. This makes the sequence of changes part of what the language model learns, giving the approach an explicit revision structure.

Training combines language-model fine-tuning with further refinement through reinforcement learning. The learned editing steps also provide something people can inspect and correct interactively. Their value is therefore twofold: they support producing revised text and offer a more interpretable route through the changes that lead to it.

The authors report superior performance on three value-alignment benchmarks and strong transfer in few-shot scenarios, where only a small number of examples are available. Extensive human evaluations further support the method's effectiveness. These findings provide evidence for learning alignment through edit sequences in the evaluated settings. The reported transfer result also suggests that the learned revision process can help when examples for a new alignment setting are scarce.
summary.tldr: Second Thoughts learns edit sequences that improve value alignment while making revisions easier to interpret and correct interactively.

title: Second Thoughts are Best: Learning to Re-Align With Human Values from Text Edits

abstract: We propose a novel reduction-to-binary (R2B) approach that enforces demographic parity for multiclass classification with non-binary sensitive attributes via a reduction to a sequence of binary debiasing tasks. We prove that R2B satisfies optimality and bias guarantees and demonstrate empirically that it can lead to an improvement over two baselines: (1) treating multiclass problems as multi-label by debiasing labels independently and (2) transforming the features instead of the labels. Surprisingly, we also demonstrate that independent label debiasing yields competitive results in most (but not all) settings. We validate these conclusions on synthetic and real-world datasets from social science, computer vision, and healthcare.

We validate these conclusions on synthetic and real-world datasets from social science, computer vision, and healthcare.

paragraphs: Debiasing a classification dataset becomes more complicated when there are several possible classes and sensitive attributes can take more than two values. This paper addresses that setting through demographic parity, a fairness requirement concerning differences in class outcomes across sensitive groups. Its goal is to handle this richer setting using a sequence of binary debiasing tasks.

The proposed reduction-to-binary method, R2B, connects those simpler tasks into a multiclass debiasing procedure. The authors prove optimality and bias guarantees for the approach. They also compare it with two alternatives: debiasing each label independently as though the problem were multi-label, and modifying input features rather than labels.

Experiments on synthetic data and datasets from social science, computer vision, and healthcare show that R2B can improve on these alternatives. However, the results also reveal that independently debiasing labels is competitive in most tested settings, though not all. The findings therefore support a principled reduction while preserving a useful practical distinction: a simpler approach can work well, but its competitiveness does not hold across every evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: R2B reduces multiclass demographic-parity debiasing to binary tasks, with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements in some settings.

title: A Reduction to Binary Approach for Debiasing Multiclass Datasets

abstract: Poisoning-based backdoor attacks are serious threat for training deep models on data from untrustworthy sources. Given a backdoored model, we observe that the feature representations of poisoned samples with trigger are more sensitive to transformations than those of clean samples. It inspires us to design a simple sensitivity metric, called feature consistency towards transformations (FCT), to distinguish poisoned samples from clean samples in the untrustworthy training set. Moreover, we propose two effective backdoor defense methods. Built upon a sample-distinguishment module utilizing the FCT metric, the first method trains a secure model from scratch using a two-stage secure training module. And the second method removes backdoor from a backdoored model with a backdoor removal module which alternatively unlearns the distinguished poisoned samples and relearns the distinguished clean samples. Extensive results on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior defense performance against eight types of backdoor attacks, to state-of-the-art backdoor defenses. Codes are available at: https://github.com/SCLBD/Effective_backdoor_defense.

The paper starts from an observation about an already backdoored network: triggered examples have internal feature representations that change more under transformations than those of clean examples. That difference offers a way to distinguish suspicious training samples.

The authors turn the observation into a metric called feature consistency towards transformations, or FCT. A sample-distinguishing module uses this metric to separate likely poisoned and clean data. The paper then builds two defenses around that shared component, allowing the same signal to support different starting situations.

The first defense trains a model from scratch through a two-stage secure-training procedure. The second repairs an existing backdoored model by alternating between unlearning identified poisoned samples and relearning identified clean samples. Experiments on three benchmark datasets and eight attack types report better defense performance than state-of-the-art alternatives. The results support transformation sensitivity as a useful empirical signal for both training and repair.
summary.tldr: Feature sensitivity to transformations helps identify poisoned examples and supports defenses for both fresh training and backdoor removal.

title: Effective Backdoor Defense by Exploiting Sensitivity of Poisoned Samples

abstract: Symbolic regression, the task of predicting the mathematical expression of a function from the observation of its values, is a difficult task which usually involves a two-step procedure: predicting the "skeleton" of the expression up to the choice of numerical constants, then fitting the constants by optimizing a non-convex loss function. The dominant approach is genetic programming, which evolves candidates by iterating this subroutine a large number of times. Neural networks have recently been tasked to predict the correct skeleton in a single try, but remain much less powerful.In this paper, we challenge this two-step procedure, and task a Transformer to directly predict the full mathematical expression, constants included. One can subsequently refine the predicted constants by feeding them to the non-convex optimizer as an informed initialization. We present ablations to show that this end-to-end approach yields better results, sometimes even without the refinement step. We evaluate our model on problems from the SRBench benchmark and show that our model approaches the performance of state-of-the-art genetic programming with several orders of magnitude faster inference.

Neural networks have recently been tasked to predict the correct skeleton in a single try, but remain much less powerful.In this paper, we challenge this two-step procedure, and task a Transformer to directly predict the full mathematical expression, constants included. paragraphs: Symbolic regression tries to recover a mathematical expression from observed function values. A common procedure first chooses the expression's structure and then fits its numerical constants through nonconvex optimization. Genetic programming repeats this process across evolving candidates, while earlier neural approaches predict an expression structure directly but remain less powerful.

This paper asks a Transformer to predict the complete expression, including its constants, in one step. The predicted constants can then serve as an informed starting point for optional numerical refinement. This changes the model's responsibility: it learns to propose both the form of the equation and the numbers needed to make that equation useful.

Ablation experiments support the end-to-end approach, with improvements sometimes appearing even without refinement. On problems from SRBench, the model approaches the performance of leading genetic-programming methods while providing inference several orders of magnitude faster. The stated result combines competitive equation recovery with much faster prediction, without claiming that the Transformer consistently surpasses genetic programming in accuracy.
summary.tldr: A Transformer predicts complete equations with constants, approaching leading genetic-programming performance with much faster inference.

title: End-to-end Symbolic Regression with Transformers

abstract: Video action detection requires annotations at every frame, which drastically increases the labeling cost. In this work, we focus on efficient labeling of videos for action detection to minimize this cost. We propose active sparse labeling (ASL), a novel active learning strategy for video action detection. Sparse labeling will reduce the annotation cost but poses two main challenges; 1) how to estimate the utility of annotating a single frame for action detection as detection is performed at video level?, and 2) how these sparse labels can be used for action detection which require annotations on all the frames? This work attempts to address these challenges within a simple active learning framework. For the first challenge, we propose a novel frame-level scoring mechanism aimed at selecting most informative frames in a video. Next, we introduce a novel loss formulation which enables training of action detection model with these sparsely selected frames. We evaluate the proposed approach on two different action detection benchmark datasets, UCF-101-24 and J-HMDB-21, and observed that active sparse labeling can be very effective in saving annotation costs. We demonstrate that the proposed approach performs better than random selection, outperforming all other baselines, with performance comparable to supervised approach using merely 10% annotations.

paragraphs: Video action detection normally requires annotations throughout a video, making labeling expensive. This paper investigates whether carefully selected frames can supply enough supervision to train an effective detector. The central difficulty is that annotation decisions happen at the frame level, while the detection task operates over videos.

The proposed active sparse labeling framework addresses both selection and training. A frame-level scoring mechanism estimates which frames would be most informative to annotate. A new loss formulation then allows the action detector to learn from these sparse annotations. These two components work together: selecting useful frames is valuable only if the training procedure can make effective use of the incomplete labels.

On UCF-101-24 and J-HMDB-21, the authors report results better than random selection and all other evaluated baselines. Using only 10% of annotations, performance is comparable to the supervised approach. The findings show that, in these evaluations, annotation value varies enough across frames for selective labeling to substantially reduce the amount of human annotation needed.
summary.tldr: Active sparse labeling selects informative video frames and trains on their labels, reaching comparable supervised performance with 10% of annotations in the reported evaluations.

title: Are all Frames Equal? Active Sparse Labeling for Video Action Detection

abstract: Many networked systems such as electric networks, the brain, and social networks of opinion dynamics are known to obey conservation laws. Examples of this phenomenon include the Kirchoff laws in electric networks and opinion consensus in social networks. Conservation laws in networked systems are modeled as balance equations of the form $X = B^\ast Y$, where the sparsity pattern of $B^\ast \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ captures the connectivity of the network on $p$ nodes, and $Y, X \in \mathbb{R}^p$ are vectors of ''potentials'' and ''injected flows'' at the nodes respectively. The node potentials $Y$ cause flows across edges which aim to balance out the potential difference, and the flows $X$ injected at the nodes are extraneous to the network dynamics. In several practical systems, the network structure is often unknown and needs to be estimated from data to facilitate modeling, management, and control. To this end, one has access to samples of the node potentials $Y$, but only the statistics of the node injections $X$. Motivated by this important problem, we study the estimation of the sparsity structure of the matrix $B^\ast$ from $n$ samples of $Y$ under the assumption that the node injections $X$ follow a Gaussian distribution with a known covariance $\Sigma_X$. We propose a new $\ell_{1}$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for tackling this problem in the high-dimensional regime where the size of the network may be vastly larger than the number of samples $n$. We show that this optimization problem is convex in the objective and admits a unique solution. Under a new mutual incoherence condition, we establish sufficient conditions on the triple $(n,p,d)$ for which exact sparsity recovery of $B^\ast$ is possible with high probability; $d$ is the degree of the underlying graph. We also establish guarantees for the recovery of $B^\ast$ in the element-wise maximum, Frobenius, and operator norms. Finally, we complement these theoretical results with experimental validation of the performance of the proposed estimator on synthetic and real-world data.

We propose a new $\ell_{1}$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for tackling this problem in the high-dimensional regime where the size of the network may be vastly larger than the number of samples $n$. We show that this optimization problem is convex in the objective and admits a unique solution. Under a new mutual incoherence condition, we establish sufficient conditions on the triple $(n,p,d)$ for which exact sparsity recovery of $B^\ast$ is possible with high probability; $d$ is the degree of the underlying graph. We also establish guarantees for the recovery of $B^\ast$ in the element-wise maximum, Frobenius, and operator norms. Finally, we complement these theoretical results with experimental validation of the performance of the proposed estimator on synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a network’s connections from measurements governed by a conservation law. In its balance equation, a matrix maps node potentials to externally injected flows, and the matrix’s nonzero pattern describes connectivity. The available data consist of potential measurements and statistical information about injections, rather than complete observations of both.

The method assumes Gaussian injections with known covariance and estimates the connectivity matrix using maximum likelihood with an L1 penalty that encourages sparsity. It targets high-dimensional settings where the network can contain far more nodes than there are observed samples. The authors show that the optimization has a convex objective and a unique solution.

Under a mutual incoherence condition, they establish sufficient relationships among sample count, network size, and graph degree for exact connection recovery with high probability. They also bound matrix estimation error under several norms. Experiments on synthetic and real data complement these guarantees, connecting the statistical analysis to practical recovery of networks governed by balance equations.
summary.tldr: A sparse likelihood estimator recovers conservation-governed network structure with conditional theoretical guarantees and experimental validation.

title: Learning the Structure of Large Networked Systems Obeying Conservation Laws

abstract: We propose Differentiable Temporal Logic (DTL), a model-agnostic framework that introduces temporal constraints to deep networks. DTL treats the outputs of a network as a truth assignment of a temporal logic formula, and computes a temporal logic loss reflecting the consistency between the output and the constraints. We propose a comprehensive set of constraints, which are implicit in data annotations, and incorporate them with deep networks via DTL. We evaluate the effectiveness of DTL on the temporal action segmentation task and observe improved performance and reduced logical errors in the output of different task models. Furthermore, we provide an extensive analysis to visualize the desirable effects of DTL.

paragraphs: Temporal action segmentation assigns action labels over time. A useful prediction must capture both the actions present and their temporal relationships. This paper introduces Differentiable Temporal Logic, or DTL, as a way to incorporate temporal constraints into deep networks through their training loss.

DTL interprets a network's outputs as truth assignments for a temporal logic formula. It then computes a loss measuring how well those outputs agree with the specified constraints. The authors develop a collection of constraints that are implicit in existing annotations and incorporate them through this mechanism. Because the framework is model-agnostic, the same general approach can be used with different task models.

In temporal action segmentation experiments, adding DTL improves performance and reduces logical errors across the evaluated models. The paper also provides visual analysis of the effects on predictions. These findings suggest that temporal relationships contained in annotations can serve as useful training information beyond individual action labels. The contribution is a differentiable connection between explicit temporal rules and the output behavior of learned models.
summary.tldr: Differentiable Temporal Logic turns temporal constraints into a training loss that improves action segmentation and reduces logical errors.

title: Don't Pour Cereal into Coffee: Differentiable Temporal Logic for Temporal Action Segmentation

abstract: Multi-armed bandit problems provide a framework to identify the optimal intervention over a sequence of repeated experiments. Without additional assumptions, minimax optimal performance (measured by cumulative regret) is well-understood. With access to additional observed variables that d-separate the intervention from the outcome (i.e., they are a d-separator), recent "causal bandit" algorithms provably incur less regret. However, in practice it is desirable to be agnostic to whether observed variables are a d-separator. Ideally, an algorithm should be adaptive; that is, perform nearly as well as an algorithm with oracle knowledge of the presence or absence of a d-separator. In this work, we formalize and study this notion of adaptivity, and provide a novel algorithm that simultaneously achieves (a) optimal regret when a d-separator is observed, improving on classical minimax algorithms, and (b) significantly smaller regret than recent causal bandit algorithms when the observed variables are not a d-separator. Crucially, our algorithm does not require any oracle knowledge of whether a d-separator is observed. We also generalize this adaptivity to other conditions, such as the front-door criterion.

paragraphs: In a bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses interventions and observes their outcomes, trying to avoid losing too much reward while learning which intervention is best. Additional observed variables can improve this process when they form a d-separator between intervention and outcome. The practical difficulty is that a learner may not know whether those variables satisfy the required causal condition.

This paper formalizes adaptivity to that uncertainty. The desired behavior is to approach the performance of a method that already knows whether a d-separator is available. The proposed algorithm uses the observed variables without requiring that advance knowledge, addressing the risk of relying on a causal relationship that does not actually hold.

When a d-separator is observed, the algorithm achieves optimal regret and improves on classical minimax methods. When the variables are not a d-separator, it incurs substantially less regret than recent causal bandit algorithms. The paper also extends its adaptivity framework to conditions including the front-door criterion, broadening the kinds of causal information it can accommodate.
summary.tldr: An adaptive causal bandit algorithm benefits from observed d-separators without needing advance knowledge that they are present.

title: Adaptively Exploiting d-Separators with Causal Bandits

abstract: Neural signals are typical nonstationary data where the functional mapping between neural activities and the intentions (such as the velocity of movements) can occasionally change. Existing studies mostly use a fixed neural decoder, thus suffering from an unstable performance given neural functional changes. We propose a novel evolutionary ensemble framework (EvoEnsemble) to dynamically cope with changes in neural signals by evolving the decoder model accordingly. EvoEnsemble integrates evolutionary computation algorithms in a Bayesian framework where the fitness of models can be sequentially computed with their likelihoods according to the incoming data at each time slot, which enables online tracking of time-varying functions. Two strategies of evolve-at-changes and history-model-archive are designed to further improve efficiency and stability. Experiments with simulations and neural signals demonstrate that EvoEnsemble can track the changes in functions effectively thus improving the accuracy and robustness of neural decoding. The improvement is most significant in neural signals with functional changes.

paragraphs: Neural decoding translates neural activity into quantities such as intended movement velocity. The relationship between activity and intention can change over time, making a fixed decoder unreliable. EvoEnsemble addresses this problem by adapting the decoder as the incoming signal changes, treating the changing functional relationship as something to track online.

The framework combines evolutionary computation with Bayesian modeling. At each time slot, incoming data provide likelihoods used to assess the fitness of candidate models. This supplies an ongoing basis for evolving the decoder ensemble in response to the current mapping between neural signals and intended outputs.

Two additional strategies, evolve-at-changes and history-model-archive, are designed to improve efficiency and stability. Experiments using both simulations and neural signals show that EvoEnsemble can track functional changes effectively, improving decoding accuracy and robustness. The largest improvements occur in neural signals with functional changes, aligning the empirical benefit with the problem the framework was designed to solve. The work therefore supports adaptive model evolution as a response to changing neural decoding relationships.
summary.tldr: EvoEnsemble evolves a Bayesian ensemble online to track changing neural-signal relationships and improve decoding robustness.

title: Tracking Functional Changes in Nonstationary Signals with Evolutionary Ensemble Bayesian Model for Robust Neural Decoding

abstract: While deep reinforcement learning has proven to be successful in solving control tasks, the ``black-box'' nature of an agent has received increasing concerns. We propose a prototype-based post-hoc \emph{policy explainer}, ProtoX, that explains a black-box agent by prototyping the agent's behaviors into scenarios, each represented by a prototypical state. When learning prototypes, ProtoX considers both visual similarity and scenario similarity. The latter is unique to the reinforcement learning context since it explains why the same action is taken in visually different states. To teach ProtoX about visual similarity, we pre-train an encoder using contrastive learning via self-supervised learning to recognize states as similar if they occur close together in time and receive the same action from the black-box agent. We then add an isometry layer to allow ProtoX to adapt scenario similarity to the downstream task. ProtoX is trained via imitation learning using behavior cloning, and thus requires no access to the environment or agent. In addition to explanation fidelity, we design different prototype shaping terms in the objective function to encourage better interpretability. We conduct various experiments to test ProtoX. Results show that ProtoX achieved high fidelity to the original black-box agent while providing meaningful and understandable explanations.

paragraphs: ProtoX explains a trained reinforcement-learning agent by organizing its behavior into scenarios represented by prototype states. The aim is to make an opaque policy understandable through representative situations. A key distinction is between states that look similar and states that play a similar role in the task, since visually different situations can lead to the same action.

The method first trains an encoder with self-supervised contrastive learning. States are treated as similar when they occur close together in time and receive the same action from the original agent. An isometry layer then lets ProtoX adapt scenario similarity to the downstream task, incorporating more than visual resemblance when learning its prototypes.

ProtoX learns through behavior cloning, using imitation learning without requiring access to the environment or agent during this training process. Its objective includes prototype-shaping terms intended to improve interpretability alongside explanation fidelity. Experiments report high fidelity to the original policy and meaningful, understandable explanations. The prototypes therefore provide a behavior-based account of the agent's decisions.
summary.tldr: ProtoX explains a reinforcement-learning policy through representative states that capture both visual resemblance and task-relevant scenario similarity.

title: ProtoX: Explaining a Reinforcement Learning Agent via Prototyping

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial examples, which can produce erroneous predictions by injecting imperceptible perturbations. In this work, we study the transferability of adversarial examples, which is significant due to its threat to real-world applications where model architecture or parameters are usually unknown. Many existing works reveal that the adversarial examples are likely to overfit the surrogate model that they are generated from, limiting its transfer attack performance against different target models. To mitigate the overfitting of the surrogate model, we propose a novel attack method, dubbed reverse adversarial perturbation (RAP). Specifically, instead of minimizing the loss of a single adversarial point, we advocate seeking adversarial example located at a region with unified low loss value, by injecting the worst-case perturbation (the reverse adversarial perturbation) for each step of the optimization procedure. The adversarial attack with RAP is formulated as a min-max bi-level optimization problem. By integrating RAP into the iterative process for attacks, our method can find more stable adversarial examples which are less sensitive to the changes of decision boundary, mitigating the overfitting of the surrogate model. Comprehensive experimental comparisons demonstrate that RAP can significantly boost adversarial transferability. Furthermore, RAP can be naturally combined with many existing black-box attack techniques, to further boost the transferability. When attacking a real-world image recognition system, Google Cloud Vision API, we obtain 22% performance improvement of targeted attacks over the compared method. Our codes are available at https://github.com/SCLBD/Transfer_attack_RAP.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples created against one neural network may fail against another because they exploit details specific to the first model. This paper studies how to improve that transfer, which matters when the eventual target's architecture or parameters are unknown. Its proposed method, reverse adversarial perturbation, aims to reduce overfitting to the surrogate network used to generate the examples.

Instead of optimizing only the attack loss at a single point, RAP seeks a surrounding region with consistently low loss. Each optimization step introduces a worst-case reverse perturbation, producing a two-level min-max problem. The intended result is an adversarial example whose effectiveness is less sensitive to changes in the model's decision boundary.

Experiments show significant improvements in transferability, and RAP can be incorporated into several existing black-box attack techniques for further gains. On the Google Cloud Vision image-recognition system, the authors report a 22% improvement in targeted-attack performance over the compared method. These findings support the idea that stability around an adversarial example can improve its ability to affect a different model.
summary.tldr: Reverse adversarial perturbation improves attack transfer by seeking adversarial examples that remain effective throughout a surrounding region.

title: Boosting the Transferability of Adversarial Attacks with Reverse Adversarial Perturbation

abstract: Most off-policy evaluation methods for contextual bandits have focused on the expected outcome of a policy, which is estimated via methods that at best provide only asymptotic guarantees. However, in many applications, the expectation may not be the best measure of performance as it does not capture the variability of the outcome. In addition, particularly in safety-critical settings, stronger guarantees than asymptotic correctness may be required. To address these limitations, we consider a novel application of conformal prediction to contextual bandits. Given data collected under a behavioral policy, we propose \emph{conformal off-policy prediction} (COPP), which can output reliable predictive intervals for the outcome under a new target policy. We provide theoretical finite-sample guarantees without making any additional assumptions beyond the standard contextual bandit setup, and empirically demonstrate the utility of COPP compared with existing methods on synthetic and real-world data.
