paragraphs: Evaluating a new decision policy from data collected by another policy often centers on its expected outcome. An average, however, does not describe how widely individual outcomes can vary. This paper addresses that gap in contextual bandits, where decisions depend on the available context, by predicting intervals for outcomes under a new target policy.

The proposed method, conformal off-policy prediction, applies conformal prediction to data gathered by a behavioral policy. Its output is a predictive interval rather than only an estimate of average performance. This changes the evaluation question from how well a policy performs on average to what range of outcomes its use may produce.

The authors establish finite-sample guarantees without adding assumptions beyond the standard contextual bandit setup. These guarantees apply at finite data sizes rather than only asymptotically, which motivates their relevance to safety-critical decisions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the method's utility against existing approaches. The contribution joins outcome variability and finite-sample reliability in off-policy assessment.
summary.tldr: COPP predicts outcome intervals for a new contextual-bandit policy from another policy's data, with finite-sample guarantees.

title: Conformal Off-Policy Prediction in Contextual Bandits

abstract: Infinite width limit has shed light on generalization and optimization aspects of deep learning by establishing connections between neural networks and kernel methods. Despite their importance, the utility of these kernel methods was limited in large-scale learning settings due to their (super-)quadratic runtime and memory complexities. Moreover, most prior works on neural kernels have focused on the ReLU activation, mainly due to its popularity but also due to the difficulty of computing such kernels for general activations. In this work, we overcome such difficulties by providing methods to work with general activations. First, we compile and expand the list of activation functions admitting exact dual activation expressions to compute neural kernels. When the exact computation is unknown, we present methods to effectively approximate them. We propose a fast sketching method that approximates any multi-layered Neural Network Gaussian Process (NNGP) kernel and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) matrices for a wide range of activation functions, going beyond the commonly analyzed ReLU activation. This is done by showing how to approximate the neural kernels using the truncated Hermite expansion of any desired activation functions. While most prior works require data points on the unit sphere, our methods do not suffer from such limitations and are applicable to any dataset of points in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Furthermore, we provide a subspace embedding for NNGP and NTK matrices with near input-sparsity runtime and near-optimal target dimension which applies to any \emph{homogeneous} dual activation functions with rapidly convergent Taylor expansion. Empirically, with respect to exact convolutional NTK (CNTK) computation, our method achieves $106\times$ speedup for approximate CNTK of a 5-layer Myrtle network on CIFAR-10 dataset.

Empirically, the approximation achieves a 106-fold speedup over exact convolutional NTK computation for a five-layer Myrtle network on CIFAR-10, demonstrating a substantial computational benefit in that evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Fast neural-kernel approximations support broader activation functions and input data, with stronger efficiency guarantees under specific activation conditions.

title: Fast Neural Kernel Embeddings for General Activations

abstract: Synthesizing novel view images from a few views is a challenging but practical problem. Existing methods often struggle with producing high-quality results or necessitate per-object optimization in such few-view settings due to the insufficient information provided. In this work, we explore leveraging the strong 2D priors in pre-trained diffusion models for synthesizing novel view images. 2D diffusion models, nevertheless, lack 3D awareness, leading to distorted image synthesis and compromising the identity. To address these problems, we propose $\textit{DreamSparse}$, a framework that enables the frozen pre-trained diffusion model to generate geometry and identity-consistent novel view images. Specifically, DreamSparse incorporates a geometry module designed to capture features about spatial information from sparse views as a 3D prior. Subsequently, a spatial guidance model is introduced to convert rendered feature maps as spatial information for the generative process. This information is then used to guide the pre-trained diffusion model toencourage the synthesis of geometrically consistent images without further tuning. Leveraging the strong image priors in the pre-trained diffusion models, DreamSparse is capable of synthesizing high-quality novel views for both object and object-centric scene-level images and generalising to open-set images.Experimental results demonstrate that our framework can effectively synthesize novel view images from sparse views and outperforms baselines in both trained and open-set category images. More results can be found on our project page: https://sites.google.com/view/dreamsparse-webpage.

paragraphs: Generating an image from a new viewpoint is difficult when only a few views of the subject are available. Pretrained image diffusion models provide strong knowledge about visual appearance, but their lack of three-dimensional awareness can produce distorted geometry or alter the subject's identity. DreamSparse combines this image knowledge with spatial information extracted from the available views.

Its geometry module captures spatial features from the sparse input images, supplying a three-dimensional prior. A separate spatial guidance model converts rendered feature maps into information that guides image generation. The pretrained diffusion model remains frozen, allowing the framework to use its existing visual knowledge while encouraging consistency with the recovered spatial structure.

The framework handles both individual objects and object-centric scenes, and the authors report generalization to open-set images. Experiments show better novel-view synthesis than the tested baselines for both trained and open-set categories. The approach matters because it provides geometric guidance to a strong image generator without requiring further tuning of that pretrained diffusion model.
summary.tldr: DreamSparse guides a frozen diffusion model with spatial features from sparse views to generate more geometrically and identity-consistent viewpoints.

title: DreamSparse: Escaping from Plato’s Cave with 2D Diffusion Model Given Sparse Views

abstract: Achieving an immersive experience enabling users to explore virtual environments with six degrees of freedom (6DoF) is essential for various applications such as virtual reality (VR). Wide-baseline panoramas are commonly used in these applications to reduce network bandwidth and storage requirements. However, synthesizing novel views from these panoramas remains a key challenge. Although existing neural radiance field methods can produce photorealistic views under narrow-baseline and dense image captures, they tend to overfit the training views when dealing with wide-baseline panoramas due to the difficulty in learning accurate geometry from sparse $360^{\circ}$ views. To address this problem, we propose PanoGRF, Generalizable Spherical Radiance Fields for Wide-baseline Panoramas, which construct spherical radiance fields incorporating $360^{\circ}$ scene priors. Unlike generalizable radiance fields trained on perspective images, PanoGRF avoids the information loss from panorama-to-perspective conversion and directly aggregates geometry and appearance features of 3D sample points from each panoramic view based on spherical projection. Moreover, as some regions of the panorama are only visible from one view while invisible from others under wide baseline settings, PanoGRF incorporates $360^{\circ}$ monocular depth priors into spherical depth estimation to improve the geometry features. Experimental results on multiple panoramic datasets demonstrate that PanoGRF significantly outperforms state-of-the-art generalizable view synthesis methods for wide-baseline panoramas (e.g., OmniSyn) and perspective images (e.g., IBRNet, NeuRay).

paragraphs: Widely spaced panoramic captures can reduce storage and bandwidth needs for virtual environments, but generating views between those captures is difficult. Sparse 360-degree images provide limited geometric evidence, and some scene regions appear in only one image. Existing radiance-field methods can consequently overfit the supplied views.

PanoGRF builds spherical radiance fields using information directly from panoramic images. For each sampled 3D point, it gathers geometry and appearance features through spherical projection. This avoids losing information by first converting panoramas into perspective images. The design makes the full panoramic representation part of the view-synthesis process rather than an input that must be reformatted.

To help with regions visible from only one viewpoint, PanoGRF incorporates monocular 360-degree depth priors into spherical depth estimation. These priors strengthen the geometry features where cross-view evidence is limited. Experiments on multiple panoramic datasets show significant improvements over leading generalizable view-synthesis methods developed for both panoramas and perspective images, supporting the value of combining panorama-native aggregation with depth information.
summary.tldr: PanoGRF combines direct spherical feature aggregation with panoramic depth priors to improve view synthesis from widely spaced panoramas.

title: PanoGRF: Generalizable Spherical Radiance Fields for Wide-baseline Panoramas

abstract: We present Prompt Diffusion, a framework for enabling in-context learning in diffusion-based generative models. Given a pair of task-specific example images, such as depth from/to image and scribble from/to image, and a text guidance, our model automatically understands the underlying task and performs the same task on a new query image following the text guidance. To achieve this, we propose a vision-language prompt that can model a wide range of vision-language tasks and a diffusion model that takes it as input. The diffusion model is trained jointly on six different tasks using these prompts. The resulting Prompt Diffusion model becomes the first diffusion-based vision-language foundation model capable of in-context learning. It demonstrates high-quality in-context generation for the trained tasks and effectively generalizes to new, unseen vision tasks using their respective prompts. Our model also shows compelling text-guided image editing results. Our framework aims to facilitate research into in-context learning for computer vision. We share our code and pre-trained models at https://github.com/Zhendong-Wang/Prompt-Diffusion.
originalAbstract: We present Prompt Diffusion, a framework for enabling in-context learning in diffusion-based generative models. Given a pair of task-specific example images, such as depth from/to image and scribble from/to image, and a text guidance, our model automatically understands the underlying task and performs the same task on a new query image following the text guidance. To achieve this, we propose a vision-language prompt that can model a wide range of vision-language tasks and a diffusion model that takes it as input. The diffusion model is trained jointly on six different tasks using these prompts. The resulting Prompt Diffusion model becomes the first diffusion-based vision-language foundation model capable of in-context learning. It demonstrates high-quality in-context generation for the trained tasks and effectively generalizes to new, unseen vision tasks using their respective prompts. Our model also shows compelling text-guided image editing results. Our framework aims to facilitate research into in-context learning for computer vision. We share our code and pre-trained models at https://github.com/Zhendong-Wang/Prompt-Diffusion.

The input includes a task-specific pair of images, a new query image, and text guidance. The example pair communicates a relationship, such as transforming depth into an image or an image into a scribble, which the model then applies to the query.

The authors design a vision-language prompt that expresses multiple tasks in this common format and train a diffusion model to consume it. Training jointly covers six tasks. This shared prompt structure gives the model a consistent way to use visual demonstrations and language, allowing task information to be supplied through the current input.

The resulting model produces high-quality in-context outputs on the trained tasks and generalizes effectively to new vision tasks in the reported demonstrations. It also supports text-guided image editing. These findings show that demonstration-based task specification can work within a diffusion framework, while distinguishing the model’s joint training stage from its subsequent ability to respond to new example prompts.
summary.tldr: Prompt Diffusion learns to apply visual tasks from example image pairs and text, including reported generalization to unseen tasks.

title: In-Context Learning Unlocked for Diffusion Models

abstract: In this paper, we propose to approximate the softmax output, which is the key product of the attention mechanism, to reduce its activation memory usage when training attention-based networks (aka Transformers). During the forward pass of the network, the proposed softmax output approximation method stores only a small fraction of the entire softmax output required for back-propagation and evicts the rest of the softmax output from memory. Then, during the backward pass, the evicted softmax activation output is approximated to compose the gradient to perform back-propagation for model training. Considering most attention-based models heavily rely on the softmax-based attention module that usually takes one of the biggest portions of the network, approximating the softmax activation output can be a simple yet effective way to decrease the training memory requirement of many attention-based networks. The experiment with various attention-based models and relevant tasks, i.e., machine translation, text classification, and sentiment analysis, shows that it curtails the activation memory usage of the softmax-based attention module by up to 84% (6.2× less memory) in model training while achieving comparable or better performance, e.g., up to 5.4% higher classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Training attention-based networks requires retaining intermediate values for the later computation of gradients. Softmax outputs in attention can account for a substantial share of this activation memory. This paper reduces that cost by keeping only a small fraction of those outputs and approximating the discarded values when they are needed.

During the forward pass, the method stores the selected portion of the softmax output and removes the rest from memory. During the backward pass, it reconstructs an approximation of the missing activations and uses it to form gradients. The saving therefore comes from changing what is retained between the two passes, with approximate activation values supporting back-propagation.

Experiments span machine translation, text classification, and sentiment analysis using various attention-based models. The paper reports reductions of up to 84% in the activation memory of the softmax-based attention module, equivalent to 6.2 times less memory, with comparable or better task performance. Reported gains include up to 5.4% higher classification accuracy. These results concern the targeted attention activations and demonstrate their value as a focus for training-memory reduction.
summary.tldr: Keeping only part of attention's softmax output and approximating the rest during back-propagation substantially reduces activation memory.

title: Softmax Output Approximation for Activation Memory-Efficient Training of Attention-based Networks

abstract: Sparse linear regression is a central problem in high-dimensional statistics. We study the correlated random design setting, where the covariates are drawn from a multivariate Gaussian $N(0,\Sigma)$, and we seek an estimator with small excess risk. If the true signal is $t$-sparse, information-theoretically, it is possible to achieve strong recovery guarantees with only $O(t\log n)$ samples. However, computationally efficient algorithms have sample complexity linear in (some variant of) the *condition number* of $\Sigma$. Classical algorithms such as the Lasso can require significantly more samples than necessary even if there is only a single sparse approximate dependency among the covariates.We provide a polynomial-time algorithm that, given $\Sigma$, automatically adapts the Lasso to tolerate a small number of approximate dependencies. In particular, we achieve near-optimal sample complexity for constant sparsity and if $\Sigma$ has few ``outlier'' eigenvalues.Our algorithm fits into a broader framework of *feature adaptation* for sparse linear regression with ill-conditioned covariates. With this framework, we additionally provide the first polynomial-factor improvement over brute-force search for constant sparsity $t$ and arbitrary covariance $\Sigma$.

paragraphs: Sparse linear regression seeks a predictive relationship involving only a small subset of many features. This paper considers correlated Gaussian features, where relationships among inputs can make learning computationally difficult. Although strong recovery is information-theoretically possible from relatively few samples, efficient methods can need many more when the covariance matrix is poorly conditioned.

The authors give a polynomial-time algorithm that uses the known covariance matrix to adapt the Lasso to a small number of approximate dependencies among features. This targets a specific source of difficulty: even one sparse approximate dependency can substantially increase the samples required by classical methods. For constant sparsity and covariance matrices with few outlier eigenvalues, the proposed method achieves near-optimal sample complexity.

The algorithm belongs to a broader feature-adaptation framework for ill-conditioned inputs. That framework also yields a polynomial-factor improvement over brute-force search for constant sparsity and arbitrary covariance. The results distinguish favorable covariance structures, where strong sample guarantees are possible, from the broader setting, where the stated advance is a computational improvement.
summary.tldr: Using known covariance structure, feature adaptation improves sparse regression under approximate dependencies and accelerates search for arbitrary covariance at constant sparsity.

title: Feature Adaptation for Sparse Linear Regression

abstract: Despite recent success in large language model (LLM) reasoning, LLMs struggle with hierarchical multi-step reasoning tasks like generating complex programs. For these tasks, humans often start with a high-level algorithmic design and implement each part gradually. We introduce Parsel, a framework enabling automatic implementation and validation of complex algorithms with code LLMs. With Parsel, we automatically decompose algorithmic tasks into hierarchical natural language function descriptions and then search over combinations of possible function implementations using tests. We show that Parsel can be used across domains requiring hierarchical reasoning, including program synthesis and robotic planning. We find that, using Parsel, LLMs solve more competition-level problems in the APPS dataset, resulting in pass rates over 75\% higher than prior results from directly sampling AlphaCode and Codex, while often using a smaller sample budget. Moreover, with automatically generated tests, we find that Parsel can improve the state-of-the-art pass@1 performance on HumanEval from 67\% to 85\%. We also find that LLM-generated robotic plans using Parsel are more than twice as likely to be considered accurate than directly generated plans. Lastly, we explore how Parsel addresses LLM limitations and discuss how Parsel may be useful for human programmers. We release our code at https://github.com/ezelikman/parsel.

paragraphs: Complex programs require coordinating several levels of reasoning, a task that language models can struggle to complete in one attempt. Parsel follows a process resembling hierarchical software design. It first decomposes an algorithmic task into natural-language descriptions of functions, then seeks implementations that work together.

The framework searches combinations of candidate function implementations and uses tests to validate them. This makes the decomposition operational: a high-level plan becomes a set of parts whose compatibility can be checked. The authors apply the framework to program synthesis and robotic planning, two domains that require coordinated sequences of decisions.

On competition-level APPS problems, reported pass rates are over 75% higher than earlier direct-sampling results from AlphaCode and Codex, often with fewer samples. With automatically generated tests, HumanEval pass@1 rises from 67% to 85%. Generated robotic plans are more than twice as likely to be judged accurate as directly generated plans. These results support combining hierarchical decomposition with implementation search and validation to improve the evaluated reasoning tasks.
summary.tldr: Parsel combines hierarchical task descriptions, implementation search, and tests to improve language-model programming and robotic planning.

title: Parsel🐍: Algorithmic Reasoning with Language Models by Composing Decompositions

abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) stands as one of the most effective and scalable methods for training transferable vision models using paired image and text data. CLIP models are trained using contrastive loss, which typically relies on data augmentations to prevent overfitting and shortcuts. However, in the CLIP training paradigm, data augmentations are exclusively applied to image inputs, while language inputs remain unchanged throughout the entire training process, limiting the exposure of diverse texts to the same image. In this paper, we introduce Language augmented CLIP (LaCLIP), a simple yet highly effective approach to enhance CLIP training through language rewrites. Leveraging the in-context learning capability of large language models, we rewrite the text descriptions associated with each image. These rewritten texts exhibit diversity in sentence structure and vocabulary while preserving the original key concepts and meanings. During training, LaCLIP randomly selects either the original texts or the rewritten versions as text augmentations for each image. Extensive experiments on CC3M, CC12M, RedCaps and LAION-400M datasets show that CLIP pre-training with language rewrites significantly improves the transfer performance without computation or memory overhead during training. Specifically for ImageNet zero-shot accuracy, LaCLIP outperforms CLIP by 8.2% on CC12M and 2.4% on LAION-400M.

paragraphs: CLIP learns transferable visual representations from paired images and text. Its training commonly varies the images through augmentation while keeping their descriptions fixed. This means a given image repeatedly appears with the same wording, limiting the diversity of language the model encounters for the concepts shown in that image.

Language augmented CLIP, or LaCLIP, adds variation on the text side. The authors use a large language model's in-context learning ability to rewrite image descriptions with different vocabulary and sentence structures while preserving their key meanings. Training randomly selects either the original description or a rewritten version for each image.

For ImageNet zero-shot accuracy, the abstract reports improvements over CLIP of 8.2% with CC12M and 2.4% with LAION-400M. The findings support language diversity as a useful training ingredient: several ways of describing the same image can improve the representations learned from image-text pairs.
summary.tldr: LaCLIP improves CLIP transfer performance by randomly training on original image captions or meaning-preserving language-model rewrites.

title: Improving CLIP Training with Language Rewrites

abstract: Sliced Wasserstein (SW) distance suffers from redundant projections due to independent uniform random projecting directions. To partially overcome the issue, max K sliced Wasserstein (Max-K-SW) distance ($K\geq 1$), seeks the best discriminative orthogonal projecting directions. Despite being able to reduce the number of projections, the metricity of the Max-K-SW cannot be guaranteed in practice due to the non-optimality of the optimization. Moreover, the orthogonality constraint is also computationally expensive and might not be effective. To address the problem, we introduce a new family of SW distances, named Markovian sliced Wasserstein (MSW) distance, which imposes a first-order Markov structure on projecting directions. We discuss various members of the MSW by specifying the Markov structure including the prior distribution, the transition distribution, and the burning and thinning technique. Moreover, we investigate the theoretical properties of MSW including topological properties (metricity, weak convergence, and connection to other distances), statistical properties (sample complexity, and Monte Carlo estimation error), and computational properties (computational complexity and memory complexity). Finally, we compare MSW distances with previous SW variants in various applications such as gradient flows, color transfer, and deep generative modeling to demonstrate the favorable performance of the MSW.

paragraphs: Sliced Wasserstein methods compare distributions through projections, but independently sampled directions can provide redundant information. Seeking highly discriminative orthogonal directions can reduce the number of projections, yet introduces expensive constraints and practical difficulties guaranteeing a valid distance when optimization is imperfect. This paper proposes a different way to organize projection directions.

Markovian sliced Wasserstein distances link successive directions through a first-order Markov structure: each new direction depends on the previous one. Different choices of starting distribution, transition distribution, burn-in, and thinning produce members of this family. This construction makes dependence between projections an explicit design choice.

The authors examine whether these distances satisfy metric properties, how they relate to weak convergence and other distances, and their sampling and estimation behavior. They also analyze computation and memory costs. Comparisons in gradient flows, color transfer, and deep generative modeling show favorable performance against earlier sliced Wasserstein variants, providing empirical support alongside the mathematical study of dependent projections.
summary.tldr: Markovian sliced Wasserstein distances connect successive projection directions and combine theoretical analysis with favorable results across several applications.

title: Markovian Sliced Wasserstein Distances: Beyond Independent Projections

abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is a sample-efficient optimization algorithm widely employed across various applications. In some challenging BO tasks, input uncertainty arises due to the inevitable randomness in the optimization process, such as machining errors, execution noise, or contextual variability. This uncertainty deviates the input from the intended value before evaluation, resulting in significant performance fluctuations in the final result. In this paper, we introduce a novel robust Bayesian Optimization algorithm, AIRBO, which can effectively identify a robust optimum that performs consistently well under arbitrary input uncertainty. Our method directly models the uncertain inputs of arbitrary distributions by empowering the Gaussian Process with the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and further accelerates the posterior inference via Nystrom approximation. Rigorous theoretical regret bound is established under MMD estimation error and extensive experiments on synthetic functions and real problems demonstrate that our approach can handle various input uncertainties and achieve a state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches efficiently for good settings of an expensive objective. In practice, the setting requested may differ from the one actually evaluated because of execution noise, machining errors, or changing context. AIRBO addresses this problem by seeking an optimum that performs consistently well when its inputs are uncertain.

The method models uncertain inputs as distributions, accommodating arbitrary distributional forms. It equips a Gaussian process with Maximum Mean Discrepancy, allowing the model to account directly for these uncertain inputs. A Nyström approximation accelerates posterior inference, addressing the computational burden of using this representation during optimization.

The authors establish a theoretical regret bound that accounts for error in estimating Maximum Mean Discrepancy. They also report experiments on synthetic functions and real problems showing that AIRBO handles varied input uncertainties and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The contribution combines a flexible representation of input randomness with faster inference and an analysis that explicitly includes estimation error, supporting optimization for reliable performance under the evaluated uncertainties.
summary.tldr: AIRBO models uncertain inputs as distributions to search efficiently for settings that perform consistently despite input randomness.

title: Efficient Robust Bayesian Optimization for Arbitrary Uncertain inputs

abstract: The widely observed 'benign overfitting phenomenon' in the neural network literature raises the challenge to the `bias-variance trade-off' doctrine in the statistical learning theory.Since the generalization ability of the 'lazy trained' over-parametrized neural network can be well approximated by that of the neural tangent kernel regression,the curve of the excess risk (namely, the learning curve) of kernel ridge regression attracts increasing attention recently.However, most recent arguments on the learning curve are heuristic and are based on the 'Gaussian design' assumption.In this paper, under mild and more realistic assumptions, we rigorously provide a full characterization of the learning curve in the asymptotic senseunder a power-law decay condition of the eigenvalues of the kernel and also the target function.The learning curve elaborates the effect and the interplay of the choice of the regularization parameter, the source condition and the noise.In particular, our results suggest that the 'benign overfitting phenomenon' exists in over-parametrized neural networks only when the noise level is small.

paragraphs: Benign overfitting describes the possibility that an overparameterized model generalizes well despite fitting its training data very closely. Kernel regression is relevant because it can approximate the generalization behavior of neural networks in the lazy-training regime. This paper studies how kernel ridge regression’s excess prediction risk behaves asymptotically.

The analysis assumes power-law decay for the kernel eigenvalues and the target function. Under assumptions described as mild and more realistic than Gaussian design, it rigorously characterizes the learning curve. That curve captures how the regularization choice, the target’s source condition, and observation noise interact in determining excess risk.

This gives a formal account of relationships that earlier learning-curve arguments often treated heuristically. In particular, the results suggest that benign overfitting in overparameterized neural networks occurs only when noise is small. That implication is presented as a suggestion from the analysis, with the neural-network connection grounded in the kernel approximation. The contribution is an asymptotic characterization under the stated decay conditions.
summary.tldr: Under power-law decay conditions, the paper rigorously characterizes kernel ridge regression learning curves and suggests small noise is needed for benign overfitting.

title: On the Asymptotic Learning Curves of Kernel Ridge Regression under Power-law Decay

abstract: We describe an approach to predict open-vocabulary 3D semantic voxel occupancy map from input 2D images with the objective of enabling 3D grounding, segmentation and retrieval of free-form language queries. This is a challenging problem because of the 2D-3D ambiguity and the open-vocabulary nature of the target tasks, where obtaining annotated training data in 3D is difficult. The contributions of this work are three-fold. First, we design a new model architecture for open-vocabulary 3D semantic occupancy prediction. The architecture consists of a 2D-3D encoder together with occupancy prediction and 3D-language heads. The output is a dense voxel map of 3D grounded language embeddings enabling a range of open-vocabulary tasks. Second, we develop a tri-modal self-supervised learning algorithm that leverages three modalities: (i) images, (ii) language and (iii) LiDAR point clouds, and enables training the proposed architecture using a strong pre-trained vision-language model without the need for any 3D manual language annotations. Finally, we demonstrate quantitatively the strengths of the proposed model on several open-vocabulary tasks:Zero-shot 3D semantic segmentation using existing datasets; 3D grounding and retrieval of free-form language queries, using a small dataset that we propose as an extension of nuScenes. You can find the project page here https://vobecant.github.io/POP3D.

paragraphs: POP-3D aims to turn two-dimensional images into a three-dimensional map that can be queried with free-form language. The map represents occupied space using voxels, or three-dimensional cells, and associates them with language embeddings. The task is difficult because images do not uniquely specify three-dimensional structure, and manual language annotations for three-dimensional scenes are hard to obtain.

The architecture combines a 2D-to-3D encoder with separate occupancy and 3D-language heads. Its dense output supports locating, segmenting, and retrieving scene content through language. To train it, the authors develop a self-supervised method combining images, language, and LiDAR point clouds. A strong pretrained vision-language model supplies supervision without requiring manually created 3D language annotations.

The paper evaluates zero-shot 3D semantic segmentation on existing datasets, along with grounding and retrieval for free-form language queries. For the latter tasks, it introduces a small extension of nuScenes. The reported quantitative results demonstrate the model’s strengths across these tasks. The approach connects image-based 3D occupancy prediction to language-compatible representations, while using LiDAR as part of its multimodal training procedure.
summary.tldr: POP-3D predicts language-queryable 3D occupancy maps from images using multimodal training without manual 3D language annotations.

title: POP-3D: Open-Vocabulary 3D Occupancy Prediction from Images

abstract: A recent line of work in high-dimensional statistics working under the Gaussian mixture hypothesis has led to a number of results in the context of empirical risk minimization, Bayesian uncertainty quantification, separation of kernel methods and neural networks, ensembling and fluctuation of random features. We provide rigorous proofs for the applicability of these results to a general class of datasets $(\mathbf{x_i},y_i, {i=1,\dots,n})$ containing independent samples from a mixture distribution $\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}} \rho_{c}P_{c}^{\mathbf{x}}$. Specifically, we consider the hypothesis class of generalized linear models $\hat{y} = F(\mathbf{\Theta}^{\top}\mathbf{x})$ and investigate the asymptotic joint statistics of a family of generalized linear estimators $(\mathbf{\Theta}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathbf{\Theta}^{(M)})$, obtained either from (a) minimizing an empirical risk $\hat{R_n}^{(m)}(\mathbf{\Theta}^{(m)};\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})$ or (b) sampling from the associated Gibbs measure $\exp(-\beta n \hat{R_n}^{(m)}(\mathbf{\Theta}^{(m)};\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y}))$. Our main contribution is to characterize under which conditions the asymptotic joint statistics of this family depends (on a weak sense) only on the means and covariances of the class conditional features distribution $P_{c}^{\mathbf{x}}$. This allows us to prove the universality of different quantities of interest, including training, generalization errors, as well as the geometrical properties and correlations of the estimators.

paragraphs: Gaussian mixture models have supported many theoretical results in high-dimensional statistics, but applying those results to more general data requires justification. This paper asks when detailed distributional structure can be replaced by the means and covariances of mixture components without changing the relevant asymptotic statistics.

The analysis considers independent samples from a mixture distribution and generalized linear models that apply a function to linear projections of the input. It studies families of estimators obtained either by minimizing empirical risk or by sampling from an associated Gibbs distribution. Looking at the family jointly allows the analysis to address relationships among estimators as well as their individual behavior.

The main result characterizes conditions under which those joint statistics depend, in a weak asymptotic sense, only on component means and covariances. This yields universality results for training and generalization errors, estimator geometry, and correlations. The contribution is a rigorous basis for extending Gaussian-mixture calculations to a broader class of datasets when the required conditions hold, rather than treating the Gaussian assumption as automatically representative.
summary.tldr: Conditional universality results show when generalized linear estimators' asymptotic behavior depends only on mixture-component means and covariances.

title: Universality laws for Gaussian mixtures in generalized linear models

abstract: Image classification and segmentation are common applications of deep learning to radiology. While many tasks can be framed using either classification or segmentation, classification has historically been cheaper to label and more widely used. However, recent work has drastically reduced the cost of training segmentation networks. In light of this recent work, we reexamine the choice of training classification vs. segmentation models. First, we use an information theoretic approach to analyze why segmentation vs. classification models may achieve different performance on the same dataset and overarching task. We then implement multiple methods for using segmentation models to classify medical images, which we call *segmentation-for-classification*, and compare these methods against traditional classification on three retrospective datasets. We use our analysis and experiments to summarize the benefits of switching from segmentation to classification, including: improved sample efficiency, enabling improved performance with fewer labeled images (up to an order of magnitude lower), on low-prevalence classes, and on certain rare subgroups (up to 161.1\% improved recall); improved robustness to spurious correlations (up to 44.8\% improved robust AUROC); and improved model interpretability, evaluation, and error analysis.

paragraphs: A medical image can be analyzed by assigning a label to the whole image or by identifying the regions associated with a finding. Classification has historically been cheaper to label, but reduced costs for training segmentation models motivate this paper to revisit that choice. The authors ask how these two formulations affect performance on the same underlying task.

They first use information theory to examine why classification and segmentation can learn differently from the same dataset. They then implement several ways of using segmentation outputs to classify medical images and compare these approaches with conventional classification on three retrospective datasets. This connects the conceptual analysis to practical alternatives for producing image-level decisions.

Reported benefits include learning with up to an order of magnitude fewer labeled images, improved performance for low-prevalence classes, and up to 161.1% improved recall for certain rare subgroups. The abstract also reports up to 44.8% improved robust AUROC against spurious correlations, alongside better interpretability and error analysis. These are reported advantages in the studied settings, with the largest gains describing particular cases.
summary.tldr: The paper examines using segmentation to classify medical images and reports gains in sample efficiency, robustness, and interpretability across three retrospective datasets.

title: A case for reframing automated medical image classification as segmentation

abstract: Survival analysis is a crucial semi-supervised task in machine learning with significant real-world applications, especially in healthcare. The most common approach to survival analysis, Cox’s partial likelihood, can be interpreted as a ranking model optimized on a lower bound of the concordance index. We follow these connections further, with listwise ranking losses that allow for a relaxation of the pairwise independence assumption. Given the inherent transitivity of ranking, we explore differentiable sorting networks as a means to introduce a stronger transitive inductive bias during optimization. Despite their potential, current differentiable sorting methods cannot account for censoring, a crucial aspect of many real-world datasets. We propose a novel method, Diffsurv, to overcome this limitation by extending differentiable sorting methods to handle censored tasks. Diffsurv predicts matrices of possible permutations that accommodate the label uncertainty introduced by censored samples. Our experiments reveal that Diffsurv outperforms established baselines in various simulated and real-world risk prediction scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate the algorithmic advantages of Diffsurv by presenting a novel method for top-k risk prediction that surpasses current methods.

paragraphs: Survival analysis predicts outcomes involving the time until an event, often with incomplete observations caused by censoring. The paper approaches this task as a ranking problem. It builds on the connection between Cox's partial likelihood and the concordance index, then considers losses that evaluate whole lists rather than relying on pairwise independence.

The proposed method, Diffsurv, extends differentiable sorting to accommodate censored observations. Its predictions are matrices representing possible permutations, allowing uncertainty in the observed labels to remain part of the ordering problem. Sorting also introduces a stronger preference for transitive rankings: relationships among multiple items should fit together into a coherent order.

This matters because censoring can leave several orderings compatible with the available evidence. Diffsurv incorporates that uncertainty into sorting-based optimization. The authors report better performance than established baselines across simulated and real-world risk prediction settings. They also introduce a top-k risk prediction method that surpasses the methods compared, showing how the formulation can support identifying a highest-risk subset.
summary.tldr: Diffsurv adapts differentiable sorting to censored outcomes, improving evaluated risk-ranking and top-k prediction tasks.

title: Differentiable sorting for censored time-to-event data.

abstract: Road traffic forecasting plays a critical role in smart city initiatives and has experienced significant advancements thanks to the power of deep learning in capturing non-linear patterns of traffic data. However, the promising results achieved on current public datasets may not be applicable to practical scenarios due to limitations within these datasets. First, the limited sizes of them may not reflect the real-world scale of traffic networks. Second, the temporal coverage of these datasets is typically short, posing hurdles in studying long-term patterns and acquiring sufficient samples for training deep models. Third, these datasets often lack adequate metadata for sensors, which compromises the reliability and interpretability of the data. To mitigate these limitations, we introduce the LargeST benchmark dataset. It encompasses a total number of 8,600 sensors in California with a 5-year time coverage and includes comprehensive metadata. Using LargeST, we perform in-depth data analysis to extract data insights, benchmark well-known baselines in terms of their performance and efficiency, and identify challenges as well as opportunities for future research. We release the datasets and baseline implementations at: https://github.com/liuxu77/LargeST.

paragraphs: Traffic forecasting models can perform well on public datasets without demonstrating that they suit practical traffic networks. This paper identifies three reasons: datasets may cover too few sensors, span too little time, or provide insufficient sensor metadata. These shortcomings restrict the scale, long-term patterns, and contextual understanding available for evaluating forecasting methods.

LargeST addresses these issues with measurements from 8,600 sensors in California over five years, accompanied by comprehensive metadata. The larger sensor network supports studying forecasting at a broader scale, while the longer coverage supports analysis of long-term patterns and supplies more training samples. Metadata adds information needed to interpret the sensor observations.

The contribution also includes detailed data analysis and benchmarks of established methods for both forecasting performance and efficiency. These evaluations are used to identify challenges and opportunities for further research. LargeST therefore supplies a setting for examining how methods behave on a larger and longer-running traffic dataset, rather than presenting a new forecasting model as its central result.
summary.tldr: LargeST provides five years of data from 8,600 California traffic sensors to benchmark forecasting at larger scales.

title: LargeST: A Benchmark Dataset for Large-Scale Traffic Forecasting

abstract: Coupling normalizing flows allow for fast sampling and density evaluation, making them the tool of choice for probabilistic modeling of physical systems. However, the standard coupling architecture precludes endowing flows that operate on the Cartesian coordinates of atoms with the SE(3) and permutation invariances of physical systems. This work proposes a coupling flow that preserves SE(3) and permutation equivariance by performing coordinate splits along additional augmented dimensions. At each layer, the flow maps atoms' positions into learned SE(3) invariant bases, where we apply standard flow transformations, such as monotonic rational-quadratic splines, before returning to the original basis.Crucially, our flow preserves fast sampling and density evaluation, and may be used to produce unbiased estimates of expectations with respect to the target distribution via importance sampling.When trained on the DW4, LJ13, and QM9-positional datasets, our flow is competitive with equivariant continuous normalizing flows and diffusion models, while allowing sampling more than an order of magnitude faster.Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to learn the full Boltzmann distribution of alanine dipeptide by only modeling the Cartesian positions of its atoms.Lastly, we demonstrate that our flow can be trained to approximately sample from the Boltzmann distribution of the DW4 and LJ13 particle systems using only their energy functions.

paragraphs: Coupling normalizing flows offer fast sampling and density evaluation, but their standard architecture obstructs the symmetries needed when modeling atomic coordinates. This paper introduces a flow that preserves equivariance under rotations, translations, and atom permutations while retaining those computational advantages.

The method performs coordinate splits along extra, augmented dimensions. Each layer maps atomic positions into learned invariant bases, applies standard flow transformations there, and returns to the original basis. The resulting model can also support unbiased estimates of target-distribution expectations through importance sampling, connecting efficient generation with a way to estimate physical quantities.

On DW4, LJ13, and QM9-positional data, the flow is competitive with equivariant continuous flows and diffusion models while sampling more than an order of magnitude faster. The authors also report learning alanine dipeptide’s full Boltzmann distribution using only Cartesian atomic positions, a first to their knowledge. For DW4 and LJ13, they demonstrate approximate Boltzmann sampling learned directly from energy functions.
summary.tldr: Augmented coupling flows preserve physical symmetries while enabling fast sampling and density evaluation for atomic systems.

title: SE(3) Equivariant Augmented Coupling Flows

abstract: Harmful memes have proliferated on the Chinese Internet, while research on detecting Chinese harmful memes significantly lags behind due to the absence of reliable datasets and effective detectors.To this end, we present the comprehensive detection of Chinese harmful memes.We introduce ToxiCN MM, the first Chinese harmful meme dataset, which consists of 12,000 samples with fine-grained annotations for meme types. Additionally, we propose a baseline detector, Multimodal Knowledge Enhancement (MKE), designed to incorporate contextual information from meme content, thereby enhancing the model's understanding of Chinese memes.In the evaluation phase, we conduct extensive quantitative experiments and qualitative analyses on multiple baselines, including LLMs and our MKE. Experimental results indicate that detecting Chinese harmful memes is challenging for existing models, while demonstrating the effectiveness of MKE.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the detection of harmful memes on the Chinese Internet, where the authors identify a shortage of reliable datasets and effective detectors. They introduce ToxiCN MM, described as the first Chinese harmful-meme dataset. It contains 12,000 samples with fine-grained annotations for meme types, providing organized material for studying this detection problem.

The paper also proposes Multimodal Knowledge Enhancement, or MKE, as a baseline detector. MKE incorporates contextual information from meme content to improve the model's understanding of Chinese memes. The method makes context part of the detection approach, connecting the interpretation of a meme's content to the decision about whether it is harmful.

The evaluation combines quantitative experiments with qualitative analysis across multiple baselines, including large language models and MKE. Results show that the task remains challenging for existing models while supporting MKE's effectiveness. The dataset and detector contribute complementary resources: one establishes a basis for examining the problem, and the other tests a context-enhanced approach to solving it.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a 12,000-sample Chinese harmful-meme dataset and a context-enhanced detector that proves effective on a challenging task.

title: Towards Comprehensive Detection of Chinese Harmful Memes

abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) models are being increasingly adopted in diverse global communities where they create visual representations of their unique cultures. Current T2I benchmarks primarily focus on faithfulness, aesthetics, and realism of generated images, overlooking the critical dimension of *cultural competence*. In this work, we introduce a framework to evaluate cultural competence of T2I models along two crucial dimensions: cultural awareness and cultural diversity, and present a scalable approach using a combination of structured knowledge bases and large language models to build a large dataset of cultural artifacts to enable this evaluation. In particular, we apply this approach to build CUBE (CUltural BEnchmark for Text-to-Image models), a first-of-its-kind benchmark to evaluate cultural competence of T2I models. CUBE covers cultural artifacts associated with 8 countries across different geo-cultural regions and along 3 concepts: cuisine, landmarks, and art. CUBE consists of 1) CUBE-1K, a set of high-quality prompts that enable the evaluation of cultural awareness, and 2) CUBE-CSpace, a larger dataset of cultural artifacts that serves as grounding to evaluate cultural diversity. We also introduce cultural diversity as a novel T2I evaluation component, leveraging quality-weighted Vendi score. Our evaluations reveal significant gaps in the cultural awareness of existing models across countries and provide valuable insights into the cultural diversity of T2I outputs for underspecified prompts. Our methodology is extendable to other cultural regions and concepts and can facilitate the development of T2I models that better cater to the global population.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether generated images represent cultures competently, beyond looking attractive, realistic, or faithful to a prompt. It proposes evaluating two dimensions: cultural awareness and cultural diversity. Separating them allows the evaluation to examine both models' knowledge of cultural artifacts and the breadth of cultural representations appearing in their outputs.

The authors introduce CUBE, covering eight countries across different cultural regions and three categories: cuisine, landmarks, and art. They combine structured knowledge bases with large language models to assemble the evaluation material. CUBE-1K supplies high-quality prompts for assessing awareness, while the larger CUBE-CSpace dataset provides reference material for assessing diversity. A quality-weighted Vendi score supports the diversity evaluation.

The evaluations reveal substantial cultural-awareness gaps across countries and examine diversity when prompts leave cultural details unspecified. This matters because an underspecified request can expose which cultural representations a model tends to produce. The authors describe their construction method as extendable to additional regions and concepts, offering a route to broader cultural evaluation.
summary.tldr: CUBE evaluates cultural awareness and diversity in text-to-image models, revealing substantial awareness gaps across the countries studied.

title: Beyond Aesthetics: Cultural Competence in Text-to-Image Models

abstract: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced natural language processing, but these models often generate factually incorrect information, known as "hallucination." Initial retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods like the "Retrieve-Read" framework was inadequate for complex reasoning tasks. Subsequent prompt-based RAG strategies and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) methods improved performance but required frequent retraining and risked altering foundational LLM capabilities. To cope with these challenges, we propose Assistant-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (AssistRAG), integrating an intelligent information assistant within LLMs. This assistant manages memory and knowledge through tool usage, action execution, memory building, and plan specification. Using a two-phase training approach—Curriculum Assistant Learning and Reinforced Preference Optimization—AssistRAG enhances information retrieval and decision-making. Experiments show AssistRAG significantly outperforms benchmarks, especially benefiting less advanced LLMs, by providing superior reasoning capabilities and accurate responses.

Initial retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods like the "Retrieve-Read" framework was inadequate for complex reasoning tasks. Subsequent prompt-based RAG strategies and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) methods improved performance but required frequent retraining and risked altering foundational LLM capabilities. To cope with these challenges, we propose Assistant-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (AssistRAG), integrating an intelligent information assistant within LLMs. This assistant manages memory and knowledge through tool usage, action execution, memory building, and plan specification. Using a two-phase training approach—Curriculum Assistant Learning and Reinforced Preference Optimization—AssistRAG enhances information retrieval and decision-making. Experiments show AssistRAG significantly outperforms benchmarks, especially benefiting less advanced LLMs, by providing superior reasoning capabilities and accurate responses.

paragraphs: AssistRAG addresses the problem of language models producing factually incorrect answers even when retrieval is available. The paper argues that simply retrieving information and asking a model to read it is inadequate for complex reasoning. It also identifies drawbacks in later prompting and fine-tuning approaches, including frequent retraining and the risk of changing foundational model capabilities.

The proposed system adds an intelligent information assistant that manages knowledge and memory. Its responsibilities include using tools, executing actions, building memory, and specifying plans. Retrieval therefore becomes part of a broader process for organizing information and deciding what to do with it, rather than an isolated step before answer generation.

The assistant is trained in two phases, called Curriculum Assistant Learning and Reinforced Preference Optimization, to improve retrieval and decision-making. Experiments report significant improvements over benchmarks, with particularly strong benefits for less advanced language models. These findings suggest that a capable information-management component can improve the reasoning and accuracy of the overall system, especially when the underlying language model is weaker.
summary.tldr: AssistRAG adds a trained information assistant to improve retrieval, reasoning, and answer accuracy, particularly for less advanced language models.

title: Boosting the Potential of Large Language Models with an Intelligent Information Assistant

abstract: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) provides a pipeline to extract quantitative and powerful topological descriptors from structured objects. This enables the definition of topological loss functions, which assert to which extent a given object exhibits some topological properties. One can then use these losses to perform topological optimization via gradient descent routines. While theoretically sounded, topological optimization faces an important challenge: gradients tend to be extremely sparse, in the sense that the loss function typically depends (locally) on only very few coordinates of the input object, yielding dramatically slow optimization schemes in practice. In this work, focusing on the central case of topological optimization for point clouds, we propose to overcome this limitation using diffeomorphic interpolation, turning sparse gradients into smooth vector fields defined on the whole space. In particular, this approach combines efficiently with subsampling techniques routinely used in TDA, as the diffeomorphism derived from the gradient computed on the subsample can be used to update the coordinates of the full and possibly large input object. We then illustrate the usefulness of our approach on black-box autoencoder (AE) regularization, where we aim at applying some topological priors on the latent spaces associated to fixed, black-box AE models without modifying their (unknown) architectures and parameters. We empirically show that, while vanilla topological optimization has to be re-run every time that new data comes out of the black-box models, learning a diffeomorphic flow can be done once and then re-applied to new data in linear time. Moreover, reverting the flow allows us to generate data by sampling the topologically-optimized latent space directly, allowing for better interpretability of the model.

paragraphs: Topological optimization adjusts data to encourage desired properties of its overall shape. A practical obstacle is that the corresponding loss often responds locally to only a few coordinates. For point clouds, this produces sparse gradients: an optimization step directly tells very few points how to move, making progress slow.

The authors use diffeomorphic interpolation to turn those sparse directions into a smooth, invertible deformation defined throughout the surrounding space. This also works with subsampling. A gradient calculated from a smaller collection of points can determine a deformation that updates the full point cloud, connecting cheaper topological calculations to larger datasets.

The paper applies this idea to latent representations from fixed, black-box autoencoders, without changing their architectures or parameters. Experiments show that a learned deformation can be reused on new latent data in linear time, whereas ordinary topological optimization must run again. Reversing the deformation also lets the authors sample the optimized latent space and map those samples back for generation, supporting greater model interpretability.
summary.tldr: Smooth, invertible deformations spread sparse topological gradients across point clouds and can be reused to reshape new autoencoder representations.

title: Diffeomorphic interpolation for efficient persistence-based topological optimization

abstract: Beyond traditional binary relational facts, n-ary relational knowledge graphs (NKGs) are comprised of n-ary relational facts containing more than two entities, which are closer to real-world facts with broader applications. However, the construction of NKGs remains at a coarse-grained level, which is always in a single schema, ignoring the order and variable arity of entities. To address these restrictions, we propose Text2NKG, a novel fine-grained n-ary relation extraction framework for n-ary relational knowledge graph construction. We introduce a span-tuple classification approach with hetero-ordered merging and output merging to accomplish fine-grained n-ary relation extraction in different arity. Furthermore, Text2NKG supports four typical NKG schemas: hyper-relational schema, event-based schema, role-based schema, and hypergraph-based schema, with high flexibility and practicality. The experimental results demonstrate that Text2NKG achieves state-of-the-art performance in F1 scores on the fine-grained n-ary relation extraction benchmark. Our code and datasets are publicly available.

paragraphs: Many facts involve more than two entities, so representing knowledge only as pairs can miss richer relational structure. N-ary knowledge graphs accommodate these multi-entity facts. The paper argues that existing construction methods remain coarse because they often assume a single representation schema and overlook entity order or variation in the number of participating entities.

Text2NKG extracts these relations from text through span-tuple classification. It combines this approach with hetero-ordered merging and output merging to handle relations of different arities. The framework also supports four knowledge-graph schemas: hyper-relational, event-based, role-based, and hypergraph-based representations, broadening the forms in which extracted facts can be organized.

Experiments report state-of-the-art F1 scores on the fine-grained n-ary relation-extraction benchmark. The authors also release their code and datasets. The contribution brings more detailed relation extraction together with flexibility in output structure, supporting knowledge-graph construction when facts vary in how many entities they connect and how those entities participate.
summary.tldr: Text2NKG extracts multi-entity relations of varying arity from text and supports four different knowledge-graph schemas.

title: Text2NKG: Fine-Grained N-ary Relation Extraction for N-ary relational Knowledge Graph Construction

abstract: Maximizing the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) is a popular approach to imbalanced binary classification problems. Existing AUC maximization methods usually assume that training and test distributions are identical. However, this assumption is often violated in practice due to {\it a positive distribution shift}, where the negative-conditional density does not change but the positive-conditional density can vary. This shift often occurs in imbalanced classification since positive data are often more diverse and time-varying than negative data. To deal with this shift, we theoretically show that the AUC on the test distribution can be expressed by using the positive and marginal training densities and the marginal test density. Based on this result, we can maximize the AUC on the test distribution by using positive and unlabeled data in the training distribution and unlabeled data in the test distribution. The proposed method requires only positive labels in the training distribution as supervision. Moreover, the derived AUC has a simple form and thus is easy to implement. The effectiveness of the proposed method is shown with four real-world datasets.

paragraphs: AUC measures how well a binary classifier ranks positive examples above negative ones, making it useful when the classes are imbalanced. Methods that maximize it commonly assume training and test examples follow the same distribution. This paper considers a particular departure from that assumption: positive examples can change, while the distribution of examples within the negative class stays fixed.

Under this positive distribution shift, the authors derive an expression for test-distribution AUC using three ingredients: the positive training density, the overall training density, and the overall test density. This connects the desired test-time ranking objective to information available without collecting labeled test examples.

The resulting method uses labeled positives and unlabeled examples from training, together with unlabeled examples from the test distribution. Only the training positives require labels. The authors describe the objective as simple to implement and demonstrate effectiveness on four real-world datasets. Its significance is that adaptation targets test AUC directly under the stated shift assumption, rather than treating training AUC as an unchanged proxy.
summary.tldr: The paper derives an AUC objective that adapts to changing positive examples using labeled training positives and unlabeled training and test data.

title: AUC Maximization under Positive Distribution Shift

abstract: Transformer models can face practical limitations due to their high computational requirements. At the same time, such models exhibit significant activation sparsity, which can be leveraged to reduce the inference cost by converting parts of the network into equivalent Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers. Despite the crucial role played by activation sparsity, its impact on this process remains unexplored. We demonstrate that the efficiency of the conversion can be significantly enhanced by a proper regularization of the activation sparsity of the base model. Moreover, motivated by the high variance of the number of activated neurons for different inputs, we introduce a more effective dynamic-$k$ expert selection rule that adjusts the number of executed experts on a per-token basis. To achieve further savings, we extend this approach to multi-head attention projections. Finally, we develop an efficient implementation that translates these computational savings into actual wall-clock speedup. The proposed method, Dense to Dynamic-$k$ Mixture-of-Experts (D2DMoE), outperforms existing approaches on common NLP and vision tasks, reducing inference cost by up to 60\% without significantly impacting performance.
originalAbstract: Transformer models can face practical limitations due to their high computational requirements. At the same time, such models exhibit significant activation sparsity, which can be leveraged to reduce the inference cost by converting parts of the network into equivalent Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers. Despite the crucial role played by activation sparsity, its impact on this process remains unexplored. We demonstrate that the efficiency of the conversion can be significantly enhanced by a proper regularization of the activation sparsity of the base model. Moreover, motivated by the high variance of the number of activated neurons for different inputs, we introduce a more effective dynamic-$k$ expert selection rule that adjusts the number of executed experts on a per-token basis. To achieve further savings, we extend this approach to multi-head attention projections. Finally, we develop an efficient implementation that translates these computational savings into actual wall-clock speedup. The proposed method, Dense to Dynamic-$k$ Mixture-of-Experts (D2DMoE), outperforms existing approaches on common NLP and vision tasks, reducing inference cost by up to 60\% without significantly impacting performance.

paragraphs: Transformers require substantial computation, but many of their neurons are inactive for a given input. This activation sparsity creates an opportunity to replace parts of a dense network with mixture-of-experts layers that execute selected groups of computations. The paper investigates how the base model’s sparsity affects the efficiency of this conversion.

D2DMoE combines sparsity regularization with a dynamic expert-selection rule. Regularization makes the original model more suitable for efficient conversion. Dynamic-k selection then adjusts the number of experts executed for each token, reflecting the observation that different inputs activate very different numbers of neurons. The method also extends this strategy to projections in multi-head attention.

The authors develop an implementation that turns reduced computation into measured execution-time improvements. Across common language and vision tasks, the method outperforms existing approaches and reduces inference cost by up to 60% without significantly affecting performance. These findings show the value of coordinating model preparation, token-specific computation, and implementation efficiency when exploiting activation sparsity.
summary.tldr: D2DMoE combines sparsity regularization and per-token expert selection to reduce transformer inference cost by up to 60%.

title: Exploiting Activation Sparsity with Dense to Dynamic-k Mixture-of-Experts Conversion

abstract: Neural representations for 3D scenes have made substantial advancements recently, yet object removal remains a challenging yet practical issue, due to the absence of multi-view supervision over occluded areas. Diffusion Models (DMs), trained on extensive 2D images, show diverse and high-fidelity generative capabilities in the 2D domain. However, due to not being specifically trained on 3D data, their application to multi-view data often exacerbates inconsistency, hence impacting the overall quality of the 3D output. To address these issues, we introduce "In-N-Out", a novel approach that begins by inpainting a prior, i.e., the occluded area from a single view using DMs, followed by outstretching it to create multi-view inpaintings via latents alignments. Our analysis identifies that the variability in DMs' outputs mainly arises from initially sampled latents and intermediate latents predicted in the denoising process. We explicitly align of initial latents using a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to establish a consistent foundational structure in the inpainted area, complemented by an implicit alignment of intermediate latents through cross-view attention during the denoising phases, enhancing appearance consistency across views. To further enhance rendering results, we apply a patch-based hybrid loss to optimize NeRF. We demonstrate that our techniques effectively mitigate the challenges posed by inconsistencies in DMs and substantially improve the fidelity and coherence of inpainted 3D representations.

paragraphs: Removing an object from a reconstructed 3D scene exposes regions that were hidden in the original views. A diffusion model can invent plausible content for one image, but generating each viewpoint independently can produce conflicting geometry or appearance. In-N-Out addresses the challenge of making these invented regions agree across views.

The method first fills the hidden region in a single view, then extends that result to other views by aligning latent representations. The authors identify two main sources of output variation: the initial sampled latents and the intermediate latents produced during denoising. A Neural Radiance Field aligns the initial latents to establish a consistent structure, while cross-view attention aligns intermediate information to improve appearance consistency.

A patch-based hybrid loss further optimizes the Neural Radiance Field for rendering. The reported results show improved fidelity and coherence in the completed 3D representations. The approach matters because it coordinates the generative process across viewpoints, allowing knowledge learned from 2D images to support a more consistent 3D reconstruction after object removal.
summary.tldr: In-N-Out aligns diffusion latents across viewpoints to fill regions exposed by 3D object removal with more consistent structure and appearance.

title: In-N-Out: Lifting 2D Diffusion Prior for 3D Object Removal via Tuning-Free Latents Alignment

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable efficacy across knowledge-intensive tasks. Nevertheless, their untapped potential in crop science presents an opportunity for advancement. To narrow this gap, we introduce CROP, which includes a novel instruction tuning dataset specifically designed to enhance LLMs’ professional capabilities in the crop science sector, along with a benchmark that serves as a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs’ understanding of the domain knowledge. The CROP dataset is curated through a task-oriented and LLM-human integrated pipeline, comprising 210,038 single-turn and 1,871 multi-turn dialogues related to crop science scenarios. The CROP benchmark includes 5,045 multiple-choice questions covering three difficulty levels. Our experiments based on the CROP benchmark demonstrate notable enhancements in crop science-related tasks when LLMs are fine-tuned with the CROP dataset. To the best of our knowledge, CROP dataset is the first-ever instruction tuning dataset in the crop science domain. We anticipate that CROP will accelerate the adoption of LLMs in the domain of crop science, ultimately contributing to global food production.

paragraphs: This paper develops CROP to help language models acquire and demonstrate crop-science expertise. It addresses two connected needs: suitable examples for teaching models how to respond in the domain, and a benchmark for measuring their knowledge. Providing both makes it possible to assess whether specialized training actually improves performance on crop-science questions.

The instruction-tuning dataset is assembled through a task-oriented process combining language models and human involvement. It contains 210,038 single-turn dialogues and 1,871 multi-turn dialogues involving crop-science scenarios. The accompanying benchmark contains 5,045 multiple-choice questions organized into three difficulty levels, providing a structured assessment of domain understanding.

Experiments show notable gains on the CROP benchmark after models are fine-tuned using the dataset. That finding supports the usefulness of domain-specific instruction data for the evaluated crop-science tasks. The authors also anticipate wider adoption of language models in crop science and eventual contributions to food production; these are prospective motivations, distinct from the demonstrated improvements in benchmark performance.
summary.tldr: CROP supplies crop-science instruction data and a knowledge benchmark, with fine-tuning experiments showing improved domain performance.

title: Empowering and Assessing the Utility of Large Language Models in Crop Science

abstract: Evaluating the performance of deep models in new scenarios has drawn increasing attention in recent years due to the wide application of deep learning techniques in various fields. However, while it is possible to collect data from new scenarios, the annotations are not always available. Existing Domain Adaptive Object Detection (DAOD) works usually report their performance by selecting the best model on the validation set or even the test set of the target domain, which is highly impractical in real-world applications. In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised model selection approach for domain adaptive object detection, which is able to select almost the optimal model for the target domain without using any target labels. Our approach is based on the flat minima principle, i.e., models located in the flat minima region in the parameter space usually exhibit excellent generalization ability. However, traditional methods require labeled data to evaluate how well a model is located in the flat minima region, which is unrealistic for the DAOD task. Therefore, we design a Detection Adaptation Score (DAS) approach to approximately measure the flat minima without using target labels. We show via a generalization bound that the flatness can be deemed as model variance, while the minima depend on the domain distribution distance for the DAOD task. Accordingly, we propose a Flatness Index Score (FIS) to assess the flatness by measuring the classification and localization fluctuation before and after perturbations of model parameters and a Prototypical Distance Ratio (PDR) score to seek the minima by measuring the transferability and discriminability of the models. In this way, the proposed DAS approach can effectively represent the degree of flat minima and evaluate the model generalization ability on the target domain. We have conducted extensive experiments on various DAOD benchmarks and approaches, and the experimental results show that the proposed DAS correlates well with the performance of DAOD models and can be used as an effective tool for model selection after training. The code will be released at https://github.com/HenryYu23/DAS.
