paragraphs: Choosing an object detector for a new domain is difficult when images are available but labels are not. Existing domain-adaptation studies often select models using labeled target validation or test data. This paper proposes Detection Adaptation Score, a way to rank trained detectors without target labels and identify models close to the best target-domain choice.

The score approximates whether a model occupies a flat minimum, where small parameter changes produce limited variation. Its Flatness Index Score measures changes in classification and localization after parameter perturbations. A second component, the Prototypical Distance Ratio, assesses transferability and discriminability. A generalization bound connects flatness to model variance and the location of minima to distance between domain distributions.

Together, the components estimate properties relevant to target-domain generalization without directly measuring labeled target accuracy. Experiments across multiple adaptation benchmarks and methods show that the score correlates well with detector performance. The findings support its use for model selection after training, addressing the practical gap between adapting a detector without labels and choosing which adapted detector to deploy.
summary.tldr: Detection Adaptation Score ranks adapted object detectors without target labels using perturbation stability and measures of transferability and discriminability.

title: Towards Unsupervised Model Selection for Domain Adaptive Object Detection

abstract: Exploration in reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge.RL algorithms rely on observing rewards to train the agent, and if informative rewards are sparse the agent learns slowly or may not learn at all. To improve exploration and reward discovery, popular algorithms rely on optimism. But what if sometimes rewards are unobservable, e.g., situations of partial monitoring in bandits and the recent formalism of monitored Markov decision process? In this case, optimism can lead to suboptimal behavior that does not explore further to collapse uncertainty.With this paper, we present a novel exploration strategy that overcomes the limitations of existing methods and guarantees convergence to an optimal policy even when rewards are not always observable. We further propose a collection of tabular environments for benchmarking exploration in RL (with and without unobservable rewards) and show that our method outperforms existing ones.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents usually learn from rewards they observe after acting. Sparse rewards already make exploration difficult, but a further complication arises when some rewards cannot be observed at all. The paper examines this distinction in settings connected to partial monitoring and monitored Markov decision processes.

A common exploration principle is optimism: favor possibilities that might turn out well while uncertainty remains. The authors explain that this principle can produce suboptimal behavior when rewards are sometimes hidden. An optimistic agent may fail to take the additional exploratory actions needed to resolve its uncertainty, leaving it without the information required to improve its decisions.

The paper proposes an exploration strategy that addresses this failure and establishes convergence to an optimal policy in the setting studied, even with intermittently unobservable rewards. It also introduces tabular benchmark environments covering both observable and unobservable rewards. Reported comparisons show the proposed method outperforming existing approaches, supporting the value of exploration strategies that explicitly address whether reward information can be acquired.
summary.tldr: A new exploration strategy addresses failures of optimism when rewards are sometimes unobservable and guarantees convergence in the studied setting.

title: Beyond Optimism: Exploration With Partially Observable Rewards

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit advanced reasoning skills, enabling robots to comprehend natural language instructions and strategically plan high-level actions through proper grounding. However, LLM hallucination may result in robots confidently executing plans that are misaligned with user goals or even unsafe in critical scenarios. Additionally, inherent ambiguity in natural language instructions can introduce uncertainty into the LLM's reasoning and planning. We propose introspective planning, a systematic approach that guides LLMs to refine their own uncertainty in alignment with inherent task ambiguity. Our approach constructs a knowledge base containing introspective reasoning examples as post-hoc rationalizations of human-selected safe and compliant plans, which are retrieved during deployment. Evaluations on three tasks, including a new safe mobile manipulation benchmark, indicate that introspection substantially improves both compliance and safety over state-of-the-art LLM-based planning methods. Additionally, we empirically show that introspective planning, in combination with conformal prediction, achieves tighter confidence bounds, maintaining statistical success guarantees while minimizing unnecessary user clarification requests.

paragraphs: Language models can help robots interpret instructions and plan high-level actions, but confident mistakes can produce unsafe behavior or plans that miss the user’s goal. Instructions can also be genuinely ambiguous. Introspective planning aims to make a planner’s uncertainty better reflect that ambiguity, improving its decisions about both action and clarification.

The method builds a knowledge base of reasoning examples associated with safe, compliant plans selected by humans. These explanations are constructed after the plans are chosen and retrieved during deployment. They guide the language model in refining its own reasoning and uncertainty using examples grounded in human judgments about appropriate plans.

Evaluations on three tasks, including a new safe mobile manipulation benchmark, show substantial improvements in safety and compliance over state-of-the-art language-model planning approaches. When combined with conformal prediction, introspective planning empirically yields tighter confidence bounds while maintaining statistical success guarantees and reducing unnecessary clarification requests. The findings connect improved uncertainty handling with more useful robot behavior, without treating every ambiguous instruction as requiring another question.
summary.tldr: Introspective planning retrieves reasoning examples to improve robot safety and compliance while better matching uncertainty to ambiguous instructions.

title: Introspective Planning: Aligning Robots' Uncertainty with Inherent Task Ambiguity

abstract: We address the problem of multi-object 3D pose control in image diffusion models. Instead of conditioning on a sequence of text tokens, we propose to use a set of per-object representations, *Neural Assets*, to control the 3D pose of individual objects in a scene. Neural Assets are obtained by pooling visual representations of objects from a reference image, such as a frame in a video, and are trained to reconstruct the respective objects in a different image, e.g., a later frame in the video. Importantly, we encode object visuals from the reference image while conditioning on object poses from the target frame, which enables learning disentangled appearance and position features. Combining visual and 3D pose representations in a sequence-of-tokens format allows us to keep the text-to-image interface of existing models, with Neural Assets in place of text tokens. By fine-tuning a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model with this information, our approach enables fine-grained 3D pose and placement control of individual objects in a scene. We further demonstrate that Neural Assets can be transferred and recomposed across different scenes. Our model achieves state-of-the-art multi-object editing results on both synthetic 3D scene datasets, as well as two real-world video datasets (Objectron, Waymo Open).

paragraphs: Controlling several objects in a generated scene requires specifying both their appearance and their individual positions and orientations. This paper introduces Neural Assets, per-object representations that replace text tokens as conditioning inputs to an image diffusion model. The goal is fine-grained control over each object’s three-dimensional pose and placement.

A Neural Asset pools visual information about an object from a reference image. During training, the model reconstructs that object in another image using its reference appearance together with its target pose. Separating the sources of appearance and pose information enables the model to learn distinct features for what an object looks like and where it belongs. The resulting representations retain the token-sequence interface used by existing text-to-image models.

After fine-tuning a pretrained diffusion model, the approach supports individual object editing and transfer or recomposition of assets across scenes. The authors report state-of-the-art multi-object editing on synthetic 3D scenes and the Objectron and Waymo Open video datasets. These results demonstrate the usefulness of object-level representations for controllable scene generation.
summary.tldr: Neural Assets separate object appearance from target pose to enable precise multi-object editing and recomposition with image diffusion models.

title: Neural Assets: 3D-Aware Multi-Object Scene Synthesis with Image Diffusion Models

abstract: We study transfer learning for estimation in latent variable network models. In our setting, the conditional edge probability matrices given the latent variables are represented by $P$ for the source and $Q$ for the target. We wish to estimate $Q$ given two kinds of data: (1) edge data from a subgraph induced by an $o(1)$ fraction of the nodes of $Q$, and (2) edge data from all of $P$. If the source $P$ has no relation to the target $Q$, the estimation error must be $\Omega(1)$. However, we show that if the latent variables are shared, then vanishing error is possible. We give an efficient algorithm that utilizes the ordering of a suitably defined graph distance. Our algorithm achieves $o(1)$ error and does not assume a parametric form on the source or target networks. Next, for the specific case of Stochastic Block Models we prove a minimax lower bound and show that a simple algorithm achieves this rate. Finally, we empirically demonstrate our algorithm's use on real-world and simulated graph transfer problems.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a well-observed source network can help estimate a sparsely observed target network. The quantity to recover is the target’s matrix of edge probabilities conditional on latent variables. Available data includes source-network edges and target edges only within a subgraph containing a fraction of nodes that tends to zero.

If the networks are unrelated, estimation error must remain bounded away from zero. The authors show that shared latent variables can make vanishing error possible. Their efficient algorithm uses the ordering induced by a suitably defined graph distance and achieves error tending to zero without specifying a parametric form for either network.

For stochastic block models, the paper further establishes a minimax lower bound and gives a simple algorithm attaining that rate. Experiments on simulated and real graph transfer problems illustrate the approach. The central message is that shared hidden structure can make extremely limited target observations useful, while the lack of any source–target relationship prevents the same estimation conclusion.
summary.tldr: Shared latent variables can enable accurate target-network estimation from a fully observed source and a vanishing fraction of target nodes.

title: Transfer Learning for Latent Variable Network Models

abstract: This work investigates the offline formulation of the contextual bandit problem, where the goal is to leverage past interactions collected under a behavior policy to evaluate, select, and learn new, potentially better-performing, policies. Motivated by critical applications, we move beyond point estimators. Instead, we adopt the principle of _pessimism_ where we construct upper bounds that assess a policy's worst-case performance, enabling us to confidently select and learn improved policies. Precisely, we introduce novel, fully empirical concentration bounds for a broad class of importance weighting risk estimators. These bounds are general enough to cover most existing estimators and pave the way for the development of new ones. In particular, our pursuit of the tightest bound within this class motivates a novel estimator (LS), that _logarithmically smoothes_ large importance weights. The bound for LS is provably tighter than its competitors, and naturally results in improved policy selection and learning strategies. Extensive policy evaluation, selection, and learning experiments highlight the versatility and favorable performance of LS.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to evaluate and improve contextual-bandit policies using interactions already collected by a different behavior policy. A single estimated performance value does not express how uncertain that judgment is. The authors therefore use pessimism: they construct upper bounds on risk to assess a policy conservatively before selecting or learning it.

Their main theoretical contribution is a set of fully empirical concentration bounds for a broad family of importance-weighted risk estimators. These estimators adjust for the difference between the data-collecting policy and the policy being evaluated. Searching for a tighter bound motivates LS, an estimator that uses logarithmic smoothing to reduce the influence of large importance weights.

The authors prove that LS has a tighter bound than its competitors in the comparison they develop. That bound also leads to improved policy-selection and learning strategies. Experiments spanning evaluation, selection, and learning report favorable performance, supporting the practical value of designing an estimator around a conservative performance guarantee.
summary.tldr: Logarithmic smoothing of large importance weights produces tighter pessimistic risk bounds and improves offline policy evaluation, selection, and learning.

title: Logarithmic Smoothing for Pessimistic Off-Policy Evaluation, Selection and Learning

abstract: We present a general method for lossless compression of unordered data structures, including multisets and graphs. It is a variant of shuffle coding that is many orders of magnitude faster than the original and enables 'one-shot' compression of single unordered objects. Our method achieves state-of-the-art compression rates on various large-scale network graphs at speeds of megabytes per second, efficiently handling even a multi-gigabyte plain graph with one billion edges. We release an implementation that can be easily adapted to different data types and statistical models.

paragraphs: Unordered data structures, including multisets and graphs, require compression methods that respect the object being represented without losing information. This paper presents a general lossless method based on shuffle coding. Its main advance is practical efficiency: the proposed variant is many orders of magnitude faster than the original approach.

The method also supports one-shot compression of a single unordered object. This makes an individual graph or multiset a direct target for the compressor. The combination of generality and single-object operation matters because the method is presented as applicable across unordered data types, with an implementation that can be adapted to different statistical models.

The reported evaluations achieve state-of-the-art compression rates on various large network graphs while processing data at megabytes per second. The method also handles a multi-gigabyte graph containing one billion edges. These results establish both compactness and practical scale in the evaluated graph settings. The contribution is therefore a usable form of shuffle coding that combines lossless representation, substantially improved speed, and support for very large individual objects.
summary.tldr: A faster shuffle-coding method losslessly compresses individual unordered objects and achieves strong compression on large network graphs.

title: Practical Shuffle Coding

abstract: Model Inversion (MI) attacks pose a significant threat to the privacy of Deep Neural Networks by recovering training data distribution from well-trained models. While existing defenses often rely on regularization techniques to reduce information leakage, they remain vulnerable to recent attacks. In this paper, we propose the Trapdoor-based Model Inversion Defense (Trap-MID) to mislead MI attacks. A trapdoor is integrated into the model to predict a specific label when the input is injected with the corresponding trigger. Consequently, this trapdoor information serves as the "shortcut" for MI attacks, leading them to extract trapdoor triggers rather than private data. We provide theoretical insights into the impacts of trapdoor's effectiveness and naturalness on deceiving MI attacks. In addition, empirical experiments demonstrate the state-of-the-art defense performance of Trap-MID against various MI attacks without the requirements for extra data or large computational overhead. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ntuaislab/Trap-MID.

This creates a privacy risk even when the original data are not directly available. The paper notes that defenses based on regularization still remain vulnerable to recent attacks and proposes a method designed to misdirect the inversion process.

Trap-MID inserts a trapdoor into the model: an input containing a particular trigger is associated with a specified label. That association gives an inversion attack a shortcut to the label it seeks. The intended result is that the attack extracts the trapdoor trigger instead of recovering private training information.

The authors provide theoretical insights into how the trapdoor's effectiveness and naturalness influence its ability to deceive attacks. Experiments report state-of-the-art defense performance against various model inversion methods, without requiring additional data or large computational overhead. The contribution is a deliberate change to what information the attack finds useful, with the reported evaluations supporting trapdoors as an effective defense mechanism against the tested inversion attacks.
summary.tldr: Trap-MID embeds label-associated triggers that redirect model inversion attacks toward trapdoor information instead of private training data.

title: Trap-MID: Trapdoor-based Defense against Model Inversion Attacks

abstract: We propose **Quan**tum-informed **T**ensor **A**daptation (**QuanTA**), a novel, easy-to-implement, fine-tuning method with no inference overhead for large-scale pre-trained language models. By leveraging quantum-inspired methods derived from quantum circuit structures, QuanTA enables efficient *high-rank* fine-tuning, surpassing the limitations of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)---low-rank approximation may fail for complicated downstream tasks. Our approach is theoretically supported by the universality theorem and the rank representation theorem to achieve efficient high-rank adaptations. Experiments demonstrate that QuanTA significantly enhances commonsense reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, and scalability compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, QuanTA shows superior performance with fewer trainable parameters compared to other approaches and can be designed to integrate with existing fine-tuning algorithms for further improvement, providing a scalable and efficient solution for fine-tuning large language models and advancing state-of-the-art in natural language processing.

Its motivation is that low-rank approximations, such as those used by LoRA, may be insufficient for complicated downstream tasks. The paper seeks a way to represent richer adaptations without giving up the efficiency benefits of training relatively few parameters.

The method draws on structures inspired by quantum circuits to construct tensor adaptations. A universality theorem and a rank representation theorem provide theoretical support for its ability to express efficient high-rank updates. The authors describe the method as straightforward to implement and report that it adds no overhead during inference.

Experiments show improved commonsense reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, and scalability compared with traditional methods. The paper also reports stronger performance with fewer trainable parameters than competing approaches. QuanTA can additionally be designed to work with existing fine-tuning algorithms. These findings support high-rank adaptation as a practical option when restricting updates to low rank may constrain downstream performance.
summary.tldr: QuanTA uses quantum-inspired tensor structures for parameter-efficient high-rank language model adaptation without added inference overhead.

title: QuanTA: Efficient High-Rank Fine-Tuning of LLMs with Quantum-Informed Tensor Adaptation

abstract: This paper explores the weakly-supervised referring image segmentation (WRIS) problem, and focuses on a challenging setup where target localization is learned directly from image-text pairs. We note that the input text description typically already contains detailed information on how to localize the target object, and we also observe that humans often follow a step-by-step comprehension process (\ie, progressively utilizing target-related attributes and relations as cues) to identify the target object. Hence, we propose a novel Progressive Comprehension Network (PCNet) to leverage target-related textual cues from the input description for progressively localizing the target object.Specifically, we first use a Large Language Model (LLM) to decompose the input text description into short phrases. These short phrases are taken as target-related cues and fed into a Conditional Referring Module (CRM) in multiple stages, to allow updating the referring text embedding and enhance the response map for target localization in a multi-stage manner.Based on the CRM, we then propose a Region-aware Shrinking (RaS) loss to constrain the visual localization to be conducted progressively in a coarse-to-fine manner across different stages.Finally, we introduce an Instance-aware Disambiguation (IaD) loss to suppress instance localization ambiguity by differentiating overlapping response maps generated by different referring texts on the same image. Extensive experiments show that our method outperforms SOTA methods on three common benchmarks.

paragraphs: Referring image segmentation asks a model to identify the image region described by text. This paper studies a weakly supervised setting where target localization is learned directly from image-text pairs. Its starting observation is that descriptions already contain useful attributes and relationships that can guide a sequence of increasingly precise localization decisions.

The proposed Progressive Comprehension Network first uses a large language model to split a description into short phrases. A Conditional Referring Module processes those cues over multiple stages, updating the text representation and the image response map. This lets the model progressively incorporate information about the target instead of relying on a single localization step.

Two training losses support this progression. Region-aware Shrinking encourages localization to narrow from coarse regions toward finer ones. Instance-aware Disambiguation separates overlapping response maps produced by different descriptions of the same image, reducing ambiguity between instances. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art methods on three common benchmarks, supporting the value of staged comprehension in this weakly supervised setting.
summary.tldr: PCNet progressively uses phrases from a description to narrow down the target object and reduce ambiguity in weakly supervised segmentation.

title: Boosting Weakly Supervised Referring Image Segmentation via Progressive Comprehension

abstract: Spatio-temporal (ST) prediction has garnered a De facto attention in earth sciences, such as meteorological prediction, human mobility perception. However, the scarcity of data coupled with the high expenses involved in sensor deployment results in notable data imbalances. Furthermore, models that are excessively customized and devoid of causal connections further undermine the generalizability and interpretability. To this end, we establish a causal framework for ST predictions, termed CaPaint, which targets to identify causal regions in data and endow model with causal reasoning ability in a two-stage process. Going beyond this process, we utilize the back-door adjustment to specifically address the sub-regions identified as non-causal in the upstream phase. Specifically, we employ a novel image inpainting technique. By using a fine-tuned unconditional Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) as the generative prior, we in-fill the masks defined as environmental parts, offering the possibility of reliable extrapolation for potential data distributions. CaPaint overcomes the high complexity dilemma of optimal ST causal discovery models by reducing the data generation complexity from exponential to quasi-linear levels. Extensive experiments conducted on five real-world ST benchmarks demonstrate that integrating the CaPaint concept allows models to achieve improvements ranging from 4.3% to 77.3%. Moreover, compared to traditional mainstream ST augmenters, CaPaint underscores the potential of diffusion models in ST enhancement, offering a novel paradigm for this field. Our project is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/12345-DFCC.

paragraphs: Predicting processes that vary across space and time is difficult when observations are scarce or unevenly distributed. Expensive sensor deployment can worsen these imbalances, while highly customized models can struggle to generalize. CaPaint addresses this problem through a causal framework that identifies relevant regions in the data and seeks to give prediction models a basis for causal reasoning.

The approach first distinguishes causal regions from regions treated as environmental or non-causal. It then uses back-door adjustment together with diffusion-based inpainting to address those environmental regions. A fine-tuned unconditional diffusion model fills the corresponding masks, supplying generated variations of the surrounding context. This offers a possible route to extrapolation across potential data distributions.

The paper reports reducing data-generation complexity from exponential to quasi-linear relative to the optimal spatio-temporal causal discovery models it discusses. Across five real-world benchmarks, incorporating CaPaint produces reported improvements ranging from 4.3% to 77.3%. These results support the usefulness of combining causal region identification with generative augmentation, while the abstract presents reliable extrapolation as a possibility rather than a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: CaPaint combines causal region identification with diffusion inpainting to augment spatio-temporal data and improve prediction across five benchmarks.

title: Causal Deciphering and Inpainting in Spatio-Temporal Dynamics via Diffusion Model

abstract: We study the proportional clustering problem of Chen et al. (ICML'19) and relate it to the area of multiwinner voting in computational social choice. We show that any clustering satisfying a weak proportionality notion of Brill and Peters (EC'23) simultaneously obtains the best known approximations to the proportional fairness notion of Chen et al., but also to individual fairness (Jung et al., FORC'20) and the ``core'' (Li et al., ICML'21). In fact, we show that any approximation to proportional fairness is also an approximation to individual fairness and vice versa. Finally, we also study stronger notions of proportional representation, in which deviations do not only happen to single, but multiple candidate centers, and show that stronger proportionality notions of Brill and Peters imply approximations to these stronger guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper connects fairness in clustering with proportional representation in multiwinner voting. Both settings involve selecting representatives, expressed as cluster centers in one case and election winners in the other. The authors use this connection to relate several fairness guarantees that had been studied through different mathematical definitions.

They show that any clustering satisfying a particular weak proportionality condition also attains the best known approximations to proportional fairness, individual fairness, and the core. They further establish a two-way relationship: an approximation to proportional fairness is also an approximation to individual fairness, and conversely. These results make one fairness property informative about another.

The paper then examines stronger proportional representation requirements, allowing deviations involving several candidate centers rather than only one. Stronger proportionality notions from voting imply approximations to these stronger clustering guarantees. The contribution is a set of theoretical connections showing how representation conditions can deliver several guarantees simultaneously, including guarantees that account for groups considering multiple alternative centers.
summary.tldr: Proportional representation conditions from voting imply multiple clustering fairness guarantees and reveal links between proportional and individual fairness.

title: Proportional Fairness in Clustering: A Social Choice Perspective

abstract: In this study, we aim to reduce generation latency for Named Entity Recognition (NER) with Large Language Models (LLMs). The main cause of high latency in LLMs is the sequential decoding process, which autoregressively generates all labels and mentions for NER, significantly increase the sequence length. To this end, we introduce Parallel Decoding in LLM for NE} (PaDeLLM-NER), a approach that integrates seamlessly into existing generative model frameworks without necessitating additional modules or architectural modifications. PaDeLLM-NER allows for the simultaneous decoding of all mentions, thereby reducing generation latency. Experiments reveal that PaDeLLM-NER significantly increases inference speed that is 1.76 to 10.22 times faster than the autoregressive approach for both English and Chinese. Simultaneously it maintains the quality of predictions as evidenced by the performance that is on par with the state-of-the-art across various datasets. All resources are available at https://github.com/GeorgeLuImmortal/PaDeLLM_NER.

paragraphs: Named entity recognition identifies entity mentions in text and assigns their labels. When a language model generates all mentions and labels sequentially, the resulting output can be long, increasing the time needed to obtain a prediction. This paper focuses on reducing that generation delay.

PaDeLLM-NER changes the decoding process so that mentions can be decoded simultaneously. The method fits into existing generative-model frameworks without adding modules or changing the architecture. Its central idea is to reduce the sequential work associated with producing multiple mentions, making the organization of generation itself the target of the efficiency improvement.

Experiments in English and Chinese report inference speeds between 1.76 and 10.22 times those of the autoregressive approach. Prediction quality remains comparable to state-of-the-art results across the evaluated datasets. These findings indicate that parallel mention decoding can deliver substantial latency reductions while preserving competitive recognition quality in the tested settings. The range of reported gains also makes clear that the improvement varies across evaluations.
summary.tldr: PaDeLLM-NER decodes entity mentions in parallel, reporting 1.76–10.22 times faster inference while maintaining competitive recognition quality.

title: PaDeLLM-NER: Parallel Decoding in Large Language Models for Named Entity Recognition

abstract: Deep learning technologies have demonstrated remarkable performance in vulnerability detection. Existing works primarily adopt a uniform and consistent feature learning pattern across the entire target set. While designed for general-purpose detection tasks, they lack sensitivity towards target code comprising multiple functional modules or diverse vulnerability subtypes. In this paper, we present a knowledge fusion-based vulnerability detection method (KF-GVD) that integrates specific vulnerability knowledge into the Graph Neural Network feature learning process. KF-GVD achieves accurate vulnerability detection across different functional modules of the Linux kernel and vulnerability subtypes without compromising general task performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that KF-GVD outperforms SOTAs on function-level and statement-level vulnerability detection across various target tasks, with an average increase of 40.9% in precision and 26.1% in recall. Notably, KF-GVD discovered 9 undisclosed vulnerabilities when employing on C/C++ open-source projects without ground truth.

paragraphs: Code vulnerability detectors often learn features in the same way across all target code. That uniform approach can miss differences among functional modules or vulnerability subtypes. This paper investigates how incorporating knowledge suited to a particular detection task can improve the representations used to identify vulnerable code.

KF-GVD integrates specific vulnerability knowledge into a graph neural network's feature-learning process. The method aims to support detection across different Linux kernel modules and vulnerability subtypes while preserving general-task performance. Its central idea is to make the learned representation responsive to the kind of code and vulnerability being examined, rather than applying one undifferentiated feature-learning pattern throughout.

Experiments cover both function-level and statement-level detection across multiple target tasks. The authors report that KF-GVD outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, with average increases of 40.9% in precision and 26.1% in recall. Applied to open-source C/C++ projects without ground-truth labels, it also discovered nine previously undisclosed vulnerabilities. These findings provide evidence for task-oriented knowledge fusion in both benchmark detection and practical vulnerability discovery.
summary.tldr: KF-GVD injects task-specific vulnerability knowledge into graph learning to improve detection across code modules and vulnerability types.

title: Suitable is the Best: Task-Oriented Knowledge Fusion in Vulnerability Detection

abstract: We present a theoretical analysis of the Elo rating system, a popular method for ranking skills of players in an online setting. In particular, we study Elo under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model and, using techniques from Markov chain theory, show that Elo learns the model parameters at a rate competitive with the state-of-the-art. We apply our results to the problem of efficient tournament design and discuss a connection with the fastest-mixing Markov chain problem.
originalAbstract: We present a theoretical analysis of the Elo rating system, a popular method for ranking skills of players in an online setting. In particular, we study Elo under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model and, using techniques from Markov chain theory, show that Elo learns the model parameters at a rate competitive with the state-of-the-art. We apply our results to the problem of efficient tournament design and discuss a connection with the fastest-mixing Markov chain problem.

paragraphs: Elo is a system for updating estimates of player skill as match results arrive. This paper asks a theoretical question about that familiar procedure: how quickly does it learn the underlying skill parameters? The analysis studies Elo under the Bradley–Terry–Luce model, so its conclusions concern a specified mathematical model of match outcomes.

The authors use techniques from Markov chain theory to analyze the rating process. Within the studied setting, they show that Elo learns the model parameters at a rate competitive with state-of-the-art methods. This gives a formal learning-rate justification for Elo beyond its popularity as an online ranking procedure.

The paper also applies the analysis to efficient tournament design and discusses a connection to the fastest-mixing Markov chain problem. That connection brings the choice of tournament structure into the same mathematical picture as rating convergence. The contribution links how results are gathered with how efficiently a rating system can extract skill information, while retaining the Bradley–Terry–Luce model as the basis of the analysis.
summary.tldr: A Markov chain analysis shows that Elo learns skill parameters at a competitive rate under the Bradley–Terry–Luce model and informs tournament design.

title: An Analysis of Elo Rating Systems via Markov Chains

abstract: Benefiting from the powerful language expression and planning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), LLM-based autonomous agents have achieved promising performance in various downstream tasks. Recently, based on the development of single-agent systems, researchers propose to construct LLM-based multi-agent systems to tackle more complicated tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, named COPPER, to enhance the collaborative capabilities of LLM-based agents with the self-reflection mechanism. To improve the quality of reflections, we propose to fine-tune a shared reflector, which automatically tunes the prompts of actor models using our counterfactual PPO mechanism. On the one hand, we propose counterfactual rewards to assess the contribution of a single agent’s reflection within the system, alleviating the credit assignment problem. On the other hand, we propose to train a shared reflector, which enables the reflector to generate personalized reflections according to agent roles, while reducing the computational resource requirements and improving training stability. We conduct experiments on three datasets to evaluate the performance of our model in multi-hop question answering, mathematics, and chess scenarios. Experimental results show that COPPER possesses stronger reflection capabilities and exhibits excellent generalization performance across different actor models.

paragraphs: When multiple language-model agents collaborate, useful self-reflection must account for each agent’s role and contribution. COPPER is a framework designed to improve that collaboration by training a shared reflector. The reflector generates feedback that automatically adjusts the prompts used by the acting models, making reflection part of the system’s learning process.

The training method uses counterfactual PPO and counterfactual rewards to assess the contribution of an individual agent’s reflection. This addresses the credit assignment problem: a collective result does not by itself reveal which reflection helped. Sharing the reflector also lets it produce role-specific feedback while reducing computational requirements and improving training stability.

The authors evaluate COPPER on three datasets spanning multihop question answering, mathematics, and chess. They report stronger reflection capabilities and strong generalization across different actor models. The approach matters because it treats reflection quality as something to optimize explicitly, while using a common mechanism to coordinate personalized guidance across the participating agents.
summary.tldr: COPPER trains a shared, role-aware reflector with counterfactual rewards to improve collaboration among language-model agents.

title: Reflective Multi-Agent Collaboration based on Large Language Models

abstract: Although pre-trained transformers and reprogrammed text-based LLMs have shown strong performance on time series tasks, the best-performing architectures vary widely across tasks, with most models narrowly focused on specific areas, such as time series forecasting. Unifying predictive and generative time series tasks within a single model remains challenging. We introduce UniTS, a unified multi-task time series model that utilizes task tokenization to integrate predictive and generative tasks into a single framework. UniTS employs a modified transformer block to capture universal time series representations, enabling transferability from a heterogeneous, multi-domain pre-training dataset—characterized by diverse dynamic patterns, sampling rates, and temporal scales—to a wide range of downstream datasets with varied task specifications and data domains. Tested on 38 datasets across human activity sensors, healthcare, engineering, and finance, UniTS achieves superior performance compared to 12 forecasting models, 20 classification models, 18 anomaly detection models, and 16 imputation models, including adapted text-based LLMs. UniTS also demonstrates strong few-shot and prompt capabilities when applied to new domains and tasks. In single-task settings, UniTS outperforms competitive task-specialized time series models. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/mims-harvard/UniTS.

paragraphs: Time-series models are often specialized for forecasting, classification, anomaly detection, or imputation. UniTS brings predictive and generative tasks into one framework through task tokenization and a modified Transformer block designed for shared time-series representations.

Pretraining draws on heterogeneous domains with different dynamics, sampling rates, and time scales. The aim is to transfer a common model to downstream datasets with differing task specifications rather than train unrelated architectures for each objective.

Evaluation spans 38 datasets in human activity, healthcare, engineering, and finance. Comparisons include 12 forecasting, 20 classification, 18 anomaly-detection, and 16 imputation models, with superior reported performance and strong few-shot and prompting capabilities. The abstract does not provide per-dataset metrics. Its evidence supports broad multitask usefulness in the tested collection, including competitive single-task settings, without claiming one model dominates every possible time-series application.
summary.tldr: UniTS uses task tokens and shared representations to support multiple time-series objectives.

title: UniTS: A Unified Multi-Task Time Series Model

abstract: Gaze to the Stars is an AI-mediated participatory public art installation that transforms the MIT Great Dome into a platform for collective emotional storytelling. 200 Participants engage in reflective conversations with a large language model, their responses encoded as Braille into their iris videos and projected onto the Dome. Using affective narrative embedding, iris segmentation, and emotional clustering, the project visualizes both shared and personal affect. Through Gaze to the Stars, we frame AI not as a tool for efficiency, but as a companion—inviting self-reflection and fostering civic empathy within public space.

paragraphs: Gaze to the Stars is a participatory artwork that uses the MIT Great Dome as a surface for collective emotional storytelling. The project brings personal reflection into a shared public setting through conversations with AI and large-scale projection. Its focus is the relationship between an individual’s feelings and emotions shared across a group.

Two hundred participants engage in reflective conversations with a large language model. Their responses are encoded in Braille within videos of their irises, and the resulting material is projected onto the Dome. The system combines affective narrative embedding, iris segmentation, and emotional clustering to represent personal accounts alongside patterns of shared feeling.

The artwork connects a conversational encounter with an intimate bodily image and a public architectural display. That combination gives the project its approach to moving between personal and collective experience. The authors frame AI as a companion that invites reflection and civic empathy. The contribution is an artistic realization of that framing: a public installation organized around emotional expression, participation, and the visibility of shared experience.
summary.tldr: Gaze to the Stars turns AI-guided personal reflections and iris videos into a public installation about shared emotion.

title: Gaze to the Stars: AI and Public Art from Personal Affect and Collective Empathy

abstract: Boltzmann Generators have emerged as a promising machine learning tool for generating samples from equilibrium distributions of molecular systems using Normalizing Flows and importance weighting. Recently, Flow Matching has helped speed up Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs), scale them to more complex molecular systems, and minimize the length of the flow integration trajectories. We investigate the benefits of using path gradients to fine-tune CNFs initially trained by Flow Matching, in the setting where a target energy is known. Our experiments show that this hybrid approach yields up to a threefold increase in sampling efficiency for molecular systems, all while using the same model, a similar computational budget and without the need for additional sampling. Furthermore, by measuring the length of the flow trajectories during fine-tuning, we show that path gradients largely preserve the learned structure of the flow.

paragraphs: Boltzmann generators use learned transformations and importance weighting to sample equilibrium distributions of molecular systems. Flow matching has made continuous normalizing flows more practical by improving speed, supporting more complex systems, and shortening integration trajectories. This paper asks whether further training can improve sampling efficiency while retaining the useful structure learned through flow matching.

The proposed approach fine-tunes a flow-matching-trained model using path gradients. It applies in a setting where the target energy is known, providing information for the refinement stage. The study combines an initial training method that builds efficient flows with a subsequent gradient-based adjustment aimed at improving sampling from the desired molecular distribution.

Experiments show up to a threefold increase in sampling efficiency using the same model and a similar computational budget, without additional sampling. The authors also measure flow-trajectory lengths during fine-tuning and find that path gradients largely preserve the learned flow structure. This supports the hybrid approach as a way to improve sampling while retaining benefits of the original training.
summary.tldr: When target energy is known, path-gradient fine-tuning improves molecular sampling efficiency by up to threefold after flow matching.

title: Path Gradients after Flow Matching

abstract: Instance-dependent Partial Label Learning (ID-PLL) aims to learn a multi-class predictive model given training instances annotated with candidate labels related to features, among which correct labels are hidden fixed but unknown. The previous works involve leveraging the identification capability of the training model itself to iteratively refine supervision information. However, these methods overlook a critical aspect of ID-PLL: within the original label space, the model may fail to distinguish some incorrect candidate labels that are strongly correlated with features from correct labels. This leads to poor-quality supervision signals and creates a bottleneck in the training process. In this paper, we propose to leverage reduction-based pseudo-labels to alleviate the influence of incorrect candidate labels and train our predictive model to overcome this bottleneck. Specifically, reduction-based pseudo-labels are generated by performing weighted aggregation on the outputs of a multi-branch auxiliary model, with each branch trained in a label subspace that excludes certain labels. This approach ensures that each branch explicitly avoids the disturbance of the excluded labels, allowing the pseudo-labels provided for instances troubled by these excluded labels to benefit from the unaffected branches. Theoretically, we demonstrate that reduction-based pseudo-labels exhibit greater consistency with the Bayes optimal classifier compared to pseudo-labels directly generated from the training predictive model.

paragraphs: In instance-dependent partial-label learning, each example comes with several candidate labels, one of which is correct but unknown. Incorrect candidates can be strongly associated with the example's features. A predictive model may therefore struggle to distinguish them from the true label, weakening methods that repeatedly use that same model to refine its own supervision.

The proposed method generates replacement training targets through a separate, multi-branch auxiliary model. Each branch learns in a reduced label space that excludes certain labels. Weighted aggregation then combines the branches' predictions into pseudo-labels. When an example is confused by a particular incorrect candidate, branches that exclude that candidate can contribute predictions without its interference.

The resulting pseudo-labels are used to train the main predictive model. The authors provide a theoretical result showing greater consistency with the Bayes-optimal classifier than pseudo-labels generated directly by the training predictor. This supports the central idea that deliberately reducing label spaces can improve supervision when feature-correlated incorrect labels obstruct learning.
summary.tldr: The method combines predictions from reduced label spaces to generate better pseudo-labels for examples with feature-correlated incorrect candidate labels.

title: Reduction-based Pseudo-label Generation for Instance-dependent Partial Label Learning

abstract: Variance-dependent regret bounds have received increasing attention in recent studies on contextual bandits. However, most of these studies are focused on upper confidence bound (UCB)-based bandit algorithms, while sampling based bandit algorithms such as Thompson sampling are still understudied. The only exception is the `LinVDTS` algorithm (Xu et al., 2023), which is limited to linear reward function and its regret bound is not optimal with respect to the model dimension. In this paper, we present `FGTSVA`, a variance-aware Thompson Sampling algorithm for contextual bandits with general reward function with optimal regret bound. At the core of our analysis is an extension of the decoupling coefficient, a technique commonly used in the analysis of Feel-good Thompson sampling (FGTS) that reflects the complexity of the model space. With the new decoupling coefficient denoted by $\mathrm{dc}$, `FGTS-VA` achieves the regret of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{\mathrm{dc}\cdot\log|\mathcal{F}|\sum_{t=1}^T\sigma_t^2}+\mathrm{dc})$, where $|\mathcal{F}|$ is the size of the model space, $T$ is the total number of rounds, and $\sigma_t^2$ is the subgaussian norm of the noise (e.g., variance when the noise is Gaussian) at round $t$. In the setting of contextual linear bandits, the regret bound of `FGTSVA` matches that of UCB-based algorithms using weighted linear regression (Zhou and Gu, 2022).

summary.tldr: FGTS-VA gives variance-aware Thompson sampling regret guarantees for general reward functions and matches established UCB bounds in linear contextual bandits.

title: Variance-Aware Feel-Good Thompson Sampling for Contextual Bandits

abstract: Intracortical Brain-Computer Interfaces (iBCI) decode behavior from neural population activity to restore motor functions and communication abilities in individuals with motor impairments. A central challenge for long-term iBCI deployment is the nonstationarity of neural recordings, where the composition and tuning profiles of the recorded populations are unstable across recording sessions. Existing approaches attempt to address this issue by explicit alignment techniques; however, they rely on fixed neural identities and require test-time labels or parameter updates, limiting their generalization across sessions and imposing additional computational burden during deployment. In this work, we address the problem of cross-session nonstationarity in long-term iBCI systems and introduce SPINT - a Spatial Permutation-Invariant Neural Transformer framework for behavioral decoding that operates directly on unordered sets of neural units. Central to our approach is a novel context-dependent positional embedding scheme that dynamically infers unit-specific identities, enabling flexible generalization across recording sessions. SPINT supports inference on variable-size populations and allows few-shot, gradient-free adaptation using a small amount of unlabeled data from the test session. We evaluate SPINT on three multi-session datasets from the FALCON Benchmark, covering continuous motor decoding tasks in human and non-human primates. SPINT demonstrates robust cross-session generalization, outperforming existing zero-shot and few-shot unsupervised baselines while eliminating the need for test-time alignment and fine-tuning. Our work contributes an initial step toward a robust and scalable neural decoding framework for long-term iBCI applications.

paragraphs: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces decode behavior from recorded neural activity, but the recorded population can change across sessions. Individual units may appear, disappear, or change their tuning. SPINT addresses this instability by treating the input as an unordered collection of neural units, reducing dependence on a fixed arrangement or persistent unit identities.

Its context-dependent positional embeddings infer unit-specific identities dynamically. The model can therefore process populations of different sizes and adapt using a small amount of unlabeled data from a new session. This few-shot adaptation requires no gradient updates, avoiding test-time fine-tuning and explicit alignment.

The authors evaluate SPINT on three multi-session FALCON datasets covering continuous motor decoding in humans and non-human primates. It outperforms the compared zero-shot and few-shot unsupervised baselines and demonstrates robust generalization between sessions. The result supports a representation designed around changing neural populations as an alternative to repeatedly realigning recordings. The authors frame this as an initial step toward scalable, reliable decoding for long-term brain-computer interface use.
summary.tldr: SPINT decodes behavior from changing, unordered neural populations and adapts across sessions using limited unlabeled data without gradient updates.

title: SPINT: Spatial Permutation-Invariant Neural Transformer for Consistent Intracortical Motor Decoding

abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for supervising intermediate reasoning steps in large language models (LLMs). Previous PRMs are primarily trained on model final output responses and struggle to evaluate intermediate thinking trajectories robustly, especially in the emerging setting of trajectory–response outputs generated by frontier reasoning models like Deepseek-R1. In this work, we introduce ReasonFlux-PRM, a novel trajectory-aware PRM explicitly designed to evaluate the trajectory-response type of reasoning traces. ReasonFlux-PRM incorporates both step-level and trajectory-level supervision, enabling fine-grained reward assignment aligned with structured chain-of-thought data. We adapt ReasonFlux-PRM to support reward supervision under both offline and online settings, including (i) selecting high-quality model distillation data for downstream supervised fine-tuning of smaller models, (ii) providing dense process-level rewards for policy optimization during reinforcement learning, and (iii) enabling reward-guided Best-of-N test-time scaling. Empirical results on challenging downstream benchmarks such as AIME, MATH500, and GPQA-Diamond demonstrate that ReasonFlux-PRM-7B selects higher quality data than strong PRMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-72B) and human-curated baselines. Furthermore, ReasonFlux-PRM-7B yields consistent performance improvements, achieving average gains of 12.1\% in supervised fine-tuning, 4.5\% in reinforcement learning, and 6.3\% in test-time scaling. We also release an efficient ReasonFlux-PRM-1.5B for resource-constrained applications and edge deployment. Our code and models are released at https://github.com/Gen-Verse/ReasonFlux.

Existing versions often learn from final output responses and struggle with traces that contain a separate thinking trajectory followed by a response. ReasonFlux-PRM is designed around this trajectory–response structure, using supervision at both individual-step and whole-trajectory levels.

They can select reasoning examples for distilling a larger model into a smaller one, provide dense feedback during reinforcement learning, and guide selection among multiple answers at test time. These uses connect the evaluation of a reasoning process with concrete decisions about data, policy updates, and final responses.

title: ReasonFlux-PRM: Trajectory-Aware PRMs for Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs

abstract: Recent work studying the generalization of diffusion models with locally linear UNet-based denoisers reveals inductive biases that can be expressed via geometry-adaptive harmonic bases. For such locally linear UNets, these geometry-adaptive harmonic bases can be conveniently visualized through the eigen-decomposition of a UNet’s Jacobian matrix. In practice, however, more recent denoising networks are often transformer-based, e.g., the diffusion transformer (DiT). Due to the presence of nonlinear operations, similar eigen-decomposition analyses cannot be used to reveal the inductive biases of transformer-based denoisers. This motivates our search for alternative ways to explain the strong generalization ability observed in DiT models. Investigating a DiT’s pivotal attention modules, we find that locality of attention maps in a DiT’s early layers are closely associated with generalization. To verify this finding, we modify the generalization of a DiT by restricting its attention windows and observe an improvement in generalization. Furthermore, we empirically find that both the placement and the effective attention size of these local attention windows are crucial factors. Experimental results on the CelebA, ImageNet, MSCOCO, and LSUN data show that strengthening the inductive bias of a DiT can improve both generalization and generation quality when less training data is available. Source code is available at https://github.com/DiT-Generalization/DiT-Generalization.

paragraphs: This paper asks which architectural preferences help diffusion transformers generalize. Earlier work studied locally linear UNet denoisers through eigen-decompositions of their Jacobians. The nonlinear operations in transformer denoisers prevent the same analysis from revealing their inductive biases, motivating a different investigation centered on attention.

The authors find that local attention in early transformer layers is closely associated with generalization. They then restrict attention windows and observe improved generalization, providing an intervention beyond the initial association. Their experiments also show that the placement of these windows and their effective attention size are crucial.

Results on CelebA, ImageNet, MSCOCO, and LSUN show that strengthening this architectural preference can improve both generalization and image quality when training data is limited. The finding is specific about where the benefit comes from: local attention must be configured appropriately. It offers an empirical explanation and a design direction for diffusion transformers under reduced data availability, rather than establishing that every restriction on attention improves generation.
summary.tldr: Appropriately placed local attention windows improve diffusion-transformer generalization and generation quality in experiments with limited training data.

title: On Inductive Biases That Enable Generalization in Diffusion Transformers

abstract: In modern sequential decision-making systems, the construction of an optimal candidate action space is critical to efficient inference. However, existing approaches either rely on manually defined action spaces that lack scalability or utilize unstructured spaces that render exhaustive search computationally prohibitive. In this paper, we propose a novel framework named \textsc{DynaAct} for automatically constructing a compact action space to enhance sequential reasoning in complex problem-solving scenarios. Our method first estimates a proxy for the complete action space by extracting general sketches observed in a corpus covering diverse complex reasoning problems using large language models. We then formulate a submodular function that jointly evaluates candidate actions based on their utility to the current state and their diversity, and employ a greedy algorithm to select an optimal candidate set. Extensive experiments on six diverse standard benchmarks demonstrate that our approach significantly improves overall performance, while maintaining efficient inference without introducing substantial latency. The implementation is available at \url{https://github.com/zhaoxlpku/DynaAct}.

paragraphs: Sequential reasoning requires choosing what to do next at each stage of a problem. A manually specified menu of actions can be difficult to scale, while an unrestricted menu can make search prohibitively expensive. DynaAct addresses this tension by automatically constructing a compact set of candidate actions suited to the current reasoning state.

The framework first uses large language models to extract general action sketches from a corpus of varied, complex reasoning problems. These sketches provide an approximation to the complete action space. It then scores candidate sets using a submodular function that combines usefulness for the current state with diversity, and applies a greedy selection algorithm.

This design makes action selection itself part of the reasoning process: the system seeks relevant options without filling its candidate set with similar alternatives. Experiments on six standard benchmarks report significant overall performance improvements while preserving efficient inference without substantial additional latency. The findings support compact, dynamically selected action spaces as a practical way to improve sequential problem solving.
summary.tldr: DynaAct improves sequential reasoning by dynamically selecting compact action sets that balance immediate usefulness with diversity.

title: DynaAct: Large Language Model Reasoning with Dynamic Action Spaces

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) incurs high communication costs in both uplink and downlink. The literature largely focuses on lossy compression of model updates in deterministic FL. In contrast, stochastic (Bayesian) FL considers distributions over parameters, enabling uncertainty quantification, better generalization, and, crucially, inherent communication-regularized training through a mirror-descent structure. In this paper, we consider both uplink and downlink communication in stochastic FL, and propose a communication framework based on remote source generation. Employing Minimal Random Coding (MRC) for remote generation, we allow the server and the clients to sample from local and global posteriors (sources), respectively, rather than transmitting locally sampled updates. The framework encompasses communication-regularized local optimization and principled compression of model updates, leveraging gradually updated prior distributions as side information. Through extensive simulations, we show that our method achieves $5-32\times$ reduction in total communication cost while preserving accuracy. We further analyze the communication cost, refining existing MRC bounds and enabling precise quantification of uplink and downlink trade-offs. We also extend our method to conventional FL via stochastic quantization and prove a contraction property for the biased MRC compressor to facilitate convergence analysis.

summary.tldr: Remote sampling from parameter distributions reduces communication in both directions of federated learning while preserving accuracy in simulations.

title: Bi-Directional Communication-Efficient Stochastic FL via Remote Source Generation

abstract: We introduce LOKI, a compute-efficient framework for co-designing morphologies and control policies that generalize across unseen tasks. Inspired by biological adaptation—where animals quickly adjust to morphological changes—our method overcomes the inefficiencies of traditional evolutionary and quality-diversity algorithms. We propose learning convergent functions: shared control policies trained across clusters of morphologically similar designs in a learned latent space, drastically reducing the training cost per design. Simultaneously, we promote divergent forms by replacing mutation with dynamic local search, enabling broader exploration and preventing premature convergence. The policy reuse allows us to explore $\sim780\times$ more designs using 78\% fewer simulation steps and 40\% less compute per design. Local competition paired with a broader search results in a diverse set of high-performing final morphologies. Using the UNIMAL design space and a flat-terrain locomotion task, LOKI discovers a rich variety of designs—ranging from quadrupeds to crabs, bipedals, and spinners—far more diverse than those produced by prior work. These morphologies also transfer better to unseen downstream tasks in agility, stability, and manipulation domains (e.g. $2 \times$ higher reward on bump and push box incline tasks). Overall, our approach produces designs that are both diverse and adaptable, with substantially greater sample efficiency than existing co-design methods.

summary.tldr: LOKI reuses controllers across similar robot bodies to explore more designs efficiently and improve transfer to unseen tasks.

title: Convergent Functions, Divergent Forms

abstract: Generative video modeling has made significant strides, yet ensuring structural and temporal consistency over long sequences remains a challenge. Current methods predominantly rely on RGB signals, leading to accumulated errors in object structure and motion over extended durations. To address these issues, we introduce WorldWeaver, a robust framework for long video generation that jointly models RGB frames and perceptual conditions within a unified long-horizon modeling scheme. Our training framework offers three key advantages. First, by jointly predicting perceptual conditions and color information from a unified representation, it significantly enhances temporal consistency and motion dynamics. Second, by leveraging depth cues, which we observe to be more resistant to drift than RGB, we construct a memory bank that preserves clearer contextual information, improving quality in long-horizon video generation. Third, we employ segmented noise scheduling for training prediction groups, which further mitigates drift and reduces computational cost. Extensive experiments on both diffusion and rectified flow-based models demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldWeaver in reducing temporal drift and improving the fidelity of generated videos.

paragraphs: Long generated videos can gradually lose consistency as errors in object structure and motion accumulate. WorldWeaver addresses this drift by jointly modeling color frames and perceptual conditions over long sequences. Its premise is that RGB information alone does not provide the strongest basis for maintaining coherent structure through time.

The framework predicts perceptual conditions and color from a shared representation to improve temporal consistency and motion dynamics. It also builds a memory bank using depth cues, which the authors observe to resist drift better than RGB. A segmented noise schedule for training prediction groups further reduces drift and computational cost.

The contribution combines richer predicted information, depth-based contextual memory, and a training schedule designed for extended generation. These results support using perceptual structure throughout the generation process to help preserve context and motion over longer videos.
summary.tldr: WorldWeaver combines perceptual prediction, depth-based memory, and segmented noise scheduling to reduce drift in long video generation.

title: WorldWeaver: Generating Long-Horizon Video Worlds via Rich Perception

abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models, common in sequence generation, are limited in many biological tasks like de novo peptide sequencing and protein modeling by their unidirectional nature, failing to capture crucial global bidirectional token dependencies. Non-Autoregressive (NAR) models offer holistic, bidirectional representations but face challenges with generative coherence and scalability. To transcend this, we propose a hybrid framework enhancing AR generation by dynamically integrating rich contextual information from non-autoregressive mechanisms. Our approach couples a shared input encoder with two decoders: a non-autoregressive one learning latent bidirectional biological features, and an AR decoder synthesizing the biological sequence by leveraging these bidirectional features. A novel cross-decoder attention module enables the AR decoder to iteratively query and integrate these bidirectional features, enriching its predictions. This synergy is cultivated via a tailored training strategy with importance annealing for balanced objectives and cross-decoder gradient blocking for stable, focused learning. Evaluations on a demanding 9-species benchmark of de novo peptide sequencing task show our model substantially surpasses AR and NAR baselines. It uniquely harmonizes AR stability with NAR contextual awareness, delivering robust, superior performance on diverse downstream data. This research advances biological sequence modeling techniques and contributes a novel architectural paradigm for augmenting AR models with enhanced bidirectional understanding for complex sequence generation. Our code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/BEAM-Labs/denovo

paragraphs: Biological sequence generation benefits from dependencies that extend in both directions across a sequence. Autoregressive models generate sequentially, limiting their access to this global context. Non-autoregressive models can learn bidirectional representations, but face difficulties with coherent generation and scalability. This paper combines the two approaches so sequential generation can draw on richer biological context.

A shared input encoder feeds two decoders. The non-autoregressive decoder learns latent bidirectional features, while the autoregressive decoder generates the sequence. Cross-decoder attention allows the generating decoder to repeatedly query those features. Training uses importance annealing to balance objectives and blocks gradients across decoders to support stable, focused learning.

On a nine-species benchmark for de novo peptide sequencing, the authors report substantial improvements over both autoregressive and non-autoregressive baselines. They also report strong performance on diverse downstream data. The central contribution is an architecture that brings bidirectional information into autoregressive prediction through a separate learned representation, preserving the sequential decoder’s role in producing a coherent output.
summary.tldr: A hybrid biological sequence model improves autoregressive generation by letting it attend to bidirectional features learned by a second decoder.

title: Bidirectional Representations Augmented Autoregressive Biological Sequence Generation

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong generative capabilities but remain prone to inconsistencies and hallucinations. We introduce Peer Elicitation Games (PEG), a training-free, game-theoretic framework for aligning LLMs through a peer elicitation mechanism involving a generator and multiple discriminators instantiated from distinct base models. Discriminators interact in a peer evaluation setting, where utilities are computed using a determinant-based mutual information score that provably incentivizes truthful reporting without requiring ground-truth labels. We establish theoretical guarantees showing that each agent, via online learning, achieves sublinear regret in the sense their cumulative performance approaches that of the best fixed truthful strategy in hindsight. Moreover, we prove last-iterate convergence to a truthful Nash equilibrium, ensuring that the actual policies used by agents converge to stable and truthful behavior over time. Empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements in factual accuracy. These results position PEG as a practical approach for eliciting truthful behavior from LLMs without supervision or fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Peer Elicitation Games addresses language-model inconsistencies and hallucinations through interaction among models. The framework uses a generator and several discriminators instantiated from distinct base models. It requires neither ground-truth labels nor fine-tuning, instead designing a peer evaluation game whose incentives encourage participants to report truthfully.

Discriminator utilities are calculated with a determinant-based mutual information score. The authors prove that this mechanism incentivizes truthful reporting and that agents using online learning achieve sublinear regret relative to the best fixed truthful strategy in hindsight. This means the cumulative performance gap grows more slowly than the number of interactions.

The paper also proves convergence of the agents’ actual policies to a truthful Nash equilibrium, going beyond a guarantee about cumulative performance alone. These results combine formal guarantees about behavior within the proposed game with measured gains in model outputs, supporting peer elicitation as a practical route to better factual responses without supervised retraining.
summary.tldr: Peer Elicitation Games uses theoretically grounded incentives among models to encourage truthful reporting and improve factual accuracy without labels or fine-tuning.

title: Incentivizing Truthful Language Models via Peer Elicitation Games

abstract: We explore the concept of replicability, which ensures algorithmic consistency despite input data variations, for online pricing problems, specifically prophet inequalities and delegation. Given the crucial role of replicability in enhancing transparency in economic decision-making, we present a replicable and nearly optimal pricing strategy for prophet inequalities, achieving a sample complexity of $\textnormal{poly}(\log^* |\mathcal{X}|)$, where $\mathcal{X}$ is the ground set of distributions. Furthermore, we extend these findings to the delegation problem and establish lower bound that proves the necessity of the $\log^*|\mathcal{X}|$ dependence. En route to obtaining these results, we develop a number of technical contributions which are of independent interest. Most notably, we propose a new algorithm for a variant of the heavy hitter problem, which has a nearly linear dependence on the inverse of the heavy hitter parameter, significantly improving upon existing results which have a cubic dependence.

paragraphs: This paper studies online pricing algorithms that remain consistent despite variation in their input data. Such replicability matters for transparency in economic decisions: the analysis asks how to obtain stable algorithmic behavior while retaining strong pricing performance. The authors investigate this requirement for prophet inequalities and extend their findings to delegation.

They construct a replicable, nearly optimal pricing strategy whose sample complexity is polynomial in log-star of the size of the distribution ground set. Log-star is an iterated logarithm, making this a very slowly growing dependence on the ground-set size. A lower bound shows that dependence on this iterated-logarithm quantity is necessary, so it cannot simply be eliminated.

The proof development also produces an algorithm for a variant of the heavy hitter problem. Its dependence on the inverse heavy hitter parameter is nearly linear, improving on an existing cubic dependence. The contribution therefore includes both pricing guarantees and a separate technical improvement. The pricing result establishes near-optimality together with replicability, rather than treating consistency as an informal property of repeated runs.
summary.tldr: The paper develops nearly optimal replicable pricing with iterated-logarithmic sample dependence and proves that this dependence is necessary.

title: Replicable Online pricing

abstract: The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (AFDB) offers unparalleled structural coverage at near-experimental accuracy, positioning it as a valuable resource for data-driven protein design. However, its direct use in training deep models that are sensitive to fine-grained atomic geometry—such as inverse folding—exposes a critical limitation. Comparative analysis of structural feature distributions reveals that AFDB structures exhibit distinct statistical regularities, reflecting a systematic geometric bias that deviates from the conformational diversity found in experimentally determined structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). While AFDB structures are cleaner and more idealized, PDB structures capture the intrinsic variability and physical realism essential for generalization in downstream tasks. To address this discrepancy, we introduce a Debiasing Structure AutoEncoder (DeSAE) that learns to reconstruct native-like conformations from intentionally corrupted backbone geometries. By training the model to recover plausible structural states, DeSAE implicitly captures a more robust and natural structural manifold. At inference, applying DeSAE to AFDB structures produces debiased structures that significantly improve inverse folding performance across multiple benchmarks. This work highlights the critical impact of subtle systematic biases in predicted structures and presents a principled framework for debiasing, significantly boosting the performance of structure-based learning tasks like inverse folding.

paragraphs: Inverse folding uses a protein’s structure to guide sequence design, making the details of atomic geometry important. The paper examines whether the enormous AlphaFold Protein Structure Database can directly support this task. Its analysis finds systematic differences between predicted structures and experimentally determined structures: AlphaFold structures are more idealized, while experimental structures contain a broader range of conformations.

The authors introduce a Debiasing Structure AutoEncoder, or DeSAE, to address that mismatch.
