The result shows why high overall structural accuracy can coexist with biases that matter for downstream learning. For protein design models sensitive to fine geometry, adjusting the structural training material can therefore provide benefits beyond merely increasing its quantity.
summary.tldr: DeSAE corrects systematic geometric biases in AlphaFold structures and improves inverse folding performance across multiple benchmarks.

title: AlphaFold Database Debiasing for Robust Inverse Folding

abstract: Synthesizing radio-frequency (RF) data given the transmitter and receiver positions, e.g., received signal strength indicator (RSSI), is critical for wireless networking and sensing applications, such as indoor localization. However, it remains challenging due to complex propagation interactions, including reflection, diffraction, and scattering. State-of-the-art neural radiance field (NeRF)-based methods achieve high-fidelity RF data synthesis but are limited by long training times and high inference latency. We introduce GSRF, a framework that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from the optical domain to the RF domain, enabling efficient RF data synthesis. GSRF realizes this adaptation through three key innovations: First, it introduces complex-valued 3D Gaussians with a hybrid Fourier–Legendre basis to model directional and phase-dependent radiance. Second, it employs orthographic splatting for efficient ray–Gaussian intersection identification. Third, it incorporates a complex-valued ray tracing algorithm, executed on RF-customized CUDA kernels and grounded in wavefront propagation principles, to synthesize RF data in real time. Evaluated across various RF technologies, GSRF preserves high-fidelity RF data synthesis while achieving significant improvements in training efficiency, shorter training time, and reduced inference latency.

paragraphs: Predicting radio-frequency measurements from transmitter and receiver positions supports applications such as wireless networking and indoor localization. The task is difficult because signals undergo reflection, diffraction, and scattering. Neural radiance field methods can synthesize detailed RF data, but their training time and prediction latency motivate a more efficient representation.

GSRF adapts three-dimensional Gaussian splatting from optical rendering to radio signals. Its complex-valued Gaussians represent phase-dependent behavior, while a hybrid Fourier–Legendre basis models directional variation. Orthographic splatting helps identify intersections between rays and Gaussians efficiently. These components adapt the representation and geometric processing to the specific requirements of RF synthesis.

A complex-valued ray-tracing algorithm then generates RF data using wavefront propagation principles and CUDA kernels customized for the task. Evaluations across multiple RF technologies report high-fidelity synthesis alongside improved training efficiency, shorter training times, and lower inference latency, including real-time generation. The findings show that adapting both signal representation and computation can preserve synthesis quality while reducing the cost of modeling radio propagation.
summary.tldr: GSRF adapts Gaussian splatting to radio waves for high-fidelity RF synthesis with faster training and real-time inference.

title: GSRF: Complex-Valued 3D Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Radio-Frequency Data Synthesis

abstract: Driven by the applications in autonomous driving, robotics, and augmented reality, 3D object annotation is a critical task compared to 2D annotation, such as spatial complexity, occlusion, and viewpoint inconsistency. The existing methods relying on single models often struggle with these issues. In this paper, we introduce Tri-MARF, a novel framework that integrates tri-modal inputs (i.e., 2D multi-view images, text descriptions, and 3D point clouds) with multi-agent collaboration to enhance the 3D annotation process. Our Tri-MARF consists of three specialized agents: a vision-language model agent that generates multi-view descriptions, an information aggregation agent that selects optimal descriptions, and a gating agent that aligns text descriptions with 3D geometries for more refined captioning. Extensive experiments on the Objaverse-LVIS, Objaverse-XL, and ABO datasets demonstrate the superiority of our Tri-MARF, which achieves a CLIPScore of 88.7 (compared to 78.6–82.4 for other SOTA methods), retrieval accuracy of 45.2/43.8 (ViLT R@5), and an impressive throughput of 12,000 objects per hour on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

paragraphs: Annotating a 3D object requires reconciling what different views reveal about its shape and identity. Occlusion can hide important features, and descriptions from separate viewpoints can disagree. Tri-MARF addresses these difficulties by combining images from multiple views, text descriptions, and 3D point clouds within a framework of three collaborating agents.

Each agent handles a different part of the annotation process. A vision-language agent produces descriptions from the images. An aggregation agent selects the most suitable descriptions, while a gating agent aligns the selected language with the object's 3D geometry. This division connects visual description, information selection, and geometric checking to produce more refined captions.

The framework reaches a CLIPScore of 88.7, against 78.6–82.4 for other state-of-the-art approaches, and processes 12,000 objects per hour on one NVIDIA A100 GPU. These findings support both the annotation quality and processing efficiency of combining complementary inputs with specialized agents in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Tri-MARF combines multiple views, text, and 3D geometry through three specialized agents to improve the quality and speed of 3D object annotation.

title: 3D-Agent: A Tri-Modal Multi-Agent Responsive Framework for Comprehensive 3D Object Annotation

abstract: Recent advances in graph neural network (GNN)-based neural operators have demonstrated significant progress in solving partial differential equations (PDEs) by effectively representing computational meshes. However, most existing approaches overlook the intrinsic physical and topological meaning of higher-order elements in the mesh, which are closely tied to differential forms. In this paper, we propose a higher-order GNN framework that incorporates higher-order interactions based on discrete and finite element exterior calculus. The time-independent boundary value problems (BVPs) in electromagnetism are instantiated to illustrate the proposed framework. It can be easily generalized to other PDEs that admit differential form formulations. Moreover, the novel physics-informed loss terms, integrated form estimators, and theoretical support are derived correspondingly. Experiments show that our proposed method outperforms the existing neural operators by large margins on BVPs in electromagnetism. Our code is available at https://github.com/Supradax/Higher-Order-Differential-Topology-aware-GNN.

title: Boundary-Value PDEs Meet Higher-Order Differential Topology-aware GNNs

abstract: In this paper, we propose \textbf{Jasmine}, the first Stable Diffusion (SD)-based self-supervised framework for monocular depth estimation, which effectively harnesses SD’s visual priors to enhance the sharpness and generalization of unsupervised prediction. Previous SD-based methods are all supervised since adapting diffusion models for dense prediction requires high-precision supervision. In contrast, self-supervised reprojection suffers from inherent challenges (\textit{e.g.}, occlusions, texture-less regions, illumination variance), and the predictions exhibit blurs and artifacts that severely compromise SD's latent priors. To resolve this, we construct a novel surrogate task of mix-batch image reconstruction. Without any additional supervision, it preserves the detail priors of SD models by reconstructing the images themselves while preventing depth estimation from degradation. Furthermore, to address the inherent misalignment between SD's scale and shift invariant estimation and self-supervised scale-invariant depth estimation, we build the Scale-Shift GRU. It not only bridges this distribution gap but also isolates the fine-grained texture of SD output against the interference of reprojection loss. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Jasmine achieves SoTA performance on the KITTI benchmark and exhibits superior zero-shot generalization across multiple datasets.

paragraphs: Jasmine adapts Stable Diffusion’s learned visual knowledge to self-supervised depth estimation from a single image. The difficulty is that reprojection-based training can introduce blur and artifacts when images contain occlusion, little texture, or changing illumination. Those imperfect training signals can undermine the detailed visual information that makes the pretrained diffusion model useful.

This auxiliary task preserves the model’s detail priors while protecting depth estimation from degradation. The results support adapting a diffusion model’s visual priors through carefully designed self-supervised objectives, rather than relying on the high-precision supervision used by the earlier Stable Diffusion depth methods described in the abstract.
summary.tldr: Jasmine combines image reconstruction and scale-shift adaptation to use Stable Diffusion’s visual priors for self-supervised depth estimation.

title: Jasmine: Harnessing Diffusion Prior for Self-supervised Depth Estimation

abstract: This paper introduces a novel iterative method for missing data imputation that sequentially reduces the mutual information between data and the corresponding missingness mask. Inspired by GAN-based approaches that train generators to decrease the predictability of missingness patterns, our method explicitly targets this reduction in mutual information. Specifically, our algorithm iteratively minimizes the KL divergence between the joint distribution of the imputed data and missingness mask, and the product of their marginals from the previous iteration. We show that the optimal imputation under this framework can be achieved by solving an ODE whose velocity field minimizes a rectified flow training objective. We further illustrate that some existing imputation techniques can be interpreted as approximate special cases of our mutual-information-reducing framework. Comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the efficacy of our proposed approach, demonstrating its superior imputation performance. Our implementation is available at \url{https://github.com/yujhml/MIRI-Imputation}.

paragraphs: This paper approaches missing-value imputation by reducing the dependence between completed data and the pattern of missing entries. The missingness mask records which values were absent. The central idea is that imputed data should become less informative about this mask, making the missingness pattern harder to infer from the completed values.

The algorithm works iteratively. At each step, it minimizes the KL divergence between the joint distribution of completed data and masks and a product of their marginal distributions from the previous step. This turns the broad goal of reducing mutual information into a sequence of distribution-matching problems.

The authors show that optimal imputation within this framework can be obtained by solving an ordinary differential equation whose velocity field is learned through a rectified-flow objective. They also interpret some existing imputation techniques as approximate special cases. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior imputation performance. The contribution therefore combines an explicit information-based objective, a flow-based procedure for solving it, and a common perspective on several earlier approaches.
summary.tldr: An iterative rectified-flow method fills missing values by reducing statistical dependence between completed data and missingness patterns.

title: Missing Data Imputation by Reducing Mutual Information with Rectified Flows

abstract: Efficient equilibrium sampling of molecular conformations remains a core challenge in computational chemistry and statistical inference. Classical approaches such as molecular dynamics or Markov chain Monte Carlo inherently lack amortization; the computational cost of sampling must be paid in-full for each system of interest. The widespread success of generative models has inspired interest into overcoming this limitation through learning sampling algorithms. Despite performing on par with conventional methods when trained on a single system, learned samplers have so far demonstrated limited ability to transfer across systems. We prove that deep learning enables the design of scalable and transferable samplers by introducing Ensemble, a 200 million parameter all-atom transferable normalizing flow trained on a corpus of peptide molecular dynamics trajectories up to 8 residues in length. Ensemble draws zero-shot uncorrelated proposal samples for arbitrary peptide systems, achieving the previously intractable transferability across sequence length, whilst retaining the efficient likelihood evaluation of normalizing flows. Through extensive empirical evaluation we demonstrate the efficacy of Ensemble as a proposal for a variety of sampling algorithms, finding a simple importance sampling-based finetuning procedure to achieve superior performance to established methods such as sequential Monte Carlo. We open-source the Ensemble codebase, model weights, and training dataset, to further stimulate research into amortized sampling methods and finetuning objectives.

paragraphs: Sampling molecular shapes at equilibrium is expensive because conventional simulation methods must repeat substantial computation for each molecular system. Learned samplers offer a way to spread training costs across future sampling tasks, but previous approaches have transferred poorly between systems. This paper introduces Ensemble to make that reuse possible across peptide systems and sequence lengths.

Ensemble is a normalizing flow with 200 million parameters that represents all atoms and is trained on peptide simulation trajectories containing up to eight residues. It produces uncorrelated proposal samples for peptide systems without system-specific training, including transfer across sequence length. Its flow structure also preserves efficient evaluation of sample likelihoods, which supports its use within sampling algorithms.

The authors evaluate Ensemble as a proposal generator for several sampling methods. They find that a simple fine-tuning procedure based on importance sampling outperforms established methods such as sequential Monte Carlo in their evaluations. The distinction between proposals and equilibrium samples matters: the framework supplies reusable learned proposals that sampling procedures can exploit. Code, weights, and training data are released to support further work.
summary.tldr: Ensemble learns transferable molecular sampling proposals that work across peptide lengths and support effective importance-sampling-based fine-tuning.

title: Amortized Sampling with Transferable Normalizing Flows

abstract: Recent advances in video generation models have sparked interest in world models capable of simulating realistic environments. While navigation has been well-explored, physically meaningful interactions that mimic real-world forces remain largely understudied. In this work, we investigate using physical forces as a control signal for video generation and propose force prompts which enable users to interact with images through both localized point forces, such as poking a plant, and global wind force fields, such as wind blowing on fabric. We demonstrate that these force prompts can enable videos to respond realistically to physical control signals by leveraging the physical prior in the original pretrained model, without using any 3D asset or physics simulator at inference. The primary challenge of force prompting is the difficulty in obtaining high quality paired force-video training data, both in the real world due to the difficulty of obtaining force signals, and in synthetic data due to limitations in the visual quality and domain diversity of physics simulators. Our key finding is that video generation models can *generalize* remarkably well when adapted to follow physical force conditioning from videos synthesized by Blender, even with limited demonstrations of few objects (e.g., flying flags, rolling balls, etc.). Our method can generate videos which simulate forces across diverse geometries, settings, and materials. We also try to understand the source of this generalization and perform ablations on the training data that reveal two key elements: visual diversity and the use of specific text keywords during training. Our approach is trained on only around 15k training examples for a single day on four A100 GPUs, and outperforms existing methods on force adherence and physics realism, bringing world models closer to real-world physics interactions. All datasets, code, and model weights will be open-sourced. Video examples can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/force-prompting-neurips2025
originalAbstract: Recent advances in video generation models have sparked interest in world models capable of simulating realistic environments. While navigation has been well-explored, physically meaningful interactions that mimic real-world forces remain largely understudied. In this work, we investigate using physical forces as a control signal for video generation and propose force prompts which enable users to interact with images through both localized point forces, such as poking a plant, and global wind force fields, such as wind blowing on fabric. We demonstrate that these force prompts can enable videos to respond realistically to physical control signals by leveraging the physical prior in the original pretrained model, without using any 3D asset or physics simulator at inference. The primary challenge of force prompting is the difficulty in obtaining high quality paired force-video training data, both in the real world due to the difficulty of obtaining force signals, and in synthetic data due to limitations in the visual quality and domain diversity of physics simulators. Our key finding is that video generation models can *generalize* remarkably well when adapted to follow physical force conditioning from videos synthesized by Blender, even with limited demonstrations of few objects (e.g., flying flags, rolling balls, etc.). Our method can generate videos which simulate forces across diverse geometries, settings, and materials. We also try to understand the source of this generalization and perform ablations on the training data that reveal two key elements: visual diversity and the use of specific text keywords during training. Our approach is trained on only around 15k training examples for a single day on four A100 GPUs, and outperforms existing methods on force adherence and physics realism, bringing world models closer to real-world physics interactions. All datasets, code, and model weights will be open-sourced. Video examples can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/force-prompting-neurips2025

paragraphs: Force prompting lets users control generated video through physical signals, such as a push at one location or a wind field across a scene. The paper investigates whether pretrained video models can turn these controls into realistic motion. A central obstacle is collecting paired forces and videos: real forces are difficult to measure, while simulated videos have limited appearance quality and diversity.

The authors adapt a pretrained model using Blender-generated examples involving a limited collection of objects. The model then generalizes force-conditioned generation across varied geometries, environments, and materials. At inference, it uses the physical prior learned by the video model without requiring a physics simulator or a three-dimensional asset.

Training uses around 15,000 examples and one day on four A100 GPUs. The approach outperforms the compared methods on force adherence and physical realism. Ablations identify visual diversity and specific training text keywords as important to generalization. These findings suggest that limited simulated demonstrations can help expose useful physical control capabilities in pretrained video models.
summary.tldr: Force prompting adapts pretrained video models with simulated examples so generated scenes respond to physical controls without a simulator at inference.

title: Force Prompting: Video Generation Models Can Learn And Generalize Physics-based Control Signals

abstract: Contrastive learning involves learning representations via a loss function that encourages each (unlabeled) sample to be far from other samples, but close to its own *augmentation*. In this paper, we aim to understand why this simple idea performs remarkably well, by theoretically analyzing it for a simple, natural problem setting: dimensionality reduction in Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs). Note that the standard GMM setup lacks the concept of augmentations. We study an intuitive extension: we define the pair of data sample and its augmentation as a coupled random draw from the GMM such that the marginal over the "noisy" augmentation is *biased* towards the component of the data sample. For this setup, we show that vanilla contrastive loss, e.g., InfoNCE, is able to find the *optimal* lower-dimensional subspace even when the Gaussian components are non-isotropic. In particular, we show that InfoNCE can match the performance of a fully supervised algorithm, e.g., LDA, (where each data point is labeled with the mixture component it comes from) even when the augmentations are "noisy". We further extend our setup to the multi-modal case, and develop a GMM-like setting to study the contrastive CLIP loss. We corroborate our theoretical with real-data experiments on CIFAR100; representations learned by InfoNCE loss match the performance of LDA on clustering metrics.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning draws a sample's representation toward its augmented version while separating it from other samples. This paper investigates why that objective can produce useful representations by analyzing dimensionality reduction in Gaussian mixture models. The setting provides a structured way to study what information contrastive learning can recover without mixture-component labels.

Because an ordinary Gaussian mixture model does not define augmentations, the authors introduce coupled sample pairs. The augmentation is noisy but biased toward the component that generated the original sample. In this setting, they show that InfoNCE can recover the optimal lower-dimensional subspace even when Gaussian components are non-isotropic. It can match supervised linear discriminant analysis despite the noisy augmentations.

The paper also extends its modeling setup to multiple modalities to study the CLIP contrastive loss. Experiments on CIFAR100 provide supporting empirical evidence: representations learned with InfoNCE match linear discriminant analysis on clustering metrics. The theoretical conclusion is tied to the proposed mixture and augmentation setting, while the real-data result shows a corresponding comparison in the reported experiment.
summary.tldr: In a Gaussian-mixture setting with noisy coupled augmentations, InfoNCE can recover an optimal subspace and match supervised linear discriminant analysis.

title: Understanding Contrastive Learning via Gaussian Mixture Models

abstract: Understanding how the test risk scales with model complexity is a central question in machine learning. Classical theory is challenged by the learning curves observed for large over-parametrized deep networks. Capacity measures based on parameter count typically fail to account for these empirical observations. To tackle this challenge, we consider norm-based capacity measures and develop our study for random features based estimators, widely used as simplified theoretical models for more complex networks. In this context, we provide a precise characterization of how the estimator’s norm concentrates and how it governs the associated test error. Our results show that the predicted learning curve admits a phase transition from under- to over-parameterization, but no double descent behavior. This confirms that more classical U-shaped behavior is recovered considering appropriate capacity measures based on models norms rather than size. From a technical point of view, we leverage deterministic equivalence as the key tool and further develop new deterministic quantities which are of independent interest.

paragraphs: How test error changes with model complexity depends partly on how complexity is measured. Counting parameters often fails to explain the behavior of large, overparameterized networks. This paper instead studies capacity measures based on model norms, using random-feature estimators as a simplified theoretical setting for understanding more complex networks.

The authors precisely characterize how the estimator's norm concentrates and how it governs test error. Their main mathematical tool is deterministic equivalence, and they develop new deterministic quantities as part of the analysis. This connects a norm-based description of the fitted model with predictions about its generalization behavior.

In this setting, the predicted learning curve has a transition between underparameterization and overparameterization but does not show double descent. Using the norm-based capacity measure recovers a more classical U-shaped relationship. The result shows how the chosen complexity measure can change the apparent shape of generalization, with the formal characterization established for the random-feature estimators studied rather than for every deep network.
summary.tldr: For random-feature estimators, norm-based capacity analysis recovers a U-shaped generalization curve without double descent.

title: The $\varphi$ Curve: The Shape of Generalization through the Lens of Norm-based Capacity Control

abstract: Controlling specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities is a central challenge for safe and reliable artificial intelligence deployment. Current steering methods, such as vector addition and directional ablation, are constrained within a two-dimensional subspace defined by the activation and feature direction, making them sensitive to chosen parameters and potentially affecting unrelated features due to unintended interactions in activation space. We introduce Angular Steering, a novel and flexible method for behavior modulation that operates by rotating activations within a fixed two-dimensional subspace. By formulating steering as a geometric rotation toward or away from a target behavior direction, Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors such as refusal and compliance. We demonstrate this method using refusal steering emotion steering as use cases. Additionally, we propose Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant that rotates only activations aligned with the target feature, further enhancing stability and coherence. Angular Steering generalizes existing addition and orthogonalization techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework, simplifying parameter selection and maintaining model stability across a broader range of adjustments. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show that Angular Steering achieves robust behavioral control while maintaining general language modeling performance, underscoring its flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches. Code and artifacts are available at \url{https://github.com/lone17/angular-steering/}.

paragraphs: Angular Steering addresses how to change a language model’s behavior while preserving its broader language abilities. Existing approaches modify internal activations by adding a feature direction or removing a component along it. The paper argues that these operations can be sensitive to parameter choices and can unintentionally interact with unrelated features.

The proposed method expresses steering as a rotation within a fixed two-dimensional activation subspace. Rotating toward or away from a behavior direction provides a continuous way to adjust its influence. The authors demonstrate refusal and emotion steering. An adaptive version applies rotations selectively to activations already aligned with the target feature, aiming to improve stability and coherence.

The paper places addition and orthogonalization methods within a shared geometric framework, making steering parameters easier to manage. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes report robust behavioral control while retaining general language modeling performance. These findings support rotation as a flexible control mechanism over the tested adjustments, rather than establishing that every behavioral intervention preserves all capabilities.
summary.tldr: Angular Steering controls language-model behavior through activation rotations, with experiments showing stable adjustments while preserving general language modeling performance.

title: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space

abstract: Backdoor learning is a critical research topic for understanding the vulnerabilities of deep neural networks. While the diffusion model (DM) has been broadly deployed in public over the past few years, the understanding of its backdoor vulnerability is still in its infancy compared to the extensive studies in discriminative models. Recently, many different backdoor attack and defense methods have been proposed for DMs, but a comprehensive benchmark for backdoor learning on DMs is still lacking. This absence makes it difficult to conduct fair comparisons and thoroughly evaluate existing approaches, thus hindering future research progress. To address this issue, we propose *BackdoorDM*, the first comprehensive benchmark designed for backdoor learning on DMs. It comprises nine state-of-the-art (SOTA) attack methods, four SOTA defense strategies, and three useful visualization analysis tools. We first systematically classify and formulate the existing literature in a unified framework, focusing on three different backdoor attack types and five backdoor target types, which are restricted to a single type in discriminative models. Then, we systematically summarize the evaluation metrics for each type and propose a unified backdoor evaluation method based on multimodal large language model (MLLM). Finally, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation and highlight several important conclusions. We believe that BackdoorDM will help overcome current barriers and contribute to building a trustworthy artificial intelligence generated content (AIGC) community. The codes are released in https://github.com/linweiii/BackdoorDM.

paragraphs: Research on diffusion-model backdoors has produced multiple attacks and defenses, but comparing them fairly requires shared definitions and evaluation procedures. BackdoorDM addresses this evaluation problem. It brings existing methods into a common benchmark so that differences in attack setup or measurement do not remain separate, incompatible research conventions.

The benchmark includes nine attack methods, four defense strategies, and three visualization tools. Its organizing framework distinguishes three attack types and five target types, reflecting the variety of backdoor behavior studied in diffusion models. This classification gives researchers a common language for specifying what an attack attempts to produce and how a defense should be assessed.

The authors also summarize evaluation metrics for the different types and propose a unified evaluator based on a multimodal large language model. They conduct a comprehensive evaluation using the framework. The contribution is an infrastructure for systematic comparison and analysis: combining implementations, categories, metrics, and visualizations makes it easier to examine diffusion-model vulnerabilities within one experimental setting.
summary.tldr: BackdoorDM unifies diffusion-model backdoor attacks, defenses, and evaluation tools in a comprehensive benchmark.

title: BackdoorDM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Backdoor Learning on Diffusion Model

abstract: Power flow (PF) calculations are the backbone of real-time grid operations, across workflows such as contingency analysis (where repeated PF evaluations assess grid security under outages) and topology optimization (which involves PF-based searches over combinatorially large action spaces). Running these calculations at operational timescales or across large evaluation spaces remains a major computational bottleneck. Additionally, growing uncertainty in power system operations from the integration of renewables and climate-induced extreme weather also calls for tools that can accurately and efficiently simulate a wide range of scenarios and operating conditions. Machine learning methods offer a potential speedup over traditional solvers, but their performance has not been systematically assessed on benchmarks that capture real-world variability. This paper introduces PF∆, a benchmark dataset for power flow that captures diverse variations in load, generation, and topology. PF∆ contains 859,800 solved power flow instances spanning six different bus system sizes, capturing three types of contingency scenarios (N , N –1, and N –2), and including close-to-infeasible cases near steady-state voltage stability limits. We evaluate traditional solvers and GNN-based methods, highlighting key areas where existing approaches struggle, and identifying open problems for future research. Our dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/pfdelta/pfdelta/tree/main and our code with data generation scripts and model implementations is at https: //github.com/MOSSLab-MIT/pfdelta

Repeating these calculations for outage analysis or topology searches can become a computational bottleneck. Machine learning could accelerate the process, but evaluating that promise requires benchmarks covering the variability that power systems encounter.

PF∆ provides 859,800 solved power-flow instances across six bus-system sizes. The dataset varies electricity demand, generation, and network topology, and includes N, N−1, and N−2 contingency settings. It also contains cases close to infeasibility near steady-state voltage stability limits, extending evaluation to conditions where the grid is approaching an important operating boundary.

The authors evaluate traditional solvers and methods based on graph neural networks, identifying areas of difficulty and open research problems. The benchmark’s contribution is to make performance under varied operating conditions available for systematic study. Its coverage is motivated by uncertainty from renewable integration and extreme weather, as well as the large scenario spaces encountered in grid operations. The reported evaluation highlights challenges rather than claiming that learned methods have resolved them.
summary.tldr: PF∆ benchmarks power-flow methods on 859,800 solved cases covering varied operating conditions, contingencies, and near-infeasible states.

title: PF∆: A Benchmark Dataset for Power Flow under Load, Generation, and Topology Variations

abstract: As the field progresses toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), there is a pressing need for more comprehensive and insightful evaluation frameworks that go beyond aggregate performance metrics. This paper introduces a unified rating system that jointly models the difficulty of individual test cases and the competency of AI models (or humans) across vision, language, and action domains. Unlike existing metrics that focus solely on models, our approach allows for fine-grained, difficulty-aware evaluations through competitive interactions between models and tasks, capturing both the long-tail distribution of real-world challenges and the competency gap between current models and full task mastery. We validate the generalizability and robustness of our system through extensive experiments on multiple established datasets and models across distinct AGI domains. The resulting rating distributions offer novel perspectives and interpretable insights into task difficulty, model progression, and the outstanding challenges that remain on the path to achieving full AGI task mastery. We have made our code and results publicly available at https://ss47816.github.io/AGI-Elo/.

paragraphs: An aggregate benchmark score describes how often a model succeeds, but it gives a limited picture of which challenges remain. AGI-Elo approaches evaluation by rating both the capability of the system being tested and the difficulty of individual test cases. The framework is intended to cover AI models or humans across vision, language, and action.

Its ratings arise from competitive interactions between models and tasks. Treating task difficulty as something to estimate makes evaluation sensitive to the distribution of challenges, including difficult cases in the long tail. This supports a more detailed account of the gap between current competence and mastery of a task than a model-only summary provides.

The authors evaluate the system across multiple established datasets and models from different domains, reporting evidence of robustness and generalizability. The resulting rating distributions help interpret task difficulty, model progress, and unresolved challenges. The contribution is a shared evaluation framework for examining those relationships, rather than merely compressing performance into another aggregate score.
summary.tldr: AGI-Elo jointly rates model competence and test-case difficulty to reveal performance gaps hidden by aggregate benchmark scores.

title: AGI-Elo: How Far Are We From Mastering A Task?

abstract: Grounding language in perception and action is a key challenge when building situated agents that can interact with humans, or other agents, via language. In the past, addressing this challenge has required manually designing the language grounding or curating massive datasets that associate language with the environment. We propose Ground-Compose-Reinforce, an end-to-end, neurosymbolic framework for training RL agents directly from high-level task specifications—without manually designed reward functions or other domain-specific oracles, and without massive datasets. These task specifications take the form of Reward Machines, automata-based representations that capture high-level task structure and are in some cases autoformalizable from natural language. Critically, we show that Reward Machines can be grounded using limited data by exploiting compositionality. Experiments in a custom Meta-World domain with only 350 labelled pretraining trajectories show that our framework faithfully elicits complex behaviours from high-level specifications—including behaviours that never appear in pretraining—while non-compositional approaches fail.

paragraphs: An agent that follows high-level instructions must connect those instructions to what it perceives and does. Building that connection has often required manually specified grounding or large collections of language-environment examples. Ground-Compose-Reinforce studies whether agents can instead learn from limited labeled experience by reusing and combining pieces of task structure.

The framework represents high-level tasks with Reward Machines, automata that encode how a task is organized. In some cases, these representations can be produced automatically from natural language. The method combines symbolic task structure with learned grounding and reinforcement learning, without manually designed reward functions or domain-specific oracles. Its central idea is to exploit compositionality when grounding the Reward Machines.

In a custom Meta-World domain, the authors use only 350 labeled pretraining trajectories. They report that the resulting agents faithfully perform complex specified behaviors, including behaviors absent from pretraining, while non-compositional approaches fail. This provides evidence that combining grounded components can extend the usefulness of limited demonstrations. The result concerns the evaluated domain and supports compositional learning as a route to more data-efficient instruction grounding.
summary.tldr: Ground-Compose-Reinforce uses compositional Reward Machines to learn complex agent behaviors from limited labeled trajectories.

title: Ground-Compose-Reinforce: Grounding Language in Agentic Behaviours using Limited Data

abstract: We revisit the problem of private online learning, in which a learner receives a sequence of $T$ data points and has to respond at each time-step a hypothesis. It is required that the entire stream of output hypotheses should satisfy differential privacy. Prior work of Golowich and Livni [2021] established that every concept class $\mathcal{H}$ with finite Littlestone dimension $d$ is privately online learnable in the realizable setting. In particular, they proposed an algorithm that achieves an $O_{d}(\log T)$ mistake bound against an oblivious adversary. However, their approach yields a suboptimal $\tilde{O}\_{d}(\sqrt{T})$ bound against an adaptive adversary. In this work, we present a new algorithm with a mistake bound of $O_{d}(\log T)$ against an adaptive adversary, closing this gap. We further investigate the problem in the agnostic setting, which is more general than the realizable setting as it does not impose any assumptions on the data. We give an algorithm that obtains a sublinear regret of $\tilde{O}_d(\sqrt{T})$ for generic Littlestone classes, demonstrating that they are also privately online learnable in the agnostic setting.

paragraphs: In private online learning, a learner receives data sequentially and releases a hypothesis at every step. Privacy must hold for the entire sequence of released hypotheses. This paper studies how well such a learner can perform when an adversary adapts future data to the interaction, making the setting harder than a sequence chosen independently beforehand.

For concept classes with finite Littlestone dimension d, the authors give an algorithm with a mistake bound growing logarithmically with the number of rounds T in the realizable setting. This setting assumes the data can be explained by a hypothesis in the class. The result closes a gap between earlier guarantees for oblivious and adaptive adversaries.

The paper also treats the agnostic setting, which removes that realizability requirement. Here, the algorithm achieves regret scaling roughly with the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors and dependence on d. Sublinear regret means the average excess loss relative to the best comparator decreases over time, establishing private online learnability in this broader setting.
summary.tldr: New algorithms establish strong private online learning guarantees against adaptive adversaries in both realizable and agnostic settings.

title: Private Online Learning against an Adaptive Adversary: Realizable and Agnostic Settings

abstract: Open-source foundation models have seen rapid adoption and development, enabling powerful general-purpose capabilities across diverse domains. However, fine-tuning large foundation models for domain-specific or personalized tasks remains prohibitively expensive for most users due to the significant memory overhead beyond that of inference. We introduce EMLoC, an Emulator-based Memory-efficient fine-tuning framework with LoRA Correction, which enables model fine-tuning within the same memory budget required for inference. EMLoC constructs a task-specific light-weight emulator using activation-aware singular value decomposition (SVD) on a small downstream calibration set. Fine-tuning then is performed on this lightweight emulator via LoRA. To tackle the misalignment between the original model and the compressed emulator, we propose a novel compensation algorithm to correct the fine-tuned LoRA module, which thus can be merged into the original model for inference. EMLoC supports flexible compression ratios and standard training pipelines, making it adaptable to a wide range of applications. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EMLoC outperforms other baselines across multiple datasets and modalities. Moreover, without quantization, EMLoC enables fine-tuning of a 38B model, which originally required 95GB of memory, on a single 24GB consumer GPU—bringing efficient and practical model adaptation to individual users.

paragraphs: Adapting a large foundation model usually requires more memory than running it for inference, putting customization beyond many users' hardware budgets. EMLoC addresses this gap by performing fine-tuning on a compressed, task-specific emulator and transferring the learned adaptation back to the original model.

The emulator is built using activation-aware singular value decomposition on a small calibration dataset from the downstream task. LoRA then learns the adaptation on this lightweight model. Compression changes the model on which those updates were learned, so simply transferring them can create a mismatch. EMLoC introduces a compensation algorithm that corrects the fine-tuned LoRA module before merging it into the original model for inference.

The framework supports different compression ratios and standard training pipelines. Experiments across datasets and modalities outperform the compared baselines. A reported demonstration fine-tunes a 38-billion-parameter model on one 24 GB consumer GPU without quantization, where the original requirement was 95 GB. This illustrates how emulator training plus correction can bring adaptation within an inference-sized memory budget.
summary.tldr: EMLoC fine-tunes a compressed emulator and corrects its LoRA updates for the original model, reducing adaptation memory requirements.

title: EMLoC: Emulator-based Memory-efficient Fine-tuning with LoRA Correction

abstract: We introduce a full-stack framework that scales up reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) to long videos, leveraging reinforcement learning. We address the unique challenges of long video reasoning by integrating three critical components: (1) a large-scale dataset, LongVideo-Reason, comprising 104K long video QA pairs with high-quality reasoning annotations across diverse domains such as sports, games, and vlogs; (2) a two-stage training pipeline that extends VLMs with chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning (CoT-SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL); and (3) a training infrastructure for long video RL, named Multi-modal Reinforcement Sequence Parallelism (MR-SP), which incorporates sequence parallelism and a vLLM-based engine tailored for long video, using cached video embeddings for efficient rollout and prefilling. In our experiments, LongVILA-R1-7B achieves strong performance on video benchmarks, reaching 65.1% and 71.1% accuracy on VideoMME without and with subtitles, respectively, and consistently outperforming LongVILA-7B across multiple benchmarks. Moreover, LongVILA-R1-7B supports processing up to 8,192 video frames per video, and configurable FPS settings. Notably, our MR-SP system achieves up to 2.1x speedup on long video RL training. In addition, we release our training system for public availability that supports RL training on various modalities (video, text, and audio), various models (VILA and Qwen series), and even image and video generation models. On a single A100 node (8 GPUs), it supports RL training on hour-long videos (e.g., 3,600 frames). Code and models are available at https://github.com/NVlabs/Long-RL

title: Scaling RL to Long Videos

abstract: We approach the problem of estimating the parameters of a latent tree graphical model from a hierarchical tensor decomposition point of view. In this new view, the marginal probability table of the observed variables in a latent tree is treated as a tensor, and we show that: (i) the latent variables induce low rank structures in various matricizations of the tensor; (ii) this collection of low rank matricizations induce a hierarchical low rank decomposition of the tensor. Exploiting these properties, we derive an optimization problem for estimating the parameters of a latent tree graphical model, i.e., hierarchical decomposion of a tensor which minimizes the Frobenius norm of the difference between the original tensor and its decomposition. When the latent tree graphical models are correctly specified, we show that a global optimum of the optimization problem can be obtained via a recursive decomposition algorithm. This algorithm recovers previous spectral algorithms for hidden Markov models (Hsu et al., 2009; Foster et al., 2012) and latent tree graphical models (Parikh et al., 2011; Song et al., 2011) as special cases, elucidating the global objective these algorithms are optimizing for. When the latent tree graphical models are misspecified, we derive a better decomposition based on our framework, and provide approximation guarantee for this new estimator. In both synthetic and real world data, this new estimator significantly improves over the-state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate the parameters of a tree-shaped probabilistic model containing hidden variables. It treats the joint probability table of the observed variables as a tensor, or multidimensional array. Hidden variables create low-rank structure when that array is reshaped into different matrices, and those structures together imply a hierarchical tensor decomposition.

This perspective gives parameter estimation a shared optimization objective: minimize the Frobenius-norm difference between the probability tensor and its decomposition. When the latent tree model is correctly specified, the authors show that a recursive decomposition algorithm can reach a global optimum. Existing spectral algorithms for hidden Markov models and latent trees emerge as special cases, clarifying the objective behind them.

The framework also addresses model misspecification, where the chosen model does not correctly describe the data. For that case, the authors derive an improved decomposition and provide an approximation guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real data report significant improvements over leading methods. The contribution therefore combines an explanation of established estimators with a new estimator for imperfectly specified models.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical tensor objective unifies latent-tree estimators and yields an improved estimator for misspecified models.

title: Hierarchical Tensor Decomposition of Latent Tree Graphical Models

abstract: The performance of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) depends critically on how learning rates are tuned and decreased over time. We propose a method to automatically adjust multiple learning rates so as to minimize the expected error at any one time. The method relies on local gradient variations across samples. In our approach, learning rates can increase as well as decrease, making it suitable for non-stationary problems. Using a number of convex and non-convex learning tasks, we show that the resulting algorithm matches the performance of the best settings obtained through systematic search, and effectively removes the need for learning rate tuning.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent updates a model using noisy information from sampled data. Its performance depends heavily on the learning rates that control update size and on how those rates change during training. This paper proposes adjusting multiple learning rates automatically, with the objective of minimizing expected error at the current point in learning.

The method bases its adjustments on local variations in gradients across samples. Those variations provide information for choosing update sizes from the learning process itself. Rates are allowed to rise as well as fall, giving the procedure flexibility when the problem changes over time. The abstract identifies this property as making the approach suitable for non-stationary problems.

Across a collection of convex and non-convex tasks, the resulting algorithm matches the performance of the best settings found through systematic search. These experiments support the claim that the method effectively removes the need for learning-rate tuning in the evaluated tasks. The practical contribution is to replace that tuning effort with an adaptive rule driven by observed gradient behavior.
summary.tldr: Gradient variation drives automatic learning-rate adjustments that match systematically tuned settings in the reported experiments.

title: No more pesky learning rates

abstract: Cross-validation is an essential tool in machine learning and statistics. The typical procedure, in which data points are randomly assigned to one of the test sets, makes an implicit assumption that the data are exchangeable. A common case in which this does not hold is when the data come from multiple sources, in the sense used in transfer learning. In this case it is common to arrange the cross-validation procedure in a way that takes the source structure into account. Although common in practice, this procedure does not appear to have been theoretically analysed. We present new estimators of the variance of the cross-validation, both in the multiple-source setting and in the standard iid setting. These new estimators allow for much more accurate confidence intervals and hypothesis tests to compare algorithms.

paragraphs: Ordinary cross-validation randomly distributes data points among test sets, implicitly treating the observations as exchangeable. That assumption can fail when data come from multiple sources, as in transfer learning. Source identity then matters to the evaluation, and practitioners commonly organize cross-validation to respect that structure.

The paper develops theory for this practice by introducing estimators of cross-validation variance. Variance describes the uncertainty surrounding an evaluation result, which is essential when deciding how confidently to interpret an apparent performance difference. The authors provide estimators for both the multiple-source setting and the standard setting with independent, identically distributed data.

The stated benefit is substantially more accurate confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for comparing algorithms. This shifts attention from obtaining a cross-validation score to assessing how reliable that score and its comparisons are. By accounting for source structure in the uncertainty calculation, the work supports more trustworthy interpretation of evaluations involving multiple data sources, while also improving uncertainty estimation in the standard setting.
summary.tldr: New cross-validation variance estimators improve confidence intervals and algorithm comparisons for both multiple-source and standard IID data.

title: Multiple-source cross-validation

abstract: Subspace clustering separates data points approximately lying on union of affine subspaces into several clusters. This paper presents a novel nonparametric Bayesian subspace clustering model that infers both the number of subspaces and the dimension of each subspace from the observed data. Though the posterior inference is hard, our model leads to a very efficient deterministic algorithm, DP-space, which retains the nonparametric ability under a small-variance asymptotic analysis. DP-space monotonically minimizes an intuitive objective with an explicit tradeoff between data fitness and model complexity. Experimental results demonstrate that DP-space outperforms various competitors in terms of clustering accuracy and at the same time it is highly efficient.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups observations that lie approximately within several affine subspaces. The challenge includes deciding how many subspaces are needed and how many dimensions each should have. This paper introduces a Bayesian nonparametric model that infers both quantities from observed data, allowing different clusters to have different dimensional complexity.

Direct posterior inference is difficult, so the authors use small-variance asymptotics to derive a deterministic algorithm called DP-space. The resulting procedure retains the ability to infer the number and dimensions of subspaces. Its objective explicitly balances how well the subspaces fit the data against the complexity of the resulting model.

DP-space decreases this objective monotonically, providing a clear optimization criterion for its updates. That property describes improvement of the objective rather than a claim of finding a global optimum. Experiments report better clustering accuracy than several competing methods while also showing high efficiency. The contribution therefore combines adaptive model structure with a practical optimization procedure and favorable results on the evaluated clustering problems.
summary.tldr: DP-space efficiently learns both the number and dimensions of clustering subspaces by balancing data fit against model complexity.

title: DP-space: Bayesian Nonparametric Subspace Clustering with Small-variance Asymptotics

abstract: The Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithm has recently regained popularity for machine learning applications due to its projection-free property and its ability to handle structured constraints. However, in the stochastic learning setting, it is still relatively understudied compared to the gradient descent counterpart. In this work, leveraging a recent variance reduction technique, we propose two stochastic Frank-Wolfe variants which substantially improve previous results in terms of the number of stochastic gradient evaluations needed to achieve 1-εaccuracy. For example, we improve from O(\frac1ε) to O(\ln\frac1ε) if the objective function is smooth and strongly convex, and from O(\frac1ε^2) to O(\frac1ε^1.5) if the objective function is smooth and Lipschitz. The theoretical improvement is also observed in experiments on real-world datasets for a multiclass classification application.

paragraphs: Frank–Wolfe optimization is useful for structured constraints because it avoids projection steps. This paper develops its stochastic form, where optimization relies on stochastic gradient information. The authors introduce two variants that use variance reduction to improve the number of gradient evaluations required to reach the stated accuracy target.

The improvements depend on properties of the objective. For smooth, strongly convex objectives, the reported gradient-evaluation requirement improves from O(1/ε) to O(log(1/ε)). For smooth, Lipschitz objectives, it improves from O(1/ε²) to O(1/ε^1.5). These are conditional complexity results, and they concern stochastic gradient evaluations rather than an unconditional statement about every component of running time.

Experiments on real-world datasets for multiclass classification also exhibit the theoretical improvement. The contribution connects the projection-free handling of constraints with more efficient use of stochastic gradient information. That combination matters because retaining a useful constraint-handling strategy need not mean accepting the previously reported gradient-evaluation costs in the settings covered by the analysis.
summary.tldr: Variance reduction lowers stochastic gradient-evaluation requirements for two projection-free Frank–Wolfe variants under stated objective assumptions.

title: Variance-Reduced and Projection-Free Stochastic Optimization

abstract: The collection and analysis of user data drives improvements in the app and web ecosystems, but comes with risks to privacy. This paper examines discrete distribution estimation under local privacy, a setting wherein service providers can learn the distribution of a categorical statistic of interest without collecting the underlying data. We present new mechanisms, including hashed k-ary Randomized Response (KRR), that empirically meet or exceed the utility of existing mechanisms at all privacy levels. New theoretical results demonstrate the order-optimality of KRR and the existing RAPPOR mechanism at different privacy regimes.

New theoretical results demonstrate the order-optimality of KRR and the existing RAPPOR mechanism at different privacy regimes.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a service can estimate the distribution of a categorical statistic without collecting users’ underlying data. The target is an aggregate description, such as how frequently different categories occur. Local privacy constrains the information available for that estimation, creating a tradeoff between protecting individual data and retaining useful population-level information.

The authors introduce new mechanisms, including hashed k-ary Randomized Response. Their empirical results show utility that matches or exceeds existing mechanisms across all privacy levels considered. This addresses the practical side of the problem: whether privacy-preserving collection still provides enough information to estimate the categorical distribution effectively.

The theoretical results establish order-optimality for k-ary Randomized Response and the existing RAPPOR mechanism in different privacy regimes. Order-optimality concerns the scaling of estimation performance, rather than an assertion that every numerical detail is best possible. Together, the results show why privacy strength matters when choosing a mechanism: the theoretical justification for different methods applies in different regimes, alongside the empirical gains from the proposed mechanisms.
summary.tldr: New locally private mechanisms improve categorical-distribution estimation, with optimal scaling guarantees for different mechanisms in different privacy regimes.

title: Discrete Distribution Estimation under Local Privacy

abstract: Deep generative models have recently yielded encouraging results in producing subjectively realistic samples of complex data. Far less attention has been paid to making these generative models interpretable. In many scenarios, ranging from scientific applications to finance, the observed variables have a natural grouping. It is often of interest to understand systems of interaction amongst these groups, and latent factor models (LFMs) are an attractive approach. However, traditional LFMs are limited by assuming a linear correlation structure. We present an output interpretable VAE (oi-VAE) for grouped data that models complex, nonlinear latent-to-observed relationships. We combine a structured VAE comprised of group-specific generators with a sparsity-inducing prior. We demonstrate that oi-VAE yields meaningful notions of interpretability in the analysis of motion capture and MEG data. We further show that in these situations, the regularization inherent to oi-VAE can actually lead to improved generalization and learned generative processes.

paragraphs: Many datasets contain naturally grouped observed variables, and understanding interactions among those groups can be as important as generating realistic samples. Traditional latent factor models offer an interpretable approach but assume linear correlation structure. This paper develops an output-interpretable variational autoencoder, oi-VAE, for modeling more complex relationships in grouped data.

The model combines generators specific to each output group with a prior that encourages sparsity. This structure connects the hidden representation to identifiable groups of observations while allowing nonlinear relationships between latent and observed variables. The design makes the organization of the outputs part of how the generative model is built.

Experiments with motion capture and MEG data demonstrate meaningful interpretations of the learned model. In those settings, the authors also find that the regularization built into oi-VAE can improve generalization and the learned generative process. The result shows that interpretability-oriented structure can bring predictive modeling benefits as well as making relationships among groups easier to understand.
summary.tldr: oi-VAE combines group-specific generators and sparsity to learn interpretable nonlinear factors, with generalization benefits in the studied datasets.

title: oi-VAE: Output Interpretable VAEs for Nonlinear Group Factor Analysis

abstract: In this paper we study leveraging confidence information induced by adversarial training to reinforce adversarial robustness of a given adversarially trained model. A natural measure of confidence is $\|F(x)\|_\infty$ (i.e. how confident $F$ is about its prediction?). We start by analyzing an adversarial training formulation proposed by Madry et al.. We demonstrate that, under a variety of instantiations, an only somewhat good solution to their objective induces confidence to be a discriminator, which can distinguish between right and wrong model predictions in a neighborhood of a point sampled from the underlying distribution. Based on this, we propose Highly Confident Near Neighbor (HCNN) a framework that combines confidence information and nearest neighbor search, to reinforce adversarial robustness of a base model. We give algorithms in this framework and perform a detailed empirical study. We report encouraging experimental results that support our analysis, and also discuss problems we observed with existing adversarial training.

We demonstrate that, under a variety of instantiations, an only somewhat good solution to their objective induces confidence to be a discriminator, which can distinguish between right and wrong model predictions in a neighborhood of a point sampled from the underlying distribution. Based on this, we propose Highly Confident Near Neighbor (HCNN) a framework that combines confidence information and nearest neighbor search, to reinforce adversarial robustness of a base model. We give algorithms in this framework and perform a detailed empirical study. We report encouraging experimental results that support our analysis, and also discuss problems we observed with existing adversarial training.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether confidence information already present in an adversarially trained model can help strengthen its robustness. It measures confidence using the largest component of the model's output. The key question is whether that value can help distinguish correct predictions from incorrect ones near a typical data point.

The authors analyze an existing adversarial training objective and show that, under a variety of instantiations, even a moderately good solution can make confidence informative in this local sense. The result links the training objective to a useful property of the resulting confidence scores. It does not assert that arbitrary models have universally reliable confidence.

Based on that analysis, the paper proposes Highly Confident Near Neighbor, a framework combining confidence information with nearest-neighbor search to reinforce a base model. The authors develop algorithms within the framework and conduct a detailed empirical study. They describe the results as encouraging and supportive of their analysis, while also reporting problems observed with existing adversarial training. The contribution centers on making locally informative confidence useful for robustness.
summary.tldr: Highly Confident Near Neighbor combines confidence induced by adversarial training with neighbor search to strengthen a base model's robustness.

title: Reinforcing Adversarial Robustness using Model Confidence Induced by Adversarial Training

abstract: We study the heavy-tailed stochastic bandit problem in the cooperative multi-agent setting, where a group of agents interact with a common bandit problem, while communicating on a network with delays. Existing algorithms for the stochastic bandit in this setting utilize confidence intervals arising from an averaging-based communication protocol known as running consensus, that does not lend itself to robust estimation for heavy-tailed settings. We propose MP-UCB, a decentralized multi-agent algorithm for the cooperative stochastic bandit that incorporates robust estimation with a message-passing protocol. We prove optimal regret bounds for MP-UCB for several problem settings, and also demonstrate its superiority to existing methods. Furthermore, we establish the first lower bounds for the cooperative bandit problem, in addition to providing efficient algorithms for robust bandit estimation of location.

Existing algorithms for the stochastic bandit in this setting utilize confidence intervals arising from an averaging-based communication protocol known as running consensus, that does not lend itself to robust estimation for heavy-tailed settings. We propose MP-UCB, a decentralized multi-agent algorithm for the cooperative stochastic bandit that incorporates robust estimation with a message-passing protocol. We prove optimal regret bounds for MP-UCB for several problem settings, and also demonstrate its superiority to existing methods. Furthermore, we establish the first lower bounds for the cooperative bandit problem, in addition to providing efficient algorithms for robust bandit estimation of location.

paragraphs: The paper studies a group of agents learning which options produce the best rewards while sharing information over a network. Communication takes time, and rewards have heavy tails, making unusually large observations an important estimation challenge. The agents must therefore coordinate exploration while dealing with both delayed information and unreliable behavior of ordinary averages.

Existing approaches use running consensus, a communication protocol built around averaging, to construct confidence intervals. The authors explain that this mechanism does not readily support robust estimation in heavy-tailed settings. Their decentralized algorithm, MP-UCB, instead combines robust reward estimation with a message-passing protocol, connecting the statistical estimator to a different way of sharing observations.

The authors prove optimal regret bounds in several problem settings and report superiority over existing methods. They also establish lower bounds for cooperative bandits, providing a reference for what algorithms can achieve, and develop efficient methods for robust location estimation. The optimality claims apply to the analyzed settings, rather than every possible communication network or reward model.
summary.tldr: MP-UCB combines robust estimation with decentralized message passing to achieve optimal regret in several cooperative heavy-tailed bandit settings.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Bandits with Heavy Tails

abstract: Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are among the most fundamental tools for binary classification. In its simplest formulation, an SVM produces a hyperplane separating two classes of data using the largest possible margin to the data. The focus on maximizing the margin has been well motivated through numerous generalization bounds. In this paper, we revisit and improve the classic generalization bounds in terms of margins. Furthermore, we complement our new generalization bound by a nearly matching lower bound, thus almost settling the generalization performance of SVMs in terms of margins.
originalAbstract: Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are among the most fundamental tools for binary classification. In its simplest formulation, an SVM produces a hyperplane separating two classes of data using the largest possible margin to the data. The focus on maximizing the margin has been well motivated through numerous generalization bounds. In this paper, we revisit and improve the classic generalization bounds in terms of margins. Furthermore, we complement our new generalization bound by a nearly matching lower bound, thus almost settling the generalization performance of SVMs in terms of margins.

paragraphs: In its simplest form, a support vector machine separates two classes with a hyperplane chosen to leave the widest possible margin around the data. Generalization bounds help explain why this geometric objective is useful: they connect margins observed in learning to guarantees about classification beyond the training examples. This paper revisits those classical guarantees.

The authors derive an improved margin-based generalization bound. This strengthens the theoretical description of how well support vector machines can generalize when performance is expressed in terms of margins. The contribution concerns the quality of that mathematical guarantee and sharpens an established justification for choosing a separator with a large margin.

The paper also establishes a lower bound that nearly matches its new guarantee. Together, the upper and lower bounds leave relatively little room for improvement in this margin-based characterization. That pairing is central to the result: an improved bound shows what can be guaranteed, while the nearly matching lower bound indicates how close that guarantee is to the attainable limit.
summary.tldr: Improved generalization bounds and a nearly matching lower bound sharply characterize support vector machine performance in terms of margins.

title: Near-Tight Margin-Based Generalization Bounds for Support Vector Machines

abstract: Decision tree optimization is notoriously difficult from a computational perspective but essential for the field of interpretable machine learning. Despite efforts over the past 40 years, only recently have optimization breakthroughs been made that have allowed practical algorithms to find optimal decision trees. These new techniques have the potential to trigger a paradigm shift, where, it is possible to construct sparse decision trees to efficiently optimize a variety of objective functions, without relying on greedy splitting and pruning heuristics that often lead to suboptimal solutions. The contribution in this work is to provide a general framework for decision tree optimization that addresses the two significant open problems in the area: treatment of imbalanced data and fully optimizing over continuous variables. We present techniques that produce optimal decision trees over variety of objectives including F-score, AUC, and partial area under the ROC convex hull. We also introduce a scalable algorithm that produces provably optimal results in the presence of continuous variables and speeds up decision tree construction by several order of magnitude relative to the state-of-the art.

paragraphs: Sparse decision trees are useful for interpretable prediction, but finding an optimal tree is computationally difficult. Common construction methods make greedy splits and later prune the result, which can leave better trees undiscovered. This paper develops a general optimization framework aimed at constructing optimal sparse trees for a wider range of practical objectives.

The work addresses two problems: handling imbalanced data and fully optimizing over continuous variables. It supports objectives including F-score, AUC, and partial area under the ROC convex hull. Supporting these objectives matters because the criterion used to select a tree need not be limited to one measure of classification performance, particularly when class frequencies are uneven.

The authors also introduce a scalable algorithm that gives provably optimal results in the presence of continuous variables. They report construction speed improvements of several orders of magnitude relative to the state of the art. The contribution combines a broader choice of optimization targets with faster tree construction, making exact optimization more practically useful within the framework studied.
summary.tldr: A decision-tree optimization framework supports imbalance-sensitive objectives and continuous variables while reporting major speed gains and provable optimality.

title: Generalized and Scalable Optimal Sparse Decision Trees

abstract: One fundamental problem in deep learning is understanding the outstanding performance of deep Neural Networks (NNs) in practice. One explanation for the superiority of NNs is that they can realize a large class of complicated functions, i.e., they have powerful expressivity. The expressivity of a ReLU NN can be quantified by the maximal number of linear regions it can separate its input space into. In this paper, we provide several mathematical results needed for studying the linear regions of CNNs, and use them to derive the maximal and average numbers of linear regions for one-layer ReLU CNNs. Furthermore, we obtain upper and lower bounds for the number of linear regions of multi-layer ReLU CNNs. Our results suggest that deeper CNNs have more powerful expressivity than their shallow counterparts, while CNNs have more expressivity than fully-connected NNs per parameter.

paragraphs: A ReLU network represents a function that is linear within different regions of its input space. Counting those regions provides one way to quantify how complicated a function the network can express. This paper develops mathematical tools for studying that measure specifically in convolutional neural networks.

For one-layer ReLU convolutional networks, the authors derive both maximal and average numbers of linear regions. For networks with multiple layers, they establish upper and lower bounds. The distinction matters: exact counts describe the one-layer setting, while bounds characterize the range of possible complexity in deeper architectures.

The results suggest that deeper convolutional networks have greater expressive power than shallow counterparts and that convolutional networks offer more expressivity per parameter than fully connected networks. These conclusions concern the linear-region measure of representation capacity. The contribution provides a mathematical account of how architecture and depth influence the complexity of functions a network can represent, giving a concrete basis for comparing capacity beyond simply counting parameters.
summary.tldr: Linear-region counts and bounds suggest that depth and convolution can increase ReLU network expressivity, including expressivity per parameter.

title: On the Number of Linear Regions of Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: We propose a novel method for exploring how neurons within neural networks interact. In particular, we consider activation values of a network for given data, and propose to mine noise-robust rules of the form X {\rightarrow} Y , where X and Y are sets of neurons in different layers. We identify the best set of rules by the Minimum Description Length Principle as the rules that together are most descriptive of the activation data. To learn good rule sets in practice, we propose the unsupervised ExplaiNN algorithm. Extensive evaluation shows that the patterns it discovers give clear insight in how networks perceive the world: they identify shared, respectively class-specific traits, compositionality within the network, as well as locality in convolutional layers. Moreover, these patterns are not only easily interpretable, but also supercharge prototyping as they identify which groups of neurons to consider in unison.
