paragraphs: Understanding a neural network involves examining how groups of neurons behave together across layers. This paper studies the activation values produced for given data and searches for noise-robust rules connecting sets of neurons in different layers. The resulting rules summarize recurring relationships within the network’s internal activity.

The authors use the Minimum Description Length principle to choose a collection of rules that jointly describes the activation data well. This treats explanation as a problem of finding a compact, informative account of the observed patterns. Their unsupervised algorithm, ExplaiNN, learns such rule sets without requiring a separate supervised rule-learning task.

Evaluations show patterns associated with traits shared across classes, traits specific to individual classes, compositional structure, and locality in convolutional layers. The authors also report that the patterns are interpretable and useful for prototyping because they identify neuron groups worth considering together. The contribution is a group-level view of internal network behavior, expressed through robust relationships that can be inspected and used during model exploration.
summary.tldr: ExplaiNN mines compact, noise-robust rules between neuron groups to reveal interpretable patterns in neural-network activations.

title: What’s in the Box? Exploring the Inner Life of Neural Networks with Robust Rules

abstract: Strategic classification studies the interaction between a classification rule and the strategic agents it governs. Agents respond by manipulating their features, under the assumption that the classifier is known. However, in many real-life scenarios of high-stake classification (e.g., credit scoring), the classifier is not revealed to the agents, which leads agents to attempt to learn the classifier and game it too. In this paper we generalize the strategic classification model to such scenarios and analyze the effect of an unknown classifier. We define the ”price of opacity” as the difference between the prediction error under the opaque and transparent policies, characterize it, and give a sufficient condition for it to be strictly positive, in which case transparency is the recommended policy. Our experiments show how Hardt et al.’s robust classifier is affected by keeping agents in the dark.

paragraphs: Strategic classification studies situations where people alter their features in response to a classifier’s rules. Standard formulations assume that those rules are known. This paper considers an opaque classifier, where people must try to learn the rule while also deciding how to manipulate their inputs to obtain a preferred outcome.

The authors extend the strategic classification model to capture this uncertainty. They define the price of opacity as the difference in prediction error between opaque and transparent policies, then characterize that quantity. This gives a concrete criterion for comparing disclosure policies: how the classifier performs after accounting for the strategic responses those policies induce.

The analysis provides a sufficient condition for the price of opacity to be strictly positive. When that condition holds, transparency is recommended because opacity increases prediction error. The claim is conditional, so it does not establish that disclosure always performs better. Experiments additionally examine how keeping agents uninformed affects Hardt and colleagues’ robust classifier, connecting the model to an existing strategic-classification approach.
summary.tldr: The paper models strategic responses to unknown classifiers and gives a sufficient condition under which opacity raises prediction error.

title: Strategic Classification in the Dark

abstract: We introduce the GANsformer, a novel and efficient type of transformer, and explore it for the task of visual generative modeling. The network employs a bipartite structure that enables long-range interactions across the image, while maintaining computation of linear efficiency, that can readily scale to high-resolution synthesis. It iteratively propagates information from a set of latent variables to the evolving visual features and vice versa, to support the refinement of each in light of the other and encourage the emergence of compositional representations of objects and scenes. In contrast to the classic transformer architecture, it utilizes multiplicative integration that allows flexible region-based modulation, and can thus be seen as a generalization of the successful StyleGAN network. We demonstrate the model’s strength and robustness through a careful evaluation over a range of datasets, from simulated multi-object environments to rich real-world indoor and outdoor scenes, showing it achieves state-of-the-art results in terms of image quality and diversity, while enjoying fast learning and better data-efficiency. Further qualitative and quantitative experiments offer us an insight into the model’s inner workings, revealing improved interpretability and stronger disentanglement, and illustrating the benefits and efficacy of our approach. An implementation of the model is available at https://github.com/dorarad/gansformer.

paragraphs: GANsformer brings a transformer architecture to visual generation, with a design intended to connect distant image regions efficiently. Its bipartite structure separates latent variables from the visual features being generated. Information passes between these two sets, enabling long-range interactions while maintaining linear computational efficiency and supporting scaling to high-resolution synthesis.

The exchange works in both directions: latent variables influence evolving visual features, and those features inform the latent variables. Repeating this interaction allows each representation to be refined in light of the other and encourages compositional representations of scenes and objects. Multiplicative integration provides flexible modulation of image regions, making the architecture a generalization of StyleGAN.

Evaluations span simulated scenes containing multiple objects and real indoor and outdoor imagery. The authors report state-of-the-art image quality and diversity, together with fast learning and improved data efficiency. Additional qualitative and quantitative analyses indicate better interpretability and stronger disentanglement. These findings support the usefulness of coordinating image generation through interactions between latent variables and visual regions.
summary.tldr: GANsformer uses efficient two-way attention between latent variables and image features to improve visual generation and compositional representations.

title: Generative Adversarial Transformers

abstract: Transfer in reinforcement learning is based on the idea that it is possible to use what is learned in one task to improve the learning process in another task. For transfer between tasks which share transition dynamics but differ in reward function, successor features have been shown to be a useful representation which allows for efficient computation of action-value functions for previously-learned policies in new tasks. These functions induce policies in the new tasks, so an agent may not need to learn a new policy for each new task it encounters, especially if it is allowed some amount of suboptimality in those tasks. We present new bounds for the performance of optimal policies in a new task, as well as an approach to use these bounds to decide, when presented with a new task, whether to use cached policies or learn a new policy.

paragraphs: An agent facing a new task may already have a useful policy in its collection of previously learned behaviors. This paper studies that possibility for tasks with the same transition dynamics but different reward functions. In this setting, successor features allow efficient computation of old policies' action values under a new reward.

Those action-value functions can induce policies for the new task, creating an opportunity to reuse prior learning. Reuse is especially attractive when some suboptimality is acceptable: the agent may not need a newly learned policy for every task it encounters. The challenge is determining whether the cached knowledge is good enough for the current task.

The authors provide new bounds on the performance of optimal policies in a new task and use them to guide that decision. Their approach chooses whether to rely on cached policies or learn a new one. This turns transfer into a decision about when existing policies suffice, within the shared-dynamics setting.
summary.tldr: New performance bounds help agents decide whether to reuse cached policies or learn a new policy when rewards change but dynamics stay fixed.

title: Policy Caches with Successor Features

abstract: Many weakly supervised classification methods employ a noise transition matrix to capture the class-conditional label corruption. To estimate the transition matrix from noisy data, existing methods often need to estimate the noisy class-posterior, which could be unreliable due to the overconfidence of neural networks. In this work, we propose a theoretically grounded method that can estimate the noise transition matrix and learn a classifier simultaneously, without relying on the error-prone noisy class-posterior estimation. Concretely, inspired by the characteristics of the stochastic label corruption process, we propose total variation regularization, which encourages the predicted probabilities to be more distinguishable from each other. Under mild assumptions, the proposed method yields a consistent estimator of the transition matrix. We show the effectiveness of the proposed method through experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: When training labels are corrupted, a noise transition matrix describes how labels from each true class can become other labels. Many methods estimate this matrix through predicted probabilities for the noisy classes. The paper identifies a weakness in that route: neural networks can be overconfident, making those probability estimates unreliable.

The proposed method learns the classifier and the noise transition matrix simultaneously, using only noisy labels. It avoids depending on a separate, error-prone estimate of the noisy class-posterior. Its key ingredient is total variation regularization, motivated by the stochastic label-corruption process and designed to make predicted probability distributions more distinguishable from one another.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove that the transition-matrix estimator is consistent, meaning that its estimate approaches the true matrix as data increases within the analyzed setting. Experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines a different estimation strategy with conditional theoretical support, addressing overconfidence at a step that other approaches rely on.
summary.tldr: Total variation regularization enables joint classifier and label-noise estimation, with consistency of the transition-matrix estimate under mild assumptions.

title: Learning Noise Transition Matrix from Only Noisy Labels via Total Variation Regularization

paragraphs: At the edge of stability, gradient descent can display oscillating loss while still making overall progress. Sharpness, measured by the largest Hessian eigenvalue, stays near twice the inverse learning rate. This paper analyzes an implicit regularization mechanism associated with that behavior, explaining how deterministic updates can favor particular minimum-loss solutions.

The analysis shows that the updates induce a deterministic flow along the manifold of minima. Under the stated regularity conditions, this flow minimizes the largest Hessian eigenvalue, linking the training dynamics to reduced sharpness. The mechanism does not depend on gradient noise or on the infinitesimal-update explanations used in many earlier implicit-bias results.

The formal results cover two constructions from a smooth loss: normalized gradient descent with a gradient-dependent learning rate, and constant-step gradient descent applied to the square root of the loss above its minimum. Both provably enter the edge-of-stability regime under the assumptions. Experiments corroborate the theoretical findings. These constructions provide a mathematical account of the phenomenon, with guarantees tied to the analyzed updates and regularity conditions.
summary.tldr: For two analyzed gradient-descent constructions, edge-of-stability dynamics induce a flow among minima that reduces the largest Hessian eigenvalue.

title: Understanding Gradient Descent on the Edge of Stability in Deep Learning

abstract: We investigate approximation guarantees provided by logistic regression for the fundamental problem of agnostic learning of homogeneous halfspaces. Previously, for a certain broad class of “well-behaved” distributions on the examples, Diakonikolas et al. (2020) proved an tilde{Omega}(OPT) lower bound, while Frei et al. (2021) proved an tilde{O}(sqrt{OPT}) upper bound, where OPT denotes the best zero-one/misclassification risk of a homogeneous halfspace. In this paper, we close this gap by constructing a well-behaved distribution such that the global minimizer of the logistic risk over this distribution only achieves Omega(sqrt{OPT}) misclassification risk, matching the upper bound in (Frei et al., 2021). On the other hand, we also show that if we impose a radial-Lipschitzness condition in addition to well-behaved-ness on the distribution, logistic regression on a ball of bounded radius reaches tilde{O}(OPT) misclassification risk. Our techniques also show for any well-behaved distribution, regardless of radial Lipschitzness, we can overcome the Omega(sqrt{OPT}) lower bound for logistic loss simply at the cost of one additional convex optimization step involving the hinge loss and attain tilde{O}(OPT) misclassification risk. This two-step convex optimization algorithm is simpler than previous methods obtaining this guarantee, all of which require solving O(log(1/OPT)) minimization problems.

paragraphs: Logistic regression optimizes a smooth loss, while classification quality ultimately depends on incorrect predictions. This paper studies how closely those objectives align when learning homogeneous halfspaces, whose decision boundaries pass through the origin. Its reference quantity, OPT, is the smallest misclassification risk achievable by such a halfspace, even when the labels cannot be classified perfectly.

The authors construct a distribution within a broad well-behaved class where even the global logistic-loss minimizer has misclassification risk at least on the order of the square root of OPT. This matches an existing upper bound and closes the stated gap. The result concerns the loss itself: finding its global minimum does not remove this worst-case separation from classification performance.

The paper also identifies two routes to stronger guarantees. Adding a radial-Lipschitzness condition allows logistic regression within a bounded ball to achieve risk proportional to OPT up to logarithmic factors. Alternatively, without that additional condition, one extra convex optimization step using hinge loss achieves that stronger rate. This gives a two-step method where earlier approaches required a logarithmic number of minimizations.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes logistic regression's worst-case classification limit and shows how an extra hinge-loss optimization step overcomes it.

title: Agnostic Learnability of Halfspaces via Logistic Loss

abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs), which have demonstrated a state-of-the-art performance in image classification, can also visualize global interpretations through attention-based contributions. However, the complexity of the model makes it difficult to interpret the decision-making process, and the ambiguity of the attention maps can cause incorrect correlations between image patches. In this study, we propose a new ViT neural tree decoder (ViT-NeT). A ViT acts as a backbone, and to solve its limitations, the output contextual image patches are applied to the proposed NeT. The NeT aims to accurately classify fine-grained objects with similar inter-class correlations and different intra-class correlations. In addition, it describes the decision-making process through a tree structure and prototype and enables a visual interpretation of the results. The proposed ViT-NeT is designed to not only improve the classification performance but also provide a human-friendly interpretation, which is effective in resolving the trade-off between performance and interpretability. We compared the performance of ViT-NeT with other state-of-art methods using widely used fine-grained visual categorization benchmark datasets and experimentally proved that the proposed method is superior in terms of the classification performance and interpretability. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/jumpsnack/ViT-NeT.

paragraphs: Vision transformers classify images effectively, but their complexity makes their decisions difficult to interpret. Attention maps offer visual clues, yet ambiguity in those maps can suggest incorrect relationships between image patches. This paper introduces ViT-NeT to make classification decisions easier to examine while improving fine-grained recognition.

A vision transformer first produces contextual representations of image patches. A neural tree decoder then uses those representations for classification. The tree structure and prototypes describe the decision process and provide visual interpretations. The architecture targets categories that can look similar to one another while also containing substantial variation within a category, a central difficulty in fine-grained recognition.

The authors compare ViT-NeT with state-of-the-art methods on widely used fine-grained visual categorization benchmarks. Their experiments show superior classification performance and interpretability in those comparisons. The results support combining a transformer backbone with an explicitly structured decoder as a way to improve both objectives together, addressing the practical tension between predictive performance and understandable decisions.
summary.tldr: ViT-NeT adds a prototype-based neural tree decoder to a vision transformer, improving fine-grained classification and interpretability in benchmarks.

title: ViT-NeT: Interpretable Vision Transformers with Neural Tree Decoder

abstract: Computational chemistry aims to autonomously design specific molecules with target functionality. Generative frameworks provide useful tools to learn continuous representations of molecules in a latent space. While modelers could optimize chemical properties, many generated molecules are not synthesizable. To design synthetically accessible molecules that preserve main structural motifs of target molecules, we propose a reaction-embedded and structure-conditioned variational autoencoder. As the latent space jointly encodes molecular structures and their reaction routes, our new sampling method that measures the path-informed structural similarity allows us to effectively generate structurally analogous synthesizable molecules. When targeting out-of-domain as well as in-domain seed structures, our model generates structurally and property-wisely similar molecules equipped with well-defined reaction paths. By focusing on the important region in chemical space, we also demonstrate that our model can design new molecules with even higher activity than the seed molecules.

paragraphs: A molecule-generation system can propose structures with attractive properties yet fail to provide molecules that can be synthesized. This paper addresses that problem while also trying to preserve important structural motifs of a target molecule. Its goal is to generate useful chemical relatives with defined routes for making them.

The proposed variational autoencoder is conditioned on structure and incorporates reaction information. Its latent representation jointly encodes molecular structures and their reaction routes. A new sampling method measures structural similarity using information about those routes, so the search for related molecules accounts for both molecular form and synthetic paths.

The authors report generating molecules similar in structure and properties to seed molecules from both within and outside the model’s domain, with well-defined reaction paths. They also demonstrate molecules with higher activity than their seeds by concentrating the search on an important region of chemical space. The approach connects structural preservation, property-oriented exploration, and synthetic accessibility within one generative framework.
summary.tldr: A reaction-aware variational autoencoder generates molecules resembling target structures while providing defined synthetic routes.

title: Path-Aware and Structure-Preserving Generation of Synthetically Accessible Molecules

abstract: In problems involving matrix computations, the concept of leverage has found a large number of applications. In particular, leverage scores, which relate the columns of a matrix to the subspaces spanned by its leading singular vectors, are helpful in revealing column subsets to approximately factorize a matrix with quality guarantees. As such, they provide a solid foundation for a variety of machine-learning methods. In this paper we extend the definition of leverage scores to relate the columns of a matrix to arbitrary subsets of singular vectors. We establish a precise connection between column and singular-vector subsets, by relating the concepts of leverage scores and principal angles between subspaces. We employ this result to design approximation algorithms with provable guarantees for two well-known problems: generalized column subset selection and sparse canonical correlation analysis. We run numerical experiments to provide further insight on the proposed methods. The novel bounds we derive improve our understanding of fundamental concepts in matrix approximations. In addition, our insights may serve as building blocks for further contributions.

paragraphs: When approximating a matrix using a subset of its columns, some columns are more useful than others. Leverage scores help identify useful choices by relating columns to spaces defined by leading singular vectors. This paper broadens that relationship so the selected singular vectors can come from an arbitrary subset.

The authors establish a precise geometric connection between these generalized scores and principal angles, which describe how subspaces align. This connects a chosen collection of columns with a chosen collection of singular vectors. It provides a mathematical basis for reasoning about column selection beyond the usual focus on leading directions.

The paper uses this relationship to design approximation algorithms with provable guarantees for generalized column subset selection and sparse canonical correlation analysis. Numerical experiments provide further insight into the methods. The resulting bounds strengthen the theoretical understanding of matrix approximation, while the geometric connection offers a potential building block for additional algorithms involving the selection and comparison of subspaces.
summary.tldr: Generalized leverage scores connect matrix-column selection to subspace geometry and yield approximation algorithms with provable guarantees.

title: Generalized Leverage Scores: Geometric Interpretation and Applications

abstract: Hypergraphs are a common model for multiway relationships in data, and hypergraph semi-supervised learning is the problem of assigning labels to all nodes in a hypergraph, given labels on just a few nodes. Diffusions and label spreading are classical techniques for semi-supervised learning in the graph setting, and there are some standard ways to extend them to hypergraphs. However, these methods are linear models, and do not offer an obvious way of incorporating node features for making predictions. Here, we develop a nonlinear diffusion process on hypergraphs that spreads both features and labels following the hypergraph structure. Even though the process is nonlinear, we show global convergence to a unique limiting point for a broad class of nonlinearities and we show that such limit is the global minimum of a new regularized semi-supervised learning loss function which aims at reducing a generalized form of variance of the nodes across the hyperedges. The limiting point serves as a node embedding from which we make predictions with a linear model. Our approach is competitive with state-of-the-art graph and hypergraph neural networks, and also takes less time to train.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships involving multiple nodes at once. In semi-supervised learning, the goal is to use a few known node labels to predict the rest. Standard diffusion and label-spreading approaches extend naturally from graphs, but their linear formulations do not provide an obvious way to incorporate node features into the predictions.

This paper develops a nonlinear diffusion process that spreads both labels and features according to the hypergraph's structure. For a broad class of nonlinearities, the authors prove global convergence to a unique limiting point. They also show that this point globally minimizes a new regularized learning objective that reduces a generalized measure of variation among nodes sharing hyperedges.

The converged representation becomes a node embedding, which a linear model then uses for prediction. Experiments show performance competitive with state-of-the-art graph and hypergraph neural networks while requiring less training time. The contribution joins a nonlinear representation-building method with a precise optimization interpretation and convergence result, with those guarantees applying to the stated class of nonlinearities.
summary.tldr: Nonlinear hypergraph diffusion combines features and labels into predictive embeddings with convergence guarantees for a broad class of nonlinearities.

title: Nonlinear Feature Diffusion on Hypergraphs

abstract: Extracting information on fluid motion directly from images is challenging. Fluid flow represents a complex dynamic system governed by the Navier-Stokes equations. General optical flow methods are typically designed for rigid body motion, and thus struggle if applied to fluid motion estimation directly. Further, optical flow methods only focus on two consecutive frames without utilising historical temporal information, while the fluid motion (velocity field) can be considered a continuous trajectory constrained by time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs). This discrepancy has the potential to induce physically inconsistent estimations. Here we propose an unsupervised learning based prediction-correction scheme for fluid flow estimation. An estimate is first given by a PDE-constrained optical flow predictor, which is then refined by a physical based corrector. The proposed approach outperforms optical flow methods and shows competitive results compared to existing supervised learning based methods on a benchmark dataset. Furthermore, the proposed approach can generalize to complex real-world fluid scenarios where ground truth information is effectively unknowable. Finally, experiments demonstrate that the physical corrector can refine flow estimates by mimicking the operator splitting method commonly utilised in fluid dynamical simulation.

paragraphs: Estimating fluid motion from images is difficult because fluid velocity evolves according to physical dynamics. The paper argues that optical flow methods designed around rigid motion and pairs of frames can miss this temporal structure. Treating each estimate in isolation can potentially produce motion estimates that are inconsistent with the governing equations.

The proposed method uses an unsupervised prediction-correction scheme. First, an optical flow predictor constrained by partial differential equations produces a velocity estimate. A physically based corrector then refines that estimate. This divides the task into an initial visual prediction and a subsequent adjustment informed by fluid dynamics.

On a benchmark dataset, the approach outperforms optical flow methods and is competitive with existing supervised learning methods. The authors also report generalization to complex real-world fluid scenarios where ground-truth motion is effectively unknowable. Further experiments show that the corrector can refine estimates by mimicking operator splitting, a technique used in fluid simulation. Together, these findings support incorporating physical evolution directly into image-based flow estimation.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised predictor and physical corrector use fluid dynamics to improve motion estimates from images.

title: Learning to Estimate and Refine Fluid Motion with Physical Dynamics

abstract: The paper uses a frame-theoretic setting to study the injectivity of a ReLU-layer on the closed ball of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its non-negative part. In particular, the interplay between the radius of the ball and the bias vector is emphasized. Together with a perspective from convex geometry, this leads to a computationally feasible method of verifying the injectivity of a ReLU-layer under reasonable restrictions in terms of an upper bound of the bias vector. Explicit reconstruction formulas are provided, inspired by the duality concept from frame theory. All this gives rise to the possibility of quantifying the invertibility of a ReLU-layer and a concrete reconstruction algorithm for any input vector on the ball.

paragraphs: A ReLU layer can discard information by setting negative activations to zero. This paper asks when the layer nevertheless preserves enough information to distinguish every input within a bounded region. The property being studied is injectivity: two different permitted inputs must produce different outputs. The authors consider a closed ball and its non-negative portion.

The analysis combines frame theory with convex geometry, emphasizing how the ball’s radius interacts with the layer’s bias vector. This matters because invertibility is examined over a specified input region, so the size of that region and the biases jointly affect which information survives. Under restrictions expressed through an upper bound on the bias vector, the authors obtain a computationally feasible injectivity check.

The paper also provides explicit reconstruction formulas inspired by duality in frame theory. These connect the question of whether reconstruction is possible with a concrete way to carry it out. The resulting framework offers a route to quantifying invertibility and reconstructing inputs on the ball when the relevant injectivity conditions hold.
summary.tldr: Frame theory and convex geometry provide conditional injectivity checks and explicit input reconstruction formulas for ReLU layers on bounded regions.

title: Convex Geometry of ReLU-layers, Injectivity on the Ball and Local Reconstruction

abstract: Adapting to regularities of the environment is critical for biological organisms to anticipate events and plan. A prominent example is the circadian rhythm corresponding to the internalization by organisms of the $24$-hour period of the Earth’s rotation. In this work, we study the emergence of circadian-like rhythms in deep reinforcement learning agents. In particular, we deployed agents in an environment with a reliable periodic variation while solving a foraging task. We systematically characterize the agent’s behavior during learning and demonstrate the emergence of a rhythm that is endogenous and entrainable. Interestingly, the internal rhythm adapts to shifts in the phase of the environmental signal without any re-training. Furthermore, we show via bifurcation and phase response curve analyses how artificial neurons develop dynamics to support the internalization of the environmental rhythm. From a dynamical systems view, we demonstrate that the adaptation proceeds by the emergence of a stable periodic orbit in the neuron dynamics with a phase response that allows an optimal phase synchronisation between the agent’s dynamics and the environmental rhythm.

paragraphs: Biological organisms use internal rhythms to anticipate regular environmental changes. This paper investigates whether similar behavior can emerge in deep reinforcement learning agents. The authors train agents on a foraging task in an environment with reliable periodic variation and systematically examine how their behavior develops during learning.

The learned rhythm is endogenous, meaning it is internally generated, and entrainable, meaning it can synchronize with an external signal. It also adapts when the environmental signal shifts in phase, without additional training. This shows that the agents' timing behavior can adjust after learning, rather than remaining fixed to the original timing of the environment.

The authors investigate the mechanism through bifurcation analysis and phase response curves. Their dynamical-systems analysis identifies a stable periodic orbit in artificial-neuron dynamics, with a phase response that supports optimal synchronization between the agent and its environment. The contribution connects observed rhythmic behavior to an internal dynamical mechanism, explaining how environmental regularity becomes represented in the agent's ongoing neural activity.
summary.tldr: Foraging agents develop internal rhythms that synchronize with periodic environments and adapt to timing shifts without retraining.

title: Emergence of Adaptive Circadian Rhythms in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning signed distance functions (SDFs) from 3D point clouds is an important task in 3D computer vision. However, without ground truth signed distances, point normals or clean point clouds, current methods still struggle from learning SDFs from noisy point clouds. To overcome this challenge, we propose to learn SDFs via a noise to noise mapping, which does not require any clean point cloud or ground truth supervision for training. Our novelty lies in the noise to noise mapping which can infer a highly accurate SDF of a single object or scene from its multiple or even single noisy point cloud observations. Our novel learning manner is supported by modern Lidar systems which capture multiple noisy observations per second. We achieve this by a novel loss which enables statistical reasoning on point clouds and maintains geometric consistency although point clouds are irregular, unordered and have no point correspondence among noisy observations. Our evaluation under the widely used benchmarks demonstrates our superiority over the state-of-the-art methods in surface reconstruction, point cloud denoising and upsampling. Our code, data, and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/mabaorui/Noise2NoiseMapping/ .

paragraphs: A signed distance function represents a surface through distances to it, with a sign distinguishing its two sides. Learning this representation from noisy 3D measurements is difficult when clean point clouds, surface normals, or correct signed distances are unavailable. This paper proposes learning through a noise-to-noise mapping instead.

The method can infer an object’s or scene’s signed distance function from multiple noisy observations or even a single noisy point cloud, without clean training targets. Its loss supports statistical reasoning while preserving geometric consistency. This is particularly relevant because point clouds are unordered and irregular, and separate observations do not provide matching identities for their points.

Modern lidar systems naturally supply repeated noisy observations, making the proposed learning setup relevant to their data. Evaluations on widely used benchmarks report advantages over state-of-the-art methods in surface reconstruction, point-cloud denoising, and upsampling. The contribution connects a way to learn without clean supervision to several geometric tasks, using the learned distance representation as the common basis for improving noisy 3D data.
summary.tldr: Noise-to-noise mapping learns signed distance functions from noisy point clouds without clean supervision and improves several 3D reconstruction tasks.

title: Learning Signed Distance Functions from Noisy 3D Point Clouds via Noise to Noise Mapping

abstract: Object placement aims to insert a foreground object into a background image with a suitable location and size to create a natural composition. To predict a diverse distribution of placements, existing methods usually establish a one-to-one mapping from random vectors to the placements. However, these random vectors are not interpretable, which prevents users from interacting with the object placement process. To address this problem, we propose an Interactive Object Placement method with Reinforcement Learning, dubbed IOPRE, to make sequential decisions for producing a reasonable placement given an initial location and size of the foreground. We first design a novel action space to flexibly and stably adjust the location and size of the foreground while preserving its aspect ratio. Then, we propose a multi-factor state representation learning method, which integrates composition image features and sinusoidal positional embeddings of the foreground to make decisions for selecting actions. Finally, we design a hybrid reward function that combines placement assessment and the number of steps to ensure that the agent learns to place objects in the most visually pleasing and semantically appropriate location. Experimental results on the OPA dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of plausibility and diversity.

paragraphs: Object placement inserts a foreground object into a background at a location and size that produce a natural composition. Existing methods often generate placement diversity from random vectors, but those vectors are difficult for people to interpret or control. This paper introduces IOPRE, which starts from an initial placement and improves it through sequential decisions.

The reinforcement-learning agent uses an action space that adjusts position and size while preserving the foreground object’s aspect ratio. To choose actions, it combines features of the composed image with sinusoidal positional embeddings describing the foreground. This representation provides information about both visual composition and the object’s current placement.

A hybrid reward combines placement assessment with the number of adjustment steps, guiding the agent toward visually pleasing and semantically appropriate results. Experiments on the OPA dataset show state-of-the-art plausibility and diversity. The interactive value comes from making location and size explicit starting conditions for a sequence of adjustments, giving users a more interpretable entry point than a random vector.
summary.tldr: IOPRE uses reinforcement learning to adjust an initial object placement through interpretable position and size changes.

title: Interactive Object Placement with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large context window is a desirable feature in large language models (LLMs). However, due to high fine-tuning costs, scarcity of long texts, and catastrophic values introduced by new token positions, current extended context windows are limited to around 128k tokens. This paper introduces LongRoPE that, for the first time, extends the context window of pre-trained LLMs to an impressive 2048k tokens, with up to only 1k fine-tuning steps at within 256k training lengths, while maintaining performance at the original short context window. This is achieved by three key innovations: (i) we identify and exploit two forms of non-uniformities in positional interpolation through an efficient search, providing a better initialization for fine-tuning and enabling an 8x extension in non-fine-tuning scenarios; (ii) we introduce a progressive extension strategy that first fine-tunes a 256k length LLM and then conducts a second positional interpolation on the fine-tuned extended LLM to achieve a 2048k context window; (iii) we readjust LongRoPE on 8k length to recover the short context window performance. Extensive experiments on LLaMA2 and Mistral across various tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Models extended via LongRoPE retain the original architecture with minor modifications to the positional embedding, and can reuse most pre-existing optimizations. Code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/LongRoPE

paragraphs: Extending a language model’s context window is difficult because long-text fine-tuning is costly and new token positions can create problematic values. LongRoPE addresses these issues by changing positional embeddings while retaining the model’s original architecture. The paper reports extending pretrained models to a 2048k-token context using up to 1k fine-tuning steps at training lengths within 256k.

The method searches for two kinds of non-uniformity in positional interpolation. This improves the starting point for fine-tuning and also enables an eightfold extension without fine-tuning in the studied scenarios. A progressive procedure first fine-tunes a model at 256k context length, then applies another positional interpolation to reach 2048k.

LongRoPE additionally readjusts the model at an 8k length to recover short-context performance. Experiments with LLaMA2 and Mistral across various tasks support the approach’s effectiveness. Because the changes are concentrated in positional embeddings, the extended models can reuse most existing optimizations. The contribution combines very long context support with an explicit step to preserve performance at the original shorter window.
summary.tldr: LongRoPE extends pretrained language models to 2048k-token contexts through searched positional interpolation and progressive extension while recovering short-context performance.

title: LongRoPE: Extending LLM Context Window Beyond 2 Million Tokens

abstract: In recent years, there has been a growing interest in visualizing the loss landscape of neural networks. Linear landscape visualization methods, such as principal component analysis, have become widely used as they intuitively help researchers study neural networks and their training process. However, these linear methods suffer from limitations and drawbacks due to their lack of flexibility and low fidelity at representing the high dimensional landscape. In this paper, we present a novel auto-encoder-based non-linear landscape visualization method called Neuro-Visualizer that addresses these shortcoming and provides useful insights about neural network loss landscapes. To demonstrate its potential, we run experiments on a variety of problems in two separate applications of knowledge-guided machine learning (KGML). Our findings show that Neuro-Visualizer outperforms other linear and non-linear baselines and helps corroborate, and sometime challenge, claims proposed by machine learning community. All code and data used in the experiments of this paper can be found at the link below.

paragraphs: A neural network's loss landscape describes how its training objective changes as its parameters change. Visualizations help researchers reason about that landscape and the training process, but reducing a high-dimensional object to a viewable form is difficult. This paper focuses on the limited flexibility and fidelity of linear visualization methods such as principal component analysis.

Neuro-Visualizer uses an autoencoder to construct a nonlinear landscape representation. The approach is intended to capture structure that a linear representation may miss, improving the usefulness of the resulting visualization. Its purpose is to provide a more faithful basis for inspecting neural-network behavior and interpreting claims about training.

The authors test the method on multiple problems within two applications of knowledge-guided machine learning. They report that it outperforms both linear and nonlinear baselines and produces insights that support some community claims while challenging others. The findings suggest that the choice of visualization method can affect the conclusions drawn from a loss landscape, making representation fidelity consequential for interpretation.
summary.tldr: Neuro-Visualizer uses a nonlinear autoencoder representation to improve loss-landscape visualization and investigate claims about neural-network training.

title: Neuro-Visualizer: A Novel Auto-Encoder-Based Loss Landscape Visualization Method With an Application in Knowledge-Guided Machine Learning

abstract: Recently, the question of adversarially robust streaming, where the stream is allowed to depend on the randomness of the streaming algorithm, has gained a lot of attention. In this work, we consider a strong white-box adversarial model (Ajtai et al. PODS 2022), in which the adversary has access to all past random coins and the parameters used by the streaming algorithm. We focus on the sparse recovery problem and extend our result to other tasks such as distinct element estimation and low-rank approximation of matrices and tensors. The main drawback of previous work is that it requires a random oracle, which is especially problematic in the streaming model since the amount of randomness is counted in the space complexity of a streaming algorithm. Also, the previous work suffers from large update time. We construct a near-optimal solution for the sparse recovery problem in white-box adversarial streams, based on the subexponentially secure Learning with Errors assumption. Importantly, our solution does not require a random oracle and has a polylogarithmic per item processing time. We also give results in a related white-box adversarially robust distributed model. Our constructions are based on homomorphic encryption schemes satisfying very mild structural properties that are currently satisfied by most known schemes.

paragraphs: Streaming algorithms process incoming data under limited memory. This paper considers a strong adversary that can choose the stream after seeing all past random choices and parameters used by the algorithm. Its main task is sparse recovery, with extensions to counting distinct elements and approximating matrices and tensors with low-rank representations.

Earlier approaches in this setting required a random oracle and incurred large update times. The oracle requirement is especially troublesome because randomness counts toward a streaming algorithm's memory use. The authors construct a near-optimal sparse recovery solution that avoids a random oracle and processes each item in polylogarithmic time.

The construction relies on the assumption that Learning with Errors remains secure against subexponential attacks. It uses homomorphic encryption schemes with mild structural requirements that, according to the abstract, most known schemes satisfy. The authors also obtain results for a related distributed setting. The significance is a stronger combination of adversarial robustness, memory-conscious randomness, and fast updates under an explicit cryptographic assumption.
summary.tldr: Under a subexponential Learning with Errors security assumption, the paper gives fast, near-optimal sparse recovery against white-box streaming adversaries without a random oracle.

title: Fast White-Box Adversarial Streaming Without a Random Oracle

abstract: Goal-conditioned planning benefits from learned low-dimensional representations of rich observations. While compact latent representations typically learned from variational autoencoders or inverse dynamics enable goal-conditioned decision making, they ignore state reachability, hampering their performance. In this paper, we learn a representation that associates reachable states together for effective planning and goal-conditioned policy learning. We first learn a latent representation with multi-step inverse dynamics (to remove distracting information), and then transform this representation to associate reachable states together in $\ell_2$ space. Our proposals are rigorously tested in various simulation testbeds. Numerical results in reward-based settings show significant improvements in sampling efficiency. Further, in reward-free settings this approach yields layered state abstractions that enable computationally efficient hierarchical planning for reaching ad hoc goals with zero additional samples.

paragraphs: Planning toward a goal becomes easier when rich observations are represented by compact states. However, a compact representation can omit a crucial relationship: whether one state is reachable from another. This paper argues that representations learned through variational autoencoders or inverse dynamics can miss that relationship, limiting their usefulness for planning and goal-conditioned decision making.

PcLast uses a two-stage approach. It first learns a representation through multistep inverse dynamics to remove distracting information. It then transforms that representation so that reachable states are associated in Euclidean space. The second stage aims to make the geometry of the representation useful for action planning, rather than relying on compactness alone.

Simulation experiments show significant sampling-efficiency improvements in reward-based settings. In reward-free settings, the approach produces layered state abstractions that support computationally efficient hierarchical planning for ad hoc goals with no additional samples. That last result concerns planning using the learned abstractions; the method still learns its representation beforehand. The findings connect planning performance to representing reachability explicitly.
summary.tldr: PcLast organizes learned states by reachability, improving sampling efficiency and enabling hierarchical planning for new goals without additional samples.

title: PcLast: Discovering Plannable Continuous Latent States

abstract: Explainable Graph Neural Network (GNN) has emerged recently to foster the trust of using GNNs. Existing GNN explainers are developed from various perspectives to enhance the explanation performance. We take the first step to study GNN explainers under adversarial attack—We found that an adversary slightly perturbing graph structure can ensure GNN model makes correct predictions, but the GNN explainer yields a drastically different explanation on the perturbed graph. Specifically, we first formulate the attack problem under a practical threat model (i.e., the adversary has limited knowledge about the GNN explainer and a restricted perturbation budget). We then design two methods (i.e., one is loss-based and the other is deduction-based) to realize the attack. We evaluate our attacks on various GNN explainers and the results show these explainers are fragile.

paragraphs: Explanations are intended to help people trust predictions from graph neural networks. This paper examines whether those explanations remain stable when an adversary makes small changes to the graph structure. Its central finding is that a model can continue predicting correctly while an explanation changes drastically under the perturbed graph.

The authors formulate an attack setting that restricts both the adversary's knowledge of the explainer and the number of permitted structural changes. They then develop two attack methods, one based on a loss and another based on deduction. The target is the explanation produced for the graph, with correct prediction retained in the demonstrated behavior.

Evaluations across multiple GNN explainers show fragility under these attacks. The results separate two properties that can otherwise appear closely linked: correctness of a prediction and robustness of its explanation. A stable or correct model output does not, in these experiments, ensure a stable account of why that output was produced. The restricted threat model makes that distinction relevant even when an adversary has limited information and modification capacity.
summary.tldr: Small adversarial graph changes can drastically alter GNN explanations while preserving correct predictions, even under restricted attack capabilities.

title: Graph Neural Network Explanations are Fragile

abstract: We introduce a novel algorithm for estimating Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) values under Local Differential Privacy (LDP) by exploiting an unexpected connection between LDP and the current status problem, a classical survival data problem in statistics. This connection leads to the development of tools for constrained isotonic estimation based on binary queries. Through mathematical proofs and extensive numerical testing, we demonstrate that our method achieves uniform and $L_2$ error bounds when estimating the entire CDF curve. By employing increasingly dense grids, the error bound can be improved, exhibiting an asymptotic normal distribution of the proposed estimator. Theoretically, we show that the error bound smoothly changes as the number of grids increases relative to the sample size $n$. Computationally, we demonstrate that our constrained isotonic estimator can be efficiently computed deterministically, eliminating the need for hyperparameters or random optimization.

This connection leads to the development of tools for constrained isotonic estimation based on binary queries. Through mathematical proofs and extensive numerical testing, we demonstrate that our method achieves uniform and $L_2$ error bounds when estimating the entire CDF curve. By employing increasingly dense grids, the error bound can be improved, exhibiting an asymptotic normal distribution of the proposed estimator. paragraphs: A cumulative distribution function gives the fraction of values at or below each threshold. This paper studies estimating that entire curve under local differential privacy. Its starting point is a connection to the current-status problem in survival statistics, where observations provide limited information about whether an event has occurred.

That connection leads to a constrained isotonic estimator based on binary queries. Isotonic estimation fits the ordered structure of a cumulative distribution curve, whose values cannot decrease as the threshold increases. The authors establish both uniform error bounds, controlling error across the curve, and L2 bounds, describing aggregate squared error.

The analysis also examines increasingly dense grids of evaluation points. It shows how error bounds change as the grid grows relative to sample size and establishes asymptotic normality of the estimator. Computationally, the constrained estimator can be obtained efficiently through a deterministic procedure without hyperparameter tuning or randomized optimization. Mathematical proofs and numerical testing therefore support both the statistical behavior and the practical computation of the proposed privacy-preserving estimator.
summary.tldr: A connection to survival statistics yields a deterministic, tuning-free CDF estimator under local differential privacy.

title: Tuning-free Estimation and Inference of Cumulative Distribution Function under Local Differential Privacy

abstract: New capabilities in foundation models are owed in large part to massive, widely-sourced, and under-documented training data collections. Existing practices in data collection have led to challenges in tracing authenticity, verifying consent, preserving privacy, addressing representation and bias, respecting copyright, and overall developing ethical and trustworthy foundation models. In response, regulation is emphasizing the need for training data transparency to understand foundation models’ limitations. Based on a large-scale analysis of the foundation model training data landscape and existing solutions, we identify the missing infrastructure to facilitate responsible foundation model development practices. abstract: Due to the high computational load of modern numerical simulation, there is a demand for approaches that would reduce the size of discrete problems while keeping the accuracy reasonable. In this work, we present an original algorithm to coarsen an unstructured grid based on the concepts of differentiable physics. We achieve this by employing $k$-means clustering, autodifferentiation and stochastic minimization algorithms. We demonstrate performance of the designed algorithm on two PDEs: a linear parabolic equation which governs slightly compressible fluid flow in porous media and the wave equation. Our results show that in the considered scenarios, we reduced the number of grid points up to 10 times while preserving the modeled variable dynamics in the points of interest. The proposed approach can be applied to the simulation of an arbitrary system described by evolutionary partial differential equations.

These components provide a computational approach to finding a coarser grid while accounting for the modeled dynamics. summary.tldr: A differentiable grid-coarsening method reduces grid points by up to tenfold in tested PDE simulations while preserving dynamics at selected points.

title: Self-Supervised Coarsening of Unstructured Grid with Automatic Differentiation

abstract: The commercialization of text-to-image diffusion models (DMs) brings forth potential copyright concerns. Despite numerous attempts to protect DMs from copyright issues, the vulnerabilities of these solutions are underexplored. In this study, we formalized the Copyright Infringement Attack on generative AI models and proposed a backdoor attack method, SilentBadDiffusion, to induce copyright infringement without requiring access to or control over training processes. Our method strategically embeds connections between pieces of copyrighted information and text references in poisoning data while carefully dispersing that information, making the poisoning data inconspicuous when integrated into a clean dataset. Our experiments show the stealth and efficacy of the poisoning data. When given specific text prompts, DMs trained with a poisoning ratio of 0.20% can produce copyrighted images. Additionally, the results reveal that the more sophisticated the DMs are, the easier the success of the attack becomes. These findings underline potential pitfalls in the prevailing copyright protection strategies and underscore the necessity for increased scrutiny to prevent the misuse of DMs.

Experiments show that models trained with a poisoning ratio of 0.20% can generate copyrighted images when given specific prompts. The results also indicate that more sophisticated diffusion models are easier to attack in the studied settings. These findings expose a potential weakness in copyright-protection strategies: stronger generative capability can coincide with greater susceptibility to this form of data poisoning.
summary.tldr: SilentBadDiffusion demonstrates that subtle data poisoning can trigger copyrighted-image generation, with stronger diffusion models more susceptible in the reported experiments.

title: The Stronger the Diffusion Model, the Easier the Backdoor: Data Poisoning to Induce Copyright BreachesWithout Adjusting Finetuning Pipeline

abstract: Audio generation is a major branch of generative AI research. Compared with prior works in this area that are commonly task-specific with heavy domain knowledge, this paper advocates building universal audio generation models that can handle various tasks in a unified manner. As recent research on large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated their strong ability to handle multiple tasks, this work presents UniAudio, an LLM-based audio generation model that supports a wide range of audio generation tasks. Based on various input conditions, such as phoneme, text description, or audio itself, UniAudio can generate speech, sound, music, and singing voice. The proposed UniAudio is built with 100k hours of multi-source open-available audio data and is scaled to 1B parameters. The audio tokenization method and language model architecture are also specifically designed for both performance and efficiency. Experimentally, UniAuido supports 11 audio generation tasks and achieves competitive results on all tasks consistently. We also show that UniAudio can support new tasks seamlessly via simple fine-tuning.

These findings support a common modeling framework for several kinds of audio generation and show a path for expanding its task coverage. The claim of universality is therefore a direction supported by a broad evaluated task set.
summary.tldr: UniAudio uses one language-model-based framework for 11 audio generation tasks, with competitive results and extension to new tasks through fine-tuning.

title: UniAudio: Towards Universal Audio Generation with Large Language Models

abstract: Recently, large-scale language-image generative models have gained widespread attention and many works have utilized generated data from these models to further enhance the performance of perception tasks. However, not all generated data can positively impact downstream models, and these methods do not thoroughly explore how to better select and utilize generated data. On the other hand, there is still a lack of research oriented towards active learning on generated data. In this paper, we explore how to perform active learning specifically for generated data in the long-tailed instance segmentation task. Subsequently, we propose BSGAL, a new algorithm that estimates the contribution of the current batch-generated data based on gradient cache. BSGAL is meticulously designed to cater for unlimited generated data and complex downstream segmentation tasks. BSGAL outperforms the baseline approach and effectually improves the performance of long-tailed segmentation.

paragraphs: Language-image generative models can supply additional training examples for visual perception, but generated examples do not all help a downstream model. This paper studies how to select and use them for long-tailed instance segmentation, where categories have uneven representation and the model must distinguish individual objects within images.

The proposed algorithm, BSGAL, applies active learning specifically to generated data. It estimates the contribution of a currently generated batch using a gradient cache. This makes the estimated usefulness of the batch part of the training-data decision, instead of treating generated examples as equally valuable. The method is designed for the combination of an unlimited generated-data supply and a complex segmentation task.

The reported results show that BSGAL outperforms the baseline and improves long-tailed segmentation performance. The finding supports a selective approach to synthetic training data: the availability of more examples makes their contribution worth evaluating. The paper’s focus is therefore on connecting generation to the needs of the downstream learner, with batch-level contribution estimates guiding how generated data is used.
summary.tldr: BSGAL estimates generated batches’ training contributions to improve active data selection for long-tailed instance segmentation.

title: Generative Active Learning for Long-tailed Instance Segmentation

abstract: With the rapid growth of data in modern applications, parallel combinatorial algorithms for maximizing non-monotone submodular functions have gained significant attention. In the parallel computation setting, the state-of-the-art approximation ratio of $1/e$ is achieved by a continuous algorithm (Ene & Nguyen, 2020) with adaptivity $\mathcal O (log(n))$. In this work, we focus on size constraints and present the first combinatorial algorithm matching this bound – a randomized parallel approach achieving $1/e - \epsilon$ approximation ratio. This result bridges the gap between continuous and combinatorial approaches for this problem. As a byproduct, we also develop a simpler $(1/4 - \epsilon)$-approximation algorithm with high probability $(\ge 1 - 1/n)$. Both algorithms achieve $\mathcal O (log(n) log(k))$ adaptivity and $\mathcal O (n log(n) log(k)) query complexity. Empirical results show our algorithms achieve competitive objective values, with the $(1/4 - $\epsilon$)$-approximation algorithm particularly efficient in queries.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to select a size-limited set when the objective has diminishing returns but adding an item can sometimes reduce its value. The computational challenge is to find a valuable set while allowing many objective evaluations to happen in parallel. The authors focus on combinatorial algorithms that work with discrete selections.

Their main randomized algorithm achieves an approximation ratio of 1/e minus epsilon, reaching arbitrarily close to the established 1/e benchmark for continuous methods. They also develop a simpler algorithm with a weaker ratio of 1/4 minus epsilon, guaranteed with probability at least 1 minus 1/n. This provides two choices with different guarantees and practical behavior.

Both algorithms require O(log(n) log(k)) sequential rounds of adaptive computation and O(n log(n) log(k)) objective queries. Thus, the approximation result does not imply matching the continuous approach's O(log(n)) adaptivity. Experiments show competitive objective values, with the simpler algorithm particularly economical in queries. The contribution is a strong approximation guarantee using a parallel combinatorial approach, alongside a simpler practical alternative.
summary.tldr: Two parallel combinatorial algorithms offer strong approximation guarantees for size-constrained non-monotone submodular maximization, including a ratio approaching 1/e.

title: Breaking Barriers: Combinatorial Algorithms for Non-Monotone Submodular Maximization with Sublinear Adaptivity and $1/e$ Approximation

abstract: Event cameras are bio-inspired vision sensors that encode visual information with high dynamic range, high temporal resolution, and low latency. Current state-of-the-art event stream processing methods rely on end-to-end deep learning techniques. However, these models are heavily dependent on data structures, limiting their stability and generalization capabilities across tasks, thereby hindering their deployment in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a chaotic dynamics event signal processing framework inspired by the dorsal visual pathway of the brain. Specifically, we utilize Continuous-coupled Neural Network (CCNN) to encode the event stream. CCNN encodes polarity-invariant event sequences as periodic signals and polarity-changing event sequences as chaotic signals. We then use continuous wavelet transforms to analyze the dynamical states of CCNN neurons and establish the high-order mappings of the event stream. The effectiveness of our method is validated through integration with conventional classification networks, achieving state-of-the-art classification accuracy on the N-Caltech101 and N-CARS datasets, with results of 84.3% and 99.9%, respectively. Our method improves the accuracy of event camera-based object classification while significantly enhancing the generalization and stability of event representation.

summary.tldr: A brain-inspired framework converts event-camera streams into dynamical signals, improving their representation and reported object-classification performance.

title: A Chaotic Dynamics Framework Inspired by Dorsal Stream for Event Signal Processing

abstract: This paper investigates the convergence properties of the hypergradient descent method ($\texttt{HDM}$), a 25-year-old heuristic originally proposed for adaptive stepsize selection in stochastic first-order methods. We provide the first rigorous convergence analysis of $\texttt{HDM}$ using the online learning framework and apply this analysis to develop a new state-of-the-art adaptive gradient methods with empirical and theoretical support. Notably, $\texttt{HDM}$ automatically identifies the optimal stepsize for the local optimization landscape and achieves local superlinear convergence. Our analysis explains the instability of $\texttt{HDM}$ reported in the literature and proposes efficient strategies to address it. We also develop two $\texttt{HDM}$ variants with heavy-ball and Nesterov momentum. Experiments on deterministic convex problems show $\texttt{HDM}$ with heavy-ball momentum ($\texttt{HDM-HB}$) exhibits robust performance and significantly outperforms other adaptive first-order methods. Moreover, $\texttt{HDM-HB}$ often matches the performance of $\texttt{L-BFGS}$, an efficient and practical quasi-Newton method, using less memory and cheaper iterations.

The authors use the resulting understanding to develop adaptive gradient methods with both theoretical support and empirical evidence.

Together, these results connect an established learning-rate heuristic to a rigorous analysis and show practical benefits in the tested optimization setting.
summary.tldr: An online-learning analysis explains hypergradient descent’s convergence and instability, supporting momentum variants with strong results on deterministic convex problems.

title: Provable and Practical Online Learning Rate Adaptation with Hypergradient Descent

abstract: We consider a framework for clustering edge-colored hypergraphs, where the goal is to cluster (equivalently, to color) objects based on the primary type of multiway interactions they participate in. One well-studied objective is to color nodes to minimize the number of unsatisfied hyperedges—those containing one or more nodes whose color does not match the hyperedge color. We motivate and present advances for several directions that extend beyond this minimization problem. We first provide new algorithms for maximizing satisfied edges, which is the same at optimality but is much more challenging to approximate, with all prior work restricted to graphs. We develop the first approximation algorithm for hypergraphs, and then refine it to improve the best-known approximation factor for graphs. We then introduce new objective functions that incorporate notions of balance and fairness, and provide new hardness results, approximations, and fixed-parameter tractability results.

paragraphs: An edge-colored hypergraph represents objects participating in different types of group interactions. Clustering assigns a color to each object, and an interaction is satisfied only when all its objects match its color. This paper extends the usual goal of minimizing unsatisfied interactions to other objectives that capture different priorities.

The first extension maximizes satisfied interactions. Although maximizing successes and minimizing failures have the same optimal solutions here, their approximation guarantees behave differently. The authors provide the first approximation algorithm for the maximization problem on hypergraphs, where interactions can involve more than two objects. They then refine the method to improve the best-known approximation factor for ordinary graphs.

The paper also introduces objectives incorporating balance and fairness. For these formulations, it establishes hardness results, approximation algorithms, and fixed-parameter tractability results. These contributions explain both what can be computed efficiently and where difficulty remains. The broader message is that choosing an objective changes the available algorithmic guarantees, even when two objectives agree on the ideal solution.
summary.tldr: The paper develops approximation algorithms for satisfied-edge maximization and studies balance and fairness in edge-colored hypergraph clustering.

title: Edge-Colored Clustering in Hypergraphs: Beyond Minimizing Unsatisfied Edges

abstract: Semantic Dependency refers to the relationship between words in a sentence where the meaning of one word depends on another, which is important for natural language understanding. In this paper, we investigate the role of semantic dependencies in answering questions for transformer models, which is achieved by analyzing how token values shift in response to changes in semantics. Through extensive experiments on models including the BERT series, GPT, and LLaMA, we uncover the following key findings: 1). Most tokens primarily retain their original semantic information even as they propagate through multiple layers. 2). Models can encode truthful semantic dependencies in tokens in the final layer. 3). Mistakes in model answers often stem from specific tokens encoded with incorrect semantic dependencies. Furthermore, we found that addressing the incorrectness by directly adjusting parameters is challenging because the same parameters can encode both correct and incorrect semantic dependencies depending on the context. Our findings provide insights into the causes of incorrect information generation in transformers and help the future development of robust and reliable models.

paragraphs: This paper studies transformer mistakes through semantic dependencies: relationships in which one word’s meaning depends on another. The researchers examine how token representations change when sentence meaning changes, using question answering to connect internal representations with model behavior. Their experiments cover models from the BERT family, GPT, and LLaMA.

The analysis finds that most tokens largely preserve their original semantic information as they pass through successive layers. At the same time, tokens in the final layer can encode correct relationships between meanings. These findings suggest that retaining information about an individual word and representing its relationship to other words can coexist inside a transformer.

Incorrect answers often involve particular tokens that encode the wrong semantic dependencies. Fixing these errors by directly changing parameters is difficult because the same parameters can represent correct relationships in one context and incorrect ones in another. The contribution is an interpretable account of some answer failures, together with evidence that their causes depend on context.
summary.tldr: Transformer answer errors often involve tokens encoding incorrect semantic relationships, whose context dependence makes direct parameter fixes difficult.

title: A Lens into Interpretable Transformer Mistakes via Semantic Dependency

abstract: Censored survival data are common in clinical trials, but small control groups can pose challenges, particularly in rare diseases or where balanced randomization is impractical. Recent approaches leverage external controls from historical studies or real-world data to strengthen treatment evaluation for survival outcomes. However, using external controls directly may introduce biases due to data heterogeneity. We propose a doubly protected estimator for the treatment-specific restricted mean survival time difference that is more efficient than trial-only estimators and mitigates biases from external data. Our method adjusts for covariate shifts via doubly robust estimation and addresses outcome drift using the DR-Learner for selective borrowing. The approach can incorporate machine learning to approximate survival curves and detect outcome drifts without strict parametric assumptions, borrowing only comparable external controls. Extensive simulation studies and a real-data application evaluating the efficacy of Galcanezumab in mitigating migraine headaches have been conducted to illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

paragraphs: Clinical trials with small control groups can benefit from control observations collected elsewhere, but differences between data sources can bias treatment comparisons. This paper studies that problem for censored survival outcomes, where some event times are not fully observed. Its target is the difference between treatment-specific restricted mean survival times, which summarizes survival over a restricted time horizon.

The proposed estimator addresses two forms of mismatch. Doubly robust estimation adjusts for shifts in measured covariates between the trial and external data. A DR-Learner then supports selective borrowing by identifying outcome drift, allowing the method to use comparable external controls. Machine learning can estimate survival curves and detect these differences without imposing strict parametric forms.

The authors describe the resulting estimator as more efficient than estimators using only trial data while mitigating bias from external observations. Simulations and an application involving Galcanezumab for migraine headaches illustrate the framework. The methodological contribution is to combine adjustment with selective borrowing, so that additional controls contribute information according to their comparability rather than merely their availability.
summary.tldr: The proposed survival estimator combines covariate adjustment and selective borrowing to improve trial efficiency while mitigating bias from external controls.

title: Doubly Protected Estimation for Survival Outcomes Utilizing External Controls for Randomized Clinical Trials

abstract: Similar to surprising performance in the standard deep learning, deep nets trained by adversarial training also generalize well for unseen clean data (natural data). However, despite adversarial training can achieve low robust training error, there exists a significant robust generalization gap. We call this phenomenon the Clean Generalization and Robust Overfitting (CGRO). In this work, we study the CGRO phenomenon in adversarial training from two views: representation complexity and training dynamics. Specifically, we consider a binary classification setting with $N$ separated training data points. First, we prove that, based on the assumption that we assume there is $\operatorname{poly}(D)$-size clean classifier (where $D$ is the data dimension), ReLU net with only $O(N D)$ extra parameters is able to leverages robust memorization to achieve the CGRO, while robust classifier still requires exponential representation complexity in worst case. Next, we focus on a structured-data case to analyze training dynamics, where we train a two-layer convolutional network with $O(N D)$ width against adversarial perturbation. We then show that a three-stage phase transition occurs during learning process and the network provably converges to robust memorization regime, which thereby results in the CGRO. Besides, we also empirically verify our theoretical analysis by experiments in real-image recognition datasets.
