In this work, we study the CGRO phenomenon in adversarial training from two views: representation complexity and training dynamics. Specifically, we consider a binary classification setting with $N$ separated training data points. First, we prove that, based on the assumption that we assume there is $\operatorname{poly}(D)$-size clean classifier (where $D$ is the data dimension), ReLU net with only $O(N D)$ extra parameters is able to leverages robust memorization to achieve the CGRO, while robust classifier still requires exponential representation complexity in worst case. Next, we focus on a structured-data case to analyze training dynamics, where we train a two-layer convolutional network with $O(N D)$ width against adversarial perturbation. We then show that a three-stage phase transition occurs during learning process and the network provably converges to robust memorization regime, which thereby results in the CGRO. Besides, we also empirically verify our theoretical analysis by experiments in real-image recognition datasets.

paragraphs: Adversarially trained networks can perform well on unseen natural inputs while failing to extend their training-set robustness to unseen inputs. This paper calls that combination clean generalization and robust overfitting. It studies the phenomenon through two complementary questions: what a network can represent, and what its training dynamics lead it to learn.

For binary classification with N separated training points in D dimensions, the authors assume a clean classifier of size polynomial in D exists. Under that assumption, a ReLU network can exhibit the phenomenon through robust memorization using only O(ND) extra parameters. By comparison, representing a robust classifier can require exponential complexity in the worst case.

The training analysis considers structured data and a two-layer convolutional network of O(ND) width trained against adversarial perturbations. It proves a three-stage learning transition that ends in robust memorization, producing the same generalization mismatch. Experiments on real-image recognition datasets support the analysis. The results explain how fitting adversarial training examples can remain compatible with good clean performance yet inadequate robust generalization.
summary.tldr: Under specified theoretical settings, robust memorization explains how adversarial training can yield good clean generalization but poor robust generalization.

title: On the Clean Generalization and Robust Overfitting in Adversarial Training from Two Theoretical Views: Representation Complexity and Training Dynamics

abstract: Jailbreak attacks bypass the guardrails of large language models to produce harmful outputs. In this paper, we ask whether the model outputs produced by existing jailbreaks are actually useful. For example, when jailbreaking a model to give instructions for building a bomb, does the jailbreak yield good instructions? Since the utility of most unsafe answers (e.g., bomb instructions) is hard to evaluate rigorously, we build new jailbreak evaluation sets with known ground truth answers, by aligning models to refuse questions related to benign and easy-to-evaluate topics (e.g., biology or math). Our evaluation of eight representative jailbreaks across five utility benchmarks reveals a consistent drop in model utility in jailbroken responses, which we term the jailbreak tax. For example, while all jailbreaks we tested bypass guardrails in models aligned to refuse to answer math, this comes at the expense of a drop of up to 92% in accuracy. Overall, our work proposes jailbreak utility as a new important metric in AI safety, and introduces benchmarks to evaluate existing and future jailbreaks. We make the benchmark available at https://github.com/ethz-spylab/jailbreak-tax

paragraphs: A jailbreak can make a language model answer a prohibited question, but that does not establish whether the answer is useful or correct. This paper separates those outcomes. It studies whether bypassing refusal also reduces the quality of the resulting response, calling the observed loss in utility the jailbreak tax.

To make answer quality rigorously measurable, the authors align models to refuse benign topics with known answers, such as mathematics or biology. They then evaluate eight representative jailbreaks across five utility benchmarks. This setup allows them to measure correctness after refusal is bypassed without needing to judge the practical effectiveness of dangerous instructions.

The evaluations show a consistent utility drop in jailbroken responses. All tested jailbreaks bypass the math-refusal guardrails, yet accuracy falls by as much as 92%. These results establish that successful bypass and useful output can diverge sharply in the studied settings. The paper introduces benchmarks and proposes output utility as an additional metric for evaluating jailbreaks.
summary.tldr: Jailbreaks that successfully bypass refusals can substantially reduce answer correctness, motivating a separate measure of output utility.

title: The Jailbreak Tax: How Useful are Your Jailbreak Outputs?

abstract: Linear attention offers the advantages of linear inference time and fixed memory usage compared to Softmax attention. However, training large-scale language models with linear attention from scratch remains prohibitively expensive and exhibits significant performance gaps compared to Softmax-based models. To address these challenges, we focus on transforming pre-trained Softmax-based language models into linear attention models. We unify mainstream linear attention methods using a high-order QK integration theory and a multi-level vocabulary decomposition. Specifically, the QK integration theory explains the efficacy of combining linear and sparse attention from the perspective of information collection across different frequency bands. The multi-level vocabulary decomposition exponentially expands memory capacity by recursively exploiting compression loss from compressed states. Through detailed error analysis, we demonstrate superior approximation of Softmax attention achieved by our approach. To further improve performance and reduce training costs, we adopt a soft integration strategy with attention scores, effectively combining a sliding window mechanism. With less than 100M tokens, our method fine-tunes models to achieve linear complexity while retaining 99% of their original performance. Compared to state-of-the-art linear attention model and method, our approach improves MMLU scores by 1.2 percentage points with minimal fine-tuning. Furthermore, even without the sliding window mechanism, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on all test sets with 10B tokens.

MVA instead converts pretrained Softmax-attention models. The aim is to retain the capabilities already learned while gaining the computational properties of linear attention.

The paper unifies several linear-attention methods through high-order query-key integration and multi-level vocabulary decomposition. The first explains combinations of linear and sparse attention in terms of collecting information across frequency bands. summary.tldr: MVA converts pretrained language models to linear attention while retaining most reported performance with limited fine-tuning.

title: MVA: Linear Attention with High-order Query-Keys Integration and Multi-level Vocabulary Decomposition

abstract: We propose methods for auditing multiclass classifiers for fairness under multiclass equalized odds, by estimating the deviation from equalized odds when the classifier is not completely fair. We generalize to multiclass classifiers the measure of Disparate Conditional Prediction (DCP), originally suggested by Sabato & Yom-Tov (2020) for binary classifiers. DCP is defined as the fraction of the population for which the classifier predicts with conditional prediction probabilities that differ from the closest common baseline. We provide new local-optimization methods for estimating the multiclass DCP under two different regimes, one in which the conditional confusion matrices for each protected sub-population are known, and one in which these cannot be estimated, for instance, because the classifier is inaccessible or because good-quality individual-level data is not available. These methods can be used to detect classifiers that likely treat a significant fraction of the population unfairly. Experiments demonstrate the accuracy of the methods. The code for the experiments is provided as supplementary material.

paragraphs: Fairness auditing needs more than a yes-or-no answer about whether a classifier meets a fairness condition. This paper studies how far multiclass classifiers depart from equalized odds. It extends Disparate Conditional Prediction, previously proposed for binary classification, so that the measure can describe classifiers choosing among more than two outcomes.

The measure expresses the fraction of the population whose conditional prediction probabilities differ from the closest shared baseline. That population-based interpretation makes the size of a departure easier to connect to how broadly it affects predictions. The authors introduce local-optimization methods to estimate the measure under two different information settings.

In the first setting, conditional confusion matrices are known for each protected group. In the second, those matrices cannot be estimated, potentially because the classifier is inaccessible or suitable individual-level data is unavailable. Experiments demonstrate the methods’ accuracy. The resulting estimates can help flag classifiers likely to treat a substantial share of the population unfairly under the specified fairness criterion.
summary.tldr: The paper extends a population-based measure of unfair prediction to multiclass classifiers and develops estimators for two different data-access settings.

title: Disparate Conditional Prediction in Multiclass Classifiers

abstract: This paper investigates the convergence behavior of score-based graph generative models (SGGMs). Unlike common score-based generative models (SGMs) that are governed by a single stochastic differential equation (SDE), SGGMs utilize a system of dependent SDEs, where the graph structure and node features are modeled separately, while accounting for their inherent dependencies. This distinction makes existing convergence analyses from SGMs inapplicable for SGGMs. In this work, we present the first convergence analysis for SGGMs, focusing on the convergence bound (the risk of generative error) across three key graph generation paradigms: (1) feature generation with a fixed graph structure, (2) graph structure generation with fixed node features, and (3) joint generation of both graph structure and node features. Our analysis reveals several unique factors specific to SGGMs (e.g., the topological properties of the graph structure) which significantly affect the convergence bound. Additionally, we offer theoretical insights into the selection of hyperparameters (e.g., sampling steps and diffusion length) and advocate for techniques like normalization to improve convergence. To validate our theoretical findings, we conduct a controlled empirical study using a synthetic graph model. The results in this paper contribute to a deeper theoretical understanding of SGGMs and offer practical guidance for designing more efficient and effective SGGMs.

paragraphs: Generating a graph involves coordinating its connections with the features attached to its nodes. The score-based models studied here describe these two parts through dependent stochastic differential equations. Because the equations interact, convergence analyses developed for models governed by a single equation do not directly apply. The paper develops an analysis that explicitly handles this dependence.

The authors bound generative error in three settings: generating node features while keeping the graph fixed, generating graph structure while keeping features fixed, and generating both together. This separation clarifies how the generation task changes the analysis. Their results identify graph-specific influences on the error bound, including topological properties that describe how the graph is connected.

The analysis also provides guidance for choosing sampling steps and diffusion length, and supports normalization as a way to improve convergence. A controlled study using synthetic graphs checks the theoretical findings empirically. The contribution therefore connects mathematical understanding of coupled graph generation with practical choices involved in building and running these models.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds error in score-based graph generation while accounting for dependencies between graph structure and node features.

title: A Non-Asymptotic Convergent Analysis for Scored-Based Graph Generative Model via a System of Stochastic Differential Equations

abstract: Building helpful and harmless large language models (LLMs) requires effective model alignment approach based on human instructions and feedback, which necessitates high-quality human-labeled data. Constructing such datasets is often expensive and hard to scale, and may face potential limitations on diversity and generalization. To address these challenges, we introduce Mixture of Agents Alignment (MoAA), that leverages the collective strengths of various language models to provide high-quality data for model alignment. By employing MoAA, we enhance both supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization, leading to improved performance compared to using a single model alone to generate alignment data (e.g. using GPT-4o alone). Evaluation results show that our approach can improve win rate of LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct from 19.5 to 48.3 on Arena-Hard and from 22.33 to 57.23 on AlpacaEval2, highlighting a promising direction for model alignment through this new scalable and diverse synthetic data recipe. Furthermore, we demonstrate that MoAA enables a self-improvement pipeline, where models fine-tuned on MoA-generated data surpass their own initial capabilities, providing evidence that our approach can push the frontier of open-source LLMs without reliance on stronger external supervision. Data and code will be released.

The authors also demonstrate a self-improvement pipeline in which models trained on mixture-generated data exceed their initial capabilities. This provides evidence that combining available models can improve alignment without stronger external supervision in the demonstrated setting. The contribution is a data-generation recipe whose collective output proves useful for subsequent training, with benchmark gains supporting its promise for open-source language models.
summary.tldr: MoAA combines multiple models to generate alignment data that improves fine-tuning, preference optimization, and demonstrated self-improvement.

title: Improving Model Alignment Through Collective Intelligence of Open-Source Models

abstract: This paper studies a class of convex Finite-sum Coupled Compositional Optimization (cFCCO) problems with applications including group distributionally robust optimization (GDRO) and learning with imbalanced data. To better address these problems, we introduce an efficient single-loop primal-dual block-coordinate stochastic algorithm called ALEXR. The algorithm employs block-coordinate stochastic mirror ascent with extrapolation for the dual variable and stochastic proximal gradient descent updates for the primal variable. We establish the convergence rates of ALEXR in both convex and strongly convex cases under smoothness and non-smoothness conditions of involved functions, which not only improve the best rates in previous works on smooth cFCCO problems but also expand the realm of cFCCO for solving more challenging non-smooth problems such as the dual form of GDRO. Finally, we derive lower complexity bounds, demonstrating the (near-)optimality of ALEXR within a broad class of stochastic algorithms for cFCCO. Experimental results on GDRO and partial Area Under the ROC Curve (pAUC) maximization demonstrate the promising performance of our algorithm.

paragraphs: Some learning objectives combine a finite collection of terms through nested functions, making their optimization more involved than minimizing a simple average. This paper studies the convex version of this problem class, called cFCCO. Its applications include learning from imbalanced data and group distributionally robust optimization, where performance across groups matters.

The proposed algorithm, ALEXR, coordinates primal and dual updates within a single loop. It updates selected blocks of the dual variables using stochastic mirror ascent with extrapolation, while updating the primal variables through stochastic proximal gradient steps. This combines several complementary optimization operations in one stochastic procedure.

The authors establish convergence rates for convex and strongly convex objectives, covering both smooth and nonsmooth functions. Their rates improve previous results for smooth cFCCO and extend the analysis to harder nonsmooth cases, including a dual formulation of group robustness. Lower complexity bounds establish near-optimality within a broad class of stochastic algorithms. Experiments on group robustness and partial ROC-area maximization provide additional evidence of practical promise.
summary.tldr: ALEXR combines single-loop stochastic updates with improved convergence guarantees for convex compositional optimization.

title: A Near-Optimal Single-Loop Stochastic Algorithm for Convex Finite-Sum Coupled Compositional Optimization

abstract: Flow matching (FM) is a family of training algorithms for fitting continuous normalizing flows (CNFs). Conditional flow matching (CFM) exploits the fact that the marginal vector field of a CNF can be learned by fitting least-squares regression to the conditional vector field specified given one or both ends of the flow path. In this paper, we extend the CFM algorithm by defining conditional probability paths along "streams”, instances of latent stochastic paths that connect data pairs of source and target, which are modeled with Gaussian process (GP) distributions. The unique distributional properties of GPs help preserve the “simulation-free” nature of CFM training. We show that this generalization of the CFM can effectively reduce the variance in the estimated marginal vector field at a moderate computational cost, thereby improving the quality of the generated samples under common metrics. Additionally, adopting the GP on the streams allows for flexibly linking multiple correlated training data points (e.g., time series). We empirically validate our claim through both simulations and applications to image and neural time series data.

paragraphs: Flow matching trains continuous normalizing flows by learning a vector field that moves between distributions. Conditional flow matching makes this learning tractable through regression against conditional vector fields defined using one or both endpoints of a path. This paper extends that construction to richer stochastic paths called streams.

The streams connect source and target data pairs and are modeled with Gaussian-process distributions. Properties of those distributions preserve the simulation-free character of conditional flow-matching training. They also allow multiple correlated data points to be linked within the construction, making the approach relevant to data with relationships across time rather than only isolated pairs.

The authors show that the extension can reduce variance in the estimated marginal vector field at a moderate computational cost, improving generated samples under common evaluation metrics. They test the approach through simulations and applications to images and neural time series. The contribution is a more flexible specification of training paths that can improve estimation and accommodate correlations while retaining a key computational advantage of conditional flow matching.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-process streams extend conditional flow matching to reduce vector-field estimation variance and connect correlated training observations.

title: Stream-level Flow Matching with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) face significant deployment challenges due to their substantial resource requirements. While low-bit quantized weights can reduce memory usage and improve inference efficiency, current hardware lacks native support for mixed-precision General Matrix Multiplication (mpGEMM), resulting in inefficient dequantization-based implementations. Moreover, uniform quantization methods often fail to capture weight distributions adequately, leading to performance degradation. We propose GANQ (GPU-Adaptive Non-Uniform Quantization), a layer-wise post-training non-uniform quantization framework optimized for hardware-efficient lookup table-based mpGEMM. GANQ achieves superior quantization performance by utilizing a training-free, GPU-adaptive optimization algorithm to efficiently reduce layer-wise quantization errors. Extensive experiments demonstrate GANQ’s ability to reduce the perplexity gap from the FP16 baseline compared to state-of-the-art methods for both 3-bit and 4-bit quantization. Furthermore, when deployed on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, GANQ’s quantized models achieve up to 2.57$\times$ speedup over the baseline, advancing memory and inference efficiency in LLM deployment.

paragraphs: Reducing the bits used to store language-model weights can save memory, but practical speed depends on how those weights are processed. The paper identifies two obstacles: inefficient implementations that must dequantize weights for mixed-precision matrix multiplication, and uniform quantization that poorly represents weight distributions. GANQ addresses representation quality and GPU execution together.

GANQ is a post-training, non-uniform quantization framework that operates layer by layer. Its training-free optimization adapts to the GPU while reducing each layer's quantization error. The resulting representation is designed for hardware-efficient mixed-precision matrix multiplication based on lookup tables, tying the choice of quantization to the computation used during inference.

Experiments with 3-bit and 4-bit weights show a smaller perplexity gap from the FP16 baseline than the compared state-of-the-art methods. On a single NVIDIA RTX 4090, the quantized models reach up to 2.57 times the baseline speed. These results connect better preservation of model behavior with measured hardware efficiency, with the stated speedup applying to the reported deployment setting.
summary.tldr: GANQ combines GPU-adaptive non-uniform quantization with lookup-table computation to improve low-bit language-model quality and inference speed.

title: GANQ: GPU-Adaptive Non-Uniform Quantization for Large Language Models

abstract: As Large Language Models transition to autonomous agents, user inputs frequently violate cooperative assumptions (e.g., implicit intent, missing parameters, false presuppositions, or ambiguous expressions), creating execution risks that text-only evaluations do not capture. Existing benchmarks typically assume well-specified instructions or restrict evaluation to text-only, single-turn clarification, and thus do not measure multi-turn disambiguation under grounded execution risk. We introduce DRIFT-BENCH, the first diagnostic benchmark that evaluates agentic pragmatics under input faults through multi-turn clarification across state-oriented and service-oriented execution environments. Grounded in classical theories of communication, DRIFT-BENCH provides a unified taxonomy of cooperative breakdowns and employs a persona-driven user simulator with the Rise evaluation protocol. Experiments show substantial performance drops under these faults, with clarification effectiveness varying across user personas and fault types. DRIFT-BENCH connects clarification studies with agent benchmarking, providing a framework to diagnose failures arising from faulty user inputs.

paragraphs: Users often give agents instructions with unstated intentions, missing parameters, mistaken assumptions, or ambiguous wording. For an agent that executes actions, misunderstanding those instructions can affect the environment. DRIFT-BENCH evaluates whether agents can repair such communication failures through multiple turns of clarification before or during grounded execution.

The benchmark organizes input faults using a taxonomy drawn from theories of cooperative communication. It covers both state-oriented and service-oriented execution environments, and combines a persona-driven user simulator with the Rise evaluation protocol. This setup makes clarification part of an ongoing interaction with a particular kind of user, rather than a single isolated response to an unclear prompt.

Experiments show substantial performance declines when these input faults are introduced. The usefulness of clarification also varies with the user persona and the type of fault. Those differences make the benchmark diagnostic: it can help reveal which communication breakdowns an agent handles poorly. The paper connects conversational clarification with agent evaluation by treating successful understanding as part of successful execution.
summary.tldr: DRIFT-BENCH measures how agents clarify faulty user instructions across multiple turns and shows that such faults substantially reduce performance.

title: DRIFT-BENCH: Diagnosing CoopeRative Breakdowns in LLM Agents under Input Faults via Multi-Turn Interaction

abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards is an effective route for post-training to strengthen the reasoning capability of large language models. However, as training proceeds, the learning signal can collapse thus makes the training gain become marginal and ineffective. Specifically, a growing fraction of prompts’ rollouts become advantage-degenerated: all the self-generated rollouts show verified-success, making the standard deviation over their rewards be zero; accordingly each rollout’s advantage becomes degenerated (zero) as well. Given such rollouts’ advantages, the policy-gradient for model optimization eventually vanishes, capping the training performance. We argue that some of these rollouts still contain valuable learning signals but unfortunately omitted with the existing RLVR methods. In this paper, inspired through analyzing the entropy pattern behind golden trajectories produced by external expert models, we propose EchoRL for better exploiting the advantage-degenerated rollouts to further improve the training performance. EchoRL is a lightweight module that first identifies an EchoClip from verified-success rollouts based on their step-level entropy values, and then feeds this clip back as an auxiliary supervision signal in the RL objective. Extensive experiments across 10 benchmarks, 5 LLM backbones, and 7 popular RLVR post-training methods demonstrate that EchoRL consistently improves RLVR post-training with minimal overhead.

EchoRL is a lightweight module that first identifies an EchoClip from verified-success rollouts based on their step-level entropy values, and then feeds this clip back as an auxiliary supervision signal in the RL objective. Extensive experiments across 10 benchmarks, 5 LLM backbones, and 7 popular RLVR post-training methods demonstrate that EchoRL consistently improves RLVR post-training with minimal overhead.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can lose a useful training signal when every sampled response to a prompt succeeds. With identical successful rewards, reward variation becomes zero, and the corresponding advantages also become zero. Those responses then contribute no policy-gradient signal through that advantage calculation, even though parts of them may still be valuable to learn.

EchoRL extracts additional supervision from such successful responses. Motivated by entropy patterns in expert-generated trajectories, it examines step-level entropy within verified-success rollouts and selects a segment called an EchoClip. That clip is fed back into the training objective as auxiliary supervision.

The approach gives successful trajectories another way to contribute when the usual reward comparison has become uninformative. Across 10 benchmarks, five language-model backbones, and seven reinforcement-learning post-training methods, the authors report consistent improvements with minimal overhead. The findings support the paper’s central claim that some advantage-degenerated rollouts still contain useful learning information that standard reward-based updates leave unused.
summary.tldr: EchoRL reuses entropy-selected segments of successful rollouts as supervision when identical rewards make their usual learning advantages vanish.

title: EchoRL: Reinforcement Learning via Rollout Echoing

abstract: Flow Matching shows great promise in offline reinforcement learning (RL), yet optimizing these iterative policies via Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) is unstable. While prevailing paradigms circumvent this by distilling multi-step flows into single-step approximations, such methods may limit the benefits of iterative refinement. To avoid these sacrifices, we propose Direct Flow Q-Learning (DFQL), a streamlined framework that attains superior results by optimizing flow matching policies without BPTT or distillation. DFQL derives a surrogate objective that directly injects terminal Q-value gradients as a guidance term into each step velocity field, ensuring stable optimization while preserving iterative expressive capacity. Across 73 challenging tasks in OGBench and D4RL, DFQL achieves state-of-the-art results. Additionally, DFQL extends seamlessly to the offline-to-online setting, delivering substantial performance gains without further modification.

This connects the value of the eventual action to the updates that construct it, while preserving the policy's multiple refinement steps.

The authors report stable optimization and state-of-the-art results across 73 tasks in OGBench and D4RL. They also apply the same framework to an offline-to-online setting, obtaining substantial gains without further modification. The stated findings suggest that directly guiding the flow's individual steps can retain its expressive capacity while avoiding the training difficulty associated with differentiating through the entire trajectory.
summary.tldr: Direct Flow Q-Learning trains iterative flow policies with terminal value guidance, avoiding both backpropagation through time and distillation.

title: Direct Flow Q-Learning

abstract: How can we generate samples from a conditional distribution that we never fully observe? This question arises across a broad range of applications in both modern machine learning and classical statistics, including image post-processing in computer vision, approximate posterior sampling in simulation-based inference, and conditional distribution modeling in complex data settings. In such settings, compared with unconditional sampling, additional feature information can be leveraged to enable more adaptive and efficient sampling. Building on this, we introduce Conditional Generator using MMD (CGMMD), a novel framework for conditional sampling. Unlike many contemporary approaches, our method frames the training objective as a simple, adversary-free direct minimization problem. A key feature of CGMMD is its ability to produce conditional samples in a single forward pass of the generator, enabling practical one-shot sampling with low test-time complexity. We establish rigorous theoretical bounds on the loss incurred when sampling from the CGMMD sampler, and prove convergence of the estimated distribution to the true conditional distribution. In the process, we also develop a uniform concentration result for nearest-neighbor based functionals, which may be of independent interest. Finally, we show that CGMMD performs competitively on synthetic tasks involving complex conditional densities, as well as on practical applications such as image denoising and image super-resolution.

This arises in tasks such as image restoration and inference from simulations. Conditional Generator using MMD, or CGMMD, uses that feature information to learn a generator designed for efficient sampling.

The method trains through direct minimization of an objective without an adversarial model. Once trained, it produces a conditional sample in a single forward pass, keeping test-time computation low. summary.tldr: CGMMD learns an adversary-free conditional generator that samples in one forward pass and comes with distributional convergence guarantees.

title: One-shot Conditional Sampling: MMD meets Nearest Neighbors

abstract: Generalization under distribution shift remains a core challenge in modern machine learning, yet existing learning bound theory is limited to narrow, idealized settings and is non-estimable from samples. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theory and practical applications. We first show that existing definition of concept shift breaks when the source and target supports mismatch. Leveraging entropic optimal transport, we propose a key notion: $\gamma^\ast$-concept shifts, and derive a general error bound unifying covariate and $\gamma^\ast$-concept shifts, which applies to broad loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling. We further develop estimators for these shifts with concentration guarantees, and the DataShifts algorithm, which can quantify distribution shifts and estimate the error bound in most applications - a rigorous and general tool for analyzing learning error under distribution shift.

paragraphs: This paper seeks to make distribution-shift theory usable for measuring how changes between training and deployment data affect prediction error. It identifies a problem with an existing definition of concept shift: the definition breaks when source and target distributions cover different regions of the input space. That mismatch matters for describing shifts beyond idealized settings.

The authors use entropic optimal transport to introduce a new notion called γ*-concept shift. They derive an error bound that combines this notion with covariate shift, bringing changes in inputs and changes in labeling into one framework. The bound accommodates broad classes of losses and label spaces, including settings where labeling is stochastic.

The work also develops sample-based estimators with concentration guarantees and an algorithm called DataShifts. These provide a route from the theoretical quantities to measurements and an estimated error bound in most applications, as stated in the abstract. The contribution therefore connects a more general definition of shift with tools intended to quantify its implications for learning error.
summary.tldr: DataShifts connects a transport-based definition of concept shift with sample-based estimates and a general prediction-error bound.

title: General Quantification of Covariate and Concept Shifts

abstract: Self-supervised learning for physiological time-series aims to captures the identity of the underlying dynamical process while filtering irrelevant noise. However, existing approaches may obscure the clinical semantics important for downstream transferability. Weakly constrained pretext tasks (i.e. contrastive learning, MAE) may incorrectly ignore the underlying dynamical structure, while structurally constrained models (i.e. SVAEs) are unable to selectively filter sample-specific noise. To bridge this gap, we propose ${\bf PULSE}$, a novel pretraining objective that simultaneously preserves dynamical relationships important to physiological time-series while selectively removing irrelevant noise. We achieve this by formulating a dynamical systems model to identify transferable and non-transferable information between time-series windows, and target the former through a novel cross-reconstruction objective. We establish theory that provides conditions for when transferrable information is recovered, and empirically validate it through synthetic experiments. On several real-world datasets, PULSE effectively distinguishes clinical semantic classes, increases label efficiency, and improves transfer learning performance.

paragraphs: PULSE addresses a tension in self-supervised learning for physiological signals: representations should preserve the underlying process while filtering irrelevant noise. The paper argues that weakly constrained learning tasks may overlook meaningful dynamics, while strongly structured models may retain sample-specific noise. Either problem can reduce the usefulness of representations for clinical transfer tasks.

The proposed pretraining objective uses a dynamical-systems model to distinguish information that transfers between time-series windows from information that does not. A cross-reconstruction objective targets the transferable portion. This gives the learning task a specific structural aim: preserve relationships associated with the physiological process while selectively removing noise that does not carry across windows.

The authors establish conditions under which transferable information is recovered and validate the theory through synthetic experiments. On several real-world datasets, PULSE better distinguishes clinical semantic classes, increases label efficiency, and improves transfer learning. The recovery claim is conditional, while the empirical results support the practical usefulness of combining dynamical structure with selective noise removal.
summary.tldr: PULSE learns physiological representations by preserving transferable dynamics across signal windows while selectively filtering irrelevant noise.

title: Self-Supervised Dynamical System Representations for Physiological Time-Series

abstract: Reliable automatic seizure detection from long-term electroencephalogram recordings (EEG) remains an unsolved challenge, as current models often fail to generalize across patients or clinical settings. Manual EEG review still is the standard of care, highlighting the need for robust models and standardized evaluation. The current literature often reports high efficacy, yet these models frequently fail when deployed to unseen patient populations. To rigorously assess this generalization gap, we conducted a large-scale empirical study evaluating 28 state-of-the-art algorithmic architectures, ranging from classical feature engineering to modern Deep Learning. These algorithms were collected by organizing a competition. A strictly held-out private dataset of continuous EEG recordings from 65 subjects, totaling 4,360 hours of data, was utilized to evaluate algorithm performance. Expert neurophysiologists annotated these recordings, establishing the ground truth for seizure events. Algorithms were evaluated using event-based metrics from the SzCORE framework, including sensitivity, precision, F1-score, and false positive rate per day. Results revealed significant performance variability among state-of-the-art approaches, with the top F1 score of 32% (sensitivity 37%, precision 29%), highlighting the persistent difficulty of this task for current machine learning methodologies. Our analysis uncovered a discordance between peak performance and population-level stability. The algorithms achieving the highest aggregate F1-scores did not achieve the most consistent ranking across subjects, indicating high performance variance and susceptibility to failure on outlier patients. This independent evaluation also exposed a notable gap between self-reported efficacies and hold-out performance, underscoring the critical need for standardized, rigorous benchmarking in developing clinically viable ML models. A comparison with previous challenges and commercial systems indicates that the best algorithm in this study surpassed prior methods. Critically, the evaluation infrastructure transitions into a continuously open benchmarking platform, fostering reproducible research and accelerating the development of robust seizure detection algorithms by allowing ongoing submissions and integration of additional private datasets. Clinical centers can also adopt this platform to evaluate seizure detection algorithms on their EEG data using a standardized, reproducible framework.

title: Quantifying the Generalization Gap in Seizure Detection: A Large-Scale Empirical Benchmark via the SzCORE Challenge

abstract: Multimodal LLMs struggle to systematically model the temporal evolution of visual scenes in videos or multi-image sequences. Such inputs require models to predict or simulate multiple levels of dynamic constituents, such as actions taken in the visual sequence, and the associated changes to the visual environment that result. To address this challenge, we propose a dynamic schema-guided world model, DynaVieW, optimized for visual dynamic prediction and simulation. DynaVieW achieves an in-depth understanding of visual dynamics by learning interleaved state-transition sequences, where states cover broad visual scenes from video keyframes, and transitions capture comprehensive dynamic constituents within a hierarchical schema. DynaVieW jointly models transition prediction and state simulation under a mixture-of-experts architecture, with a cross-expert selective attention and a schema token re-weighted loss, to ensure effective and robust learning. DynaVieW’s superior visual dynamic understanding boosts its downstream performances on both visual narrative creation and world simulation, showing improved consistency and controllability of visual generation and better instruction-following ability.

paragraphs: Understanding a video requires tracking both what a scene contains and how actions change it. The paper argues that multimodal language models struggle to organize these changes systematically across videos or image sequences. DynaVieW addresses this by making scene states and transitions explicit parts of a learned world model.

Training uses alternating sequences of states and transitions. States describe broad scenes drawn from video keyframes, while transitions organize dynamic elements within a hierarchical schema. A mixture-of-experts architecture jointly learns to predict transitions and simulate resulting states. Selective attention across experts and a loss that reweights schema tokens support learning of these structured descriptions.

This organization links an account of what happens to an account of what the visual world becomes afterward. The reported gains extend to visual narrative creation and world simulation, including more consistent and controllable generation and improved instruction following. The findings support structured modeling of visual change as a useful way to improve downstream generation, rather than treating temporal understanding as an implicit by-product of processing image sequences.
summary.tldr: DynaVieW learns structured sequences of scene states and transitions to improve visual prediction, simulation, and controllable generation.

title: DynaVieW: Schema-Guided World Modeling for Understanding Hierarchical Visual Dynamics

abstract: Explanations of model behavior are commonly evaluated via proxy properties weakly tied to the purposes explanations serve in practice. We contribute a decision theoretic framework that treats explanations as information signals valued by the expected improvement they enable on a specified decision task. This approach yields three distinct estimands: (i) a theoretical benchmark that upper-bounds achievable performance by any agent with the explanation, (ii) a human-complementary value that quantifies the theoretically attainable value that is not already captured by a baseline human decision policy, and (iii) a behavioral value representing the causal effect of providing the explanation to human decision-makers. We instantiate these definitions in a practical validation workflow, and apply them to assess explanation potential and interpret behavioral effects in human–AI decision support and mechanistic interpretability.

paragraphs: An explanation is useful partly because of what it enables someone to do. This paper builds that idea into evaluation by treating explanations as information signals for a specified decision task. Their value is measured through expected improvement in decisions, tying assessment directly to the purpose the explanation serves.

The framework distinguishes three quantities. One is an upper bound on the performance any agent could achieve with the explanation. Another measures theoretically attainable value beyond what a baseline human decision policy already captures. The third measures the causal effect of actually providing the explanation to human decision-makers. These separate information potential, additional value relative to people, and realized behavioral impact.

The authors turn these definitions into a practical validation workflow and apply it to human–AI decision support and mechanistic interpretability. The distinction between the three quantities helps interpret why an explanation's potential and its observed effect need not coincide. Evaluation therefore asks both whether the information could improve the specified decision and whether giving it to people actually does so.
summary.tldr: A decision-theoretic framework evaluates explanations by their potential, additional, and realized value for a specified decision task.

title: Explanations are a Means to an End: Decision Theoretic Explanation Evaluation

abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) integrate into writing workflows, precise governance requires distinguishing ”how AI participated” rather than merely ”whether AI was used.” Traditional binary detection often misclassifies “AI-polished” content as generated, creating fairness risks. We propose shifting from passive post-hoc detection to active intent attribution, focusing on the distinction between Editing (source-anchored) and Generation (unanchored). We introduce IACW-Instruct, a corpus of diverse editing operations constructed via a Director–Actor–Judge pipeline to enable systematic evaluation. Building on this benchmark, we propose Intent-Aware Controllable Watermarking (IACW), featuring intent-adaptive entropy gating for semantically lossless embedding. Experiments show that IACW achieves 95% attribution accuracy under 20% token deletion while preserving near-unwatermarked semantic fidelity, establishing a practical paradigm for fine-grained provenance.

paragraphs: A binary judgment that text involved AI can obscure the difference between polishing an existing source and generating new content. The paper argues that confusing these roles creates fairness risks. It therefore focuses on attributing the mode of AI participation, distinguishing editing anchored to source material from generation without such an anchor.

The authors introduce IACW-Instruct, a collection of varied editing operations constructed through a Director–Actor–Judge pipeline. This corpus supports systematic evaluation of the distinction. Their watermarking method, IACW, actively embeds attribution information and uses entropy gating that adapts to intent. The embedding mechanism is designed to preserve meaning while making the type of AI involvement detectable.

Experiments report 95% attribution accuracy after deletion of 20% of the tokens, alongside semantic fidelity close to unwatermarked text. These findings support the feasibility of finer-grained provenance under the tested editing conditions. The attributed distinction concerns source-anchored editing versus unanchored generation, making the role of AI participation more explicit than a simple generated-text label.
summary.tldr: IACW embeds intent-sensitive watermarks to distinguish AI editing from generation while maintaining near-unwatermarked semantic fidelity.

title: IACW: Intent-Aware Controllable Watermarking for Scalable Authorial Intent Attribution

abstract: By integrating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in robotic manipulation, particularly by improving generalization and interpretability. However, the security of CoT-based reasoning mechanisms remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that CoT reasoning introduces a novel attack vector for targeted behavior hijacking—for example, causing a robot to mistakenly deliver a knife to a person instead of an apple—without modifying the user’s instruction. We first provide empirical evidence that CoT strongly governs action generation, even when it is semantically misaligned with the input instructions. Building on this observation, we propose TRAP, the first targeted behavior-hijacking adversarial attack against CoT-reasoning VLA models. By targeting the reasoning-to-action pathway, TRAP uses an adversarial patch (e.g., a tablecloth placed on the table) to steer intermediate CoT reasoning and downstream actions toward adversary-defined behaviors. Extensive evaluations on three representative reasoning VLAs, spanning distinct CoT reasoning mechanisms, demonstrate the effectiveness of TRAP. Notably, we implemented the patch by printing it on paper in a real-world setting. Our findings highlight the urgent need to secure CoT reasoning in VLA systems. The project page is available at https://zhengxian-huang.github.io/TRAP-website/.

paragraphs: Adding chain-of-thought reasoning to robotic vision-language-action models can improve generalization and make their decisions easier to inspect. This paper investigates a security consequence of that design: intermediate reasoning may become a route for redirecting physical actions. The authors first show empirically that reasoning strongly influences action generation even when it conflicts with the user’s instruction.

TRAP targets this reasoning-to-action connection using an adversarial visual patch in the robot’s environment. The patch steers intermediate reasoning toward an attacker-chosen behavior, which can then influence downstream actions without changing the user’s request. This makes the interaction between visual input, generated reasoning, and control central to the attack mechanism.

Evaluations demonstrate effectiveness on three representative reasoning-based VLA models with different reasoning mechanisms. The authors also implement a printed-paper patch in a real-world setting. These results establish the reported vulnerability across multiple tested designs and a physical implementation. They motivate protecting the intermediate reasoning pathway as part of securing robotic action generation.
summary.tldr: TRAP demonstrates that visual patches can redirect robotic actions by manipulating intermediate reasoning without changing the user’s instruction.

title: TRAP: Hijacking VLA CoT-Reasoning via Adversarial Patches

abstract: Effectively modeling non-stationary dynamics in probabilistic multivariate time series(MTS) forecasting requires balancing expressiveness with robustness. Existing parametric approaches benefit from strong inductive biases but lack flexibility, whereas deep generative models struggle to capture complex temporal dependencies without extensive data and computation. We introduce Parametric Prior Mapping (PPM), a framework that injects parametric structural priors into a generative modeling process. Specifically, PPM utilizes a parametric estimator to derive a dynamic, adaptive prior that guides the learning of a complex predictive distribution via a learnable mapping. This design allows the model to retain the efficiency of parametric methods while exploiting the expressive power of generative models. Trained with a hybrid objective, PPM yields precise forecasts with well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. Empirical results show that PPM outperforms existing baselines in handling non-stationary data, offering a superior trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/ljl8336/PPM.

paragraphs: Parametric Prior Mapping addresses forecasting multiple related time series whose behavior changes over time. Probabilistic forecasting must describe both expected outcomes and uncertainty. The paper starts from a tension: parametric methods offer useful structure and efficiency, while flexible generative models can demand substantial data and computation to capture temporal relationships.

PPM combines these approaches by using a parametric estimator to construct a dynamic, adaptive prior. A learnable mapping then uses that prior to guide a richer predictive distribution. The parametric component supplies structural guidance, while the generative component provides flexibility beyond the initial estimate. A hybrid training objective supports the combined forecasting process.

The authors report precise forecasts with well-calibrated uncertainty and stronger performance than existing baselines on non-stationary data. They also report a better balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. These findings suggest that adaptive structural priors can help a flexible model handle changing temporal behavior efficiently. The contribution lies in making the prior an active, learned bridge between a compact estimator and a more expressive predictive distribution.
summary.tldr: PPM guides generative time-series forecasting with adaptive parametric priors to combine expressive predictions, calibrated uncertainty, and computational efficiency.

title: Parametric Prior Mapping Framework for Non-stationary Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting

abstract: The rapid evolution of GUI-enabled agents has rendered traditional CAPTCHAs obsolete. While previous benchmarks like OpenCaptchaWorld established a baseline for evaluating multimodal agents, recent advancements in reasoning-heavy models, such as Gemini3-Pro-High and GPT-5.2-Xhigh have effectively collapsed this security barrier, achieving pass rates as high as 90% on complex logic puzzles like ”Bingo”. In response, we introduce Next-Gen CAPTCHAs, a scalable defense framework designed to secure the next-generation web against the advanced agents. Unlike static datasets, our benchmark is built upon a robust data generation pipeline, allowing for large-scale and easily scalable evaluations, notably, for backend-supported types, our system is capable of generating effectively unbounded CAPTCHA instances. We exploit the persistent human–agent “Cognitive Gap” in interactive perception, memory, decision-making, and action. By engineering dynamic tasks that require adaptive intuition rather than granular planning, we re-establish a robust distinction between biological users and artificial agents, offering a scalable and diverse defense mechanism for the agentic era.

paragraphs: Next-Gen CAPTCHAs responds to the growing ability of agents to solve web challenges through graphical interfaces. The authors report that recent reasoning-heavy models reach pass rates as high as 90% on complex puzzles such as Bingo in earlier evaluations. This motivates challenges built around capabilities that still separate people from agents.

The proposed framework focuses on interactive perception, memory, decision-making, and action. Its dynamic tasks are designed to demand adaptive intuition rather than detailed advance planning. The underlying idea is to exploit a persistent human–agent cognitive gap through interactions that require users to respond as the task unfolds. The authors present this as a way to restore a useful distinction between human users and automated agents.

A generation pipeline supports scalable evaluation instead of relying on a fixed collection of challenges. For challenge types supported by the backend, the system can produce effectively unbounded instances. This qualification matters: the instance-generation claim applies to those supported types. The framework combines diverse interactive challenges with scalable generation as a proposed defense against increasingly capable GUI agents.
summary.tldr: Next-Gen CAPTCHAs proposes scalable interactive challenges that exploit remaining differences between human and GUI-agent capabilities.

title: Next-Gen CAPTCHAs: Leveraging the Cognitive Gap for Scalable and Diverse GUI-Agent Defense

abstract: Time series prototype learning is fundamentally challenged by observational ambiguity. Discrete architectures fail to resolve this, as they lack the capacity to decouple stochastic noise from continuous dynamics. Furthermore, rigid closed-set assumptions fail to capture unseen diversity. To address these limitations, we propose a hierarchical ordinary differential equation clustering network, which utilizes neural ordinary differential equation to model latent state evolution as a continuous integral curve. This formulation enforces temporal continuity to effectively disentangle smooth feature trends from stochastic noise, while our adaptive hierarchical mechanism autonomously determines the appropriate number of prototypes without rigid prior constraints. Validated on the early link failure detection task with irregularly sampled time series, the proposed method effectively extracts underlying physical prototypes, thereby enabling robust failure detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/NJ-LNN/Hierarchical-ODE.

paragraphs: Learning representative patterns from time series is difficult when observations mix underlying dynamics with random noise. The paper addresses this ambiguity in early link failure detection, where measurements can arrive at irregular intervals. It also challenges a fixed set of pattern categories, because that restriction may fail to capture previously unseen variation.

The proposed clustering network represents latent state evolution through a neural ordinary differential equation. This produces a continuous trajectory rather than only a sequence of disconnected states. Enforcing temporal continuity helps separate smooth feature trends from stochastic fluctuations. Alongside this continuous-time model, an adaptive hierarchy determines the number of prototypes instead of requiring a rigid count in advance.

Validation on early link failure detection shows that the method extracts underlying physical prototypes from irregularly sampled data and enables robust detection. The two design choices address different sources of ambiguity: continuous dynamics organize how features evolve, while the adaptive hierarchy accommodates diversity in the patterns being learned. The reported findings support their combined use for recognizing failure-related behavior in this task.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical neural ODE learns continuous-time prototypes and their number adaptively to support early link failure detection.

title: Hierarchical ODE: Learning Continuous-Time Physical Prototypes for Early Link Failure Detection

abstract: Large-scale models are at the forefront of time series (TS) forecasting, dominated by two paradigms: fine-tuning text-based Large Language Models for TS (LLM4TS) and training Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) from scratch. Both approaches share a foundational assumption that scaling up model capacity and data volume leads to improved performance. However, we observe a scaling paradox in TS models, revealing a puzzling phenomenon that larger models do NOT always achieve better performance. Through extensive experiments on two model families across four scales (100M to 1.7B parameters) and diverse data (up to 6B observations), we rigorously confirm that the scaling paradox is a pervasive issue. We then diagnose its root cause by analyzing internal representations, identifying a phenomenon we call few-layer dominance: only a small subset of layers are functionally important, while the majority are redundant, under-utilized, and can even distract training. Based on this discovery, we propose a practical method to automatically identify and retain only these dominant layers. In our models, retaining only 21% of the parameters achieves up to a 12% accuracy improvement and a 2.7x inference speedup. We validate the universality of our method on 8 prominent SOTA models (LLM4TS and TSFMs, 90M to 6B), showing that retaining less than 30% layers achieves superior accuracy in over 95% tasks.

paragraphs: Larger models and more training data are often expected to improve time-series forecasting. This paper tests that expectation for language models adapted to forecasting and foundation models trained for time series. Experiments across two model families, four sizes from 100 million to 1.7 billion parameters, and datasets containing up to six billion observations find that larger models do not always perform better.

Analysis of internal representations identifies few-layer dominance: a small subset of layers contributes most of the useful function, while many others are redundant, underused, or can distract training. The authors develop a method that automatically identifies and retains the dominant layers, using the diagnosis to guide model reduction.

In their models, retaining 21% of parameters delivers up to 12% better accuracy and a 2.7-fold inference speedup. Further evaluation on eight leading models finds that keeping fewer than 30% of layers improves accuracy on over 95% of tested tasks. These results show that selective reduction can improve both efficiency and accuracy within the evaluated forecasting models.
summary.tldr: The paper finds that a few layers dominate many time-series models and shows that retaining them can improve accuracy while reducing inference cost.

title: Revealing Scaling Paradox in Large-scale Time Series Models: Implications for More Efficient and Accurate Forecasting

abstract: Imagine Alice has a specific image $x^\ast$ in her mind, say, the view of the street in which she grew up during her childhood. To generate that exact image, she guides a generative model with multiple rounds of prompting and arrives at an image $x^{p*}$. Although $x^{p*}$ is reasonably close to $x^\ast$, Alice finds it difficult to close that gap using language prompts. This paper aims to narrow this gap by observing that even after language has reached its limits, humans can still tell when a new image $x^+$ is closer to $x^\ast$ than $x^{p*}$. Leveraging this observation, we develop MultiBO (Multi-Choice Preferential Bayesian Optimization) that carefully generates $K$ new images as a function of $x^{p*}$, gets preferential feedback from the user, uses the feedback to guide the diffusion model, and ultimately generates a new set of $K$ images. We show that within $B$ rounds of user feedback, it is possible to arrive much closer to $x^\ast$, even though the generative model has no information about $x^\ast$. Qualitative scores from $30$ users, combined with quantitative metrics compared across $5$ baselines, show promising results, suggesting that multi-choice feedback from humans can be effectively harnessed for personalized image generation.

paragraphs: A person may recognize an image that better matches what they imagine even when they cannot describe the needed change in words. This paper uses that distinction to improve personalized generation after prompting has reached its practical limits. The target image exists in the user’s mind and is never directly available to the generative model.

MultiBO generates a set of candidate images based on the current prompted result and asks the user for preferences. It then uses that feedback to guide a diffusion model and produce another candidate set. Repeating this process turns comparisons among images into a signal for searching toward the user’s intended result.

The authors show that a bounded number of feedback rounds can bring generated images substantially closer to the intended target. Evaluation combines qualitative scores from 30 users with quantitative comparisons against five baselines. The reported results are promising, suggesting that multi-choice preference feedback can refine image generation beyond what language prompts alone achieve. The method’s central contribution is making the user’s ability to compare images operational.
summary.tldr: MultiBO uses repeated user preferences among generated images to move closer to an imagined target after language prompting becomes difficult.

title: Personalized Image Generation via Human-in-the-loop Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Stochastic Frank-Wolfe is a classical optimization method for solving constrained optimization problems. On the other hand, recent optimizers such as Lion and Muon have gained quite significant popularity in deep learning. In this work, building on recent initiatives, we provide a unifying perspective by interpreting these seemingly disparate methods through the lens of Stochastic Frank-Wolfe. Specifically, we show that Lion and Muon with weight decay can be viewed as special instances of a Stochastic Frank-Wolfe, and we establish their convergence guarantees in terms of the Frank-Wolfe gap, a standard stationarity measure in non-convex optimization for Frank-Wolfe methods. We further find that convergence to this gap implies convergence to a KKT point of the original problem under a norm constraint for Lion and Muon. Moreover, motivated by recent empirical findings that stochastic gradients in modern machine learning tasks often exhibit heavy-tailed distributions, we extend Stochastic Frank-Wolfe to settings with heavy-tailed noise by developing two robust variants with strong theoretical guarantees that hold for general compact convex sets without the need for a large batch size, filling the gap in the literature on Stochastic Frank-Wolfe for non-convex optimization. Our contributions in the later part of this work, in turn, yield new variants of Lion and Muon, that better accommodate heavy-tailed gradient noise, thereby enhancing their practical scope.

paragraphs: Lion and Muon are deep-learning optimizers, while stochastic Frank-Wolfe is a classical approach to constrained optimization. This paper connects them by showing that Lion and Muon with weight decay can be interpreted as instances of stochastic Frank-Wolfe. The connection supplies a common mathematical language for analyzing their behavior.

The authors establish convergence guarantees using the Frank-Wolfe gap, a measure of stationarity suited to constrained nonconvex problems. They further show that convergence in this measure implies convergence to a Karush–Kuhn–Tucker point for the corresponding norm-constrained problem. This characterizes a constrained stationarity condition, rather than asserting that the optimizers necessarily reach a globally best solution.

The paper also develops two robust stochastic Frank-Wolfe variants for heavy-tailed gradient noise, where unusually large gradient fluctuations matter. Their theoretical guarantees apply to general compact convex constraint sets without requiring large batches. Through the earlier connection, these developments yield new Lion and Muon variants designed to better accommodate heavy-tailed noise, expanding the conditions under which the optimization framework can be used.
summary.tldr: A stochastic Frank-Wolfe interpretation gives convergence guarantees for Lion and Muon and motivates variants robust to heavy-tailed gradient noise.

title: Lions and Muons: Optimization via Stochastic Frank-Wolfe under Heavy-Tailed Noise

abstract: Label shift refers to the distribution shift scenario where the marginal label distribution changes while the class-conditional distribution remains invariant. To address this challenge in complex real-world settings, we propose Regularized Discriminative Alignment for Label Shift (RDALS), a novel framework that adapts to target domains by aligning distributions within the deep latent space. By shifting the focus from raw inputs to learned representations, RDALS effectively operates under a weaker and more practical invariance assumption. Specifically, we construct a moment-matching linear system using Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) and show that this choice maximizes numerical stability. We further provide rigorous theoretical analysis, establishing finite-sample error bounds for the importance weight estimation and the generalization bounds for the adapted classifier. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that RDALS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving superior robustness and accuracy in both data-scarce and extreme-shift regimes.

paragraphs: Label shift occurs when class frequencies change between domains while the distribution of inputs within each class remains unchanged. RDALS adapts this idea to learned deep representations. By aligning distributions in latent space, it works under a weaker invariance assumption than requiring the original input distributions to remain stable within every class.

The framework constructs a linear system that matches statistical moments using Linear Discriminant Analysis. The authors show that this choice maximizes numerical stability, addressing the reliability of estimating importance weights for adaptation. Those weights account for differences in class prevalence between the source and target domains.

The paper also provides finite-sample bounds on weight-estimation error and generalization bounds for the adapted classifier. These connect the estimation procedure to theoretical statements about its behavior with limited data. Experiments on standard benchmarks report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy and robustness, including scarce-data and extreme-shift conditions. The contribution combines a representation-level assumption, stable estimation, and empirical evidence for adaptation.
summary.tldr: RDALS handles changing class frequencies through stable alignment in learned representations, with theoretical error bounds and strong benchmark results.

title: Regularized Discriminative Alignment for Deep Representations under Label Shift

abstract: In machine unlearning, $(\varepsilon,\delta)-$unlearning is a popular framework that provides formal guarantees on the effectiveness of the removal of a subset of training data, the forget set, from a trained model. For strongly convex objectives, existing first-order methods achieve $(\varepsilon,\delta)-$unlearning, but they only use the forget set to calibrate injected noise, never as a direct optimization signal. In contrast, efficient empirical heuristics often exploit the forget samples (e.g., via gradient ascent) but come with no formal unlearning guarantees. We bridge this gap by presenting the Variance-Reduced Unlearning (VRU) algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, VRU is the first first-order algorithm that directly includes forget set gradients in its update rule, while provably satisfying $(\varepsilon,\delta)-$unlearning. We establish the convergence of VRU and show that incorporating the forget set yields strictly improved rates, i.e., a better dependence on the achieved error compared to existing first-order $(\varepsilon,\delta)-$unlearning methods. Moreover, we prove that, in a low-error regime VRU asymptotically outperforms any first-order methods that ignores the forget set. Experiments corroborate our theory, showing consistent gains over both state-of-the-art certified unlearning methods and over empirical baselines that explicitly leverage the forget set.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples, called the forget set. For strongly convex objectives, existing first-order methods provide formal epsilon–delta unlearning guarantees but use those examples only to calibrate noise. Practical heuristics often use forget-set gradients directly, yet lack the same formal guarantees.

Variance-Reduced Unlearning, or VRU, connects these approaches by including forget-set gradients in its update rule while provably satisfying epsilon–delta unlearning. The authors establish convergence and show that using this information improves the rate’s dependence on achieved error compared with existing first-order certified methods. The forget set thus becomes an optimization signal as well as information relevant to privacy-style calibration.

In a low-error regime, VRU asymptotically outperforms any first-order method that ignores the forget set, within the theoretical setting studied. Experiments corroborate the analysis through consistent gains over certified unlearning methods and empirical baselines that also use forget examples. The main contribution is evidence that directly exploiting data targeted for removal can improve optimization while preserving a formal unlearning guarantee.
summary.tldr: VRU directly uses forget-set gradients while retaining formal unlearning guarantees, improving convergence rates and reported empirical performance.

title: Variance-Reduced $(\varepsilon, δ)-$Unlearning using Forget Set Gradients

abstract: A critical challenge in developing capable AI agents is defining their "action space”—the set of possible actions they can take. These spaces can range widely, from generating code and using language skills to operating on latent representations or raw joystick controls. Through a large-scale study in Minecraft, we discovered a major dilemma: no single action space is universally best. The most effective action space is highly task-dependent, which complicates the goal of building one generalist agent that can handle everything. To solve this, we introduce Chain-of-Action (CoA), a novel framework that unifies high-level abstracted actions and low-level control actions within a single model. With CoA, an abstract goal is not just a final command; instead, it serves as an intermediate reasoning step that guides the model to generate the precise, executable actions needed to complete the task. Furthermore, we show that an All-in-One generalist agent, trained on a diverse mix of action spaces using CoA, learns a more generalizable policy. This unified agent achieves a new state-of-the-art, outperforming strong, specialized baselines. To support the research community, we are releasing the OpenHA (Open Hierarchical Agents) suite, which includes our benchmark of over 800 tasks, curated datasets, source code, and all model checkpoints at: https://github.com/ CraftJarvis/OpenHA.

paragraphs: An agent’s action space determines how it can interact with its environment, from abstract language skills to detailed control signals. A large-scale Minecraft study finds that the most effective action space depends strongly on the task. This complicates the design of a generalist agent, because choosing one space can leave it poorly suited to other tasks.

OpenHA introduces Chain-of-Action to combine abstract actions and low-level controls within one model. An abstract goal becomes an intermediate reasoning step that helps generate the detailed actions needed for execution. The authors train an All-in-One agent on a diverse mixture of action spaces using this framework.

The resulting agent learns a more generalizable policy and achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming strong specialized baselines in the study. This supports mixed action-space training as a way to build a generalist without committing to a single level of control. The OpenHA release includes a benchmark of more than 800 tasks, curated datasets, source code, and model checkpoints, providing resources for studying the approach and comparing future hierarchical agents.
summary.tldr: OpenHA combines abstract and low-level actions through Chain-of-Action, producing a Minecraft generalist that outperforms specialized baselines in the reported study.

title: OpenHA: A Series of Open-Source Hierarchical Agentic Models in Minecraft

abstract: Current approaches to enhance Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning, such as Chain-of-Thought and "Wait" prompts, primarily encourage models to think more, yet often fail to guide them toward Truth. While Representation Editing (RepE) offers a intrinsic control, its application to dynamic reasoning trajectories remains underexplored. In this work, we bridge this gap by investigating the geometry of truth within unfolding reasoning chains. We uncover three critical insights: (1) Truth is encoded at the sentence level and is entangled with latent reasoning patterns; (2) Effective intervention follows an Uncertainty Principle and a Decay Effect, requiring localization to early, high-entropy forks; (3) Naive steering vectors suffer from noise, risking collateral damage to correct trajectories. Based on these findings, we propose DynaSteer, a dynamic RepE framework. DynaSteer employs pattern clustering to disentangle reasoning manifolds and utilizes Fisher-LDA to project purified truth. By dynamically monitoring lookahead entropy, it selectively steers and rolls back trajectories only when necessary. Comprehensive experimental results on several MATH benchmark verify the effectiveness of DynaSteer, and experiments on out-of-domain coding tasks further confirm its generalization ability. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/tianlwang/DynaSteer.
