paragraphs: Encouraging a language model to reason longer does not necessarily guide it toward correct conclusions. This paper investigates how truth-related information appears inside unfolding reasoning chains and how internal representations can be edited to influence their direction. The authors find sentence-level truth signals entangled with different reasoning patterns.

Their analysis also indicates that useful intervention should target early, uncertain branching points, and that noisy steering directions can damage trajectories that were already correct. DynaSteer responds by clustering reasoning patterns and using Fisher linear discriminant analysis to isolate cleaner truth-related directions. It then monitors lookahead entropy to decide when intervention is warranted.

The framework selectively steers reasoning and rolls trajectories back when needed, making the intervention depend on the evolving reasoning state. Experiments on several MATH benchmarks demonstrate effectiveness, while coding experiments provide evidence of transfer outside the original domain. These findings support selective representation editing as a way to guide reasoning, without implying that an internal truth signal guarantees correct answers.
summary.tldr: DynaSteer selectively edits internal representations at uncertain reasoning branches to improve mathematical reasoning and transfer to coding tasks.

title: Search for Truth from Reasoning: A Dynamic Representation Editing Framework for Steering LLM Trajectories

abstract: 3D style transfer enables the creation of visually expressive 3D content, enriching the visual appearance of 3D scenes and objects. However, existing VGG- and CLIP-based methods struggle to model multi-view consistency within the model itself, while diffusion-based approaches can capture such consistency but rely on denoising directions, leading to unstable training. To address these limitations, we propose DiffStyle3D, a novel diffusion-based paradigm for 3DGS style transfer that directly optimizes in the latent space. Specifically, we introduce an Attention-Aware Loss that performs style transfer by aligning style features in the self-attention space, while preserving original content through content feature alignment. Inspired by the geometric invariance of 3D stylization, we propose a Geometry-Guided Multi-View Consistency method that integrates geometric information into self-attention to enable cross-view correspondence modeling. Based on geometric information, we additionally construct a geometry-aware mask to prevent redundant optimization in overlapping regions across views, which further improves multi-view consistency. Extensive experiments show that DiffStyle3D outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving higher stylization quality and visual realism. The code is available at https://github.com/yangyt46/DiffStyle3D.

paragraphs: Applying an artistic style to a 3D scene requires the appearance to remain coherent across viewpoints. DiffStyle3D targets this problem for scenes represented by 3D Gaussian splatting. It uses diffusion-model representations while directly optimizing in latent space, addressing the training instability associated with approaches that rely on denoising directions.

Its Attention-Aware Loss aligns style information in self-attention features and separately aligns content features to preserve the scene’s original content. Geometry is also incorporated into self-attention so that the model can connect corresponding regions across views. This makes the scene’s spatial structure part of the mechanism used to coordinate stylization.

A geometry-aware mask further prevents redundant optimization where views overlap. Together, these components link appearance changes across viewpoints while avoiding repeated treatment of the same regions. Experiments report better stylization quality and visual realism than state-of-the-art methods. The findings support using attention features and explicit geometric correspondence as complementary tools for producing consistent stylized 3D content.
summary.tldr: DiffStyle3D combines attention-based style alignment with geometric correspondence to improve the quality and cross-view consistency of stylized 3D Gaussian scenes.

title: DiffStyle3D: Consistent 3D Gaussian Stylization via Attention Optimization

abstract: Bridging the gap between data-rich training regimes and observation-sparse deployment conditions remains a central challenge in spatiotemporal field reconstruction, particularly when target domains exhibit distributional shifts, heterogeneous structure, and multi-scale dynamics absent from available training data. We present SENDAI, a hierarchical $\textbf{S}$parse-measurement, $\textbf{E}$fficie$\textbf{N}$t $\textbf{D}$ata $\textbf{A}$ss$\textbf{I}$milation Framework that reconstructs full spatial states from hyper sparse sensor observations by combining simulation-derived priors with learned discrepancy corrections. We demonstrate the performance on satellite remote sensing, reconstructing MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) derived vegetation index fields across six globally distributed sites. Using seasonal periods as a proxy for domain shift, the framework consistently outperforms established baselines that require substantially denser observations—SENDAI achieves a maximum SSIM improvement of 185% over traditional baselines and a 36% improvement over recent high-frequency-based methods. These gains are particularly pronounced for landscapes with sharp boundaries and sub-seasonal dynamics; more importantly, the framework effectively preserves diagnostically relevant structures—such as field topologies, land cover discontinuities, and spatial gradients. By yielding corrections that are more structurally and spectrally separable, the reconstructed fields are better suited for downstream inference of indirectly observed variables. The results therefore highlight a lightweight and operationally viable framework for sparse-measurement reconstruction that is applicable to physically grounded inference, resource-limited deployment, and real-time monitor and control.

abstract: KV cache in autoregressive LLMs eliminates redundant recomputation but has emerged as the dominant memory and bandwidth bottleneck during inference, notably with long contexts and test-time scaling. KV quantization is a key lever for reducing cache cost, but accuracy drops sharply as the native KV distribution lacks flatness and thus maintains a wide quantization range. Prior work focuses on isolating outliers, which caps their error but fails to flatten the overall distribution, leaving performance fragile under low-bit settings. In this work, we show that the K cache maintains a stable, context-evolving structure, while the V cache carries latent semantic regularities, with both contributing to the organization of vectors into shared patterns. Building on these insights, we propose PatternKV, a pattern-aligned residual quantization scheme. It mines representative pattern vectors online, aligns each KV vector to its nearest pattern, and quantizes only the residual. This reshaping of the KV distribution flattens the quantization target and narrows its range, thereby improving the fidelity of low-bit KV quantization. Across long-context and test-time scaling settings on multiple backbones, PatternKV delivers consistent 2-bit gains, incurs only a 0.08% average 4-bit drop relative to FP16, and improves test-time scaling accuracy by 10% on average. Compared with FP16, PatternKV further raises throughput by 1.5$\times$ and supports 1.25$\times$ larger batches.

Compressing it into very few bits risks accuracy loss because the values span a wide range. PatternKV addresses the overall distribution of cached vectors rather than focusing only on unusually large values.

The method identifies representative patterns online, associates each key or value vector with its nearest pattern, and quantizes the remaining difference. It also reports a 10% average improvement in test-time scaling accuracy. Relative to FP16, throughput rises by 1.5 times and supported batch size by 1.25 times, connecting improved compression fidelity with practical inference capacity.
summary.tldr: PatternKV compresses attention caches by quantizing differences from shared patterns, improving low-bit accuracy and reported inference throughput.

title: PatternKV: Flattening KV Representation Expands Quantization Headroom

abstract: Inspired by the idea of Positive-incentive Noise (Pi-Noise or $\pi$-Noise) that aims at learning the reliable noise beneficial to tasks, we scientifically investigate the connection between contrastive learning and $\pi$-noise in this paper. By converting the contrastive loss to an auxiliary Gaussian distribution to quantitatively measure the difficulty of the specific contrastive model under the information theory framework, we properly define the task entropy, the core concept of $\pi$-noise, of contrastive learning. It is further proved that the predefined data augmentation in the standard contrastive learning paradigm can be regarded as a kind of point estimation of $\pi$-noise. Inspired by the theoretical study, a framework that develops a $\pi$-noise generator to learn the beneficial noise (instead of estimation) as data augmentations for contrast is proposed. The designed framework can be applied to diverse types of data and is also completely compatible with the existing contrastive models. From the visualization, we surprisingly find that the proposed method successfully learns effective augmentations.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning uses augmented data to shape what a model learns to treat as related. This paper studies those augmentations through positive-incentive noise, meaning noise that benefits the learning task. Its central question is how predefined transformations relate to a formal account of useful noise, and whether that account can guide learned augmentations.

The authors convert the contrastive loss into an auxiliary Gaussian distribution and use an information-theoretic framework to define task entropy for contrastive learning. This supplies a quantitative description of task difficulty. Within that formulation, they prove that predefined augmentation in standard contrastive learning can be interpreted as a point estimate of positive-incentive noise.

The theoretical connection motivates a generator that learns beneficial noise to produce augmentations. The framework is described as applicable to different data types and compatible with existing contrastive models. Visualizations show that it learns effective augmentations. The work therefore links an interpretation of established augmentation practice to a concrete mechanism for learning task-beneficial transformations.
summary.tldr: The paper interprets predefined contrastive augmentations as estimates of beneficial noise and uses that theory to learn augmentations with a noise generator.

title: Data Augmentation of Contrastive Learning is Estimating Positive-incentive Noise

abstract: Dataset pruning remains underexplored for 3D modalities, where inherent class imbalance persists across both training and test sets. This creates a divergence in evaluation: overall accuracy favors natural frequency, reflecting practical usage; while mean accuracy demands balanced generalization. Instead of forcing a premature trade-off, we advocate for base principles that remain universally robust and beneficial across diverse priors. We cast pruning as a quadrature approximation on population risk and decompose the error bound into representation error (fidelity to the underlying manifold) and prior-mismatch bias (distribution shift), clarifying what can be improved jointly across priors. To address prior-mismatch bias, we decouple likelihood from prior in the posterior and transfer the structural likelihood via distillation with a calibrated teacher and geometry-preserving constraints. Simultaneously, to reduce representation error, we audit common pruning signals and choose geometric embedding, which exhibits greater robustness given the high inductive bias of 3D models. We also prioritize a safety floor before selection, capturing high-reward regions beneficial across priors. Finally, acknowledging that no single subset optimally satisfies divergent evaluation priors, we augment these principles with a steering wrapper that interpolates between stratified seeding and global selection. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework elevates the performance floor while offering flexibility for different prior preferences.

paragraphs: Selecting a smaller 3D training dataset is complicated by class imbalance in both training and testing. Overall accuracy gives common classes more influence, while mean accuracy emphasizes balanced performance across classes. Consequently, the best subset can depend on which class distribution the evaluation is intended to represent.

The paper views pruning as approximating population risk with a selected set of samples. It separates error into two sources: how well the subset represents the data's underlying geometry and how much its class prior differs from the desired distribution. To address the latter, it separates likelihood from prior and transfers structural information through a calibrated teacher, distillation, and geometry-preserving constraints.

For representation quality, the method selects using geometric embeddings and establishes a safety floor that captures regions useful across priors. A steering wrapper then moves between class-stratified seeding and global selection. The paper explicitly recognizes that no single subset optimally serves divergent evaluation priors. Its experiments report a stronger performance floor while preserving flexibility to accommodate different preferences about class balance.
summary.tldr: The framework prunes 3D datasets by separating geometric coverage from class-prior mismatch and allowing selection to follow different evaluation priorities.

title: Exploring 3D Dataset Pruning

abstract: Low-rank approximation has emerged as a cornerstone technique for model compression and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling substantial reductions in computation and memory without altering model architectures. However, existing approaches often overlook the shifts in feature distributions induced by the approximation process, which can lead to error amplification and unstable inference. We propose a distribution-aware whitening framework that dynamically whitens layer inputs based on the evolving feature distributions, ensuring second-order isotropy of input features. This allows that the discarded components in the low-rank approximation are those with minimal impact on model outputs, thereby minimizing cumulative approximation errors across layers. We theoretically analyze how distribution misalignment leads to error propagation and demonstrate that our approach achieves tighter control over layerwise distortion. Extensive experiments across various large language models demonstrate the superiority of our method in post-training compression. Moreover, our method can also serve as an effective initialization for LoRA-style parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Our findings highlight the importance of considering feature distributions in low-rank approximations, paving the way for reliable and effective model compression strategies.

paragraphs: This paper studies why low-rank model compression can accumulate errors across layers. Approximating a layer changes the features passed to later layers, so assumptions based on the original feature distribution may become misaligned. The authors connect these distribution shifts to amplified approximation errors and unstable inference.

Their framework dynamically whitens each layer’s inputs using the evolving feature distribution. Whitening makes the inputs isotropic in their second-order statistics, giving the approximation a distribution-aware basis for deciding what to discard. The intended effect is to remove components with minimal influence on model outputs and control the distortion that accumulates through the network.

The theoretical analysis explains how distribution mismatch propagates errors and establishes tighter control of layerwise distortion with the proposed method. Experiments across several large language models report superior post-training compression performance. The authors also find that the method provides an effective initialization for LoRA-style fine-tuning. Together, these findings emphasize that useful low-rank approximations depend on the features a compressed model actually receives.
summary.tldr: Distribution-aware whitening reduces error propagation in low-rank compression by adapting to the changing inputs of successive layers.

abstract: We propose a new kernel function for attributed molecular graphs, which is based on the idea of computing an optimal assignment from the atoms of one molecule to those of another one, including information on neighborhood, membership to a certain structural element and other characteristics for each atom. As a byproduct this leads to a new class of kernel functions. We demonstrate how the necessary computations can be carried out efficiently. Compared to marginalized graph kernels our method in some cases leads to a significant reduction of the prediction error. Further improvement can be gained, if expert knowledge is combined with our method. We also investigate a reduced graph representation of molecules by collapsing certain structural elements, like e.g. rings, into a single node of the molecular graph.

Further improvement can be gained, if expert knowledge is combined with our method. We also investigate a reduced graph representation of molecules by collapsing certain structural elements, like e.g. rings, into a single node of the molecular graph.

paragraphs: This paper proposes comparing molecules by finding an optimal assignment between their atoms. Molecules are represented as attributed graphs, so each atom carries information beyond its identity. The comparison incorporates properties such as an atom's neighborhood and its membership in a structural element, allowing the assignment to reflect molecular context.

The resulting similarity function is presented as a new kernel for molecular graphs and also leads to a broader class of kernel functions. The authors show how to perform the required computations efficiently. They additionally investigate a reduced representation in which certain structures, such as rings, are collapsed into single graph nodes.

Compared with marginalized graph kernels, the proposed method substantially reduces prediction error in some cases. Combining it with expert knowledge can provide further improvement. These findings suggest that informative atom matching and domain knowledge can strengthen molecular prediction. The reported advantage is explicitly case-dependent, while the reduced graph representation explores another way of expressing molecular structure for comparison.
summary.tldr: An atom-assignment kernel compares molecular graphs using structural attributes and reduces prediction error in some evaluated cases.

title: Optimal assignment kernels for attributed molecular graphs

abstract: We prove a quantitative connection between the expected sum of rewards of a policy and binary classification performance on created subproblems. This connection holds without any unobservable assumptions (no assumption of independence, small mixing time, fully observable states, or even hidden states) and the resulting statement is independent of the number of states or actions. The statement is critically dependent on the size of the rewards and prediction performance of the created classifiers. We also provide some general guidelines for obtaining good classification performance on the created subproblems. In particular, we discuss possible methods for generating training examples for a classifier learning algorithm.

The statement is critically dependent on the size of the rewards and prediction performance of the created classifiers. We also provide some general guidelines for obtaining good classification performance on the created subproblems. In particular, we discuss possible methods for generating training examples for a classifier learning algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper establishes a quantitative relationship between reinforcement learning and binary classification. It connects a policy’s expected total reward to the predictive performance of classifiers on constructed subproblems. This makes classification performance a mathematically grounded way to reason about the quality of the resulting policy.

The connection does not require assumptions of independence, short mixing times, fully observable states, or even hidden states. The resulting statement also does not depend on the number of states or actions. Its critical dependencies are instead the size of rewards and the prediction performance achieved on the constructed classification problems.

The paper also discusses how to obtain good classifiers for those subproblems, including possible ways to generate training examples for a classification learner. This practical component matters because the theoretical connection depends directly on prediction quality. The contribution therefore combines a broad performance relationship with guidance about the data needed to use it. It identifies reward scale and classifier performance as central quantities without requiring the listed assumptions about the environment.
summary.tldr: A theorem links policy reward to binary classification performance without dependence on the number of states or actions.

title: Relating reinforcement learning performance to classification performance

abstract: Proportional data (normalized histograms) have been frequently occurring in various areas, and they could be mathematically abstracted as points residing in a geometric simplex. A proper distance metric on this simplex is of importance in many applications including classiﬁcation and information retrieval. In this paper, we develop a novel framework to learn an optimal metric on the simplex. Major features of our approach include: 1) its ﬂexibility to handle correlations among bins/dimensions; 2) widespread applicability without being limited to ad hoc backgrounds; and 3) a “real” global solution in contrast to existing traditional local approaches. The technical essence of our approach is to ﬁt a parametric distribution to the observed empirical data in the simplex. The distribution is parameterized by aﬃnities between simplex vertices, which is learned via maximizing likelihood of observed data. Then, these aﬃnities induce a metric on the simplex, deﬁned as the earth mover’s distance equipped with ground distances derived from simplex vertex aﬃnities.

paragraphs: Normalized histograms describe proportions across bins and can be represented as points on a geometric simplex. Comparing such points requires a distance that reflects meaningful relationships between bins. This paper develops an unsupervised framework for learning that distance from observed proportional data, with classification and information retrieval among the motivating applications.

The method fits a parametric probability distribution to the observations. Its parameters describe affinities between simplex vertices, corresponding to relationships among histogram dimensions. These affinities are learned by maximizing the likelihood of the data. This allows the distance construction to account for correlations among bins rather than treating their relationships as fixed in advance.

The learned affinities then determine ground distances for an earth mover's distance on the simplex. In effect, fitting a distribution supplies the relationships used to compare entire histograms. The authors emphasize broad applicability and a global solution, contrasting their approach with traditional local methods. That optimality claim belongs to the proposed framework; the abstract does not establish that the resulting metric is best for every downstream application.
summary.tldr: The framework learns relationships between histogram bins from unlabeled data and uses them to construct an earth mover's distance.

title: Dirichlet aggregation: unsupervised learning towards an optimal metric for proportional data

abstract: We propose and analyze two strategies to learn over unordered pairs with kernels, and provide a common theoretical framework to compare them. The strategies are related to methods that were recently investigated to predict edges in biological networks. We show that both strategies differ in their loss function and in the kernels they use. We deduce in particular a smooth interpolation between the two approaches, as well as new ways to learn over unordered pairs. The different approaches are tested on the inference of missing edges in two biological networks.

We deduce in particular a smooth interpolation between the two approaches, as well as new ways to learn over unordered pairs. The different approaches are tested on the inference of missing edges in two biological networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies kernel-based learning when each input is an unordered pair. The ordering of the two members does not distinguish one input from another, as in predicting whether two entities share an edge in a network. The authors consider two strategies related to methods previously explored for biological edge prediction.

They place both strategies in a common theoretical framework so that their differences can be analyzed directly. The comparison shows that the approaches differ in two aspects: the kernels they use and the loss functions they optimize. This identifies distinct modeling choices behind methods aimed at the same pair-prediction task.

From this framework, the authors derive a smooth interpolation between the strategies as well as additional approaches for learning over unordered pairs. They test the different methods by inferring missing edges in two biological networks. The contribution is both explanatory and constructive: it clarifies how existing strategies relate and uses that relationship to develop further learning methods for pair-valued inputs.
summary.tldr: A common framework relates two kernel-learning strategies for unordered pairs and yields interpolations and new methods.

title: On learning with kernels for unordered pairs

abstract: Existing algorithms for joint clustering and feature selection can be categorized as either global or local approaches. Global methods select a single cluster-independent subset of features, whereas local methods select cluster-specific subsets of features. In this paper, we present a unified probabilistic model that can perform both global and local feature selection for clustering. Our approach is based on a hierarchical beta-Bernoulli prior combined with a Dirichlet process mixture model. We obtain global or local feature selection by adjusting the variance of the beta prior. We provide a variational inference algorithm for our model. In addition to simultaneously learning the clusters and features, this Bayesian formulation allows us to learn both the number of clusters and the number of features to retain. Experiments on synthetic and real data show that our unified model can find global and local features and cluster data as well as competing methods of each type.

In this paper, we present a unified probabilistic model that can perform both global and local feature selection for clustering. Our approach is based on a hierarchical beta-Bernoulli prior combined with a Dirichlet process mixture model. We obtain global or local feature selection by adjusting the variance of the beta prior. We provide a variational inference algorithm for our model. In addition to simultaneously learning the clusters and features, this Bayesian formulation allows us to learn both the number of clusters and the number of features to retain. Experiments on synthetic and real data show that our unified model can find global and local features and cluster data as well as competing methods of each type.

paragraphs: When clustering data, feature selection can either choose one set of useful features for every cluster or choose a different set for each cluster. These global and local approaches reflect different possibilities about which measurements matter. The paper introduces a probabilistic model that can represent both possibilities within one formulation.

The model combines a hierarchical beta-Bernoulli prior with a Dirichlet process mixture model. Adjusting the variance of the beta prior produces global or local feature selection. This gives the distinction between shared and cluster-specific features a place inside the model, instead of requiring a separate modeling framework for each approach.

A variational inference algorithm learns the clustering and feature selections together. The Bayesian formulation also allows the number of clusters and retained features to be learned. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the model can recover both global and local features and cluster data as well as competing methods specialized for each type. The evidence supports the usefulness of a unified formulation across the tested settings.
summary.tldr: A unified Bayesian clustering model learns shared or cluster-specific features, along with how many clusters and features to retain.

title: A Unified Probabilistic Model for Global and Local Unsupervised Feature Selection

abstract: Matching one set of objects to another is a ubiquitous task in machine learning and computer vision that often reduces to some form of the quadratic assignment problem (QAP). The QAP is known to be notoriously hard, both in theory and in practice. Here, we investigate if this difficulty can be mitigated when some additional piece of information is available: (a) that all QAP instances of interest come from the same application, and (b) the correct solution for a set of such QAP instances is given. We propose a new approach to accelerating the solution of QAPs based on learning parameters for a modified objective function from prior QAP instances. A key feature of our approach is that it takes advantage of the algebraic structure of permutations, in conjunction with special methods for optimizing functions over the symmetric group \m{\Sb_n} in Fourier space. Experiments show that in practical domains the new method can significantly outperform existing approaches.

paragraphs: Matching objects between two sets often leads to a quadratic assignment problem, a difficult optimization task. This paper asks whether solving such problems can become easier when they repeatedly arise from the same application and correct matchings are available for some previous instances.

The proposed method learns parameters of a modified objective function from those solved examples. It uses the algebraic structure of permutations, which encode possible assignments, together with methods for optimizing over the symmetric group in Fourier space. The learning component brings application-specific information into the objective, while the harmonic-analysis component supplies machinery for handling the space of matchings.

Experiments show that the approach can substantially outperform existing methods in practical domains. The result is tied to the paper's source of additional information: related instances from one application and known solutions for training. Its contribution is a way to use that recurring structure to accelerate matching, rather than a claim that arbitrary quadratic assignment problems become easy.
summary.tldr: Learning from solved matching problems in the same application helps accelerate quadratic assignment through permutation-based harmonic analysis.

title: Incorporating Domain Knowledge in Matching Problems via Harmonic Analysis
